title: Tirzepatide safety in EudraVigilance: descriptive and disproportionality analysis of preferred terms related to suboptimal treatment outcomes and drug-use-related issues
abstract: Objective As obesity and diabetes are on the verge of an alarming growth, so is the use of tirzepatide, a novel dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist (RA) and currently the most effective weight loss-drug. This research aimed to identify reporting patterns related to suboptimal therapeutic outcomes and tirzepatide-related drug-use issues, mining the EudraVigilance (EV). Design Retrospective pharmacovigilance study using descriptive and disproportionality analyses of reports retrieved from the EV database. Settings Analysis of individual case safety reports involving tirzepatide in comparison with other GLP-1 RAs in the overall dataset (healthcare professionals (HP) and non-HP reports combined) and in the HP group. Outcome measures Reporting ORs (RORs) with 95% CIs for selected Preferred Terms (PT) related to drug-use issues. Results Among all analysed PTs, the most frequently reported were ‘Off-label use’ (n=1521), ‘Drug ineffective’ (n=425) and ‘Off-label use device’ (n=99). PTs in HP reports showed lower reporting odds compared with non-HP reports. In the overall dataset, reports involving tirzepatide showed lower reporting odds of the PT ‘Drug ineffective’ than those involving liraglutide (ROR 0.61, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.70), dulaglutide (ROR 0.72, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.82), exenatide (ROR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.92) and semaglutide (ROR 0.81, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.91). However, in HP reports, no difference in reporting odds was observed between tirzepatide and semaglutide. A different pattern was observed for ‘off-label use’ in the full dataset, with higher reporting odds for tirzepatide vs lixisenatide, dulaglutide and liraglutide, but lower reporting odds vs semaglutide (ROR 0.52, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.55). In contrast, a higher reporting odd for the PT ‘off-label use of device’ was observed for tirzepatide versus semaglutide (ROR 43.47, 95% CI 16.00 to 118.13) in the overall reports; however, this finding should be interpreted with caution given the wide CI. Conclusions This study complements existing evidence from clinical trials and current clinical practice.

title: Efficacy and safety of narlumosbart in combination with stereotactic body radiation therapy followed by first-line chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy in advanced driver gene-negative non-small cell lung cancer patients with bone metastases: a phase II, single-arm, single-centre clinical trial protocol
abstract: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY This single-arm phase II trial uses a Simon two-stage design to evaluate the combination of narlumosbart with stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) in patients with driver gene-negative advanced non-small cell lung cancer and bone metastases. Sample size was calculated prospectively (α=0.05, power=0.8, H₀=25%, H₁=50%) with a 10% dropout adjustment. Standardised SBRT protocols (target delineation, dose constraints, daily image guidance, patient-specific quality assurance) ensure reproducibility. The trial uses a primary endpoint (objective response rate of non-irradiated lesions) as a surrogate for systemic effect, alongside predefined secondary and exploratory endpoints. The single-centre design and lack of a control group limit generalisability, requiring validation in larger randomised trials. title: Relationship between positive psychological traits, perceived spousal support and head and neck cancer-specific health-related quality of life: a cross-sectional study in oncology treatment settings
abstract: Objectives Data on how positive psychological traits and perceived spousal support are related to head and neck cancer (HNC)-specific health-related quality of life (QOL) using validated instruments in the Malay language in oncology settings are scarce. Hence, this study: (1) evaluated the association between demographic and clinical characteristics, optimism, posttraumatic growth (PTG), hope, perceived spousal support and HNC specific health-related QOL; and (2) assessed the mediation associations of PTG, perceived spousal support and hope on the relationship between optimism and HNC specific health-related QOL among a cohort of patients with HNC. Design Cross-sectional study. Settings This study was conducted in two tertiary referral centres for oncology treatment in Malaysia. Participants Data were collected from a total of 240 patients with HNC. Primary and secondary outcome measures The primary outcome was HNC specific health-related QOL assessed with the 35-item European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life-Head and Neck Module, while the secondary outcomes were optimism measured with the Life Orientation Test-Revised, PTG measured with the Posttraumatic Growth Inventory-Short Form, perceived spousal support evaluated with the Sources of Social Support Scale and hope assessed with the Dispositional Hope Scale. Results Higher perceived spousal support (B=–0.454, 95% CI –0.781 to –0.126, p=0.007) and optimism (B=–2.001, 95% CI –2.660 to –1.342, p Conclusion Optimism and perceived spousal support may have a positive association with HNC-specific health-related QOL.

title: Antibiotic prescribing practices of community health extension workers in East Central Uganda: an exploratory qualitative study
abstract: Background Antibiotic misuse at the community level remains a critical contributor to antimicrobial resistance, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs) play a pivotal role in primary healthcare delivery and antibiotic access, yet little is known about how they navigate prescribing decisions amid systemic limitations, social expectations and ethical pressures. Objective This study explored CHEWs’ perceptions, practices and experiences related to antibiotic prescribing and dispensing in resource-constrained settings, with particular attention to decision-making processes, ethical reasoning and everyday care realities. Methods An exploratory qualitative study was conducted involving in-depth interviews with 25 community health extension workers. Data were analysed thematically using an inductive approach. Themes were developed through iterative coding and constant comparison, with attention to both structural and social influences on antibiotic use. Data were collected using a semi-structured interview guide, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and translated into English. Results Four major themes emerged: (1) decision-making under resource constraints, characterised by medicine shortages, stock-outs and limited diagnostic capacity; (2) negotiating community expectations versus guidelines, where social pressure and cultural norms influenced prescribing practices; (3) ethical dilemmas and moral reasoning, reflecting CHEWs’ strong sense of responsibility for patient outcomes amid competing professional and community obligations; and (4) informal antibiotic practices and improvisation, including borrowing medicines, adjusting dosages due to financial constraints and integrating traditional knowledge. Across themes, CHEWs demonstrated adaptive, contextually grounded decision-making shaped by scarcity, trust and moral accountability. Conclusion CHEWs’ antibiotic prescribing practices are not simply acts of non-adherence to clinical guidelines but represent complex, morally informed responses to structural constraints and community realities. Effective antimicrobial stewardship in resource-limited settings must therefore move beyond individual behaviour change to address health system limitations, ethical complexity and the social dimensions of care.

title: Heterogeneity in clinical nurses core competency and its associations with self-efficacy and self-directed learning ability: a cross-sectional latent profile analysis
abstract: Objectives To identify latent profiles of core competency among hospital clinical nurses and to examine the associations of self-efficacy and self-directed learning ability with profile membership. Design A cross-sectional survey reported in accordance with Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) principles. Setting Two general hospitals in Yanji, Jilin Province, China. Participants A total of 605 registered clinical nurses who were directly engaged in clinical nursing work were recruited using convenience sampling from January to March 2026. Methods Latent profile analysis was conducted using the seven Competency Inventory for Registered Nurses (CIRN) dimension scores as continuous indicators to identify core competency profiles. Univariable analyses were used to compare demographic, occupational and psychological characteristics across profiles. Multivariable multinomial logistic regression was subsequently performed with profile membership as the outcome to examine associated factors. Main outcome measures Core competency measured using the seven dimensions of the CIRN, general self-efficacy, self-directed learning ability and latent core competency profile membership. Results Three profiles were identified: low-level core competency (266/605, 43.97%), moderate-level core competency (254/605, 41.98%) and high-level core competency (85/605, 14.05%). After adjustment for demographic and occupational variables, self-directed learning ability was positively associated with membership of the moderate-level profile (OR 1.119, 95% CI 1.077 to 1.163) and high-level profile (OR 1.142, 95% CI 1.078 to 1.210) rather than the low-level profile. General self-efficacy showed similar positive associations with the moderate-level profile (OR 1.161, 95% CI 1.113 to 1.213) and high-level profile (OR 1.578, 95% CI 1.452 to 1.715). Conclusions Clinical nurses’ core competency showed clear heterogeneity, with a relatively small high-level subgroup. Self-directed learning ability and self-efficacy were modifiable correlates of more favourable competency profiles and may inform stratified competency development strategies.

title: Adaptation and feasibility assessment of a school-based Suicide Prevention Intervention for Adolescents (SPREAD Study) in Nigeria: protocol for a cluster randomised controlled feasibility trial
abstract: Introduction Adolescent suicide constitutes a critical public health challenge in low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), where structural deficits in mental health infrastructure compound an already substantial burden. In Nigeria, where suicidal ideation among secondary school students has been documented at a lifetime prevalence of 22.9%, curative clinic-based responses are neither scalable nor sustainable. School-based universal interventions offer a pragmatic upstream alternative. The Youth Aware of Mental Health (YAM) programme has demonstrated robust efficacy in European contexts, reducing incident suicide attempts by approximately 50%; however, its transferability to the West African educational and cultural environment remains untested. This protocol describes a study designed to culturally adapt YAM for Nigerian secondary schools and assess the feasibility of conducting a definitive cluster randomised controlled trial in Lagos State. Methods and analysis This study employs a hybrid type 1 effectiveness–implementation design, structured as a two-arm parallel-group cluster randomised feasibility trial across 10 public secondary schools in Lagos State. Approximately 600 adolescents aged 13–17 years will be recruited. Prior to the trial, YAM will be systematically adapted using the Method for Programme Adaptation through Community Engagement framework, producing the YAM-Nigeria curriculum. Schools will be randomised to receive either the culturally adapted YAM-Nigeria programme (five sessions of 45–60 min each delivered by trained external facilitators) or enhanced usual practice (standard health education curriculum supplemented with suicide awareness materials). Primary feasibility outcomes include school recruitment rates (target ≥60%), student consent rates (target ≥70%), retention at the 3-month follow-up (target ≥75%), implementation fidelity (target ≥80% adherence) and acceptability (target ≥70% student satisfaction). Secondary exploratory outcomes include suicidal ideation, depression, mental health literacy, stigma and help-seeking behaviour, measured to estimate the SD and intraclass correlation coefficient required to power a future definitive trial. Progression to a definitive phase III trial will be governed by pre-specified traffic light criteria. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval has been granted by the Lagos State University Teaching Hospital Health Research Ethics Committee (Ref: LREC/06/10/2656) and the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine Research Ethics Committee (Ref: RGETEM045). A two-stage consent process requiring written parental consent and adolescent assent will be implemented. Findings will be disseminated through open-access peer-reviewed publications, policy briefs for the Lagos State Ministries of Health and Education and plain-language summaries for participating communities. Trial registration number ISRCTN registry, ISRCTN69846459 . Registered on 24 November 2025.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of a DenseNet-121 deep learning algorithm for chest radiograph triage in health assessment applicants: a prospective shadow-mode validation study in Nepal
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of a publicly available DenseNet-121 convolutional neural network (TorchXRayVision) for triaging chest radiographs of health assessment applicants at a tertiary hospital in Nepal. Design Prospective, single-centre, shadow-mode diagnostic accuracy validation study. Reported in accordance with the Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) 2015 checklist and STARD-Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Developmental and Exploratory Clinical Investigations of DEcision support systems driven by Artificial Intelligence (DECIDE-AI) guidelines. Setting Department of Radiology and Imaging, Patan Academy of Health Sciences/Patan Hospital, Lalitpur, Nepal. Participants 826 consecutive health assessment applicants (foreign employment predeparture medical examination and student migration) undergoing chest radiography from 5 June 2026 to 20 June 2026 inclusive (16 days). Two cases were excluded due to Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine technical failure. Index test DenseNet-121 algorithm (TorchXRayVision library, densenet121-res224-all pretrained weights). A maximum aggregated pathology probability score was derived per radiograph and compared against a post hoc derived threshold of 0.6258 (selected as the highest threshold achieving the prespecified ≥95% sensitivity criterion). Reference standard Single-reader-per-case review by one of three radiologists—two board-certified radiodiagnosticians (LS: 276 cases; DM: 275 cases) and one radiology resident (UB: 275 cases)—each blinded to AI output, using a standardised data collection worksheet capturing binary classification (abnormal/normal) and free-text findings. Results Of 826 radiographs, 41 (4.97%) were classified as abnormal by the reference standard. At the post hoc derived threshold of 0.6258, the DenseNet-121 algorithm achieved: sensitivity 95.12% (95% CI 83.9% to 98.7%), specificity 77.2% (95% CI 74.1% to 80.0%), area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.9583 (95% bootstrap CI 0.9225 to 0.9843), negative predictive value (NPV) 99.67% (95% Wilson CI 98.8% to 99.9%), positive predictive value 17.89% (95% Wilson CI 13.4% to 23.5%) and Cohen’s 0.237 (95% bootstrap CI 0.174 to 0.304). Brier score was 0.3621 (null Brier 0.0472) and expected calibration error was 0.564, confirming calibration failure due to score compression (range 0.52–0.72) despite preserved discrimination. The sensitivity estimate should be interpreted with caution given the relatively small number of reference-standard positives (n=41); the Wilson CI width of 14.8 percentage points (83.9–98.7%) reflects substantial uncertainty around this point estimate. Cross-validated results 10-fold cross-validation yielded bias-corrected sensitivity 95.12% (95% Wilson CI 83.9% to 98.7%; optimism 0.00 pp) and specificity 75.80% (95% Wilson CI 72.7% to 78.7%; optimism+1.40 pp), confirming by internal validation that primary metrics are not materially inflated by circular optimisation; independent external validation was not performed. Conclusions The DenseNet-121 algorithm demonstrated high point-estimate sensitivity and excellent discrimination for chest radiograph triage in a Nepali health-assessment population, supporting its potential as a radiographic abnormality rule-out triage tool (NPV 99.67%); this does not constitute microbiological exclusion of active pulmonary tuberculosis. Systematic score compression—preserved discrimination despite calibration shift—is a quantifiable marker of low- and middle-income country distributional shift. Prospective local calibration studies and independent external validation are warranted before operational deployment.

title: Past-year violence experienced by transgender women living with HIV with or without recent involvement in transactional sex: the French national cross-sectional ANRS-Trans&HIV study
abstract: Introduction Stigma and violence experienced by transgender women and women engaged in transactional sex may negatively impact health and access to HIV care. We investigated typologies of past-year violence experienced by transgender women living with HIV (TWLH), with or without involvement in transactional sex (TWLH-TS and TWLH-nTS, respectively) in France. Methods We used data from the 2020–2022 French national cross-sectional ANRS-TRANS&HIV survey, which included TWLH recruited in 36 HIV care centres. We performed latent class analyses using variables representing combinations of past-year violence type and perpetrator separately for TWLH-TS and TWLH-nTS. Correlates of the resulting past-year violence typologies among TWLH-TS were assessed using multinomial logistic regression. Results Among TWLH-TS (66% of the 501 participants), three typologies emerged: low reported violence (42% of the 501 participants), multiple-perpetrator violence (8%) and client and street violence (17%). Among TWLH-nTS (34% of the 501 participants), two typologies emerged: low reported violence (30% of the 501 participants) and multiple-perpetrator violence (3%). In TWLH-TS, correlates of client and street violence were inadequate housing, ART interruption, stimulant use and daily cannabis use, while those of multiple-perpetrator violence were depression and a lack of emotional support. Client and street violence and multiple-perpetrator violence were correlated with meeting clients in outdoor locations. Conclusion TWLH in France face intersecting forms of systemic violence and structural vulnerability. One in ten experienced multi-form, multiple-perpetrator violence, regardless of transactional sex involvement, with potential consequences for mental health. Client and street violence affected one in four TWLH-TS, and was associated with precarious housing and working conditions, as well as substance use and ART adherence difficulties. Ensuring equitable access to HIV care and mental health services for transgender women is essential and inseparable from protecting their fundamental human rights and improving their socioeconomic conditions. Trial Registration NCT04849767 .

title: Cost-effectiveness of recommended interventions for managing low back pain: A systematic review
abstract: by Stephanie Mathieson, Martin Underwood, Muhammad Ibrahim, Zhilin Hua, Zhaohua Zhu, Paulo H. Ferreira, Hema Mistry, Emily R. Atkins, Jocelyn L. Bowden, Jillian P. Eyles, Andrew M. Briggs, David J. Hunter, Manuela L. Ferreira Background Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. Although numerous treatment approaches are recommended by international clinical guidelines, there is still limited understanding of which interventions provide the best value for money. We aimed to critically appraise and summarise the evidence on the cost-effectiveness and costs of interventions endorsed in recent guidelines to manage low back pain (LBP), compared to usual care. Methods and findings We searched 10 electronic databases (e.g., MEDLINE (OvidSP), EMBASE (OvidSP), PsycINFO (OvidSP)) from inception to 9th of February 2026 for cost-effectiveness studies of guideline-recommended treatments to manage non-specific LBP. The primary outcome was cost/quality-adjusted life year (QALY), which was converted to 2024 Great British Pound values, tabulated and summarised qualitatively. Secondary outcomes were direct costs (total, interventional, health service use, community services and out-of-pocket costs) and indirect costs (e.g., lost wages, lost productivity, absenteeism). We assessed methodological quality using the Consensus Health Economics Criteria (CHEC) checklist for within-trial economic evaluations or the Philips checklist for modelling studies. Our review included 20 studies (17 within-trial economic evaluations and three modelling studies), published between 2005 and 2026. Half ( n = 10) focussed on chronic LBP (>3-month duration), and eight included mixed populations (i.e., acute, subacute and chronic). All studies were of non-pharmacological, non-surgical interventions, both single-modality and multimodal interventions (e.g., exercise plus spinal manipulation; diet plus physical activity). Most interventions are cost-effective at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £20,000. Moreover, interventions aiming to reduce fear and stress or support self-management in people with chronic LBP, as well as clinician-delivered interventions including yoga, acupuncture, cognitive therapy and self-management support are potentially cost-saving from the healthcare, societal and payer’s perspectives, as they are both more effective and less costly than usual care (e.g., first contact management, including advice and medication). All of the evidence is derived from high-income countries, and from a considerable heterogenous body of literature. Evidence on cost-effective treatments in low- and middle-income countries remains limited. Conclusions Non-pharmacological, non-surgical interventions that include education, psychological support, acupuncture and exercise seem to be cost-effective for managing LBP, compared to usual care. Improved access to and implementation of these effective treatments is urgently needed so more people can benefit from them in routine care. Registration The review was registered on PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk; CRD42024510270).

title: Co-exposure to planned power outages and wildfire PM 2.5 and acute healthcare utilization in California: A time-stratified case-crossover study
abstract: by Lauren Blair Wilner, Caitlin G. Jones-Ngo, Chen Chen, Bethany Kwoka, Vivian Do, Joel D. Kaufman, Laura C. Myers, Tarik Benmahrnia, Joan A. Casey Background To prevent wildfires, electric utilities may preemptively de-energize power lines (public safety power shutoffs [PSPS]). These PSPS events may unintentionally harm health, particularly for those with pre-existing conditions like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or who rely on electricity-dependent medical equipment. Health impacts may worsen further if a wildfire occurs despite the power shutoff. To assess the effect of PSPS events, wildfire fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) exposure, and their co-occurrence on cause-specific healthcare utilization. Methods and findings We identified PSPS events in California from 2013 to 2019, categorizing magnitude based on number of people without power by zip code. We leveraged zip code-level average daily wildfire PM 2.5 estimates and respiratory, COPD-specific, cardiovascular, and psychiatric emergency department visits and unscheduled hospital admissions among adults aged 20+ from the California Department of Health Care Access and Information. Using a time-stratified case-crossover design, we estimated the impact of same-day and lagged PSPS events alone, wildfire PM 2.5 alone, and their co-occurrence on healthcare utilization, adjusting for daily temperature.Severe PSPS events were associated with elevated odds of same-day respiratory encounters (OR = 1.06, 95% CI: 1.02, 1.11) and lag 0–3 effects were similar. These associations were stronger for COPD. Compared to no PSPS or wildfire exposure, joint PSPS and 10 μg/m 3 higher wildfire PM 2.5 was associated with higher odds of respiratory encounters (1.16 [95% CI: 1.10, 1.22]), with evidence of multiplicative interaction. Associations were null for cardiovascular and psychiatric encounters.Limitations include exposure misclassification, because we assigned exposure at the residential zip code level, aggregating circuit-level data and not accounting for individual behavior or the potential for PSPS events to impact wildfire PM 2.5 exposure. Conclusions PSPS events may increase risk of respiratory events requiring acute care utilization, especially when they co-occur with wildfire PM 2.5 .

title: Breast cancer treatment: When less is more
abstract: by Katarzyna Starowicz, on behalf of the PLOS Medicine Staff Editors Breast cancer treatment using systemic therapies has often focussed on remission and survival, but can cause severe side effects that negatively impact patient quality of life and function, sometimes with limited clinical benefit. In the era of precision oncology, one of the greatest opportunities may not be in identifying more patients for treatment, but rather in identifying those who can safely receive less to avoid overtreatment. Breast cancer treatment using systemic therapies can cause severe side effects that negatively impact patient quality of life and function, sometimes with limited clinical benefit. In this Editorial, Katarzyna Starowicz discusses how precision oncology tools may help us identify those who can safely reduce therapy to avoid overtreatment.

title: Burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance associated with modifiable human antibiotic consumption: An observational study
abstract: by Benjamin J. Singer, Alec Gleason, Isabella Impalli, Mikkel D. Nagorsen, Chungman Chae, Lauren C. Granskog, Philip C. Lee, Ramanan Laxminarayan, Joseph A. Lewnard Background Human antibiotic use is widely believed to contribute to the evolution and maintenance of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacterial pathogens. While antibiotic stewardship should thus discourage use in situations where AMR-related harms outweigh clinical benefit, evidence to inform this assessment of tradeoffs is lacking, most notably in low-resource settings where gaps in antibiotic access persist. Quantitative understanding of use-resistance relationships is thus necessary as countries navigate commitments from the 2024 UN General Assembly resolution to reduce AMR burden by 2030. Methods and findings We used global surveillance data on AMR prevalence from 2000 to 2018 representing over 30 million bacterial isolates from 114 countries, along with antibiotic consumption estimates for each country and year, to estimate elasticity relationships between AMR and antibiotic exposure. Our analyses addressed 16 bacterial pathogens and antibiotic consumption across 7 drug classes, controlling for country-level health and development indicators via weighted regression models. Across pathogens, evidence that AMR is associated with population-level antibiotic exposure is strongest for Acinetobacter spp., Streptococcus pneumoniae , Staphylococcus aureus , Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli . In a modeled counterfactual scenario, we estimate that 10% lower levels of antibiotic use, in comparison to current levels, across classes, would be associated with 38,000 (95% confidence interval: 36,000–41,000) fewer annual deaths attributable to AMR globally. Although substantial, this total represents only 0.50% of estimated bacterial disease mortality. In sub-Saharan Africa, where risk of death due to bacterial disease is greatest, the modeled avertible burden of AMR-attributable deaths comprises only 0.34% of bacterial disease mortality. Key limitations of the study include reliance on ecological relationships to infer modifiable burden, and under-representation of low-resource settings in surveillance data on antibiotic consumption and AMR. Conclusions Our findings suggest near-term achievable reductions in AMR-attributable deaths may be modest relative to the persisting burden of bacterial disease mortality. These estimates should inform assessments of the potential benefits and harms of restrictive versus permissive antibiotic use paradigms in epidemiologically distinct settings.

title: Outcomes of home-based versus facility-based care for mild diphtheria during a large epidemic in Kano State, Nigeria: A retrospective matched cohort study
abstract: by Jonathan Polonsky, Suleiman Hudu, Khadidja Uthman, Yves Katuala, Philip Eghosa Evbuomwan, Hashim Juma Omer Osman, Abdulwahab Kabir Sulaiman, Ichola Ismael Adjaho, Cheick Oumar Doumbia, Etienne Gignoux, Franck Ale Background During Nigeria’s largest recorded diphtheria epidemic (first notified on 1 December 2022; more than 40,000 confirmed cases by January 2026), hospital capacity in Kano State was overwhelmed. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) introduced home-based care (HBC) for patients with mild disease; we asked whether mortality, long-term sequelae, and household transmission differed between HBC and care in a diphtheria treatment centre (DTC). Methods and findings We conducted a retrospective matched cohort study using MSF registry data and household interviews to compare mortality, long-term sequelae, and household transmission between patients with mild diphtheria treated under HBC or in a DTC. The primary outcomes were mortality, long-term sequelae, and household transmission. Mild diphtheria cases notified between January 2023 and January 2024 were exactly matched by treatment modality (HBC or DTC) on sex, age group, vaccination status, and ward of residence, and interviewed between September and October 2024, a median of 421 days after notification. Conditional logistic regression, adjusted for age, vaccination status, and treatment delay, was used to estimate the association between treatment modality and mortality, with robustness checked with propensity score weighting and sensitivity analyses. Of the 986 originally sampled patients, 491 (49.8%) were interviewed; with 178 replacements (substitute patients of similar age, sex, vaccination status, and area, interviewed when an originally selected patient could not be), 669 patients (362 HBC, 307 DTC) were analysed. After adjustment, mortality was lower with HBC than DTC care, but the interval included 1 (odds ratio [OR] 0.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.12,1.07]; p = 0.066); treatment delay was associated with increased mortality (OR 1.29 per day, 95% CI [1.00,1.67]; p = 0.048). Adding calendar time gave a similar estimate (OR 0.35, 95% CI [0.08,1.57]; p = 0.170). Vaccination was associated with lower odds of death (OR 0.32, 95% CI [0.10,0.98]; p = 0.047). HBC was not associated with increased household transmission or long-term sequelae. Residual confounding by disease severity, the small number of deaths (24), and replacement patients limit these findings. Conclusions Vaccination and early treatment were associated with survival; care setting was not clearly associated. When supported by clinical triage and structured follow-up, decentralised care may be an option to manage mild cases during diphtheria epidemics in settings with constrained hospital capacity.

title: Cardiac screening in the young for the detection of cardiovascular disease and prevention of sudden cardiac death
abstract: by Daniel T. Tardo, Sanjay Sharma Sudden cardiac death in the young is often due to silent inherited cardiac conditions. Although evidence increasingly supports cardiac screening as a preventative strategy, policies and frameworks differ globally. Structured screening frameworks that utilise AI-enabled technologies show great potential for enhancing disease detection and risk prediction. In this Perspective, Daniel Tardo and Sanjay Sharma discuss evidence that supports cardiac screening in the young as a preventative strategy for cardiovascular disease and sudden cardiac death. They highlight the need for structured screening frameworks, and discuss the potential of AI-enabled technologies for disease detection and risk prediction.

title: How do we monitor doxy-PEP impact and when should we consider revisiting guidelines?
abstract: by Yonatan H. Grad, Rachel Mittelstaedt, Remco P. H. Peters Summary points The 2026 WHO guidelines recommending doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP) represent the first global antibiotic prophylaxis recommendation for bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with provisions for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) monitoring.Doxy-PEP should be governed as an adaptive intervention subject to periodic, transparent review, but establishing decision rules faces challenges.Doxy-PEP is expected to select for resistance, including in Neisseria gonorrhoeae , Staphylococcus aureus, and the gut and skin microbiomes; the scope of clinical consequences is incompletely understood.As STI prevalence falls, the benefit per dose declines while the AMR externality per dose is expected to grow, shifting the cost-benefit balance in ways that vary across populations and settings.Attributing changes in disease prevalence or resistance patterns to doxy-PEP is methodologically difficult, given incompletely understood and complex drivers of pre-existing trends, surveillance limitations, and heterogeneous uptake, raising questions about study designs, data sources, eligibility criteria, and governance mechanisms.A full accounting of benefits and harms is broader than reduced bacterial STI incidence and AMR. Benefits include consideration of patient-centered outcomes such as reduced anxiety regarding STI acquisition, avoidance of repeated treatment visits, and fewer STI-related complications. Harms include drug side effects, such as gastrointestinal adverse effects and concerns about use in pregnancy.

title: Guidance for defining outcomes in clinical trials
abstract: by Xiangji Ying, Tianjing Li, Joanne E. McKenzie, Matthew J. Page, Kiran Ninan, Jean-Pierre Oberste, Colby J. Vorland, Andrew W. Brown, Riaz Qureshi, Nicholas J. DeVito, Ian J. Saldanha, Martin Offringa, Nancy J. Butcher, Sirui Zhang, Phi-Yen Nguyen, Joe Menke, Veronica Ka Wai Lai, Halil Kilicoglu, Evan Mayo-Wilson Background Defining outcomes completely before conducting clinical trials helps to mitigate concerns about reporting biases; however, there is limited guidance to help investigators define outcomes completely. Methods Building on a previous framework, we developed guidance for defining trial outcomes completely and consistently. We reviewed literature, developed preliminary guidance, and refined guidance iteratively through pilot testing. We randomly selected 225 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from ClinicalTrials.gov, which evaluated 3,424 outcomes. Two raters followed a structured approach to define each outcome. When raters encountered outcomes they could not define, we refined our guidance. We continued this process until no further changes were needed. We finalized the guidance through multiple drafts and discussions among authors. Findings In clinical trials, a completely defined outcome includes six elements: outcome domain, specific measurement, specific metric, cutoff (if applicable), variable type, and time point. We developed guidance for naming specific measurements for both subjective and objective outcomes. We expanded on prior work by describing more comprehensive categories for specific metrics. To be consistent with the estimand framework, we replaced “method of aggregation” with two distinct elements that describe values in individuals (rather than summary measures): “variable type” and “cutoff.” We further defined “cutoff” with three sub-elements, and we defined “variable type” as whether the value for each individual is continuous or categorical. Conclusions Trialists and sponsors could use this framework and guidance to define outcomes in trial registrations, protocols, and results reports. When all six elements are specified, readers can better determine whether reported outcomes were prespecified and whether different trials assessed the same outcomes.

title: Seeing the invisible: Reorienting cardiovascular risk prediction across the disease trajectory
abstract: by Xun Tang, Pei Gao Current risk equations miss many cardiovascular events in people classified as low risk. Prediction is simultaneously advancing on two axes: broadening predictors toward molecular omics, and expanding outcomes toward earlier subclinical atherosclerosis and later heart failure. In this Perspective, Xun Tang and Pei Gao discuss how cardiovascular risk prediction is simultaneously advancing on two axes: broadening predictors toward molecular omics, and expanding outcomes toward earlier subclinical atherosclerosis and later heart failure.

title: Impact of violence on HIV outcomes among female sex workers: A global systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: by Joshua Dawe, Khadimul Anam Mazhar, Saher Aijaz Khan, Belinda Jackson Njiro, Victoria Bendaud, Keith Sabin, Julie Ambia, Adam Trickey, Lucy Barrass, Asra Asgharzadeh, Jack Stone, Adelina Artenie, Peter Vickerman Background Female sex workers (FSW) are a key population for HIV prevention and care. Increasing evidence suggests that social and structural barriers are key drivers of HIV transmission. This global systematic review assesses whether experiencing violence is associated with worse HIV outcomes among FSW. Methods and findings We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO databases for studies published from January 1st, 2010 to June 9th, 2026 assessing the impact of violence on HIV outcomes among FSW, without restriction to language and study design. Some studies had multiple estimates due to reporting on multiple outcomes or exposures of interest. We pooled data from eligible studies using multi-level random-effects meta-analyses to quantify associations between recent (past year) or lifetime exposure to violence (physical, sexual, emotional/psychological, and/or financial) and HIV outcomes (prevalent and incident HIV infection, HIV testing, ART use, ART adherence, and viral suppression) among FSW. We preferentially used adjusted estimates over unadjusted estimates if both were available.We included 94 studies with 226 estimates, comprising 186,613 FSWs in 39 countries. Half the included studies were in low- and middle-income countries ( n = 47, 50%), and one-fifth were in low-income countries ( n = 18; 19%). We found higher odds of prevalent HIV infection among FSWs with recent (pooled odds ratio (pOR):1.31; 95% CI [1.16,1.48]; I 2 : 63%; n = 75 estimates) and lifetime (pOR:1.35; 95% CI [1.23,1.48]; I 2 : 39%; n = 68) experiences of violence. When stratifying violence by type, we found the strongest pooled associations between recent (pOR:1.55; 95% CI [1.24,1.94]; I 2 : 69%; n = 28) and lifetime (pOR:1.40; 95% CI [1.21,1.63]; I 2 : 47%; n = 28) experiences of sexual violence and HIV prevalence. Recently experiencing violence was associated with reduced odds of ART use (pOR:0.78; 95% CI [0.64,0.94]; I 2 : 8%; n = 17). Lifetime exposure to violence was associated with reduced odds of viral suppression (pOR:0.88; 95% CI [0.79,0.98]; I 2 : 20%; n = 6). There was no evidence of associations between violence and HIV incidence, HIV testing, and ART adherence.Our study had limitations, notably the cross-sectional design of most included studies, the heterogeneity in pooled estimates, and the difficulties of measuring experiences of violence. Conclusions Experiencing violence is associated with greater odds of prevalent HIV infections, and poorer HIV treatment outcomes among FSWs. HIV interventions for FSWs must address violence as a structural determinant of HIV.

title: Plasma proteomic signatures of subclinical atherosclerosis progression for cardiovascular risk stratification: A cohort study
abstract: by Yani Huang, Ruixin Gao, Jianxin Li, Bin Yang, Keyong Huang, Shufeng Chen, Jie Cao, Xiaoqing Liu, Chong Shen, Ling Yu, Liancheng Zhao, Ying Li, Dongsheng Hu, Jianfeng Huang, Bin Lu, Dongfeng Gu, Fangchao Liu, Xiangfeng Lu Background Existing risk stratification tools inadequately identify individuals with subclinical atherosclerosis (SA) who could benefit from early intervention. This study aimed to develop protein risk scores (ProtRSs) for SA progression and assess their incremental value for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk prediction. Methods and findings In a community cohort consisting of 903 individuals undergoing repeated SA assessments (coronary artery calcium [CAC] or carotid plaque) over 6 years (2008–2009 to 2013–2014), protein biomarkers were selected from a panel of 117 proteins using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression to construct SA ProtRSs for CAC and plaque progression, respectively, and their predictive abilities for incident ASCVD risk were evaluated based on a guideline-recommended traditional risk score in a case-cohort of 1,835 individuals (2007–2008 to 2018–2021, median follow-up of 10.4 years). The ProtRSs each included 14 proteins for CAC and plaque progression, explaining 17.1% and 18.4% of respective variances. Effect sizes of these proteins on SA progression showed strong concordance with those on incident ASCVD ( r > 0.75). Each standard deviation increase in CAC and plaque ProtRSs was associated with hazard ratios of 1.36 (95% confidence interval [CI] [1.20,1.54]) and 1.38 (95% CI [1.23,1.54]) for ASCVD risk, respectively. Addition of the SA ProtRSs to the traditional risk score yielded a net reclassification improvement of 0.127 ( p Conclusions SA ProtRSs of coronary calcification and carotid plaque progression may provide additional value over traditional risk assessment, highlighting their potential in refining risk stratification and guiding targeted intervention strategies.

title: The CBI-M framework for characterization of traumatic brain injury: Evaluation of performance using data from the CENTER-TBI and TRACK-TBI prospective cohort studies
abstract: by Dana Pisică, Ana Mikolić, John K. Yue, Michael A. McCrea, Kristen Dams-O’Connor, Véronique De Keyser, Sonia Jain, Amy J. Markowitz, David K. Menon, Virginia Newcombe, Ewout W. Steyerberg, Xiaoying Sun, Hester F. Lingsma, Geoffrey T. Manley, Andrew I. R. Maas, on behalf of the CENTER-TBI and TRACK-TBI Investigators Background The CBI-M Framework, incorporating Clinical, Biomarker, Imaging, and Modifier pillars, was recently proposed to provide a comprehensive characterization of patients with acute traumatic brain injury (TBI). Such detailed characterization reflects the clinical and biological heterogeneity of TBI, and is considered essential to inform appropriate clinical management. Still unclear is the extent to which CBI-M captures clinically relevant heterogeneity in relation to diagnosis, clinical care pathways, and longer-term outcome. Prior to broad implementation into clinical practice and research, its diagnostic and prognostic performance needs to be ascertained. In this study, we aim to explore how CBI-M and its constituent pillars relate to diagnosis, clinical care pathways, and outcome in two large contemporary TBI cohorts. Methods and findings We analyzed data of patients with acute TBI enrolled in the European-based CENTER-TBI ( N = 4,509) and US-based TRACK-TBI ( N = 2,552) prospective observational studies. We assessed associations of the CBI-M Framework, its pillars, and pillar components with key clinical endpoints: diagnosis (traumatic intracranial injury on computed tomography); care pathways (hospital admission, intensive care admission, intracranial pressure monitoring, and major cranial surgery); and outcomes at 6 months post-injury (mortality, Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE), and health-related quality of life (HRQoL)). Discriminatory performance was calculated using the AUC and explained variability expressed with Nagelkerke’s pseudo-R 2 . Prognostic performance was compared to the established IMPACT-Lab and CRASH-CT prediction models in their respective target populations. For diagnostic and care path endpoints full CBI-M models achieved excellent discrimination (AUC CENTER-TBI: from 0.83 to 0.95; TRACK-TBI: from 0.88 to 0.98), and high proportions of explained variability (pseudo-R 2 CENTER-TBI: from 0.41 to 0.72; TRACK-TBI: from 0.55 to 0.80). Contributions of individual pillars varied by endpoint, with the Biomarker pillar contributing most for CT-defined abnormalities and the Imaging pillar to major cranial surgery. For mortality and unfavorable outcome (GOSE ≤ 4) similarly strong performance was observed: CENTER-TBI: AUC 0.89 (95% Confidence intervals (CI) [0.88,0.90]) and 0.92 (95% CI [0.91,0.94]) respectively; pseudo-R 2 0.53 (95% CI [0.50,0.57]) and 0.55 (95% CI [0.51,0.59]) respectively; TRACK-TBI: AUC 0.91 (95% CI [0.89,0.93]) and 0.95 (95% CI [0.93,0.97]) respectively; pseudo-R 2 0.57 (95% CI [0.52,0.62] and 0.57 (95% CI [0.50, 0.64] respectively), whereas performance for HRQoL was modest. Compared to the IMPACT-Lab and CRASH-CT models in their respective target populations, pseudo-R 2 values suggest that the full CBI-M model was more strongly associated with 6-month mortality and unfavorable outcomes. Methodological limitations include the restriction to analysis of data from high-income settings, limiting generalizability, the absence of three elements of the modifier pillar in the datasets accessed, and risk of possible reverse causality in some analyses. Conclusions CBI-M provides a robust multimodal characterization of acute TBI that aligns closely with clinical decision-making and outcomes. Further prospective validation and optimization are justified and needed to inform implementation of the CBI-M Framework in clinical practice and research.

title: Associations of major congenital anomalies, long-term health conditions, and socioeconomic deprivation with educational attainment in Wales: A population-based data linkage study
abstract: by Ieuan Scanlon, Anna Rawlings, David Tucker, Daniel S. Thayer, Hywel T. Evans, Joanne Given, Sam Jones, Maria Loane, Chloe Morgan, Joan K. Morris, Sue Jordan Background Education outcomes are associated with life chances. However, deprivation, ill-health and disability are barriers to achievement. We aimed to investigate educational attainment of children with and without major congenital anomalies in state-funded mainstream schools at ages 11 and 16 (key stages [KS] 2 and 4), accounting for maternal and child socioeconomic deprivation, demographic factors, comorbidities, and special education needs (SEN) provision. Methods and findings We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study using the Secure Anonymised Information Linkage (SAIL) Databank to link routinely collected electronic health and education records of children born in Wales between January 1st, 1998 and December 31st, 2007, who were followed up until December 31st, 2019. Education outcomes were explored using logistic regression, adjusting for: major congenital anomalies, maternal and child socioeconomic deprivation, medicated co-morbidities, hospitalisation, gestation length, child sex, year of birth, and SEN provision.Children with major congenital anomalies were less likely to achieve national academic standards, including those required for some professional courses: however, attainment was more strongly associated with socioeconomic deprivation. At age 11, 81.9% (7167/8754) with and 93.8% (232,450/247,814) without major congenital anomalies attained established standards (odds ratio [OR] 0.30; 95% confidence intervals [CI] [0.28,0.32]). At age 16, 46.8% (2070/4427) with and 56.1% (69,732/124,300) without major congenital anomalies achieved 5 General Certificates of Secondary Education (GCSEs) at grades C–A*, including English/Welsh, Maths and Science (EWMS) (OR 0.69; 95% CI [0.65,0.73]). Discrepancies narrowed in adjusted analyses, particularly when SEN provision was accounted: aOR 0.72; 95% CI [0.66,0.78] at KS2, age 11, and aOR 0.93; 95% CI [0.87,1.00] for 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS. These GCSEs were achieved by 29.7% (307/1034) children with major congenital anomalies and 38.4% (10,875/28,305) of unaffected children in the most deprived quintile (using maternal Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation: in the least deprived quintile, figures were 67.6% (547/810) and 75.0% (16,978/22,644), respectively.Children with major congenital anomalies, receiving maximum SEN support, and eligible for Free School Meals (FSM) were the least likely to achieve national academic standards: 5/192 (2.6%) obtained 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS, as did 37/354 (10.4%) ineligible for FSM. The strongest associations with 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS, were SEN statements (aOR 0.07; 95% CI [0.06,0.07]), FSM eligibility (aOR 0.39; 95% CI [0.37,0.41]), and epilepsy (aOR 0.60; 95% CI [0.45,0.80]). Study limitations included absence of data for 15%–18% of children, mainly those educated outside mainstream schools, and for some comorbidities; generalisation of findings to other settings or other countries is uncertain. Conclusions Many children with major congenital anomalies from least deprived quintiles attained national academic standards, including 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS. The children living in the most deprived quintiles or eligible for FSM and with ill-health from major congenital anomalies and/or epilepsy were two to four times less likely to attain these standards. SEN provision mitigated the associations with disadvantage, but children from socioeconomically deprived quintiles with major congenital anomalies were unlikely to achieve 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS.

title: Associations of food processing and dietary risk factors with colorectal cancer incidence in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study: A cohort study
abstract: by Leila Abar, Caitlin P. O’Connell, Hyokyoung G. Hong, Kirsten A. Herrick, Lisa Kahle, Jennifer L. Lerman, Linda M. Liao, Xuehong Zhang, Xinyuan Zhang, Longgang Zhao, Sémi Zouiouich, Rashmi Sinha, Neha Khandpur, Eurídice Martínez Steele, Erikka Loftfield Background Ultra-processed foods (UPF) account for >50% of energy intake by US adults. UPF intake can include dietary components linked to lower colorectal cancer (CRC) risk, such as whole grain and dairy products, and others linked to higher CRC risk, such as processed meats, potentially explaining the heterogeneity of evidence for an association between UPF and CRC risk. Our goal was to estimate the associations of UPF and established CRC-related dietary factors, by UPF and non-UPF source, with CRC incidence in a large cohort study. Methods and findings US adults, aged 50–71, who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study in 1995–96, self-reported dietary intake using a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). Median UPF intake was 293 g/1000 kcal/day or 43% of daily energy intake. We assigned disaggregated FFQ items to Nova classification and categorized UPF intake (g/1000 kcal/day) into sex-specific quintiles. Participants who were cancer-free at baseline ( N = 461,682) were followed for cancer incidence through 2018, and 10,075 colorectal adenocarcinoma cases were diagnosed. We used multivariable-adjusted Cox proportional hazards regression models, adjusted for demographic, lifestyle, and health-related factors, including age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, physical activity, smoking, and alcohol drinking, to estimate associations for UPF and related dietary components with CRC incidence. UPF intake was not associated with CRC incidence (hazard ratio 5th versus 1st quintile 0.97; 95% confidence interval [0.91–1.03]; p trend = 0.55). Whole grain, fiber, dairy, and calcium intakes from UPF sources were inversely but meat intake from UPF sources was positively associated with CRC incidence. The main limitations of the study relate to its observational design and include potential residual confounding and exposure misclassification owing to systematic or random error in self-reported dietary data. Conclusions Total UPF intake was not associated with incident CRC in this cohort of older, US adults. This may be explained, in part, by opposing associations of some UPF with CRC risk. Our findings support current dietary guidance to consume whole grains, fiber, dairy, and calcium and avoid processed meat for CRC prevention.

title: Evaluating the impact and cost-effectiveness of typhoid conjugate vaccine schedules across diverse settings: A multi-model comparison
abstract: by Catherine G. C. Wenger, Kyra H. Grantz, Tigist F. Menkir, Alina M. Muellenmeister, Zeaan Pithawala, Raymond Hutubessy, Vittal Mogasale, Alicia N. M. Kraay, Nick Scott, Romesh G. Abeysuriya, Jason R. Andrews, Jillian Gauld, Nathan C. Lo, Virginia E. Pitzer Background Given emerging evidence on the waning of immunity from typhoid conjugate vaccines (TCV), the World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned a multi-model comparison to determine the optimal schedule in terms of health and economic impact to inform updated recommendations for TCV use across different settings. Methods and findings To identify optimal vaccination strategies across different incidence settings and vaccine waning assumptions, we compared two agent-based and two compartmental dynamic models of typhoid transmission. All models were fitted to harmonized age-specific incidence data from medium, high, and very high incidence settings. We assessed different TCV schedules under slow- and fast-waning scenarios to evaluate the best age for routine vaccination and the potential need for booster doses and catch-up campaigns. We evaluated the public health and economic impact predicted for each model and scenario using the net-monetary-benefit framework to determine cost-effectiveness under two representative scenarios for the health outcomes and costs of vaccination and treatment. Over a 10-year time horizon, routine vaccination at 9 months with a catch-up campaign to 15 years and a booster dose at 5 years was predicted to have the greatest impact, reducing cases by a median of 40%–68% across the incidence settings. Across all four models, TCV introduction with a catch-up campaign was cost-effective above willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds of $1,250 per disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted in medium incidence settings when costs of illness and case fatality risk (CFR) are high and in high incidence settings when costs and CFR are low. The optimal strategy was to delay vaccination to 2 or 5 years of age if waning is fast, depending on the age of peak incidence. In very high incidence settings, TCV introduction at 9 months or 2 years of age was cost-saving, and adding a booster dose at 5 years was cost-effective at most WTP values across all scenarios. The study findings are limited by the data available to inform indirect vaccine protection and other simplifying assumptions made in this analysis. Conclusions Model predictions for the impact and cost-effectiveness of different TCV schedules were fairly robust to uncertainty in parameter values and model structure, but the optimal strategy depends on the typhoid incidence rate, CFR, and waning rate of vaccine protection.

title: Maternal opioid prescriptions and subsequent risk of hospital admission in offspring in South Korea: A nationwide birth cohort study
abstract: by Hyeon Jin Kim, Yesol Yim, Christa J. Nehs, Jaeyu Park, Eun Soo Kim, Sung Joon Cho, Guillaume Fond, Laurent Boyer, Jiseung Kang, Dong Keon Yon Background Prenatal opioid exposure may disrupt infant development and immune system function, potentially increasing long-term susceptibility to hospital admissions. Thus, we aimed to investigate the association between prenatal opioid exposure and the risk of hospital admission in children. Methods and findings We established a population-based birth cohort in South Korea by linking mothers and children using National Health Insurance Service data and followed from January 1, 2009, to December 31, 2023. We constructed propensity score (PS)-matched and sibling comparison cohorts and performed a multi-pronged approach, including dose-dependent and time-attenuation analyses. All 5,249,429 individuals with eligible children born between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2017, were included (2,236,167 mothers and 3,013,262 children). Infants were followed up for up to 14 years, depending on birth year. Prenatal exposure to opioids was defined as maternal receipt of two or more prescriptions within any given trimester. Adjusted incidence rate ratio (aIRR) of hospital admission among children with prenatal opioid exposure was estimated for causes including infections, non-infectious respiratory conditions, non-infectious gastrointestinal conditions, oral cavity diseases, injuries/external causes, and non-infectious genitourinary conditions. Analyses were adjusted for maternal age at delivery, infant sex, region of residence, household income level, birth season, parity, severe maternal morbidity score, number of outpatient visits and hospital admissions in the year before pregnancy, preterm birth, low birth weight, delivery type, year of delivery, maternal history of substance use and neuropsychiatric disorders, and plurality. Of the 2,928,186 children, we identified 2,809,515 (51.4% male) and 118,671 (51.3% male) infants without and with prenatal opioid exposure, respectively. The rate of hospital admissions in children with prenatal opioid exposure was 28% higher in the PS-matched cohort (aIRR 1.28 [95% CI 1.28, 1.29]; p p p p Conclusions In this nationwide birth cohort study, maternal opioid prescription during pregnancy was associated with a substantial increase in the risk of hospital admissions in the offspring across various causes of morbidities. Although the attenuated estimates in the sibling comparison analysis suggest that familial factors may partly explain this association, these findings may inform postnatal monitoring and management strategies for children born to mothers who received opioid prescriptions during pregnancy.

title: Comparative effectiveness of amlodipine versus nifedipine prescribed at discharge in patients with ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack: A nationwide 5-year follow-up registry study
abstract: by Xinya Li, Xue Xia, Meng Gao, Qin Xu, Yijun Zhang, Jing Jing, Yi Zhai, Xia Meng, Anxin Wang Background Amlodipine and nifedipine are the most commonly prescribed calcium channel blockers (CCB) for patients suffering from ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA). Nevertheless, there is a scarcity of direct comparative evidence on their effectiveness. This study aimed to compare the effectiveness of amlodipine and nifedipine in patients with ischemic stroke or TIA. Methods and findings This observational study was based on the Third China National Stroke Registry, which recruited consecutive adult patients with ischemic stroke or TIA from 2015 to 2018. In this study, ischemic stroke or TIA patients were prescribed either amlodipine or nifedipine at discharge. The primary outcome was the distribution of modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score, which assesses functional outcomes in patients with stroke, at 5 years. The intergroup differences were examined using ordinal logistic regression, yielding odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Patient age, gender, body mass index, systolic blood pressure at admission, and onset date were adjusted. To improve baseline characteristic balance, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was implemented. The amlodipine group demonstrated significantly lower 5-year mRS scores in comparison to the nifedipine group, with an OR of 0.76 (95% CI [0.65, 0.89]; p 0 at 5 years, with an OR of 0.71 (95% CI [0.61, 0.83]; p Conclusions This study revealed that amlodipine, compared to nifedipine, may be associated with improved functional recovery in ischemic stroke or TIA patients. Randomized controlled trials are warranted to confirm these findings and refine CCB therapy.

title: Genotype-informed docosahexaenoic acid dosing based on the FADS Indel to reduce preterm and prolonged gestation: A secondary analysis of the ADORE randomized trial
abstract: by Yan Ning Li, Kumar S. D. Kothapalli, Susan E. Carlson, Byron J. Gajewski, Emily A. DeFranco, J. Thomas Brenna Background Spontaneous early preterm birth (EPB Methods and findings To determine whether FADS Indel genotype modifies the effect of DHA dose on gestational length, we conducted a post hoc secondary analysis of the Assessment of DHA on Reducing Early Preterm Birth (ADORE) trial (NCT02626299). The FADS Indel, the only genetic variant measured, was selected on mechanistic grounds and genotyped blind to outcome. The analysis included all participants consenting to genetic analysis (12–20 weeks gestation) at three US medical centers. Participants received 200 or 1,000 mg/d DHA and were genotyped for FADS Indel (D/D, I/D, I/I). Primary outcomes were EPB and preterm birth (PB, n = 10,497) were screened for eligibility from June 8th 2016, to March 13th 2020, 1,032 (1,000 mg, n = 540; 200 mg, n = 492) completed the ADORE trial. A total of 761 (1,000 mg, n = 396; 200 mg, n = 365) are included in this secondary analysis. Participants carrying at least one FADS Indel I allele (I/I + I/D) receiving low-dose DHA had 4.3% EPB (9/214; 95% Credible Interval (CrI) [2.0%, 7.3%]) versus 0.8% in the D/D group (1/151; 95% CrI [0.04%, 2.7%]; Posterior Probability (PP) = 0.99), and 14.5% PB (31/214; 95% CrI [10.1%, 19.5%]) versus 8.7% in the D/D group (13/151; 95% CrI [4.7%, 13.6%]; PP = 0.96). High-dose DHA was associated with reduced EPB in the I-allele group (1.1%; 2/205; 95% CrI [0.2%, 2.8%]; PP = 0.99), and PB (9.3%; 19/205; 95% CrI [5.7%, 13.6%]; PP = 0.95), with little effect in the D/D group. Birth at ≥40 weeks was more frequent in the high-dose D/D group. Black women had higher rates of PB and EPB, have higher rates of the I allele, and benefited most from 1,000 mg/d dose. These dose effects credibly differ by genotype for EPB and prolonged gestation (genotype × dose interaction PP = 0.99 and 0.98). Both genotypes reduced PB similarly with high-dose DHA (PP = 0.56). Although genetic analysis was anticipated and genotyping was completed blind to outcome, this was a post hoc analysis and the genotype-by-dose comparison was not a prespecified trial aim. Some subgroups contained few PB and EPB events, so these estimates, particularly for PB, should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed prospectively. Conclusions The FADS Indel is a functional, mechanistically grounded polymorphism whose frequency varies with race/ethnicity. Preterm and early preterm birth were lower in the I-allele group receiving high-dose DHA (1,000 mg/d), while prolonged gestation was more frequent in the D/D group receiving high-dose DHA. FADS Indel genotypes predicted the direction of the response to high-dose DHA for EPB and prolonged gestation, whereas its modest PB benefit was shared by both genotypes. Analysis by retrospectively pairing high dose to I-carrier genotype and low dose to D/D was associated with the highest proportion of births at 37–40 weeks. These findings identify the FADS Indel as a potential predictive biomarker for DHA dose response and support a genotype-informed, precision-medicine strategy to optimize gestational length by reducing preterm birth in the I-allele group and prolonged gestation in the D/D group across racially/ethnically diverse populations. title: Potential health impacts and costs of active case finding guided by Mycobacterium tuberculosis immunoreactivity survey results in Blantyre, Malawi: A mathematical modeling study
abstract: by Sun Kim, Melike Hazal Can, Hannah M. Rickman, Mphatso D. Phiri, Marriott Nliwasa, Tisungane E. Mwenyenkulu, Kuzani Mbendera, Stéphane Verguet, Marcia C. Castro, Elizabeth L. Corbett, Peter MacPherson, Ted Cohen, Nicolas A. Menzies Background Active case finding (ACF) for tuberculosis (TB) can reduce transmission, yet efficient targeting requires high-quality surveillance data. We investigated the potential costs and impact of targeted ACF, guided by local estimates of the annual risk of TB infection (ARTI) derived from Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) immunoreactivity survey data in children aged Methods and findings Using mathematical models parameterized with local data, we compared three case-finding approaches across 33 urban neighborhoods in Blantyre, Malawi: passive case finding (PCF) only; PCF with untargeted ACF; and PCF with ARTI-guided targeted ACF. Health outcomes (life expectancy, disability-adjusted life years [DALYs]) and costs were estimated using a Markov microsimulation model. Costs were assessed from health system and societal perspectives. Results were calculated for different assumptions about the relationship between ARTI and true TB prevalence.Compared to PCF-only, untargeted ACF was estimated to improve life expectancy by 3.3 years (95% credible interval (CrI) [1.7, 5.4]) for individuals with TB disease, but at high cost. Targeted ACF covering half of the study population was estimated to identify 80% of all individuals with TB and achieved a lower cost per DALY averted (US$400, 95% CrI [20,1,000]) than untargeted ACF (US$700, 95% CrI [100, 1,500]). In the main analysis, these cost-effectiveness ratios exceeded available cost-effectiveness thresholds for Malawi, although cost-effectiveness improved under assumptions of higher TB prevalence or greater transmission reduction. The findings are based on mathematical modeling and are subject to several limitations, including assumptions regarding the relationship between ARTI and TB prevalence, which remains uncertain. Conclusions Targeting ACF using Mtb immunoreactivity survey data could substantially improve health impact and cost-effectiveness compared to untargeted approaches. However, low-cost approaches for collecting these data are needed for wider adoption.

title: A machine learning-derived aging index for risk stratification and mortality prediction in cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: A retrospective cohort study
abstract: by Zhengyang Zhu, Kejun Ren, Dong Wang, Yong Lv, Hua Jin, Lei Zhang, Yiping Wang Background The cardiovascular‑kidney‑metabolic (CKM) syndrome shows substantial heterogeneity in progression, yet existing biological age indices are not tailored to CKM pathways. We developed an aging index (CKMAI) using machine learning and evaluated its predictive performance for mortality and high‑risk CKM status. Methods and findings We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 6,896 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2005–2018, weighted for the US adult population. A two‑stage machine learning framework evaluated over 100 candidate survival models; the optimal model was selected via Pareto front optimization. Predictive performance was assessed using time‑dependent area under the curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Nonlinear relationships and threshold effects were examined with restricted cubic splines and two‑piecewise regression. Additive interactions were quantified by relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) and attributable proportion (AP). Unsupervised clustering identified aging‑metabolic phenotypes. Weighted bootstrap mediation analysis assessed the mediating role of depression.The Pareto‑optimal simple Cox model achieved a mean C‑index of 0.893. CKMAI consistently outperformed PhenoAge, KDM, and the cardiometabolic index (CMI) across all outcomes. For all‑cause mortality, CKMAI’s time‑dependent AUCs were 0.893 (95% CI [0.851, 0.925]) at 3 years, 0.907 (95% CI [0.884, 0.927]) at 5 years, and 0.890 (95% CI [0.868, 0.910]) at 10 years; for cardiovascular mortality, 0.904 (95% CI [0.840, 0.943]), 0.937 (95% CI [0.892, 0.960]), and 0.937 (95% CI [0.900, 0.959]); for high‑risk CKM status, 0.790 (95% CI [0.765, 0.816]). NRI and IDI were significant at all time points ( P P > 0.05), and DCA confirmed superior net benefit. Nonlinear associations were found for all three outcomes. Threshold analysis identified inflection points at CKMAI 61.587 (all‑cause mortality), 60.732 (cardiovascular mortality), and 34.092 (high‑risk CKM status), with steeper risk increases below each threshold. CKMAI exhibited super‑additive interactions with PhenoAge (RERI 15.06, 95% CI [8.14, 38.44]). Clustering revealed six distinct aging‑metabolic phenotypes; the frail elderly cluster had the highest mortality risk (hazard ratio [HR] 11.74, 95% CI [7.85, 17.57]). Depression partially mediated the CKMAI‑outcome associations (proportions mediated: 5.6% [95% CI 2.3%–9.0%] for all‑cause mortality, 8.2% [95% CI 2.8%–22.0%] for cardiovascular mortality, 11.1% [95% CI 6.7%–24.0%] for high‑risk CKM status). Findings were robust across prespecified subgroups and multiple sensitivity analyses. A key limitation is the lack of validation in geographically independent cohorts with complete mortality follow-up; however, temporal validation within NHANES and preliminary external validation in a hospital based Chinese cohort ( n = 261) supported the generalizability of the CKMAI for identifying high risk CKM status. Conclusions CKMAI is a valid, CKM‑specific aging index that outperforms universal biological age measures in predicting mortality and identifying high‑risk CKM status. Its super‑additive interactions with PhenoAge and the partial mediation by depression offer new mechanistic insights into CKM heterogeneity. By integrating a diverse set of clinical laboratory measures, nutritional assessments, lifestyle factors, and social determinants of health, CKMAI provides a practical, implementable tool for risk stratification and targeted prevention in CKM syndrome.

title: The association between disability and mortality among children and adolescents: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: by Maureen Moyo-Chilufya, Arthemon Nguweneza, Sara Rotenberg, Hannah Kuper, Tracey Smythe Background Mortality is a fundamental marker of population health and equity. Despite major global declines in mortality over recent decades, disparities in survival persist across childhood and adolescence, particularly by disability status. We aimed to synthesise current evidence on all-cause mortality among children and adolescents with disabilities compared to their non-disabled peers through a systematic review and meta-analysis. Methods and findings This review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251072039). We searched Embase, Global Health, MEDLINE, PubMed and PsycInfo to identify relevant studies published from January 1, 2000 to August 20, 2026. We included cohort studies that compared all-cause mortality rates for children and adolescents with and without disabilities (aged 0–19 years). We excluded studies without a clear definition of disability, disaggregated mortality data, or a control group. Two authors independently screened studies, with data extraction by one and verification by a second. We assessed risk of bias using a Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool. We conducted meta-analyses in RevMan for studies reporting age-sex-adjusted or multivariable-adjusted mortality ratios and R software to assess for publication bias. We reported heterogeneity using the I 2 and τ 2 statistics. We identified 12,664 records of which 29 studies met the inclusion criteria, representing over 35 million children/adolescents. Sixteen studies were eligible to be included in the meta-analysis. Overall, children with disabilities had a 5.31-fold (95% confidence interval (CI) [3.63,7.77]; p τ 2 = 0.88; I 2 = 98%) higher all-cause mortality than their peers. The association between disability and mortality was higher in both younger children 0–5 years (Hazard ratio (HR)=7.51: 95%CI [4.70,12.00]; p τ 2 = 0.44; I 2 = 91%) and children 6–19 years (HR = 4.68: 95%CI [2.26,9.69]; p τ 2 = 0.93; I 2 = 96%). The association varied by disability type and was most stark for children with neurological disabilities (HR = 11.71: 95%CI [7.90,17.35]; p τ 2 = 0.19; I 2 = 76%). Interpretation is limited by substantial between-study heterogeneity, differences in methods used to ascertain disability ascertainment and in the effect measures used, and the small number of studies from low-income and middle-income countries. Conclusions Children with disabilities experience substantially higher mortality than their peers without disabilities. There is an urgent need for evidence on what works to close the mortality gap.

title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and immune checkpoint blockade in solid tumors: A target trial emulation with pan-cancer transcriptomic analyses
abstract: by Po-Huang Chen, Ming-Shen Dai, Mao-Hsuan Huang, Hsin-Yu Chen, Li-Ting Kao, Tina Yi-Jin Hsieh, Hong-Jie Jhou, Cho-Hao Lee Background Preclinical evidence identifies the serotonin transporter (SERT, encoded by SLC6A4) as an immune checkpoint on CD8+ T cells, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) enhancing antitumor immunity in synergy with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1) therapy. Whether this translates into clinical benefit for patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is unknown. Using a target trial emulation framework, we compared outcomes between SSRI users and benzodiazepine (BZD) users among patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who were receiving an ICI. Separately, in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), which covers a different set of patients, we examined how SLC6A4 expression related to tumor immune-cell infiltration across cancers. Methods and findings We emulated a target trial in the TriNetX federated electronic health record network (over 187 million patients), comparing SSRI with BZD treatment at first ICI administration under an intention-to-treat-analogue estimand. Eligible patients were adults with a solid tumor, a first ICI administration between 2015 and 2025, and a depressive or anxiety disorder recorded within the prior 365 days. Exposure required an active SSRI or BZD prescription overlapping the index date or starting within the preceding 90 days, not necessarily on that date. The primary outcome was 2-year overall survival; 20 secondary outcomes across 4 mechanistic pathways were prespecified. Propensity score matching (1:1) on 49 baseline covariates yielded 1,567 pairs. Estimates are hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Transcriptomic analyses used TCGA (8,272 tumor samples from 8,172 patients, 20 tumor types). Among 3,134 matched patients, SSRI use was associated with lower 2-year all-cause mortality (23.5% versus 34.4%; HR 0.627; 95% CI [0.549, 0.716]; p E -value 2.57). Composite immune-related adverse events (irAEs) were more frequent with SSRI use (HR 1.162; 95% CI [1.039, 1.299]; p = 0.008), driven by thyroid dysfunction (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]; p = 0.006), without increases in hepatitis, pneumonitis, or colitis (all p > 0.09). Newly coded distant metastases were less frequent in the SSRI group (HR 0.629; 95% CI [0.487, 0.811]; p p > 0.76). All 5 individually analyzable SSRIs were associated with lower mortality (HR range 0.61 to 0.71). In TCGA, SLC6A4 expression was inversely correlated with T-cell inflammation in 13 of 20 cancer types, and this organ-level pattern matched that of organ-specific irAEs. The main limitation is residual confounding: performance status, a clinician’s rating of everyday functional ability that strongly predicts cancer survival, is not recorded in the network, and BZDs are prescribed in different circumstances from SSRIs, so the groups may differ in ways matching cannot capture. The TCGA analyses used bulk tumor tissue from patients not treated with ICIs, so they cannot localize SLC6A4 to particular cells or show that SSRIs alter the tumor microenvironment. Conclusions In this study, SSRI use was associated with lower mortality and organ-selective immune activation compared with BZD use among ICI-treated patients with psychiatric comorbidity. Transcriptomic evidence supports biological plausibility. These findings warrant prospective evaluation of SSRI repurposing as an ICI adjuvant.

title: Assessing a multicomponent quality improvement strategy for chronic care of cardiovascular diseases in India: The C-QIP randomized feasibility trial
abstract: by Kavita Singh, Ambuj Roy, Dimple Kondal, Kalyani Nikhare, Mareesha Gandral, Satish G. Patil, Kiran Aithal, Meenahalli Palleda Girish, Mohit Gupta, Kushal Madan, Jitendra P. S. Sawhney, Kamar Ali, Meetushi Jain, Savitesh Kushwaha, Devraj Jindal, Emily Mendenhall, Shivani A. Patel, Kabayam M. Venkat Narayan, Nikhil Tandon, Mark D. Huffman, Dorairaj Prabhakaran Background Chronic cardiovascular diseases (CVD) care quality remains suboptimal, globally. We assessed the feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and preliminary effect of a multicomponent, collaborative quality improvement (C-QIP) strategy among patients with CVD attending outpatient clinics in India. Methods and findings In this pragmatic feasibility randomized controlled trial, 410 adults with ischemic heart disease, ischemic stroke, or heart failure attending four public and private hospitals were randomized to C-QIP (electronic decision support for providers, non-physician care coordination, patient education, text-message reminders, and audit-feedback) or usual care. Primary outcomes were feasibility, fidelity, adoption, and acceptability; secondary outcomes included guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), self-reported adherence, care processes, and risk factors. At end of study (median follow-up 15 months), retention was 192/206 (93.2%) in C-QIP and 187/204 (91.7%) in usual care. Fidelity was high: 187/198 (94.4%) C-QIP participants received lifestyle counseling at end of study. C-QIP increased GDMT use for ischemic heart disease (58.3% versus 32.4%; relative risk [RR] 1.45, 95% CI [1.18, 1.78]) and ischemic stroke (76.7% versus 31.8%; RR 2.41, 95% CI [1.52, 3.81]), but not heart failure. Self-reported adherence was higher for medications (90.9% versus 82.3%; RR 1.08, 95% CI [1.04, 1.12]), diet (91.9% versus 82.3%; RR 1.07, 95% CI [1.02, 1.13]), and physical activity (91.4% versus 70.4%; RR 1.23, 95% CI [1.16, 1.30]). Limitations include feasibility design, individual randomization within shared clinics, and limited power for clinical outcomes and subgroup analysis. Conclusions The C-QIP trial demonstrated that a multicomponent strategy is feasible, acceptable, and improved chronic CVD care processes in India. Future large, confirmatory hybrid trials are needed to establish whether such quality improvement strategies can reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
