title: Vitamin D receptor rs731236 polymorphism and susceptibility to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in Brazilian girls
abstract: BackgroundThe etiology and pathogenesis of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is thought to involve genetic and environmental factors, including low bone mineral density. This study aimed to evaluate the association between vitamin D receptor gene (VDR) polymorphism (rs731236, TaqI), curve magnitude, and anthropometric characteristics in girls with AIS.MethodsA retrospective case-control study included 175 Brazilian girls with AIS and 175 healthy controls. Genotyping was performed using a validated real-time PCR assay. Associations were evaluated using binary and linear regression models.ResultsThe median Cobb angle was 48.7° (11–110°), the majority (n = 100, 57.1%) had an indication for surgical treatment (Cobb ≥45°), and 120 (68.6%) were skeletally mature (Risser IV and V). Minor allele frequencies of VDR rs731236 (A > G) polymorphism were 41%, 45%, 38%, and 35.7% for all AIS, Cobb < 45° and Cobb ≥45°, and healthy volunteers, respectively. Among underweight and normal-weight participants, however, the VDR GG genotype was associated with AIS susceptibility compared to healthy controls (OR = 4.4; CI95%=1.01–19.3). A positive correlation was observed between the presence of the VDR GG genotype and an increase in the Cobb angle of 1.2 degrees for every 1 kg/m2 increase in BMI (P = 0.035).ConclusionThe VDR rs731236 GG genotype was associated with AIS susceptibility among underweight and normal-weight Brazilian girls, suggesting that anthropometric status may modify the phenotypic expression of genetic susceptibility. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger studies, with control for genetic ancestry, before any clinical application.

title: Elevated EZH2 expression is associated with reduced NRF2-related antioxidant signaling and ferroptosis-associated features in eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps
abstract: Recurrence remains common in eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (eCRSwNP) despite surgery and type 2-directed therapy, suggesting that epithelial injury mechanisms beyond cytokine signaling remain incompletely defined. Epigenetic-redox dysregulation is a plausible contributor, but its relationship to NRF2-associated antioxidant defenses in eCRSwNP has received little attention. Current therapies suppress type 2 inflammation but may not directly address persistent epithelial redox imbalance, providing a rationale for examining complementary regulatory pathways in patients with severe recurrent disease. We explored associations among EZH2 expression, NRF2-related antioxidant readouts, oxidative injury, and ferroptosis-associated features using patient sinonasal tissues, primary nasal epithelial cells subjected to EZH2-targeting shRNA, and an exploratory AAV-treated mouse model. In human tissues, higher EZH2 expression accompanied lower NRF2-related antioxidant marker levels and a ferroptosis-associated expression pattern. In cultured cells, EZH2 targeting was accompanied by improved antioxidant readouts, lower intracellular oxidation, and less mitochondrial injury. The mouse experiment showed parallel treatment-associated differences in protein staining and sinonasal histopathology, although EZH2 target engagement in nasal mucosa was not confirmed. These findings do not establish ferroptosis because functional rescue, iron-dependence testing, and direct phospholipid-peroxidation measurements were not performed. They also do not establish NRF2 dependence, direct EZH2–NRF2 binding, or the temporal direction of the relationship among EZH2, NRF2-related readouts, and oxidative stress. The results therefore identify a preliminary epigenetic-redox association rather than a defined EZH2–NRF2 mechanism. This framework may help guide future studies incorporating time-resolved measurements, reciprocal genetic perturbation, NRF2 localization and activity assays, ferroptosis-selective rescue, and direct validation of in vivo target engagement.

title: The Duffy-null phenotype in Saudi Arabia: distribution, origins and clinical significance
abstract: BackgroundThe Duffy antigens Fya and Fyb, encoded by ACKR1 (formerly DARC), are absent from red cells in the Fy(a−b−) phenotype, which almost always arises from homozygosity for the FY*02N.01 GATA-box variant (rs2814778). It bears on two everyday problems in non-malignant hematology, red-cell alloimmunization and the interpretation of a low neutrophil count, and confers protection against Plasmodium vivax. Arabian data have been phenotypic and sparse.ObjectiveTo assemble the Saudi and Gulf evidence on Duffy-null frequency and follow it into transfusion support, neutrophil reference intervals and vivax surveillance.MethodsPubMed and Web of Science were searched from July to September 2026, pairing Duffy, ACKR1, DARC and rs2814778 with Arabian regional terms, neutropenia, reference intervals and alloimmunization. Confidence intervals are Wilson intervals recomputed from reported counts.ResultsProvincial Fy(a−b−) frequency ranges from 26.7% in the north to 78.3% in Jazan, with Oman (68.5%) nearest and lower figures in the lower Gulf, consistent with enriched African ancestry at ACKR1. In male Jazan donors the Duffy-null neutrophil interval was 1,140–5,290/µL and institutional limits classified 50.9% as neutropenic; isolated neutropenia reaches 21% locally. Duffy alloimmunization is documented at every Saudi center examined, exclusively as anti-Fya, though the rates are not directly comparable.ConclusionJazan carries among the highest Duffy-null frequencies reported outside sub-Saharan Africa, with direct consequences for transfusion support and for neutrophil reference intervals. One western Saudi cohort has been genotyped at the FY promoter; the southwest, where frequencies are highest, has not, and closing that gap is the most tractable next step.

title: Fulminant pancreatic encephalopathy with brain edema and herniation in severe hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis: a case report
abstract: Pancreatic encephalopathy (PE) is a rare but potentially devastating neurological complication of severe acute pancreatitis. Its manifestations range from confusion and agitation to seizures, coma, and cerebral edema, often making the diagnosis challenging due to its overlap with other causes of encephalopathy. We report a 23-year-old woman with hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis who rapidly progressed to severe acute pancreatitis with multiorgan failure. Within 48 h of admission, she developed agitation, seizure-like activity, and coma. Neuroimaging demonstrated diffuse cerebral and cerebellar edema, features of elevated intracranial pressure, cerebellar tonsillar herniation, and extensive restricted diffusion. After evaluation of alternative etiologies, the neurological deterioration was attributed to PE. Despite aggressive medical management, including insulin therapy, renal replacement therapy, mechanical ventilation, and hyperosmolar therapy, she did not show any signs of neurological recovery. This case demonstrates that PE may rarely progress to malignant cerebral edema and tonsillar herniation. New neuropsychiatric manifestations in patients with severe acute pancreatitis should prompt urgent neurological assessment and early neuroimaging whenever clinically feasible.

title: Clinical validation of the Swaasa® artificial intelligence platform using cough sounds for screening and aid in diagnosis of respiratory diseases
abstract: IntroductionCough sound analysis can provide clues to underlying respiratory disease. The Swaasa AI platform, a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), applies artificial intelligence to cough recordings to generate indications, including overall risk (normal vs. abnormal), spirometric pattern (obstructive, restrictive, or normal), pattern severity (mild, moderate, severe), and the presence of asthma, COPD, ILD, and bronchiectasis.MethodsPatients (≥18 years) presenting to our departments with respiratory symptoms were prospectively recruited. Cough sounds were recorded on a mobile device running the Swaasa AI platform, spirometry was performed. Spirometry served as the reference standard for physiological pattern and severity, while physician-established clinical diagnosis served as the reference for disease categories. Polychotomous variables were dichotomized as normal vs. abnormal, & multi-class output for disease condition, pattern severity, and disease categories (asthma, COPD, ILD, bronchiectasis) were defined.Trial registrationCTRI/2021/04/032742; registered on 12/04/2021; date of first enrollment: 19/04/2021; trial end date: 14/09/2023.ResultsWe recruited 2,179 patients with respiratory diseases and 827 normal individuals; 62% were male. The Swaasa AI platform achieved 90% accuracy in distinguishing normal from abnormal (respiratory condition present) and in classifying normal vs. abnormal spirometry, with descriptive performance subgroup analyses showing broadly comparable performance across age and gender groups For multi-class outcomes, the accuracy ranges were: spirometry pattern: 79%–84%, pattern severity: 76%–84.5%, and disease-type classification: 83%–93%.ConclusionSwaasa® demonstrates promising performance in distinguishing normal from abnormal respiratory conditions across demographic subgroups, indicating its promise as a screening tool. While the accuracy measures emphasize further refinement to ensure consistent high performance across specific respiratory disease scenarios and severity levels, the study shows its reasonable potential in identifying specific respiratory diseases and their severity.

title: Clinical and sonographic characteristics of gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma: a descriptive case series of 13 patients
abstract: ObjectiveGastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (G-EAC) is a distinct human papillomavirus (HPV)-independent subtype of cervical adenocarcinoma for which early diagnosis continues to pose a clinical challenge. We set out to characterize the clinical and sonographic features of G-EAC and to provide hypothesis-generating observations to guide future research.MethodsThis retrospective analysis comprised 13 patients with histopathologically confirmed G-EAC who underwent surgery at our center between August 2017 and September 2024. We reviewed and descriptively summarized the clinical presentation, HPV and cytology results, cervical biopsy findings, tumor markers, and ultrasonographic and cross-sectional imaging findings, together with all available pathological and surgical records.ResultsThe patients were aged 39–76 years (mean, 53.4 years), and all were parous. Vaginal discharge was the most common presenting symptom (8/13, 61.5%), followed by irregular vaginal bleeding (4/13, 30.8%) and postcoital bleeding (1/13, 7.7%). HPV testing was negative in 11/13 patients (84.6%); 1/13 (7.7%) tested positive for HPV 58, and another 1/13 (7.7%) carried a different high-risk HPV type. ThinPrep cytologic testing (TCT) was negative in 12/13 patients (92.3%), whereas atypical squamous cells were detected in 1/13 (7.7%). Among the 11 patients who underwent colposcopy with cervical biopsy, histopathological findings were negative in 8/11 (72.7%), mild glandular atypia was identified in 2/11 (18.2%), and rare adenocarcinoma cells were identified in 1/11 (9.1%). All 13 patients underwent preoperative ultrasound. Ultrasound findings raised suspicion of cervical malignancy in 9/13 patients (69.2%), were suggestive of benign cervical cystic lesions in 2/13 (15.4%), and were unremarkable in the remaining 2/13 (15.4%). A honeycomb sonographic pattern was present in 7/13 patients (53.8%), and abundant intralesional vascularity (Adler grade III) was present in 9/13 patients (69.2%). Preoperative MRI was performed in 10/13 patients (76.9%), 1 of whom also underwent CT, whereas the remaining 3/13 patients (23.1%) underwent neither MRI nor CT. A barrel-shaped cervix was documented in the pathological or surgical records of 4/13 patients (30.8%).ConclusionG-EAC may come to attention through a combination of clinical and imaging findings that together raise diagnostic suspicion. In this series, HPV negativity was common, and vaginal discharge was the most frequent presenting complaint. A honeycomb sonographic pattern and abundant intralesional vascularity may raise suspicion of G-EAC, although these findings remain descriptive and require validation in larger, adequately controlled studies.

title: Case report: Diagnostic value of [99mTc]Tc-sestamibi SPECT/CT in a very small renal mass: a histopathology-matched case
abstract: A 12-mm enhancing renal mass was incidentally detected in a 61-year-old man during CT urography. To refine characterization, [99mTc]Tc-sestamibi SPECT/CT was performed, showing radiotracer uptake comparable to the surrounding cortex (L/K ratio 0.95) despite the sub-centimetric size, suggestive of an oncocytic or otherwise indolent lesion. Given patient-specific factors and contralateral renal impairment, partial nephrectomy was undertaken, revealing a renal oncocytoma with typical histopathological and immunohistochemical features. This case highlights that, although technical limitations exist for lesions <2 cm, [99mTc]Tc-sestamibi SPECT/CT may still provide interpretable molecular information in selected very small renal masses, especially when integrated with CAIX-targeted radiotracers – such as girentuximab – whose complementary biological profile enhances noninvasive renal mass assessment. The concordance between imaging and histology supports further investigation into standardized acquisition and interpretation criteria to optimize noninvasive assessment and guide management of small renal masses.

title: Development of an HFACS-based risk assessment indicator system for unplanned endotracheal extubation in adult ICU patients: a Delphi and AHP study
abstract: ObjectiveTo construct a risk-assessment indicator system for unplanned endotracheal extubation (UEE) among adult ICU patients based on the Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS), and provide a structured multi-level framework for unit-level safety auditing and root-cause analysis of UEE events.MethodsInitial indicators were generated via systematic literature review and retrospective analysis of local UEE adverse-event cases. A two-round Delphi expert consultation was performed to screen and revise indicators. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) was adopted to calculate indicator weights at each hierarchical level. Content validity was evaluated using the content validity index (CVI).ResultsThe valid response rates for the two Delphi rounds were 100.0% (20/20) and 95.0% (19/20), respectively. The expert authority coefficients (Cr) were 0.893 and 0.915, indicating high expert authority. Kendall's coefficients of concordance (W) were 0.242 and 0.254 (P < 0.001), showing statistically significant yet low expert agreement. Among the four primary dimensions, the combined weights were 0.448 for unsafe behavior of clinicians, 0.257 for inadequate supervision, 0.151 for preconditions for unsafe acts, and 0.144 for organizational influence. The final risk-assessment indicator system comprised 4 primary, 13 secondary, and 63 tertiary indicators with acceptable overall content validity.ConclusionUsing HFACS, two-round Delphi consultation, and AHP, this study developed a consensus-driven preliminary indicator system for UEE risk-related safety management in adult ICUs. This framework is intended for system-oriented safety audits, training priority setting, and root-cause analysis rather than bedside individual-patient risk prediction. Further prospective clinical validation is required to verify its predictive validity, reliability and practical feasibility before widespread clinical implementation.

title: Airway stenosis alters the balance between tidal volume, air entrainment, and oxygen-source delivery during normal frequency and superimposed jet ventilation: a bench model study
abstract: BackgroundSevere airway stenosis alters gas mixing and volume delivery during open-system jet ventilation. How high-frequency (HF) superimposition and component titration modify these effects remains incompletely characterized.ObjectiveTo compare stenosis-induced changes in distal oxygen concentration (FiO2), tidal volume (VT), pressure, flow, and estimated gas composition among pure normal-frequency jet ventilation (NFJV) and superimposed HF jet ventilation (SHFJV) with titration of either the NF (SHFJV-NF) or HF component (SHFJV-HF).MethodsAn open rigid-bronchoscopy bench model was tested with and without 90% fixed airway stenosis. Pure NFJV and SHFJV-NF shared 56 NF parameter settings; SHFJV-HF included 60 HF settings with a fixed NF component. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated strategy × airway interactions and Holm-adjusted pairwise contrasts. A separate matched model assessed HF addition. Gas-component fractions and volumes were estimated at each setting using a two-source mixing model.ResultsStrategy × airway interactions were significant for all five measured outcomes (all P < 0.001). Median stenosis-induced changes were +4.7, +29.1, and +24.7 percentage points for FiO2 and −454, −577, and −232 mL for VT during pure NFJV, SHFJV-NF, and SHFJV-HF, respectively. At identical NF settings, HF addition modified the stenosis response by +24.1 percentage points for FiO2, −111.7 mL for VT (95% CI −173.6 to −49.8), +2.02 cmH2O for measured positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), and −8.11 L·min−1 for expiratory flow magnitude (all P < 0.001). Estimated entrained-air volume decreased in all strategies, whereas oxygen-source volume did not increase uniformly.ConclusionAt identical NF settings, HF addition amplified the stenosis-associated FiO2 rise, VT loss, and PEEP increase. HF-component titration produced a different response across its tested parameter range. Estimated gas-composition changes were consistent with reduced oxygen dilution. Distal FiO2 did not establish preserved ventilation or arterial oxygenation, and CO2 elimination was not measured.

title: Postoperative lateral-wall status and fixation failure after cephalomedullary nailing of extracapsular hip fractures: an ambispective cohort study
abstract: BackgroundExtracapsular hip fractures cause substantial morbidity in older adults, and cephalomedullary nailing is widely used for fixation. Although lateral-wall disruption is an established concern in extramedullary fixation, the prognostic relevance of postoperative lateral-wall status after cephalomedullary nailing remains uncertain. We evaluated its association with fixation failure among patients who achieved satisfactory reduction.MethodsAn ambispective cohort of patients with acute extracapsular hip fractures treated with cephalomedullary nailing at Beijing Hospital (January 2010–October 2025) was analyzed. Only patients who achieved excellent or acceptable reduction were included. Postoperative lateral-wall status was classified using preoperative lateral-wall thickness and fracture morphology together with any new intraoperative lateral-wall fracture identified on postoperative imaging. Radiographic fixation failure was the primary endpoint; follow-up was at least 6 months unless failure was confirmed earlier. Failure-free survival and the association between postoperative lateral-wall status and fixation failure were evaluated using Kaplan–Meier analysis and prespecified parsimonious Firth penalized logistic regression models.ResultsAmong 508 patients, 33 (6.5%) experienced fixation failure: 16 of 249 (6.4%) with complete and 17 of 259 (6.6%) with incomplete postoperative lateral-wall status. The log-rank test yielded p = 0.778. In the Firth model adjusted for age and tip–apex distance, no statistically significant association was detected between postoperative lateral-wall status and fixation failure (incomplete vs. complete: adjusted odds ratio, 1.04; 95% CI: 0.52–2.10; p = 0.915).ConclusionAmong patients with AO/OTA 31-A extracapsular hip fractures who achieved satisfactory reduction, we did not detect a statistically significant association between postoperative lateral-wall status and fixation failure after cephalomedullary nailing. Because the analysis was restricted to satisfactorily reduced fractures and the number of failure events was limited, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that lateral-wall morphology is unimportant in the broader fracture population.

title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS
abstract: BackgroundHemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges.Case presentationA 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 10⁹/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology.ConclusionSeoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

title: Early risk assessment model for sepsis-associated acute kidney injury combining quantitative contrast-enhanced ultrasound and biomarkers: a prospective pilot study
abstract: BackgroundSepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) is associated with high mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU), yet early diagnosis remains challenging due to the diagnostic lag of conventional functional biomarkers. We aimed to develop and validate a Ridge-penalized multimodal model integrating quantitative renal contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) with clinical biomarkers for early SA-AKI risk stratification.MethodsAdult septic patients were prospectively enrolled in a 35-bed general ICU. Quantitative renal CEUS parameters—including peak intensity (PI), time to peak (TTP), mean transit time (MTT), and area under the time-intensity curve (TIC-AUC)—and routine clinical variables were collected within 24 h of admission. SA-AKI was defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes criteria within 7 days. A multimodal Ridge logistic regression model (Model C) was developed using stratified 5-fold cross-validation (λ1SE rule) and compared with CEUS-only (Model A) and clinical-only (Model B) candidate models. Internal validation was performed using 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Multivariable Firth-penalized regression was used to evaluate independent predictors.ResultsAmong 63 analyzed patients, 25 (39.7%) developed SA-AKI at a median lead time of ICU day 2 (IQR: day 1–day 3) post-admission; none met AKI criteria at baseline. Quantitative CEUS revealed significant cortical hypoperfusion (PI and TIC-AUC) and prolonged microvascular transit (MTT) in the SA-AKI group (all P < 0.05), while other temporal or slope parameters showed non-significant trends. Model C achieved superior discrimination with a bias-corrected area under the curve (AUC) of 0.852 (95% CI: 0.789–0.932), outperforming Model A (0.818) and Model B (0.740). At the optimal threshold, Model C yielded 80.0% sensitivity and 84.2% specificity. Decision curve analysis confirmed higher standardized net benefit for Model C across threshold probabilities of 0.15–0.60. Adjusted age and baseline serum cystatin C confirmed lower PI (aOR = 0.31), lower TIC-AUC (aOR = 0.31), and prolonged TTP (aOR = 2.1) as independent predictors (all P < 0.05).ConclusionsQuantitative renal CEUS parameters are independent early indicators of SA-AKI. Integrating renal CEUS with clinical biomarkers offers a promising, noninvasive strategy for early SA-AKI risk stratification up to 48 h before clinical diagnosis.Clinical Trial Registrationhttps://www.chictr.org.cn/, identifier ChiCTR2300067267.

title: Family physicians’ acceptability, perceived value, and barriers of pharmacist-led medication management in primary care—a theory-based qualitative study
abstract: BackgroundPolypharmacy burdens healthcare systems and increases adverse drug events. While pharmacist-led comprehensive medication management (CMM) mitigates these issues globally, its integration into Turkish primary care remains limited.ObjectiveTo explore family physicians’ acceptability of pharmacist-led CMM in Türkiye and identify perceived barriers to interprofessional collaboration.MethodsA qualitative descriptive study was conducted among primary care family physicians in Istanbul, Türkiye, between June and August 2025. Purposive sampling was utilized to recruit participants with at least 5 years of clinical experience. We collected data through semi-structured online interviews using a guide developed by an interdisciplinary panel and piloted for structural clarity. With NVivo software, transcripts were analyzed using a hybrid thematic analysis approach, combining inductive coding to identify emergent, context-specific themes with deductive mapping to the seven constructs of the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability (TFA). Inter-coder reliability was established through independent parallel coding, and trustworthiness was reinforced via member checking. Reporting adhered to the COREQ checklist.ResultsParticipants (n = 12) facing severe daily workloads (>74 patients) viewed clinical pharmacists as a crucial safety net. Analysis revealed three core themes: (1) Needs and Opportunities: CMM offers substantial benefits by managing polypharmacy, mitigating physician fatigue, reinforcing patient medication adherence, and reducing overall workload and costs. (2) Concerns and Barriers: Major structural hurdles include physical space constraints in FHCs, data privacy (KVKK) vulnerabilities, and pharmaceutical industry apprehension. (3) Implementation Conditions: Successful integration requires integrated Electronic Health Records (EHR), formalized legal boundaries, and joint interprofessional training. Subgroup analysis indicated that early- to mid-career physicians demonstrated higher implementation readiness, while late-career peers focused more on operational burdens.ConclusionFamily physicians demonstrate highly favorable prospective acceptability toward pharmacist-led CMM. Successful real-world integration requires resolving macro-level infrastructural and legal barriers while establishing actionable interprofessional enablers, shared clinical algorithms, and compatible digital workflows.

title: Airway recanalization followed by montgomery T-tube placement for severe subglottic stenosis in an adolescent: a case report
abstract: BackgroundPost-intubation subglottic stenosis (SGS) in adolescents is a progressive acquired airway disorder that can substantially impair quality of life. Both surgical and interventional airway therapies are effective treatment options for SGS; however, each carries considerable technical demands, procedural risks, and potential complications. Interventional airway therapy relieves airway obstruction, maintains airway patency, restores airway and phonatory function, and has a less invasive profile, positioning it as a key treatment modality for SGS.Case presentationA 15-year-old girl sustained a traumatic brain injury following a motor vehicle accident. She received endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit for two weeks, followed by tracheostomy. After cognitive and motor function recovered, attempted complete occlusion of the tracheostomy tube provoked dyspnea. Subsequent bronchoscopic examination revealed subglottic stenosis.DiagnosisBronchoscopic examination demonstrated approximately 98% subglottic airway stenosis involving a segment of roughly 2 cm with a funnel-shaped morphology, consistent with acquired post-intubation SGS.InterventionsA multidisciplinary team developed an individualized treatment strategy that included rigid bronchoscopy-assisted respiratory support, airway recanalization, Montgomery T-tube placement, perioperative pulmonary hygiene management, and surveillance for procedure-related adverse events.ResultsAirway recanalization, including electrocautery incision, laser ablation, and balloon dilation, was performed successfully with rigid bronchoscopic support, restoring the tracheal lumen to approximately 1 cm in diameter. After the airway mucosa had stabilized, a Montgomery T-tube was implanted. Following T-tube placement, the patient regained phonatory function and experienced marked improvement in dyspnea. Computed tomography confirmed appropriate positioning of the Montgomery T-tube. Follow-up bronchoscopy demonstrated a patent lumen without significant secretion retention or granulation tissue formation.

title: Mid-zone hepatocytes trade proliferation for survival via Atf4-Chop axis in early acute liver injury
abstract: Hepatocytes undergo extensive proliferation to facilitate liver repair after injury, yet early adaptive changes prior to proliferation remain unclear. Using a mouse model of acetaminophen (APAP)-induced liver injury, we show that hepatocytes undergo transient proliferation suppression that is most pronounced in mid-zone hepatocytes, consistent with zonal APAP metabolism. Although spatial transcriptomics (ST) alone could not independently confirm zonal proliferative restraint, ST analysis identified a unique mid-zone stress-response program centered on the Atf4-Chop axis. By integrating Cut&Run with immunohistochemistry and functional studies, we found that the Atf4-Chop axis suppresses proliferation via the cell-cycle inhibitor Btg2. Together, our findings support a model in which mid-zone hepatocytes transiently prioritize stress adaptation over proliferation, thereby preserving regenerative capacity for subsequent liver repair.

title: Concerted changes in the pediatric single-cell intestinal ecosystem before and after anti-TNF blockade
abstract: Crohn’s disease is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) commonly treated through anti-TNF blockade. However, most patients still relapse and inevitably progress. Comprehensive single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlases have largely sampled patients with established treatment-refractory IBD, limiting our understanding of which cell types, subsets, and states at diagnosis anticipate disease severity and response to treatment. Here, through combining clinical, flow cytometry, histology, and scRNA-seq methods, we profile diagnostic human biopsies from the terminal ileum of treatment-naive pediatric patients with Crohn’s disease (pediCD; n = 14), matched repeat biopsies (pediCD-treated; n = 8) and from non-inflamed pediatric controls with functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGIDs; n = 13). To resolve and annotate epithelial, stromal, and immune cell states among the 201,883 baseline single-cell transcriptomes, we develop a principled and unbiased tiered clustering approach, ARBOL. Through flow cytometry and scRNA-seq, we observe that treatment-naive pediCD and FGID have similar broad cell type composition. However, through high-resolution scRNA-seq analysis and microscopy, we identify significant differences in cell subsets and states that arise during pediCD relative to FGID. By closely linking our scRNA-seq analysis with clinical meta-data, we resolve a vector of T cell, innate lymphocyte, myeloid, and epithelial cell states in treatment-naive pediCD (pediCD-TIME) samples, which can distinguish patients along the trajectory of disease severity and anti-TNF response. By using ARBOL with integration, we position repeat on-treatment biopsies from our patients between treatment-naive pediCD and on-treatment adult CD. We identify that anti-TNF treatment pushes the pediatric cellular ecosystem toward an adult, more treatment-refractory state. Our study jointly leverages a treatment-naive cohort, high-resolution principled scRNA-seq data analysis, and clinical outcomes to understand which baseline cell states may predict Crohn’s disease trajectory.

Translational reading frame predicts the pathogenicity of C-terminal frameshift deletions in MeCP2
abstract: Mutations in the MECP2 gene cause the severe neurological disorder Rett syndrome. A cluster of frameshift-causing C-terminal deletions (CTDs) removes ~100 amino acids and accounts for approximately 10% of RTT-causing mutations. Their pathogenicity is unexpected because this C-terminal domain is dispensable in mice. Analysis of pathogenic and benign human MECP2 variants reveals that some individuals with apparently typical CTDs do not develop Rett syndrome, confirming that C-terminal truncations are not intrinsically pathogenic. Using human sequence data and mouse models we show that pathogenicity results from a marked reduction in MeCP2 levels and depends on the presence of a proline proline stop motif (-PPX) generated by a shift to the +2 reading frame. CTDs that shift to the +1 frame avoid this motif and are benign. Replacing the stop codon of the PPX motif with tryptophan restores MeCP2 expression and rescues RTT-like phenotypes in a CTD mouse model. An adenine base editor efficiently introduces this substitution in cultured cells. These findings define a reliable prognostic distinction between benign and pathogenic CTDs and establish a potential editing strategy for correcting disease-causing CTD mutations.

title: Evaluating the applicability of replication success metrics in animal-to-human translation: A simulation study
abstract: Translation failure, in which promising animal study results cannot be reproduced in human trials, is a challenge in biomedical research. Metrics for replication success are widely used to evaluate reproducibility, that is the extent to which the results of a study agree with those of replication studies. The relevance of these metrics in assessing animal-to-human translation success (or failure) is unclear. We conducted a simulation study to examine whether these metrics can quantify translation success, and how their performance varies under different conditions. Using parameters from a meta-analysis on prenatal amino acid supplementation and maternal blood pressure, we simulated animal and human studies under 648 scenarios, varying effect sizes, heterogeneity, animal sample sizes, and number of pooled animal studies. Nine metrics were assessed, namely the two-trials rule, meta-analysis, replication Bayes factor, unweighted and weighted Edgington’s methods, golden skeptical p-value, and three versions of controlled skeptical p-value. Most metrics, except meta-analysis and replication Bayes factor, controlled false positive rates under no heterogeneity, but became liberal as heterogeneity increased, particularly between human studies. Translation power (i.e. the probability of true positive translation success) was constrained by the weaker evidence of the two findings; for example, small sample size in the animal studies resulted in lower translation power. The metric based on meta-analysis frequently indicated success when either of the species found strong evidence, while skeptical p-values were more conservative. The skeptical p-value that controls overall type-one error and the weighted version of Edgington’s method performed relatively consistently across scenarios. However, no metric was uniformly optimal. Metrics developed for replication studies can inform assessments of translation, but their utility depends on the underlying evidence and assumptions. Using multiple metrics in combination, with attention to their strengths and limitations, is recommended for evaluating the translation of animal findings to human outcomes.

title: Magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate alleviates alcohol-associated liver disease through targeting HSD11B1
abstract: While magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate (MgIG) is a clinically approved therapy for alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), its precise molecular targets and mechanisms remain uncharacterized. This study aimed to define MgIG’s hepatoprotective actions in chronic-binge ALD mouse models and ethanol/palmitic acid-exposed AML-12 hepatocytes. Through an integrated strategy encompassing RNA sequencing, molecular docking, and microscale thermophoresis, we discovered that MgIG directly binds to hydroxysteroid 11-beta dehydrogenase 1 (HSD11B1) at residue 187, a finding corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations. In vivo, MgIG markedly attenuated alcohol-induced liver injury, evidenced by ameliorated histological damage, reduced hepatic steatosis, and normalized liver-to-body weight ratios. In vitro, it effectively reduced lipid accumulation, inflammation, and apoptosis. Mechanistically, RNA sequencing identified isopentenyl diphosphate delta isomerase 1 (IDI1) as a key downstream effector. Hepatocyte-specific genetic manipulations confirmed that MgIG modulates the SREBP2–IDI1 axis, thereby suppressing lipogenesis, inflammatory responses, and apoptotic pathways. We reveal HSD11B1 as a novel direct molecular target of MgIG and elucidate its therapeutic mechanism through the HSD11B1–SREBP2–IDI1 signaling axis, which profoundly impacts ALD pathogenesis. These findings not only validate MgIG’s clinical utility but also highlight a promising new therapeutic target for ALD.

Navigating the path: Advice to physician-scientists on choosing a clinical specialty
abstract: Choosing a clinical specialty is a critical decision for physician-scientist trainees, influencing both clinical practice and research trajectory. This article provides a structured approach to specialty selection, emphasizing the importance of aligning clinical interests with long-term research goals, evaluating training pathways, and considering lifestyle implications. Physician-scientists, including MD-PhD and other dual-degree graduates, as well as MD graduates with research-intensive training, often pursue specialties with established research pathways. We outline key decision-making factors, including mentorship, clinical exposure, research commitment, and financial sustainability. Additionally, we compare research track and categorical residency pathways, detailing differences in training structure, funding opportunities, and career outcomes. The article explores the evolving role of physician-scientists across career stages, from residency through senior faculty leadership, highlighting strategies to maintain research engagement while balancing clinical responsibilities. By critically evaluating these factors and leveraging mentorship and institutional support, physician-scientists can make informed decisions that align with their aspirations, ensuring a fulfilling and impactful career in both medicine and research.

title: Differential regulation of hepatic macrophage fate by Chi3l1 in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) progression involves the replacement of protective embryo-derived Kupffer cells (KCs) by inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages (MoMFs), yet the regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify chitinase 3-like 1 (Chi3l1/YKL-40) as a critical metabolic regulator of hepatic macrophage fate. We observed high expression of Chi3l1 in both KCs and MoMFs during MASLD development. Genetic deletion of Chi3l1 specifically in KCs significantly exacerbated MASLD severity and metabolic dysfunction, whereas MoMF-specific Chi3l1 deletion showed minimal metabolic effects. Mechanistic studies revealed that this cell type-specific regulation arises from differential metabolic requirements: KCs display elevated glucose metabolism compared to MoMFs. Chi3l1 directly interacts with glucose to inhibit its cellular uptake, thereby selectively protecting glucose-dependent KCs from metabolic stress-induced cell death while having negligible effects on less glucose-dependent MoMFs. These findings uncover a novel Chi3l1-mediated metabolic checkpoint that preferentially maintains KCs populations through glucose metabolism modulation, providing important new insights into the pathogenesis of MASLD and potential therapeutic strategies targeting macrophage-specific metabolic pathways.

title: Direct MRI of collagen
abstract: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body and has an important role in healthy tissue as well as in a range of prevalent diseases. Medical research and diagnostics, hence, call for means of mapping collagen in vivo. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a natural candidate for this task, offering full 3D capability and versatile contrast non-invasively. However, collagen has so far been invisible to MRI due to extremely short lifetime of its resonances. Here, we report the direct imaging of collagen in vivo by magnetic resonance on the microsecond scale. The dynamics of resonance signals from collagen were first assessed in samples of bovine tendon and cortical bone. On this basis, imaging was performed at echo times down to 10 microseconds, yielding collagen-specific depiction by echo subtraction. The same approach was then extended for use in vivo, enabling direct collagen imaging of a human forearm. This capability suggests significant promise for biomedical science and clinical use.

title: Hyperactivated glycolysis drives spatially patterned Kupffer cell depletion in MASLD
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) progression is characterized by hepatic inflammation and cell death, yet the mechanisms underlying Kupffer cell (KC) loss remain poorly understood. Here, we sought to elucidate the metabolic basis of KC death during MASLD. Using metabolomics, immunostaining, and flow cytometry, we evaluated metabolic alterations and KC death throughout early MASLD progression. We found that KC death is an early hallmark of MASLD, exhibiting greater susceptibility and a spatial distribution consistent with KC zonation. Moreoever, KCs undergo progressive metabolic reprogramming toward enhanced glucose utilization during MASLD development, which is correlated with KC death. In combination with biochemical agonist, isotope tracing, and primary KC culture, we further demonstrated that augmented glycolytic metabolism directly drives KC death in vitro. Consistently, using Chi3l1 -deficient mice, we further demonstrated that increased glucose utilization accelerates KC death in vivo. Together, these findings establish a causal link between glycolytic activation and KC loss during MASLD progression, highlighting glucose metabolic pathways as potential therapeutic targets to preserve KC homeostasis and mitigate MASLD.

title: Teaching early-career researchers how to respond to peer reviewers
abstract: The process of publishing a research article in a scientific journal inevitably involves revising the original version of the article to respond to the concerns raised by peer reviewers. In this article we describe a course module that introduces MSc students at Utrecht University in the Netherlands to this part of the publication process. During the module the students and an invited speaker actively discuss the revision process for a recent article by the speaker. Feedback from students and speakers on the module – which could be readily transferred to other courses in the life and biomedical sciences – has been largely positive.

title: Uncovering shared and tissue-specific molecular adaptations to intermittent fasting in liver, brain, and muscle
abstract: Intermittent fasting (IF) has emerged as a powerful dietary intervention with profound metabolic benefits, yet the tissue-specific molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly understood. In this study, we employed comprehensive proteomics and transcriptomics analysis to investigate the systemic and organ-specific adaptations to IF in male C57BL/6 mice. Following a 16 hr daily fasting regimen (IF16) over 4 months, IF reduced blood glucose, HbA1c, and cholesterol levels while increasing ketone bodies, indicative of enhanced metabolic flexibility. Proteomic profiling of the liver, skeletal muscle, and cerebral cortex revealed tissue-specific responses, with the liver exhibiting the most pronounced changes, including upregulation of pathways involved in fatty acid oxidation, ketogenesis, and glycan degradation, and downregulation of steroid hormone and cholesterol metabolism. In muscle, IF enhanced pyruvate metabolism, fatty acid biosynthesis, and AMPK signaling, while suppressing oxidative phosphorylation and thermogenesis. The cerebral cortex displayed unique adaptations, with upregulation of autophagy, PPAR signaling, and metabolic pathways, and downregulation of TGF-beta and p53 signaling, suggesting a shift toward energy conservation and stress resilience. Notably, Serpin A1c emerged as the only protein commonly upregulated across all three tissues, highlighting its potential role in systemic adaptation to IF. Integrative transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed partial concordance between mRNA and protein expression, underscoring the complexity of post-transcriptional regulation. Shared biological signaling processes were identified across tissues, suggesting unifying mechanisms linking metabolic changes to cellular communication. Our findings reveal both conserved and tissue-specific responses by which IF may optimize energy utilization, enhance metabolic flexibility, and promote cellular resilience.

title: Global molecular landscape of early MASLD progression in human obesity
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is often asymptomatic early on but can progress to irreversible conditions like cirrhosis. Due to limited access to human liver biopsies, systematic and integrative molecular resources remain scarce. In this study, we performed transcriptomic analyses on liver and metabolomic analyses on liver and plasma samples from morbidly obese individuals without liver pathology or at early-stage MASLD. While the plasma metabolomic profile did not fully mirror liver histological features, dual-omics integration of liver samples revealed significantly remodeled lipid and amino acid metabolism pathways. Integrative network analysis uncoupled metabolic remodeling and gene expression as independent features of hepatic steatosis and fibrosis progression, respectively. Notably, GTPases and their regulators emerged as a novel class of genes linked to early liver fibrosis. This study offers a detailed molecular landscape of early MASLD in obesity and highlights potential targets of obesity-linked liver fibrosis.

title: Sperm motility in mice with oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia restored by in vivo injection and electroporation of naked mRNA
abstract: Oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia (OAT), a recurrent cause of male infertility, is the most frequent disorder of spermatogenesis with a predominantly genetic origin. Patients and mice bearing mutations in the ARMC2 gene exhibit reduced sperm concentration, multiple morphological defects, and impaired motility, defining a canonical OAT phenotype. Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is required to treat this condition; however, it is associated with a slightly increased risk of birth defects compared with natural conception, highlighting the need for novel targeted therapies. Here, in vivo testicular injection followed by electroporation of capped, polyadenylated naked messenger RNA (mRNA) was evaluated as a strategy to treat ARMC2 -related infertility in mice. mRNAs encoding reporter proteins were used to assess expression efficiency and kinetics using in vivo and in vitro 2D and 3D imaging. Reporter proteins were detected in germ cells for up to three weeks, demonstrating the feasibility of mRNA-based approaches. These results were compared with a non-integrative plasmid Enhanced Episomal Vector, which induced weak and transient expression in spermatogenic cells. Delivery of Armc2 mRNA restored morphologically normal and motile sperm in deficient males, capable of producing embryos via in vitro fertilization and ICSI. These findings provide proof-of-concept that mRNA electroporation can restore sperm motility and fertilizing potential, offering a novel strategy to correct monogenic male infertility.

title: Single transcript level atlas of oxytocin and the oxytocin receptor in the mouse brain
abstract: Oxytocin (OXT), a primitive nonapeptide known to regulate reproduction and social behaviors, is synthesized primarily in the hypothalamus and is secreted via the hypophyseal-portal system of the posterior pituitary gland. In line with the premise that pituitary hormones, traditionally thought of as regulators of single targets, display an array of central and peripheral actions, we found that OXT directly affects bone and body composition. The effect of OXT on bone remodeling is physiologically relevant, as elevated OXT levels during pregnancy and lactation cause calcium mobilization from the maternal skeleton for intergenerational calcium transfer towards fetal bone mineralization. There is an equally large body of evidence that has established the presence of OXT receptors (OXTRs) in the brain through which central functions, such as social bonding, and peripheral functions, such as the regulation of body composition, are exerted. To purposefully address effects of OXT on the brain, we used RNAscope to map OXT and OXTR expression, at the single transcript level, in the whole female and male mouse brains. Identification of brain nuclei with the highest OXT and OXTR transcript density sheds further light on functional OXT nodes that could be further interrogated experimentally to define new physiologic circuitry.

title: Gender differences in submission behavior exacerbate publication disparities in elite journals
abstract: Women are particularly underrepresented as leading authors of papers in journals of the highest impact factor, with substantial consequences for their careers. While a large body of research has focused on the outcome and the process of peer review, fewer articles have explicitly focused on gendered submission behavior and the explanations for these differences. In our study of nearly 5000 active authors, we find that women are less likely to report having submitted papers to journals of the highest impact (e.g., Science , Nature , or PNAS ) and to submit fewer manuscripts, on average, than men when they do submit. Women were more likely to indicate that they did not submit their papers (in general and their subsequently most cited papers) to high-impact journals because they were advised not to. In the aggregate, no statistically significant difference was observed between men and women in how they rated the quality of their work. Nevertheless, regardless of discipline, women were more likely than men to indicate that their ‘ work was not ground-breaking or sufficiently novel ’ as a rationale for not submitting to one of the listed prestigious journals. Men were more likely than women to indicate that the ‘ work would fit better in a more specialized journal ’ . We discuss the implications of these findings and interventions that can serve to mitigate the disparities caused by gendered differences in submission behavior.

title: A titin missense variant drives atrial electrical remodeling and is associated with atrial fibrillation
abstract: Rare and common genetic variants contribute to the risk of atrial fibrillation (AF). Although ion channels were among the first AF candidate genes identified, rare loss-of-function variants in structural genes, such as TTN , have also been implicated in AF pathogenesis, partly through the development of atrial myopathy; however, the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. While TTN truncating variants ( TTN tvs) have been causally linked to arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy syndromes, the role of missense variants (mvs) remains unclear. We show that rare TTNmvs are associated with worse clinical outcomes in a single-center ethnic minority clinical cohort and uncover a pathogenic mechanism by which the T32756I variant drives AF. Modeling the TTN -T32756I variant using human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived atrial cardiomyocytes (iPSC-aCMs) revealed that the mutant cells display aberrant contractility, increased activity of a cardiac potassium channel (KCNQ1, Kv7.1), and dysregulated calcium homeostasis without compromising the sarcomeric integrity of the atrial cardiomyocytes. We also show that a titin-binding protein, the Four-and-a-Half Lim domains 2 (FHL2), has increased binding with KCNQ1 and its modulatory subunit KCNE1 in the TTN- T32756I-iPSC-aCMs, enhancing the slow delayed rectifier potassium current ( I ks ). Suppression of FHL2 in mutant iPSC-aCMs normalized the I ks , supporting FHL2 as an I ks modulator. Our findings demonstrate that a single amino acid substitution in titin not only impairs its function but also remodels ion channels, contributing to AF. These findings underscore the importance of high-throughput screening to assess the pathogenicity of TTN mvs and establish a mechanistic connection between titin, potassium ion channels, and sarcomeric proteins, which may represent a novel therapeutic target.

title: Dual-modal metabolic analysis reveals hypothermia-reversible uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation in neonatal brain hypoxia-ischemia
abstract: Hypoxia-ischemia (HI), which disrupts the oxygen supply-demand balance in the brain by impairing blood oxygen supply and the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO 2 ), is a leading cause of neonatal brain injury. However, it is unclear how post-HI hypothermia helps to restore the balance, as cooling reduces CMRO 2 . Also, how transient HI leads to secondary energy failure (SEF) in neonatal brains remains elusive. Using photoacoustic microscopy, we examined the effects of HI on CMRO 2 in awake 10-day-old mice, supplemented by bioenergetic analysis of purified cortical mitochondria. Our results show that while HI suppresses ipsilateral CMRO 2 , it sparks a prolonged CMRO 2 -surge post-HI, associated with increased mitochondrial oxygen consumption, superoxide emission, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential necessary for ATP synthesis—indicating oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) uncoupling. Post-HI hypothermia prevents the CMRO 2 -surge by constraining oxygen extraction fraction, reduces mitochondrial oxidative stress, and maintains ATP and N-acetylaspartate levels, resulting in attenuated infarction at 24 hr post-HI. Our findings suggest that OXPHOS-uncoupling induced by the post-HI CMRO 2 -surge underlies SEF and blocking the surge is a key mechanism of hypothermia protection. Also, our study highlights the potential of optical CMRO 2 measurements for detecting neonatal HI brain injury and guiding the titration of therapeutic hypothermia at the bedside.

title: Are peer reviewers influenced by their work being cited?
abstract: Peer reviewers sometimes comment that their own journal articles should be cited by the journal article under review. Comments concerning relevant articles can be justified, but comments can also be unrelated coercive citations. Here, we used a matched observational study design to explore how citations influence the peer review process. We used a sample of more than 37,000 peer reviews from four journals that use open peer review and make all article versions available. We find that reviewers who were cited in versions after version 1 were more likely to make a favourable recommendation (odds ratio = 1.61; adjusted 99.4% CI: 1.16–2.23), whereas being cited in the first version did not improve their recommendation (odds ratio = 0.84; adjusted 99.4% CI: 0.69–1.03). For all versions of the articles, the reviewers who commented that their own articles should be cited were less likely to recommend approval compared to the reviewers who did not, with the strongest association after the first version (odds ratio = 0.15; adjusted 99.4% CI: 0.08–0.30). Reviewers who included a citation to their own articles were much more likely to approve a revised article that cited their articles compared to a revised article that did not (odds ratio = 3.5; 95% CI: 2.0–6.1). Some reviewers’ recommendations depend on whether they are cited or want to be cited. Reviewer citation requests can turn peer review into a transaction rather than an objective critique of the article.

title: GPR30 in spinal cholecystokinin-positive neurons modulates neuropathic pain
abstract: Neuropathic pain, a major health problem affecting 7–10% of the global population, lacks effective treatment due to its elusive mechanisms. Cholecystokinin-positive (CCK + ) neurons in the spinal dorsal horn (SDH) are critical for neuropathic pain, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that the membrane estrogen receptor G-protein coupled estrogen receptor (GPER/GPR30) in spinal neurons was significantly upregulated in chronic constriction injury (CCI) mice and that inhibition of GPR30 in CCK + neurons reversed CCI-induced neuropathic pain. Furthermore, GPR30 in spinal CCK + neurons was essential for the enhancement of AMPA-mediated excitatory synaptic transmission in CCI mice. Moreover, GPR30 was expressed in spinal CCK + neurons that received direct projection from the primary sensory cortex (S1-SDH). Chemogenetic inhibition of S1-SDH post-synaptic neurons alleviated CCI-induced neuropathic pain. Conversely, chemogenetic activation of these neurons mimicked neuropathic pain symptoms, which were attenuated by spinal inhibition of GPR30. Finally, we confirmed that GPR30 in S1-SDH post-synaptic neurons was required for CCI-induced neuropathic pain. Taken together, our findings suggest that GPR30 in spinal CCK + neurons and S1-SDH post-synaptic neurons is pivotal for neuropathic pain, thereby representing a promising therapeutic target for neuropathic pain.

title: Addressing cultural and knowledge barriers to enable preclinical sex inclusive research
abstract: For over 30 years, research has highlighted a sex bias in early research, risking the validity of biological knowledge. The first step towards change is effectively challenging misconceptions, allowing researchers to perceive sex inclusive research as doable. Utilising the theory of planned behaviour, we quantified researchers’ intention as a proxy measure for conducting sex inclusive research and explored attitude (value of the behaviour), subjective norm (perceived social pressure), and behavioural control (ability to conduct the behaviour). Additionally, we quantified the knowledge gap, prevalence of misconceptions, and assessed perceived benefits and barriers. We tested a workshop intervention that directly challenges the cultural embedded barriers. The data shows researchers’ intentions were high, but they had weak statistical knowledge and misunderstandings leading to a perception that inclusive research is prohibitive due to cost and animal use. We demonstrate that participation in the training intervention improved knowledge, altered the perceived barriers, and cultural expectations.

title: The denitrosylase SCoR2 controls cardioprotective metabolic reprogramming
abstract: Acute myocardial infarction (MI) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, and therapeutic options remain limited. Endogenously generated nitric oxide (NO) is highly cardioprotective, but protection is not replicated by nitroso-vasodilators (e.g., nitrates, nitroprusside) used in clinical practice, highlighting specificity in NO-based signaling and untapped therapeutic potential. Signaling by NO is mediated largely by S -nitrosylation, entailing specific enzymes that form and degrade S -nitrosothiols in proteins (SNO-proteins), termed nitrosylases and denitrosylases, respectively. SNO-CoA Reductase 2 (SCoR2; product of the Akr1a1 gene) is a recently discovered protein denitrosylase. Genetic variants in SCoR2 have been associated with cardiovascular disease, but its function is unknown. Here, we show that mice lacking SCoR2/AKR1A1 exhibit robust protection in an animal model of MI. SCoR2 regulates ketolytic energy availability, antioxidant levels, and polyol homeostasis via S -nitrosylation of key metabolic effectors. Human cardiomyopathy shows reduced SCoR2 expression and an S -nitrosylation signature of metabolic reprogramming, mirroring SCoR2 −/− mice. Deletion of SCoR2 thus coordinately reprograms multiple metabolic pathways—ketone body utilization, glycolysis, pentose phosphate shunt, and polyol metabolism—to limit infarct size, establishing SCoR2 as a novel regulator in the injured myocardium and a potential drug target.

title: Cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous effects of Arginase 2 on cardiac aging
abstract: Aging is a predominant risk factor for heart disease. Aging heart reveals low-grade chronic inflammation, cell apoptosis, cardiac fibrosis, and increased vulnerability to ischemic injury. The underlying molecular mechanisms responsible for cardiac aging and its susceptibility to injury are not fully understood. Although literature reports a role for mitochondrial Arginase 2 (ARG2) in heart failure, contradictory results are reported. How ARG2 participates in cardiac aging is still unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that Arg2 is not expressed in cardiomyocytes from aged mice and humans but is upregulated in non-myocyte cells, including macrophages, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. Mice with genetic deficiency of Arg2 ( Arg2 -/- ) are protected from age-associated cardiac inflammation, myocyte apoptosis, interstitial and perivascular fibrosis, endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndMT), and susceptibility to ischemic injury. Further experiments show that ARG2 mediates IL-1β release from macrophages of old mice, contributing to the cardiac aging phenotype. In addition, ARG2 enhances mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and activates cardiac fibroblasts that is inhibited by inhibition of mtROS. Thus, our study demonstrates a non-cell-autonomous effect of ARG2 on cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells mediated by IL-1β from aging macrophages as well as a cell-autonomous effect of ARG2 through mtROS in fibroblasts contributing to cardiac aging phenotype.

abstract: We’ve implemented initial support for plugins in ChatGPT. Plugins are tools designed specifically for language models with safety as a core principle, and help ChatGPT access up-to-date information, run computations, or use third-party services.

title: GPT-4
abstract: We’ve created GPT-4, the latest milestone in OpenAI’s effort in scaling up deep learning. GPT-4 is a large multimodal model (accepting image and text inputs, emitting text outputs) that, while less capable than humans in many real-world scenarios, exhibits human-level performance on various professional and academic benchmarks.

title: Transforming visual accessibility
abstract: Be My Eyes uses GPT-4 to transform visual accessibility.

title: Planning for AGI and beyond
abstract: Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence—AI systems that are generally smarter than humans—benefits all of humanity.

abstract: We’re clarifying how ChatGPT’s behavior is shaped and our plans for improving that behavior, allowing more user customization, and getting more public input into our decision-making in these areas.

title: Forecasting potential misuses of language models for disinformation campaigns and how to reduce risk
abstract: OpenAI researchers collaborated with Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology and the Stanford Internet Observatory to investigate how large language models might be misused for disinformation purposes. The collaboration included an October 2021 workshop bringing together 30 disinformation researchers, machine learning experts, and policy analysts, and culminated in a co-authored report building on more than a year of research. This report outlines the threats that language models pose to the information environment if used to augment disinformation campaigns and introduces a framework for analyzing potential mitigations. Read the full report here.

title: Delivering nuanced insights from customer feedback
abstract: Using GPT-3 to deliver fast, nuanced insights from customer feedback.

abstract: Extend creativity and tell a bigger story with DALL·E images of any size.

abstract: We are improving our AI systems’ ability to learn from human feedback and to assist humans at evaluating AI. Our goal is to build a sufficiently aligned AI system that can help us solve all other alignment problems.

abstract: We are introducing a new and improved content moderation tool. The Moderation endpoint improves upon our previous content filter, and is available for free today to OpenAI API developers.

DALL·E now available in beta
abstract: We’ll invite 1 million people from our waitlist over the coming weeks. Users can create with DALL·E using free credits that refill every month, and buy additional credits in 115-generation increments for $15.

title: Reducing bias and improving safety in DALL·E 2
abstract: Today, we are implementing a new technique so that DALL·E generates images of people that more accurately reflect the diversity of the world’s population.

title: DALL·E 2: Extending creativity
abstract: As part of our DALL·E 2 research preview, more than 3,000 artists from more than 118 countries have incorporated DALL·E into their creative workflows. The artists in our early access group have helped us discover new uses for DALL·E and have served as key voices as we’ve made decisions about DALL·E’s features.

title: DALL·E 2 pre-training mitigations
abstract: In order to share the magic of DALL·E 2 with a broad audience, we needed to reduce the risks associated with powerful image generation models. To this end, we put various guardrails in place to prevent generated images from violating our content policy.

title: Learning to play Minecraft with Video PreTraining
abstract: We trained a neural network to play Minecraft by Video PreTraining (VPT) on a massive unlabeled video dataset of human Minecraft play, while using only a small amount of labeled contractor data. With fine-tuning, our model can learn to craft diamond tools, a task that usually takes proficient humans over 20 minutes (24,000 actions). Our model uses the native human interface of keypresses and mouse movements, making it quite general, and represents a step towards general computer-using agents.

title: Evolution through large models
AI-written critiques help humans notice flaws
abstract: We trained “critique-writing” models to describe flaws in summaries. Human evaluators find flaws in summaries much more often when shown our model’s critiques. Larger models are better at self-critiquing, with scale improving critique-writing more than summary-writing. This shows promise for using AI systems to assist human supervision of AI systems on difficult tasks.

title: Techniques for training large neural networks
abstract: Large neural networks are at the core of many recent advances in AI, but training them is a difficult engineering and research challenge which requires orchestrating a cluster of GPUs to perform a single synchronized calculation.

title: Best practices for deploying language models
abstract: Cohere, OpenAI, and AI21 Labs have developed a preliminary set of best practices applicable to any organization developing or deploying large language models.

title: Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
Powering next generation applications with OpenAI Codex
abstract: Codex is now powering 70 different applications across a variety of use cases through the OpenAI API.

title: DALL·E 2 research preview update
abstract: Early users have created over 3 million images to date and helped us improve our safety processes. We’re excited to begin adding up to 1,000 new users from our waitlist each week.

title: OpenAI leadership team update
abstract: We’re happy to announce several executive role changes that reflect our recent progress and will ensure continued momentum toward our next major milestones.

Measuring Goodhart’s law
abstract: Goodhart’s law famously says: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” Although originally from economics, it’s something we have to grapple with at OpenAI when figuring out how to optimize objectives that are difficult or costly to measure.

title: New GPT-3 capabilities: Edit & insert
abstract: We’ve released new versions of GPT-3 and Codex which can edit or insert content into existing text, rather than just completing existing text.

abstract: We describe our latest thinking in the hope of helping other AI developers address safety and misuse of deployed models.

title: Solving (some) formal math olympiad problems
abstract: We built a neural theorem prover for Lean that learned to solve a variety of challenging high-school olympiad problems, including problems from the AMC12 and AIME competitions, as well as two problems adapted from the IMO.

title: Aligning language models to follow instructions
abstract: We’ve trained language models that are much better at following user intentions than GPT-3 while also making them more truthful and less toxic, using techniques developed through our alignment research. These InstructGPT models, which are trained with humans in the loop, are now deployed as the default language models on our API.

title: Introducing text and code embeddings
abstract: We are introducing embeddings, a new endpoint in the OpenAI API that makes it easy to perform natural language and code tasks like semantic search, clustering, topic modeling, and classification.

title: Text and code embeddings by contrastive pre-training
WebGPT: Improving the factual accuracy of language models through web browsing

title: Solving math word problems
abstract: We’ve trained a system that solves grade school math problems with nearly twice the accuracy of a fine-tuned GPT-3 model. It solves about 90% as many problems as real kids: a small sample of 9-12 year olds scored 60% on a test from our dataset, while our system scored 55% on those same problems.

OpenAI Codex

title: Introducing Triton: Open-source GPU programming for neural networks
abstract: We’re releasing Triton 1.0, an open-source Python-like programming language which enables researchers with no CUDA experience to write highly efficient GPU code—most of the time on par with what an expert would be able to produce.

title: Evaluating large language models trained on code
Improving language model behavior by training on a curated dataset

title: Will Hurd joins OpenAI’s board of directors
abstract: OpenAI is committed to developing general-purpose artificial intelligence that benefits all humanity, and we believe that achieving our goal requires expertise in public policy as well as technology. So, we’re delighted to announce that Congressman Will Hurd has joined our board of directors.

title: GPT-3 powers the next generation of apps
abstract: Over 300 applications are delivering GPT-3–powered search, conversation, text completion, and other advanced AI features through our API.

title: Multimodal neurons in artificial neural networks
abstract: We’ve discovered neurons in CLIP that respond to the same concept whether presented literally, symbolically, or conceptually. This may explain CLIP’s accuracy in classifying surprising visual renditions of concepts, and is also an important step toward understanding the associations and biases that CLIP and similar models learn.

title: Understanding the capabilities, limitations, and societal impact of large language models
Scaling Kubernetes to 7,500 nodes
abstract: We’ve scaled Kubernetes clusters to 7,500 nodes, producing a scalable infrastructure for large models like GPT-3, CLIP, and DALL·E, but also for rapid small-scale iterative research such as Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.

title: DALL·E: Creating images from text
abstract: We’ve trained a neural network called DALL·E that creates images from text captions for a wide range of concepts expressible in natural language.

title: CLIP: Connecting text and images
abstract: We’re introducing a neural network called CLIP which efficiently learns visual concepts from natural language supervision. CLIP can be applied to any visual classification benchmark by simply providing the names of the visual categories to be recognized, similar to the “zero-shot” capabilities of GPT-2 and GPT-3.
