authors: ["Xiong, Y., Tirta, Y. K., Wang, S., Hu, Z., Ma, W., Yuan, S."]

title: Asking the Data: Conversational Interrogation of LC-MS/MS Proteomics Data Sets with an LLM Agent
abstract: Proteomics workflows are designed to answer predefined questions, leaving analytical problems that emerge after first results difficult to investigate without additional bioinformatics work. We introduce data set interrogation, a conversational framework in which a researcher uses a large language model (LLM) agent to translate emerging questions into executable tests, check the answers against controls, and keep the code, inputs, and decisions in a dated record. Applied retrospectively to four LC-MS/MS data sets, the framework exposed problems that changed the interpretation of three in-house studies: a search database lacking one of two symbionts, a swapped pair of tandem mass tag (TMT) channels, statistics inflated by non-host proteins, and false deamidation assignments caused by selection of the 13C isotope peak as monoisotopic; the same question asked of every data set revealed failed or partial cysteine alkylation in all three. A public TMT data set was reanalyzed from raw files in 24 min, a feasibility measure without a human comparison; among spectra identified by both workflows, 99.2% received the same peptide assignment as in Proteome Discoverer, and protein fold changes correlated (r = 0.93). In seeded tests, a purpose built channel assignment check detected all 216 between strain channel swaps and none of 90 within-strain swaps. The framework couples natural language interaction with executable analyses, explicit controls, and traceable decisions, enabling researchers to investigate questions not anticipated by the original pipeline. These results establish feasibility in a limited retrospective setting with one researcher; broader evaluation across users, models, and data sets is required to determine general performance.
authors: ["da Silva de Araujo, C., Keirsebelik, M., Silas Rodrigues, A. C., Leda Valverde, A., Maciel-de-Freitas, R. d. S., Guimaraes, M. Z. P., Junqueira, M."]

title: Integrative Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Explainable AI for Disease Mechanism and Biomarker Discovery in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
abstract: Invasion is an early step in the metastatic spread of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet cells within a single tumour or cell line differ in their capacity to invade, and it is unclear which transcriptional features distinguish cells that invade from those that do not. We re-analysed the public single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset GSE329526, in which ClonMapper-barcoded MDA-MB-231 cells were separated in a transwell assay into invasive (five samples, 6,289 cells) and non-invasive (five samples, 5,983 cells) fractions and compared with the parental population (one sample, 3,022 cells). An initial cell-level analysis combined Wilcoxon differential expression, an XGBoost classifier with a random cell split, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Enrichr over-representation analysis. Because cells from the same sample are not independent, we then repeated the analysis at the sample level, using differential expression on sample means (five versus five), XGBoost with cross-validation that held out whole samples, a quality-control-metric baseline model, SHAP on held-out samples and rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA). At the sample level, 6,651 of 11,727 tested genes differed between invasive and non-invasive samples (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05), including the ten top-ranked cell-level genes such as PHLDA2, ANTXR2, VIM and HMGA1 (FDR 0.0007 to 0.0022) and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) regulators TGFBR2, JAG1, SDCBP and WWTR1. With whole samples held out, XGBoost distinguished invasive from non-invasive cells with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.92 (range across folds 0.89 to 0.95); removing ribosomal and mitochondrial genes did not change performance (AUC 0.92), whereas a model using only four quality-control metrics reached 0.63, and every held-out invasive sample received a higher mean predicted probability of invasion (0.74 to 0.79) than every non-invasive sample (0.20 to 0.28). On held-out samples, SHAP ranked inflammatory and stress-response genes highest (CCL2, LGALS12, DUSP1, CXCL3, KYNU, CXCL2), and GSEA showed higher KRAS signalling (normalised enrichment score [NES] 2.30, FDR 0.001) and E2F targets (NES 1.62, FDR 0.038) and lower interferon-alpha and interferon-gamma responses (NES -1.97 and -1.65; FDR 0.001 and 0.019) in invasive samples. The ribosomal genes that dominated the original SHAP ranking were absent from the held-out ranking. Invasive MDA-MB-231 cells therefore carry a transcriptional state that is reproducible across independent transwell samples and involves EMT-related, inflammatory and proliferative programmes. Limitations include a single cell line, sequencing of the invasive and non-invasive populations in separate libraries and the absence of external validation; the candidate genes reported here are hypotheses that require confirmation in independent experiments and patient material.
authors: ["Huda, T., BISWAS, S."]

title: Best Practices for Pre-Processing Large-Scale ATAC-Seq Data: Why Epidemiological Studies Demand Greater Stringency
abstract: Assay for transposase accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) and related techniques provide critical insight into the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate gene expression in health and disease. Accurate identification of biologically meaningful chromatin accessibility signals remains an underexplored analytical challenge. Advances in sequencing technologies have increased both the magnitude and complexity of ATAC-seq datasets, leading to demand for scalable, reproducible and robust computational analysis frameworks. Peak calling, which identifies regions of chromatin accessibility, is a critical step that underpins all downstream quantitative analyses. However, there is a lack of consensus regarding the optimal peak calling strategy. Here, we present a novel bioinformatics pipeline PIPPA (Pipeline for Integrative Peak calling in Population-scale ATAC-seq), for quality control and peak set curation of large-scale ATAC-seq datasets. Using two independent cell-type sorted ATAC-seq datasets, we show that peak calling performance is dataset-dependent and that no single significance threshold performs optimally across all scenarios. We provide practical recommendations for parameters to generate high-confidence chromatin accessibility profiles. Our peak calling approach is applicable for other genome wide epigenomic assays such as ChIP-seq and CUT&Tag. By standardising this process, the PIPPA pipeline enhances epidemiological studies focused in identifying epigenetic dysregulation associated with development and disease.
authors: ["Wells, P. M., Flores-Payan, M., Chioza, B., Burrage, J., Babtie, A., Marzi, S. J., Schalkwyk, L. C., YouthGEMS Consortium,, Dempster, E., Mill, J., Hannon, E. J."]

title: BenchMHC: a reproducible framework for peptide-MHC presentation prediction
abstract: Predicting which peptides an MHC molecule presents is the first step in neoantigen and epitope discovery pipelines. Most published predictors are released for inference only, and each is trained on a different dataset, so the effect of a new method cannot be separated from the effect of its training data. We present BenchMHC, an open framework that reproduces, retrains and evaluates pMHC presentation models on public data only, and that records every implementation decision made in a reproduction. Our NetMHCpan-4.1 reproduction reaches 0.794 per-allele Mean Top-K against 0.790 for the official webserver, and 0.0025 Median FRANK against 0.0022. It scores 280,000 peptide/allele pairs in 27 s, about 350 times faster than the original binary. We then examine the training data. In the public NetMHCpan-4.1 eluted-ligand sets, 86 to 99% of hits are found in the human proteome, against about 12% of their decoys, so a model can separate hits from decoys using this difference rather than features related to MHC binding. Redrawing the decoys within the source protein of each hit and matching their cysteine status, with no other change, raises per-allele Mean Top-K on the regenerated v2.0.0 evaluation set from 0.734 to 0.755, and increases Median FRANK on CD8 epitopes from 0.0025 to 0.0053. The same change improves one evaluation set and degrades the other. Code (Apache-2.0) and model checkpoints (CC BY-NC-4.0): https://github.com/instadeepai/BenchMHC-public.
authors: ["Borck, T., Chabrol, M., Colombo, D., Imbert, A., Perier-Dulhoste, M., Volzhenin, K., Lang, M., Lopez Carranza, S. N."]

title: How Much Can AI Virtual Cells Gain from Unified Perturbational Modeling?
abstract: Predicting how individual cells respond to perturbations is a central task in artificial intelligence virtual cell (AIVC) modeling. However, integrating perturbation datasets is challenging because they differ in measured gene sets, perturbation types and cellular contexts. Existing AIVC predictors are typically developed for specific settings, limiting their applicability across heterogeneous datasets. Here, we investigate the extent to which AIVC predictors can benefit from unified perturbational modeling (UPM), a novel paradigm designed to integrate heterogeneous Perturb-seq datasets into a single predictive model. To this end, we introduce three unification modules into a variational autoencoder (VAE)-based AIVC predictor to address these sources of heterogeneity: gene-channel alignment, shared perturbation encoding, and joint embedding of gene expression and identity. We systematically evaluate and validate the individual contributions of these modules. Building on UPM, we assemble a dataset of 110 million cells spanning over 22,000 genes, four perturbation types and 76 cellular contexts, and use 89.7 million cells from 71 contexts to train a unified AIVC predictor with more than one billion parameters. Across genetic perturbation benchmarks, UPM achieves the highest PES and gene-wise response correlation among the evaluated models. It also improves all four evaluation metrics over State on the five held-out Tahoe-100M cell lines and over Stack on the cytokine benchmark. UPM also improves combinatorial perturbation prediction relative to specialized predictors. In the HSC application, our model achieves a 40.0% improvement in accuracy on a downstream task involving the recapitulation of effects induced by the knockdown of hepatic stellate cell (HSC)-related targets. Our implementation is openly available at https://github.com/youlab2025/UPM.
authors: ["Wei, Z., Ye, Y., Cui, S., Ma, W., You, Y."]

title: ProtCell: a foundation model for single-cell proteomics
abstract: Single-cell proteomics provides a direct functional readout of cellular states, but targeted assays measure limited and non-identical protein panels, fragmenting information across experiments. Here, we present ProtCell, a foundation model developed using approximately 380 million cells from 98 datasets for pretraining and evaluation. ProtCell combines protein-identity and continuous-abundance embeddings in a transformer encoder and learns cell- and protein-level representations through masked abundance modeling. ProtCell first connects fragmented profiles through transferable annotation and batch correction while preserving biological organization. It then extends limited profiles through abundance reconstruction and inference of an unmeasured cytotoxic protein program enriched in natural killer cells and memory CD8$^+$ T cells. The learned protein dependencies further guide the selection of compact panels that retain information for profile reconstruction and biological classification. ProtCell thus provides a framework for connecting fragmented proteomic profiles, extending information beyond measured panels and guiding more informative measurements.
authors: ["Hu, B., Li, Z., Jiang, Q., Yin, Q., Liu, Z., Jiang, R."]

title: Metric-driven Pre-acquisition Diagnostics for Automated Microscopy Ultraviolet Surface Excitation (MUSE)
abstract: Background Automated microscopy enables large-scale tiled imaging but remains sensitive to variations in alignment, illumination, focus, and sample coverage that may only be detected after acquisition. We present an adaptive pre-acquisition quality-control framework for microscopy ultraviolet surface excitation (MUSE) that uses sparse scout imaging and tile-level metrics to guide acquisition and selective rescanning. Methods The framework quantifies brightness, dynamic range, focus, tissue fraction, and exposure error across the field of view. For example, in a representative 10 x 10 acquisition (100 tiles, 20-megapixel imagery), the mean p99 brightness was 0.525 (CV 10.4%), the mean dynamic range was 0.331, the median focus score was 0.0333, and the median tissue fraction was 0.943. Furthermore, applying a conservative exposure-error threshold (|error| > 0.25) identified 25% of tiles as rescan candidates. Results These results show that compact tile-level metrics can be converted into actionable quality gates, enabling early detection of local acquisition errors and targeted rescanning to improve mosaic consistency while minimizing unnecessary acquisition.
authors: ["Nunez, M., Davies, B."]

title: CATFISHR: integration of transcriptome and inferred CNV profiles for comprehensive malignant cell identification
abstract: Malignant cell identification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) remains challenging because transcriptomic cell typing, somatic variant detection and inferred copy-number approaches each have modality-specific limitations. Rare or ambiguous malignant populations are especially vulnerable to misclassification or exclusion, despite their relevance to treatment resistance, minimal residual disease, and metastasis. We developed CATFISHR, a semi-automated workflow that integrates RNA-expression similarity, inferred copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and consensus cell typing to classify malignant cells relative to high-confidence references. CATFISHR was evaluated across eight cohorts, including seven scRNA-seq datasets spanning multiple carcinomas and melanoma subtypes, and one 10x Visium spatial transcriptomics sample. Compared with available benchmarks or ground truths, CATFISHR achieved balanced accuracy > 0.85 in six of eight cohorts and F1 score > 0.80 in six of eight cohorts. Cells uniquely identified by CATFISHR as malignant ("Hidden" cells) were present in every dataset and were not consistently explained by standard quality-control metrics. In several cohorts, Hidden cells were transcriptionally closer to benchmark malignant than non-malignant compartments; in Visium data, sampled Hidden spots contained histologist-confirmed morphologically malignant cells. CATFISHR reduces missed malignant calls while preserving rare, transitional and benchmark-discordant populations for downstream investigation.
authors: ["Shukla, P., Mannino, M., Hofer, M., Lattmann, E. R., Haunerdinger, V., Turko, P., Levesque, M. P."]

title: MPFIL: Multi-Level Protein Feature Integration for Predicting Mutation-Induced Protein-Protein Binding Affinity Changes
abstract: Predicting mutation-induced changes in protein protein binding affinity ({triangleup}{triangleup}G) is challenging because mutations can affect both local residue environments and the structural organization of protein complexes. Existing approaches often rely on handcrafted physicochemical, energetic, or evolutionary features, which introduce additional computational costs and require domain-specific knowledge. In this work, we propose MPFIL, a multi-level protein feature integration framework for predicting mutation-induced protein-protein binding affin ity changes. MPFIL integrates structural and sequential infor mation to characterize mutation effects from complementary perspectives. Its structural feature extraction module captures mutation-induced structural changes and differential information between wild-type and mutant complexes, while sequence feature extraction modules model local residue context and long-range dependencies. The resulting features are integrated for {triangleup}{triangleup}G prediction. We evaluate MPFIL on three benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate competitive and consistent performance across different protein complex settings, while ablation studies verify the contribution of the structural and sequential features. These results support the effectiveness of multi-level protein feature integration for modeling mutation induced changes in protein-protein binding affinity.
authors: ["Zhang, H., Liu, Y., Yu, L., Guo, M."]

title: Mimic: A Unified Neural Network Architecture for Modelling Genomic Sequences and Module-level Comparison
abstract: There exist a wide range of Neural Networks (NNs) that have modelled genomic sequences well. The architectures of these NNs consist of three steps: k-mer embedding, sequence embedding, and output mapping. The NNs are primarily differentiated from one another by their sequence embedding components. Although different NNs have been compared before, these comparisons are often either limited or involve drastically different NNs. Another issue is that some NNs are configured for a specific sequence length, and different length sequences require manual modification of the architectures. This study examines the architectures of established NNs for genomics sequences. Based on these architectures, a novel NN called Mimic is developed that provides a unified architecture for the principled comparison of NN components. Mimic was used to model two different types of genomic datasets: protein-DNA interactions and enhancer activity. Along with other architecture components, different sequence embedding strategies were tried such as recurrent layers and convolutional layers. It was found that there exist specific NN components that yield significantly better performing models. Furthermore, Mimic significantly outperformed prevailing standard NNs, Bichrom and DeepSTARR, in modelling protein-DNA interactions and enhancer activity, respectively. This study provides a framework for more extensive studies toward a general prescription of NN architecture for modelling genomics data.
authors: ["Abdulnabi, H., Westwood, J. T."]

title: RNA-SpecFlow: RNA-Conditioned Spectral Flow for Histology Synthesis
abstract: RNA-conditioned histology synthesis models the range of tissue appearances compatible with a transcriptomic representation. We present RNA-SpecFlow, a continuous-latent FlowAR architecture that applies molecular conditioning at adjacent-scale feature transitions. A Biological Latent Adapter maps RNA representations into the generator's condition space. A shared spectral fusion module separates aligned features into complementary low- and high-frequency bands, modulates each band independently with RNA, and combines them through residual fusion. The generator uses five latent grids of sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16, with per-scale velocity flow matching and an auxiliary objective for retaining the condition in backbone features. We accompany this architectural specification with an analysis of archived outputs from five TCGA cancer cohorts, including 500 saved real/generated tile pairs. Nuclear analysis yields a concrete measurement finding: increased detection counts can coincide with reduced segmentation agreement. On 12 public images with 303 annotated nuclei, twofold enlargement increases HoVer-Net predictions from 287 to 415 while mean panoptic quality changes from 0.673 to 0.458. Switching analysis pipelines also reverses the direction of real/generated count differences in two cohorts. RNA-SpecFlow provides a design for repeated frequency-specific molecular conditioning, and the accompanying experiments establish the sensitivity of morphology-based evaluation to detector inputs and analysis choices.
authors: ["Liu, Y., He, W."]

title: Xenograft supervision and joint methylation-fragment-end encoding define a reusable molecular scoring layer for cell-free tumor DNA
abstract: Circulating tumor DNA is often scarce in plasma, and regional methylation summaries can obscure informative differences between individual molecules. Here we present ctDNA-BERT, a Transformer that scores individual bisulfite reads without predefined differentially methylated regions by jointly encoding CpG methylation state, nucleotide context and the fragment 3' end. Xenografts provide molecule-level tumor supervision. The resulting frozen scorer supported tumor-fraction estimation in synthetic and patient-derived xenograft mixtures and enriched tumor-concordant methylation and chromatin-accessibility signals in independent hepatocellular carcinoma and stage III pan-cancer plasma without cohort-specific retraining. Features derived from selected reads discriminated stage I cancers from healthy controls in a retrospective cohort of 1,477 specimens, achieving an out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.884. By separating molecular scoring from sample-level inference, ctDNA-BERT provides a reusable read-level scoring layer for cell-free DNA methylation analysis.
authors: ["Zhang, X., Sun, X., Wang, R., Zhao, N., Liu, F., Li, X., Huang, J., Sun, J., Li, H., Lou, S., Wang, H., Zhao, H., Shu, H., Zhen, P., Gu, H., Shi, J., Wang, T., Zhang, F."]

title: BLOOM: Biologically Informed Flow Matching for Transcriptomic Virtual Embryo Modeling
abstract: Constructing a virtual embryo requires a generative representation of how heterogeneous cell populations change across developmental time. Here we introduce BLOOM, a biologically informed framework for conditional generation of developmental cell populations. BLOOM integrates temporal population context with developmental and regulatory priors through conditional flow matching to generate cell-expression distributions at queried stages in either temporal direction. Evaluation spans three mouse single-cell atlases covering prenatal development, visual-cortex maturation and multi-organ endothelial specialization. In comparisons with 22 time-series forecasting baselines, BLOOM ranks first for gene- and cell-expression correlations across all three datasets. Measured-stage evaluations support recovery of developmental expression patterns, population organization and marker-specific temporal relationships. Biological analyses connect these predictions to cell-state identities, gene programmes and regulatory associations. At unmeasured stages, interpolation and autoregressive history and future rollouts extend simulated expression dynamics between and beyond measured timepoints. Analyses of marker genes and temporal descriptors identify candidate differences in the timing of muscle-associated, neural and vascular-specialization programmes. Input-based gene perturbations further probe predicted responses of edited genes and associated molecular programmes across time. Together, BLOOM supports transcriptomic virtual embryo modeling by bridging temporal sampling gaps, exploring extended developmental trajectories and prioritizing gene-dependent hypotheses for experimental investigation.
authors: ["Liang, Z., Li, S., Li, B., Huang, Y., Yu, L."]

title: Analytical performance and clinical usability of a low-cost vaginal swab for sensitive detection of high-risk human papillomavirus [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Cervical cancer remains a global health burden, with >600,000 new cases and 340,000 deaths reported in 2020. To reduce this burden, affordable and scalable human papillomavirus (HPV) diagnostics - ranging from at-home to centralized laboratory testing - are needed. Specimen collection plays a key role in analytical performance, sample integrity/stability, platform compatibility and user comfort. Methods We evaluated the analytical performance and temperature stability of high-risk HPV (hrHPV) plasmid DNA and human cervical cancer cell lines on a low-cost Steripack XpressCollect flocked nylon swab using the Atila ScreenFire HPV risk stratification (RS) assay, the Cepheid Xpert HPV assay, and the Molbio Truenat HPV-HR Plus assay. We assessed the clinical usability among women seeking sexual and reproductive healthcare in New York, New York. Results The Atila ScreenFire HPV RS assay was more sensitive in detection of HPV. We demonstrated statistically improved elution efficiency from the low-cost Steripack XpressCollect flocked nylon swab relative to Copan FLOQSwabs. Additionally, dry-stored flocked nylon swabs preserved sample integrity better than swabs stored in Tris-EDTA buffer over time with varying temperatures. Frozen HPV lysates remained stable for up to three months including during freeze/thaw cycles. Among healthcare provider-collected swabs, 7.5% were HPV positive and among the self-collected swabs, 20% were HPV positive. Of those with self-collected swabs, 97% had no previous self-swabbing experience, 71% preferred self-swabbing to healthcare provider-collected swabbing, 93% found it very easy or easy to self-swab and 100% were willing to provide self-swabbing at follow-up. Conclusion The use of dry-stored, nylon-flocked vaginal swabs paired with platform-agnostic assays, like the Atila ScreenFire HPV RS and other genotyping assay, offers a practical and robust solution for hrHPV genotyping in resource-limited settings. Additionally, self-swabbing using low-cost vaginal swabs was highly accepted and retained equivalent sensitivity, further justifying its widespread use in underserved communities.

title: Characterizing multi-criteria decision analysis, risk stratification, and hotspot analysis methods to optimise health policymaking and evidence translation for medicines in low- and middle-income countries: A scoping review [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Implementing new medicines or health interventions in lower-income and middle-income countries (LMICs) may be complex and challenging, and there is a need for practical structured approaches and tools to support the translation of evidence into practice, including the implementation of evidence-informed interventions and health policy making. Objective This scoping review aimed to characterise three data analytical methodologies - multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), risk stratification, and hotspot analysis - to evaluate their use in guiding the implementation of medicines for human health in LMICs between 2010-2025. Methods Scientific articles were searched in databases PubMed and Scopus following guidelines from the Preferred Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA). Data were extracted in relation to the study aims, geographic scope and scale, author affiliations, disease focus, medicine type (categorised as oral drugs or vaccines), target population, medicine implementation phase, use of templates or tools, and main steps of the methodological process. In addition, grey literature was searched by reviewing conference abstracts, national public health websites and journals. Results From the 4,920 articles screened, a total of 40 articles (MCDA=8, risk stratification= 22, hotspot analysis=10) were included from 28 countries across five global regions, mostly Africa. Most articles focused on communicable infectious diseases, and drugs (oral regimens) and vaccines in the pre-implementation stage at a sub-national level. The processes and techniques used for each analytical method varied widely, limiting comparability. However, common methodological steps were identified and used to construct preliminary templates to summarise the processes involved in applying each methodology and support their potential adaptations for decision-making around medicine implementation. Conclusion These analytical methodologies provide a structured basis for further developing practical templates and decision-support tools to enhance the medicine translation; however, efforts are needed to raise awareness, strengthen capacity, and facilitate greater uptake.

title: Long-acting injectables for global health: drug development considerations and applications in malaria and tuberculosis [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Long-acting injectable (LAI) drug formulations represent a transformative modality in modern therapeutics, delivering medications that maintain therapeutic effects over extended periods. While initially developed to improve patient adherence and acceptability for applications such as hormonal contraception and chronic conditions, including psychiatric disorders, their recent success in HIV treatment and prevention has catalyzed a growing interest in their application to global health priorities. While there are effective oral drug regimens available for tuberculosis (TB) treatment and malaria chemoprevention, their dosing regimens challenge patient adherence. By providing sustained pharmacological activity over extended periods, LAIs decouple therapeutic efficacy from patient adherence and simplify drug dosing regimens, enhancing real-world effectiveness. This position paper synthesizes the emerging consensus on the application of LAIs for global health from a multidisciplinary expert workshop convened by Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) and the Gates Foundation in Chicago on March 17–19, 2026. Contributions considered compound selection, formulation design, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic requirements, safety and tolerability profiles, toxicology packages for first-in-human studies, regulatory pathways, and the challenges of human dose prediction. Emphasis was placed on the importance of preclinical-to-clinical translation, particularly through the application of pharmacometric tools and model-informed drug development. The workshop highlighted strategic priorities for advancing the LAI field, including coordinated cross-sector approaches, pre-competitive data sharing, and communities of practice to address critical knowledge gaps. These actions aim to realize the potential for expanding LAI technologies to advance global health.

title: Case Report: Conducting Clinical Trials during an Outbreak: An Mpox case report [version 2; peer review: 2 approved with reservations]
abstract: Background Conducting clinical trials during infectious disease outbreaks presents operational, ethical, and methodological challenges. During the 2024–2025 Mpox outbreak in Uganda, an Mpox case occurred within an HIV-focused clinical trial requiring immediate operational and ethical response. The trial aimed to assess the feasibility of therapeutic drug monitoring and optimize antimicrobial therapy in people living with HIV. Case presentation We report the case of an adult man living with HIV enrolled in the Therapeutic Drug Monitoring for Antimicrobial Agents for People Living with HIV (TAP) trial at a tertiary HIV clinic in Uganda. Following initiation of antimicrobial therapy and study enrolment, at a scheduled study follow-up visit, he developed a vesiculopustular rash involving the face and upper limbs. Research staff promptly activated infection prevention and control measures, halted study procedures, and notified the national surveillance team. Mpox infection was confirmed by real-time polymerase chain reaction testing. The participant was transferred to a designated isolation facility for clinical management and withdrawn from the trial. Continuity of HIV care was maintained through remote (phone) adherence counselling and coordination of antiretroviral refills. No secondary cases were identified among study participants or personnel after 21 days of self-monitoring. Conclusions This report highlights the importance of outbreak preparedness, adaptive risk management, and rapid coordination with public health teams to safeguard participants and personnel, protect research integrity, and ensure continuity of essential clinical care during epidemics.

title: Using Generative AI for Behavioural Research Effectively and Responsibly: a BR-UK Statement [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the behavioural research lifecycle. It may improve the efficiency and quality of research, but rapid, uncritical adoption carries risks to research integrity: algorithmic bias, ethical concerns around consent, privacy and plagiarism, erosion of researchers’ skills and public trust, and environmental costs. This Open Letter presents Behavioural Research UK’s (BR-UK) statement on using generative AI effectively and responsibly in behavioural research. It was informed by existing guidance and expert consultation. The statement sets out BR-UK’s four key propositions: (1) research ethics and integrity principles must include AI concerns; (2) AI should assist, but not replace, researchers through a human-in-the-loop approach; (3) rigorous evaluation of AI use is essential; and (4) coordinated stakeholder action is needed to move from identifying risks to practical solutions. It then provides recommendations and points to practical tools, such as decision aids and checklists for declaring AI use, for seven stakeholder groups, namely research-generating institutions, funders, publication outlets, behavioural research networks and communities, AI platform and tool providers, individual researchers, and research users. The statement will be reviewed annually until 2028, the duration of BR-UK, as technology and evidence evolve.

title: Exploring the causal role of the human gut microbiome in breast cancer risk [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background The relationship between the human gut microbiome and breast cancer (BC) risk is uncertain. Methods We used Mendelian randomization (MR) and multivariable linear regression to investigate the causal relationship between the human gut microbiome and BC risk (overall and subtype-specific) and interrogate the role of circulating metabolites as potential mediators. Summary-level data from genome-wide association studies of gut microbial traits (N = 3,890), circulating metabolites (N = 7,824), overall (N = 247,175) and subtype-specific (N = 200,898) BC risk, including triple negative BC (TNBC; N = 120,493), alongside individual-level data from the Flemish Gut Flora Project (N = 2,242). Sensitivity analyses were applied to examine the robustness of causal estimates. Results Initial two-sample MR analyses suggested that the presence of bacteria within the Ruminococcus genus increased overall BC risk, that higher abundances of bacteria within the Parabacteroides genus decreased and presence of unclassified bacteria within the Bacteroidales order increased TNBC risk, and that several circulating metabolites altered BC risk (e.g., homostachydrine with overall BC and Luminal A BC, and betaine with TNBC). Whilst, in multivariable linear regression analyses, several of these metabolites were also associated with the microbial traits that influenced BC risk, given directional inconsistency of associations across analyses of microbial traits, metabolites and BC coupled with sensitivity analyses implying violations of MR assumptions, associations were unlikely to reflect causality nor a causal pathway between the gut microbiome, metabolites, and BC risk. Conclusions In conclusion, whilst our initial analyses suggested that the gut microbiome and certain circulating metabolites may be associated with BC risk, importantly, sensitivity analyses demonstrated that these relationships are complex and, certainly for the case of the gut microbiome, unlikely to reflect causality.

title: “The Health Facility In-Charge Cannot Go into the Community as We Do": Healthcare Workers’ Perceptions of Task-Sharing for Community-Based Psychosis Screening and Referral in Malawi. [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Tasksharing is increasingly seen as a practical way to address the shortage of qualified mental health specialists in low-resource settings. In Malawi, involving general healthcare workers, such as health surveillance assistants (HSAs), in psychosis screening and referrals could help expand mental health services to underserved communities. However, little is known about healthcare workers’ perceptions of tasksharing for community-based psychosis screening and referral. This formative qualitative study investigated the factors that support or hinder tasksharing among HSAs and assessed how feasible it is to implement this approach from the perspective of healthcare workers. Methods A qualitative formative study was conducted in the Chiradzulu and Salima districts as part of the Psychosis Recovery Orientation in Malawi by Improving Services and Engagement (PROMISE) project. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and focus group discussions with members of the district mental health team, primary healthcare providers, and HSAs. Thematic analysis guided the data analysis and interpretation. Results The findings revealed variations in the understanding of psychosis across healthcare cadres. District mental health professionals were confident in their biomedical knowledge, whereas most HSAs reported a limited understanding of psychosis. Despite this, district and primary healthcare workers expressed confidence in HSAs’ potential to support community-based screening and referrals, citing their close ties to communities and experience in health promotion. Key barriers to tasksharing included inadequate training, medication shortages, limited supervision, and divergent cultural beliefs about psychosis. These systemic and contextual challenges must be addressed for tasksharing to be effective. Conclusions Task-sharing with HSAs offers a promising strategy to enhance psychosis screening and referral at the community level in Malawi. For successful implementation, comprehensive policy support, adequate resourcing, and targeted training are essential.

title: Tele-Adaptation and Feasibility of a Brief Yoga Therapy Module for Generalized Anxiety Disorder: A Pilot Study [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is highly prevalent, but access barriers limit treatment uptake. We systematically tele-adapted a validated 90-minute yoga therapy module into a brief 30-minute format and evaluated its acceptability, feasibility, and preliminary clinical effects. Methods Using expert content validation (n = 10), we developed a 30-minute tele-yoga module comprising Sukshma Vyayama, Vibhagiya Pranayama (6:4:8:4 ratio), Chandra Anuloma Viloma (4:8 ratio), Nadishodhana Pranayama, Bhramari Pranayama, and Yoga Nidra. Twenty adults (18 to 55 years) diagnosed with GAD (GAD-7 score of 5 or higher), with or without comorbid neurotic disorder, on stable pharmacotherapy or drug-naive, received one in-person orientation followed by thrice-weekly live tele-yoga sessions and weekly yoga philosophy discussions over 8 weeks. Primary outcomes included feasibility metrics: Acceptability of Intervention Measure (AIM), Feasibility of Intervention Measure (FIM), Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ), attendance, dropout rate, and Yoga Performance Assessment (YPA). Secondary outcomes were GAD-7 and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks. The Friedman test was used for repeated-measures analysis on completers (n = 17). Results Seventeen of 20 participants (85%) completed the intervention with over 80% attendance. Three withdrew for non-intervention reasons. All feasibility criteria were met: AIM 4.52 +/− 0.21, FIM 4.45 +/− 0.18, CSQ 30.05 +/− 1.14, YPA 30.11 +/− 1.36. GAD-7 scores decreased significantly from a median of 13.0 (IQR 11.0 to 15.0) at baseline to 7.0 (IQR 6.0 to 8.0) at 8 weeks (chi-square = 33.52, p < 0.001). PSQI improved from 12.0 (IQR 11.0 to 15.0) to 7.0 (IQR 4.0 to 7.0) (chi-square = 31.39, p < 0.001). No adverse events occurred. Conclusions This brief tele-adapted yoga module is feasible, acceptable, and shows promising preliminary effects on anxiety and sleep quality in GAD. Randomized controlled trials are warranted.

title: A call for human-centred approaches to qualitative longitudinal mental-health data sharing [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Qualitative longitudinal mental health (QLMH) data provides a uniquely rich resource for understanding how experiences of mental health conditions unfold over time and are shaped by context and culture. While there has been considerable investment by researchers and clinicians in collecting meaningful data and building standardised protocols and repositories for quantitative mental health data, there has been a lack of similar efforts to standardise and contextualise data sharing for the rigorous and ethical reuse of qualitative data. Researchers and data stewards rarely document the social, ethical, personal, and situational factors that shape how participants share sensitive information. In particular, while positionality and reflexivity are crucial aspects for study design and data collection, these are not explicitly addressed when openly sharing QLMH data. These gaps are a consequence of research systems that prioritise technical over relational dimensions of data. This Open Letter outlines why human-centred infrastructure for QLMH data sharing is urgently needed and proposes a co-developed toolkit – the Human-Centred Metadata Canvas – which illustrates practical steps for researchers, clinicians, data stewards, funders, and institutions to embed human-centred documentation and ethical evaluation across the QLMH data lifecycle. Addressing these gaps is essential to ensuring that QLMH data is not only collected but also ethically preserved, meaningfully shared, and responsibly reused to benefit science, clinical practice, and the communities involved.

title: Case Report: Coombs-Negative Hemolytic Anemia as the Initial Manifestation of Wilson Disease in an Adolescent Female: A Case Report [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Wilson disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene. Although hepatic and neurological manifestations are well recognized, acute Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia as the initial presentation is uncommon and may delay diagnosis. Early recognition is essential because prompt initiation of anti-copper therapy can reverse both hematologic and hepatic abnormalities. Case Presentation A previously healthy 16-year-old female basketball player presented with progressive easy fatigability, exertional dyspnea, recurrent jaundice, and high-colored urine for three months. Laboratory evaluation revealed severe Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with a hemoglobin of 6.3 g/dL, predominantly indirect hyperbilirubinemia, markedly reduced serum alkaline phosphatase (6 U/L), elevated aspartate aminotransferase with near-normal alanine aminotransferase, prolonged international normalized ratio, and reticulocytosis. During hospitalization, hemoglobin declined further to 5.4 g/dL, necessitating packed red blood cell transfusion. Viral hepatitis and autoimmune serology were negative. Slit-lamp examination demonstrated bilateral Kayser–Fleischer rings, serum ceruloplasmin was reduced (16.97 mg/dL), and 24-hour urinary copper excretion was markedly elevated (863.23 μg/24 h), confirming Wilson disease. Oral zinc therapy was initiated while awaiting urinary copper estimation, followed by gradual introduction of D-penicillamine with pyridoxine supplementation. Serial follow-up over three months demonstrated complete resolution of symptoms, improvement in hemoglobin to 11.1 g/dL, normalization of serum bilirubin, recovery of alkaline phosphatase, and reduction in urinary copper excretion to 343.68 μg/24 h. Conclusion Wilson disease should be considered in adolescents presenting with unexplained Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia and jaundice, particularly when accompanied by disproportionately low serum alkaline phosphatase and mild hepatic dysfunction. Early diagnosis and timely initiation of anti-copper therapy can result in excellent clinical and biochemical recovery.

title: Perceptions of psychosis and pathways to care in rural Zimbabwe: A mixed-methods study from the Z Factor community and public engagement project. [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Psychosis is among the most stigmatised, poorly understood mental health conditions in low- and middle-income countries. In rural Africa, pathways to care are shaped by interactions between stigma, family decision-making, cultural explanatory models, and structural barriers, yet limited research has examined how community perceptions of psychosis are formed and enacted within social contexts. Methods This convergent mixed-methods study was nested within Z Factor, a community drama-based public engagement project implemented in rural Zimbabwe. Quantitative data were collected through a cross-sectional survey (N = 60) using an adapted Community Attitudes to Mental Illness scale. Qualitative data comprised transcripts and video recordings from seven community-authored drama performances. Data sources were analysed and integrated to examine convergence, complementarity, and divergence in community perceptions of psychosis and pathways to care. Results Survey responses showed heterogeneous and contradictory attitudes. Most respondents rejected exclusion, with 80% disagreeing that people with mental illness deserve to be locked away, yet expressed ambivalence about autonomy, risk, employment, and care pathways. 58% agreed that people with mental illness should be treated like minors, 59% disagreed that they could work like any other person, and 77% agreed that community reintegration supports recovery. Drama narratives contextualised these patterns through seven themes: crisis-based perceptions of psychosis, carer burden and delayed help-seeking, elder-led family decision-making, accessibility and familiarity in pathway choice, trust and reassurance, expectations of rapid recovery, and medication as limited, inaccessible, or insufficient. Conclusions Community perceptions reflected the interplay among stigma, caregiving responsibilities, treatment expectations, structural constraints, and cultural explanatory frameworks rather than a single belief system. Help-seeking was shaped by accessibility, familiarity, trust, and coexistence of biomedical, traditional, and faith-based care systems. Participatory arts-based approaches can generate contextually grounded insights into psychosis stigma and pathways to care, stressing the need for collaborative, family-centred, and culturally responsive mental health engagement approaches.

title: Impact of personalised risk predictions on preventive treatment initiation in tuberculosis [version 2; peer review: 2 approved with reservations]
abstract: Background Preventive treatment for clinically latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection has low uptake, partly due to poor individual risk stratification. We evaluated whether personalised tuberculosis (TB) risk prediction influenced treatment initiation. Methods We undertook a retrospective service evaluation at a single TB clinic in London May 2022–September 2024, in which the PERISKOPE-TB risk prediction model was presented within consultations with patients eligible for preventative treatment for clinically latent Mtb infection. We then examined the association between predicted risk and treatment acceptance using logistic regression, with restricted cubic splines to account for a non-linear relationship. Results are presented as an odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI’s). Results 283 patients were included in the evaluation, where 62% initiated treatment. Higher predicted TB risk was associated with increased treatment initiation; each 1% increase in risk more than doubled the odds of acceptance (OR 2.12, 95% CI 1.59–2.89). Conclusions Personalised risk prediction may improve targeting and uptake of preventive TB treatment in those that need it the most.

title: Did the emergence of the Omicron variant impact the COVID-19 vaccine sentiments in the Arab world? A Twitter-based comparative analysis [version 4; peer review: 1 approved, 2 not approved]
abstract: Background Vaccine hesitancy constitutes a major obstacle for achieving herd immunity against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Research has shown high vaccine hesitancy rates and low compliance among Arabic-speaking populations in the 2021–2022 period. The aim of this study was to analyze sentiments related to COVID-19 vaccines before and after the emergence of the COVID-19 Omicron variant in the Arab-speaking world. Methods Tweets were collected before and after the Omicron emergence period in the Arab-speaking world using Python-enabled CAMeL Tools (Arabic Natural Language Processing toolkit) libraries. A sentiment analysis on COVID-19 vaccines using Arabic keywords, a sentiment analysis by city, and a time series were conducted. Results The data sets exhibited a shift towards less negativity, more neutrality, and a possible adoption of a pragmatic discourse towards vaccine uptake. Sentiments by city showed the Gulf region registered the most presence in the Twitter data, and the time series demonstrated change in sentiments followed public health events. Conclusions Despite its limitations, the study pointed to change in sentiments in response to vaccine-related events. Increased neutral sentiments and vaccine discourse shifting towards vaccine uptake pragmatism after the onset of Omicron, indicate change is possible. Future research may focus on how change towards more vaccine acceptance can be triggered; on how Twitter vaccine discourse translates within local communities; on including other social media (for instance Facebook); on vaccine discourse analysis to get nuanced insights; and on ethical implications of vaccine policies.

title: Formative evaluation of an existing community-based intervention for alcohol addiction in the Soliga tribal community in Chamarajanagar, Karnataka [version 2; peer review: 1 approved, 1 approved with reservations]
abstract: Background Socioeconomic stressors, cultural transitions, and limited access to healthcare often influence alcohol addiction among Indigenous communities. The Soliga tribal community lacks culturally tailored de-addiction services in the Chamarajanagar district of Karnataka, India. The Hosa Jeevana (HJ) program is a community-based intervention that integrates clinical care, peer-led support, and culturally relevant awareness strategies to support addiction recovery. This study protocol outlines the plan for evaluating the HJ program’s acceptability, adoption, and short-term patient outcomes through a formative approach. Study setting The study will be conducted in the HJ clinic and 17 Soliga settlements in B.R. Hills, Karnataka, India, where the intervention is implemented. Method This study will use an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. In the first phase, clinical records, Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) scores, and program retention rates will be analysed to assess engagement, participation, and early indicators of recovery. In the second phase, in-depth interviews will explore facilitators and barriers to care-seeking and perceptions of program acceptability and adoption among Soliga individuals enrolled in the HJ program, HJ Champions (peer mentors), and other stakeholders such as community health workers and physicians. The qualitative findings will contextualise the trends observed in the quantitative analysis. Expected outcomes Implementation outcomes, i.e. acceptability, adoption and identification of barriers and facilitators of the program, are the expected outcomes of the study protocol. Discussion The study findings will help refine the existing community-driven addiction recovery program and inform scaling up the intervention. While long-term sustainability falls outside the study’s scope, insights from this evaluation will lay the foundation for future research and policy integration.

title: Process mapping of a collaborative quality improvement study to optimise the use of antibiotics in intensive care units in Argentina: a Pathfinder study [version 3; peer review: 2 approved]
abstract: Objective To systematically document the operational components, barriers, facilitators, and solutions of a quality improvement collaborative for antibiotic stewardship in intensive care units (ICUs) in the public sector of Argentina, using the Pathfinder methodological framework. Methods Retrospective, descriptive observational study using mixed methods. Data sources included a documentary review of protocols, standard operating procedures, monitoring reports, and host study publications; an online survey with closed and open-ended questions administered to research team members; interviews with team researchers to estimate effort and triangulation with findings from the host study’s previously published process evaluation, structured according to Normalisation Process Theory. Integration was performed using the Pathfinder Tracker. Analysis combined descriptive statistics with content analysis of open-ended responses. Results Eleven stages of the research process were mapped, from question formulation to dissemination, with an estimated total effort of approximately 1,020 person-hours. The stages with the highest perceived difficulty (4/5) were ethical and institutional approvals, data collection, analysis, and dissemination, which together accounted for approximately 50% of the total estimated effort. Barriers were identified across three domains: institutional and regulatory (heterogeneity of ethical requirements, absence of stable local coordinators, publication costs); operational and technical (complex data collection forms, displacement of implementation focus due to the burden of data collection, variable connectivity); and human resources and capacity (clinical workload, staff turnover, insufficient training in implementation science). Solutions included a collaborative format with mentoring, agile communication via accessible digital tools (REDCap, WhatsApp, Zoom), and the use of theoretical frameworks for structuring (NPT, CFIR). Conclusions The Pathfinder framework enabled a systematic reconstruction of the host study’s processes, revealing barriers and solutions that conventional results reports do not capture. The findings are relevant for research teams in middle-income countries designing quality improvement collaboratives in complex hospital settings.

title: Seven Key Terms in Behavioural Research: Developing Agreed Ontological Definitions [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Behavioural research is a multidisciplinary field essential for addressing societal challenges, but it suffers from inconsistent terminology that impedes knowledge synthesis and communication across disciplines. This study used consensus methods to develop informal and ontological definitions for seven key behavioural research terms: individual behaviour, population behaviour, individual behaviour change, behavioural theory, behavioural research, behavioural science, and leadership. Using a seven-step iterative method involving a literature review, expert consultations, and feedback from diverse behavioural researchers and users, the team refined definitions to enhance clarity, inclusivity, and cross-disciplinary understanding. The resulting definitions were accompanied by elaborations and examples to provide context and concrete illustrations of the terms. These shared definitions provide a standardised vocabulary to improve study and intervention design and reporting, evidence synthesis, and translation of evidence into policy and practice. While acknowledging limitations such as sample bias, this work lays a foundation for clearer communication and future advances in behavioural research.

title: Creative synthesisers: Students’ experience of interdisciplinary collaboration [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Interdisciplinarity is often promoted in research funding, and interdisciplinary collaboration is often highlighted in research policy in the UK and abroad. Funders have different routes to promoting and funding interdisciplinary research. In this paper, we focus on Wellcome’s funding of doctoral training in the biosciences, which coupled encouraging disciplinary diversity as an aspect of positive research culture, with student-centred doctoral training. Methods The context of our research was a community of practice, comprising all staff and students of the doctoral training programmes. Within the communities, we used a participative observation approach, inviting participants to reflect on their experiences in group discussions with students and staff within each of the programmes and individual interviews with key staff members. Results Working closely with the funded doctoral programmes, our research found that 1) funding that follows doctoral students rather than supervisors, within a structured pool of selection, supports and develops existing interdisciplinary collaborations, and forges new ones. 2) over and above existing well discussed research skills, synthetic understanding, which integrates information from a wide range of sources (textual and interpersonal) emerges as an important area of interdisciplinary knowledge development. Conclusion The ability to create synthetic understandings is a research skill needs to be extricated from the umbrella term of ‘soft skills’ and actively supported, through training or through some other means of making explicit how to develop it.

title: From evidence to impact: reflections on the SPECTRUM Consortium’s work on the commercial determinants of health [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: The SPECTRUM Consortium (Shaping Public hEalth poliCies To Reduce ineqUalities and harM) was a UK Prevention Research Partnership-funded, multi-university, multi-agency consortium that worked between 2019 and 2025 to shape public health policy and practice on non-communicable disease prevention and the commercial determinants of health (CDOH), focusing on tobacco, alcohol and foods high in salt, sugar and fat. Guided by a Theory of Change and an associated Impact Framework, SPECTRUM organised its work around three interconnected impact pathways: Engagement and Knowledge Exchange, SPECTRUM Research, and Research Landscape. This article reflects on the Consortium’s experience of pursuing impact across these pathways, using the Impact Framework to structure both an account of activities and outputs and a critical assessment of what worked well, what fell short, and what this suggests for future research consortia. Effective strategies included embedding knowledge brokers within policy organisations, sustained co-production with public involvement panels and citizens’ juries, and the development of shared analytical tools and conceptual models that strengthened the emerging field of CDOH. Persistent challenges included the absence of systematic monitoring and evaluation of impact, uneven integration across work packages, and tension between the pace of policy windows and the time needed for rigorous research. Reflecting across all three pathways, the Consortium found that the Theory of Change worked well as a tool for aligning stakeholders at the outset but was underused as an instrument for ongoing evaluation once the programme was under way. The experience points to the value of treating impact frameworks as evolving hypotheses rather than fixed blueprints, and of investing deliberately in structural mechanisms, such as embedded knowledge brokers and dedicated evaluation capacity, rather than relying on individual researcher effort alone to sustain the relationships and systems through which policy-relevant, cross-disciplinary research on CDOH generates impact.

title: Economic evaluation of Wolbachia programmes for dengue control: a systematic review [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Dengue imposes a substantial and growing global health and economic burden, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Wolbachia-based mosquito biocontrol has emerged as a promising strategy to reduce dengue transmission, with substantial evidence demonstrating its epidemiological effectiveness. However, economic evaluations have adopted diverse modelling approaches, analytical perspectives, and assumptions, making comparisons across studies challenging. This study systematically reviews and critically appraises economic evaluations of Wolbachia-based interventions to characterise methodological approaches and assess their influence on estimates of economic value. Methods A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. MEDLINE (Ovid), EMBASE (Ovid), PubMed, and CINAHL were searched to 31 January 2026. Methodological and reporting quality were assessed by independent reviewers using the CHEQUE framework. Results Ten studies met the inclusion criteria, covering settings in Asia and Latin America and predominantly using model-based economic evaluations. Wolbachia interventions were consistently reported as cost-effective and, in several cases cost-saving. Quality appraisal showed that reporting attributes were consistently well-addressed, whereas methodological attributes were more variable. Limitations were most evident in validation practices, handling of uncertainty, and the absence of distributional considerations. Overall quality scores ranged from 59% to 85%, indicating moderate to high quality. Conclusion Wolbachia-based interventions show strong potential as a cost-effective strategy for dengue control. However, current evidence frequently relies on several model-based assumptions and does not fully capture implementation complexity. Strengthening methodological rigour and incorporating implementation considerations will be essential to support policy-relevant decision-making and its sustainable expansion at scale.

title: Perspectives on public health interventions in the management of the COVID-19 pandemic in Thailand [version 4; peer review: 2 approved]
abstract: Background Any government needs to react quickly to a pandemic and make decisions on healthcare interventions locally and internationally with little information regarding the perceptions of people and the reactions they may receive during the implementation of restrictions. Methods We report an anonymous online survey in Thailand conducted in May 2020 to assess public perceptions of three interventions in the Thai context: isolation, quarantine and social distancing. A total of 1,020 participants, of whom 52% were women, responded to the survey. Results Loss of income was the main concern among respondents (>80% for all provinces in Thailand). Traditional media and social media were important channels for communication during the pandemic. A total of 92% of respondents reported that they changed their social behaviour even before the implementation of government policy with 94% reporting they performed social distancing, 97% reported using personal protective equipment such as masks and 95% reported using sanitizer products. Conclusions This study showed a high level of compliance from individuals with government enforced or voluntarily controls such as quarantine, isolation and social distancing in Thailand. The findings from this study can be used to inform future government measures to control the pandemic and to shape communication strategies.

title: A tool to evaluate the impact of lived experience involvement in research: the Brain and Genomics Hub Impact Log protocol. [version 2; peer review: 3 approved]
abstract: Background Despite widespread recognition of the value of lived experience involvement (LEI) in healthcare research and increased LE involvement activity, we lack established implementation methods and instruments for reporting and evaluating impact. We present a protocol for an innovative LE-led Impact Log tool and LEI framework, which may help to address some fundamental barriers to LEI. The Impact Log will be implemented within a five-year multidisciplinary transdiagnostic research project on severe mental illness and is also designed for wider adaptation and use. We include a short literature review on LEI impact, to provide in-depth background. Methods The Impact Log framework is designed to integrate inclusive impactful LEI throughout all research stages, and to use a short accessible form to record and evaluate impact across three domains: design and delivery; interpersonal and environmental aspects; systems and processes. Impact Log tool and LEI design and implementation is led by LE study leads and specialist LE advisory panel, with combined research experience and LE, fully integrated within the wider research team. All Hub research participants will be offered accessible opportunities for remunerated lived experience input, and there will be outreach to ensure diverse representation, aided by the Hub’s charity partners. Data collection and analysis will be LE led and will include iterative analysis to inform continuing development. Diverse formal and informal dissemination throughout the project will maximise wider stakeholder engagement. Conclusion The potential value of this research is to implement a novel tool and framework for facilitating, recording and evaluating LEI in complex mental health research, which can be adapted for wider use. Strengths in design are LE leadership and cross-cutting LE research integration, incorporation of multiple domains, and a focus on facilitating diversity and inclusion within LEI. Potential limitations for this project and wider adaptation may include limited resources, risk of bias and health challenges.

title: Incidence and Outcomes of Acute Kidney Injury in Critically Ill Patients: A Retrospective Study at a Tertiary Care Hospital [version 2; peer review: 2 approved]
abstract: Background Acute kidney injury is common among critically ill patients and is associated with longer ICU stay, higher resource use and increased mortality. Evidence from low- and middle-income countries, including Nepal, remains limited. This study describes the incidence, severity distribution and clinical outcomes of AKI in a tertiary care ICU. Methods We conducted a hospital based retrospective observational study at Dhulikhel Hospital, Nepal. All adults admitted to the ICU from 1st may 2023 to 30th April 2024 were screened using ICU registry. AKI was defined and staged using KDIGO serum criteria. Demographic data, comorbidities, ICU interventions and outcomes were extracted. Associations were examined using appropriate statistical tests. Results Among 1113 patients, 1064 were enrolled for analysis. The incidence of AKI was 29.6%. Patients with AKI were older (median age 60 vs 55 years, p < 0.001), had longer ICU stays (median 3 vs 2 days, p < 0.001), were more frequently on invasive mechanical ventilation (39.6%vs 26%, p < 0.001). Type 2 diabetes mellitus was significantly associated with AKI (39.0% vs 28.0%, p = 0.001). AKI severity correlated with worse outcomes including higher mortality and adverse outcomes increasing from 12.7% in patients without AKI to 38% in stage 3 AKI. Renal replacement therapy was required in 2.3% of patients, mainly in stage 2 and 3 AKI. Conclusion Acute kidney injury is a common and a serious complication among critically ill patients, associated with increased mortality and prolonged ICU stay. Early recognition and targeted management strategies, particularly for high-risk groups, are needed in resource limited settings.

title: Reflections on an experiment in research culture change [version 2; peer review: 2 approved with reservations]
abstract: Recognising that scientific research cannot be divorced from the research culture that produces it, Wellcome’s funding of PhD programmes in 2019 emphasised its role, and made positive research culture an equal criterion of evaluation to scientific excellence. This Open Letter is my own reflection on the main learnings I gleaned from working closely with the community; learnings about making research culture a priority in doctoral training, and about the terms of engagement in a community of practice in its relationship to the funding context.

title: Challenges and potential solutions for improving diagnostic uptake and antibiotic optimisation in South Africa – a multi-level qualitative study [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Diagnostic uncertainty and poor uptake of diagnostic testing contribute to inappropriate antibiotic use and rising antibiotic resistance, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where infrastructure, workforce, and logistical constraints limit access to diagnostics. South Africa’s mixed public-private health system, marked by resource disparities across provinces, provides an important setting for exploring factors shaping diagnostic adoption. We investigated these factors across different South African health settings to inform strategies for improved infection management and antibiotic stewardship. Methods Between January and May 2023, we conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with 36 stakeholders including leaders from national and provincial health departments, the National Health Laboratory Service, private laboratories, and end-user clinicians. Participants worked across primary, secondary, and tertiary care in urban, peri-urban and rural settings in four purposively selected provinces: Western Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State. Interviews were conducted online using a pre-piloted guide and analysed thematically. Results Diagnostic implementation and adoption were shaped by national directives, provincial governance, facility-level practices, and clinician-level factors, with inequities linked to provincial variation in resource and governance capacity. Inefficient procurement, frequent stock-outs, poor infrastructure and planned electricity interruptions undermined diagnostic availability. Human resource shortages, high staff turnover, and limited training undermined diagnostic stewardship, including over-testing and inappropriate use and interpretation by junior doctors. Additional challenges included poor laboratory-clinician communication, outdated equipment, unreliable information systems, and specimen transport delays. Facilities adopted mitigation strategies including backup power systems, pharmacist-led gatekeeping, and digital platforms for rapid result sharing. Conclusion Interconnected governance, infrastructure, workforce, and information-system barriers hinder effective diagnostic implementation across South Africa’s health system, disproportionately affecting under-resourced provinces and rural facilities. Strengthening procurement systems, laboratory infrastructure, workforce capacity, specimen transport networks, and digital surveillance should be prioritised within national antimicrobial resistance action plans to support rational antibiotic use and mitigate the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. title: Transforming Hekima from a Research Tool into a Mental Health Data Platform for Uganda: A Process Paper [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Rich clinical information is often stored in handwritten patient charts, but there are limited systems for converting these routine records into usable data for research, care, service improvement, and policy. This process paper describes the development of Hekima, a locally hosted, AI-assisted mental health data platform that converts paper psychiatric records into structured longitudinal datasets for research. Methods We reviewed implementation documents generated during the Digitising Psychosis Project of the Mental Health Data Prize Africa program. We reconstructed the development process, major adaptations, technical and governance decisions, early analytic outputs, capacity-building activities, public communication, and scale-up pathway. Results Hekima evolved from a psychosis chart digitisation project into a broader mental health data platform. Hekima followed a “one pipeline, two outputs” model. Each scanned document was transcribed, reviewed, redacted, and structured into a longitudinal patient record, but also prepared for patient matching with existing electronic medical record systems. The project digitised and archived 203,020 images from 7,164 files. Early OCR-based extraction demonstrated feasibility but performed poorly on handwritten psychiatric notes. This prompted a redesign toward locally hosted vision-language models, redaction of identifiable information, extraction, and mandatory human review. Lived-experience partners contributed to privacy safeguards, engagement interpretation, data-use acceptability, patient-rights protection, public communication, and independent process review. Conclusion Hekima demonstrated that handwritten psychiatric records in a low-resource setting could be transformed into usable mental health data infrastructure but required data governance, lived-experience oversight, capacity building, communication, and engagement with policymakers.

title: Modelling Simian malaria disease dynamics in Southern Thailand to inform surveillance strategies for emerging zoonotic diseases. [version 1; peer review: 1 approved with reservations]
abstract: Background Zoonotic malaria caused by Plasmodium knowlesi poses a growing threat to malaria elimination. In Thailand, Ranong Province reports the highest incidence nationally, yet the role of long-tailed macaques (Macaca fascicularis) as reservoir hosts across heterogeneous landscapes remains poorly characterized. Methods We describe a prospective, multidisciplinary study on Ko Chang using a spatial grid-cell framework, with dominant land-use type assigned per cell. We will produce a fine-scale land-use classification by combining satellite data with ground-truth observations, distinguishing easily confused land-use types, such as plantations and forest, and addressing the misclassification common in conventional datasets. Audio recording devices and camera traps will be deployed across the landscape and over time to measure macaque and, human presence across land-use classes. Household questionnaires will characterise human exposure. Existing P. knowlesi case records (2013–2024) and entomological data (2011–2022) will be integrated within a unified spatial framework to estimate land-use-specific exposure. Satellite imagery will be classified into land-use types using supervised learning model. Macaque detections will be summarised as a relative abundance index and modelled in an occupancy framework to estimate the probability of site use. Human distribution and movement will be derived from interviews, camera-trap and acoustic detections. Macaque and human abundance, with secondary entomological data, will be assigned to land-use classes as inputs to a population-attributable risk (PAR) model. These land-use-explicit abundance estimates will then be combined with zoonotic malaria prevalence from the literature as inputs to a transmission-dynamics model. Expected outcome is a fine-scale land-use map of Ko Chang; land-use-explicit estimates of macaque and human site use and relative abundance; land-use-specific estimates of population-attributable risk and transmission parameters. Conclusion This study will generate fine-scale, ground-validated landscape and reservoir-host–vector data, improving understanding of how macaque movement, human exposure, and land-use change drive spillover risk, and informing targeted interventions.

abstract: We present a genome assembly from a specimen of Pione sp. (Porifera; Demospongiae; Clionaida; Clionaidae). The genome sequence has a total length of 149.53 megabases. title: Strengthening sustainable clinical trial models for greater health impact: Expert discussion from the Annual Wellcome Major International Programme Regional Meeting 2024. [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Despite growing clinical trial activity in low- and middle- income countries (LMICs), global research inequities persist, with industry funding often prioritizing high-income markets over LMIC health needs. Academic clinical trial units (CTUs) in LMICs play a critical role in delivering locally relevant research, building capacity, and supporting sustainable trial ecosystems. This manuscript reports findings from the 2024 Wellcome Major International Programmes (MIPs) Regional Annual Meeting on sustainable clinical trial models in LMICs. Methods The meeting was held from 16–18 October 2024 at the Oxford University Clinical Research Unit in Vietnam and included representatives from research institutions across Africa, Asia, and the United Kingdom (UK). A dedicated workshop explored collaborative research networks, innovative trial designs, emerging technologies, and sustainable funding models. Presentations, breakout discussions, and plenary reflections were recorded, transcribed, and analysed thematically. Results Participants identified common challenges including limited clinical trial literacy, unstable funding, workforce recruitment and retention difficulties, inequitable research partnerships, regulatory and ethics bottlenecks, operational inefficiencies, and barriers to conducting trials in remote settings. Proposed solutions included locally led research agendas, diversified funding mechanisms, stronger engagement with regulators and communities, and investment in workforce development. Participants also advocated for more efficient trial designs, including adaptive and platform trials, decentralized research models, shared monitoring systems, and interoperable electronic data platforms. A major outcome of the meeting was an agreement to explore the establishment a formal collaborative alliance between MIPs to support shared infrastructure, training, advocacy, and cross-site trial delivery. Conclusions LMIC-based CTUs are well positioned to lead more equitable, context-responsive, and sustainable clinical trial ecosystems. Strengthening collaboration through formalized regional networks may enhance trial capacity, improve efficiency, and support greater regional self-reliance in clinical research.
