title: High-risk without safeguards? The EU AI Act and the push for deregulation of medical AI
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in clinical decision-making, yet recent proposals to simplify the European Union (EU) Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) have reopened the question of whether AI-enabled medical devices should remain subject to the AI Act’s full high-risk regime. Under the current framework, AI-enabled medical devices are regulated through a combination of sectoral medical device legislation (the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation (IVDR)) and additional AI-specific safeguards contained in the AI Act. This narrative review analyses the Health Innovation Package and related legislative developments under the EU simplification agenda and examines their impact on the relationship between the AI Act and medical device law. It shows that the proposed reform would retain the high-risk classification of AI-enabled medical devices while removing most associated AI Act obligations. In effect, this decouples risk classification from the safeguards that give it regulatory meaning, including requirements on data governance, risk management, human oversight and postmarket monitoring. Rather than resolving regulatory overlap, the amendments shift the centre of gravity back to product-focused medical device law without ensuring equivalent AI-specific safeguards. These changes may narrow attention to fundamental rights, weaken oversight in clinical use and increase legal uncertainty regarding accountability and responsibility. In a domain where AI systems directly shape clinical decisions and patient outcomes, these changes risk undermining the conditions for safe, equitable and accountable deployment of medical AI.
authors: ["Van Kolfschooten, H., Solaiman, B., Onitiu, D."]

title: Me, my doctor and AI: a qualitative interview study on patients requirements for trustworthy use of AI-CDSS in ophthalmology
abstract: Objective Artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) are increasingly entering care and redefining how medical decisions are made. As patients are directly affected by hybrid physician-AI decisions without interacting with the system itself, trust, transparency and involvement in decision-making become important concerns. This study explored patients’ requirements for trustworthy use of AI-CDSS in ophthalmology, with particular attention to expectations regarding disclosure of AI use and informational needs. Methods and analysis We conducted semi-structured interviews with 23 ophthalmology patients and caregivers (aged 22–84 years) in Germany between January and March 2026. Participants were recruited via patient organisations, ophthalmology practices, clinics, social media, or purposively, with the aim of obtaining a sample diverse in age, gender and eye conditions. We used inductive qualitative content analysis to examine their perceptions of AI-assisted decision-making, factors shaping trust in AI-supported medical decisions and expectations regarding communication and AI disclosure. Results Participants were generally open to the use of AI-CDSS in ophthalmology but had several requirements for trustworthy use of AI-CDSS. These related to three domains: the physician (eg, AI competence, critical evaluation of outputs), the AI system (eg, performance, explanations) and governance of its use (eg, transparency, consent). Participants considered it essential that physicians be able to identify incorrect AI output. Relatedly, the physician emerged as an important trust mediator: some indicated that pre-existing trust in the physician would extend to trust in the use of AI-CDSS, while for others, trust appears to depend on the perceived physician-AI interaction. Transparency about AI use was particularly important in this context. Almost all participants expected to be informed when AI-CDSS were used, although preferences regarding the amount and format of information varied. Conclusion The findings suggest that patients’ comfort with AI-assisted clinical decision-making depends strongly on the perceived physician-AI interaction and physician-patient communication. Specifically, disclosure appears to be important for informational purposes and for enabling patients to assess the trustworthiness of physician-AI decisions and remain involved in decision-making. As implementation and governance decisions likely shape how patients experience AI-assisted decision-making, they should be made with explicit attention to patient concerns.

title: Priorities for artificial intelligence education: clinicians perspectives
abstract: Objective Educating clinicians about artificial intelligence (AI) is urgent as the UK General Medical Council places liability with practitioners and the European Union AI Act with employers for appropriate training, but also because AI, like any tool, requires training to use safely. National Health Service England (NHSE) Capability Framework provides guidance, but frontline clinicians’ perspectives are unknown, so we sought to identify their priorities. Methods and analysis Iterative interviews with residents, educators and experts synthesised 10 contextualised AI-related problem statements. We surveyed residents and consultant-educators in the East of England, who rated their confidence and importance. Participants also ranked their preferred learning modality. Results We received 317 responses. Clinicians’ priorities, defined by high importance (I) and low confidence (C), were: ‘understanding liability implications’ (I: 40%; C: 1.82/5), ‘determining appropriate levels of confidence in AI algorithms’ (I: 36.5%; C: 1.98/5) and ‘mitigating security and privacy risks’ (I: 34%; C: 1.68). Confidence was low (mean 20, range 10–50), with no significant difference between educators and residents. Residents preferred integration of training into regional teaching, while consultant–educators favoured webinars. Conclusion Our findings show that clinicians prioritise practical concerns, such as liability and determining confidence in algorithmic outputs. In contrast, critical appraisal and explaining AI to patients were deprioritised, despite their relevance to clinical safety. This study enhances the NHSE Capability Framework by contextualising AI-related capabilities for clinicians as users and identifying priorities with which to develop scalable training.
authors: ["Jeffrey, M., Auyoung, E., Pak, D."]

title: In vivo clinical effectiveness of artificial intelligence screening for acute coronary syndrome: testing real-world performance
abstract: Objective Many predictive models are being developed, but few are deployed in clinical care. Hence, model performance within live real-world care is often not known. We trained a predictive model (in vitro) to (1) estimate patients’ risk of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) on arrival to the emergency department (ED) and (2) identify those with highest risk for ST-segment myocardial infarction (STEMI) to receive an early ECG. We embedded this model into clinical care as clinical decision support (CDS) and using dynamic real-world data (in vivo), ran a silent pilot. We aimed to test the CDS’s replication of the original model’s screening performance and compare to standard of care screening by human staff. Methods and analysis The CDS prospectively assessed each patient arriving in the ED between November 2023 and April 2024. It calculated each patient’s risk for ACS, recorded a decision about whether the patient should receive an early ECG and was programmed to not exceed the total number of ECGs performed in human practice, approximately 33%. We used raw agreement and Cohen’s Kappa to compare the screening decisions of the in vivo CDS and original in vitro model. We then measured sensitivity for ACS, our primary outcome, and specificity, which we compared between the CDS’s and human screening decisions. Results 32 346 visits were seen in the ED and processed by the CDS. 1.0% had ACS and 0.1% STEMI. Raw agreement between the CDS and original model was 96.8%, and Kappa was 91.2% (95% CI 90.7% to 91.8%). Sensitivity for ACS was 81.7% (95% CI 77.1% to 85.8%) in CDS versus 80.2% (95% CI 75.4% to 84.4%) observed in humans. Specificity for ACS was 67.3% (95% CI 66.8% to 67.9%) versus 67.4% (95% CI 66.9 to 67.9%), respectively. Conclusion We found very good raw agreement and Kappa scores between the CDS and original model. Sensitivity and specificity between the CDS and human practice did not differ. This suggests that, when CDS is deployed independent of human decision-making, we can expect very high, although not perfect, performance replication. These differences need to be quantified and considered to estimate the real-world impact of models before deployment.

title: How data drift impacts the safety and interpretability of machine learning models predicting risk from blood glucose control
abstract: Objective Predictive algorithms trained from historical data and deployed in dynamic environments are at risk from data drift. Machine learning models using data collected by sensors making continuous measurements could be impacted by both changes in the device itself and their users, driving drift and impacting safety. To maintain predictive performance, algorithms must be continuously monitored and tuned to overcome fundamental changes to both input data (covariate shift) and the relationship with the output (concept drift). Here, we aim to understand how changes to user behaviour, physiology and sensors could impact the safety of models using automated sensor readings from continuous glucose monitors (CGM). Methods and analysis In this paper, we investigate how data drift in a machine learning model trained to predict short-term risk from blood glucose control for individuals with type-1 diabetes. We simulate how changes in both user behaviour and accuracy of the sensor could lead to covariate shift and concept drift. For each scenario, we quantify the changes to input data (Jensen-Shannon divergence), the impact to model performance metrics and the explainability of the model (ie, shift in feature importance). Results We demonstrate that using a combination of covariate shift detection, multiple performance metrics and feature importance offers a powerful methodology of identifying different types of drifts in sensor data. For blood glucose management, our scenarios focused on user behaviour (ie, changes to blood glucose dynamics and CGM use) and device/sensor noise and variability, finding more simplistic approaches to drift detection could incorrectly identify risk to model safety. Conclusion Machine learning and AI can enhance clinical decision-making, but often lack the transparency required to ensure ongoing safety. Combining complementary monitoring techniques enables clearer identification of changes in data or model behaviour, helping determine when retraining or intervention is needed.

title: An extensible deep learning framework for multi-type chromatin interaction prediction through hierarchical adaptation strategies
abstract: by Shuaibin Wang, Tong Chen, Weixu Liu, Xuejie Zheng, Zhongxin Yang, Zhen Liang, Yin Shen Three-dimensional chromatin interactions play essential roles in gene regulation, yet computational prediction of diverse interaction types remains largely dependent on specialized, single-task models. Here, we present UniLoopNet, a multi-task deep learning framework that predicts multiple types of chromatin interactions including enhancer–promoter interactions, enhancer–enhancer interactions, CTCF-mediated loops, and stripe-associated interactions from DNA sequences. UniLoopNet employs a shared encoder–decoder architecture with hierarchical adaptation strategies, integrating multi-task, transfer, and continual learning based on task semantic similarity. Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple cell lines demonstrates that UniLoopNet outperforms existing specialized and multi-task approaches, with AUROCs exceeding 0.90 in most tasks. Under stringent evaluation settings, including chromosome-matched, distance-matched, realistic imbalanced, and locus-disjoint tests, AUROCs range from 0.8934 to 0.9366. In the realistic 1:5 class-imbalance setting, the AUPRCs for enhancer–promoter and enhancer–enhancer interaction prediction are 0.7956 and 0.6935, respectively. Cross-cell-line transfer experiments further show that applying UniLoopNet to another cell line requires adaptation by supervised fine-tuning on target-cell-line data, after which performance is comparable to that of within-cell-line training. Notably, the framework exhibits data efficiency in experiments with substantially reduced training data. Interpretability analyses reveal that the learned sequence features are associated with known transcription factor binding sites and uncover differential regulatory effects of disease-associated variants. UniLoopNet provides a versatile and data-efficient framework for sequence-based prediction and interpretation of diverse 3D genome interactions, complementing existing sequence-to-map approaches while improving the understanding of sequence-encoded regulatory potential.

title: Evolutionary and dynamic constraints converge on a conserved coupling sector in thermally adapted GH1 β-glucosidases
abstract: by Li-Ting Zheng, Yi Li, Xian He, Lian-Tao Yang, De-Rui Zhao, Meng-Ting Liu, Peng Sang, Li-Quan Yang How protein sequences evolve to maintain functional conformational dynamics under thermal stress remains an important question in molecular evolution. Thermophilic enzymes are often considered to achieve stability primarily through enhanced structural rigidity, yet thermal adaptation may also involve the preservation or reorganization of correlated motions across the protein scaffold. Here, we compared three glycoside hydrolase family 1 β-glucosidases—BsBgl1A, 9UPT, and LQBG8—that share a conserved (β/α) 8 TIM-barrel fold but display distinct optimal temperatures of approximately 45, 65, and 70 °C, respectively. By integrating comparative structural analysis, three independent 1 μs molecular dynamics simulations at 300, 325, and 350 K, neural relational inference of residue-level dynamic coupling, and family-level coevolutionary analysis, we identified distinct dynamic strategies associated with their thermal phenotypes. All three enzymes retained their global compactness and principal secondary-structure framework across the simulated temperatures, indicating that differences in RMSD and residue flexibility did not reflect large-scale unfolding. BsBgl1A showed the strongest temperature sensitivity, with increased structural deviation and residue mobility at 350 K. Its inferred interaction network exhibited a non-monotonic response, characterized by pronounced overcoupling at 325 K followed by reduced connectivity at 350 K. In contrast, 9UPT maintained relatively restrained residue dynamics and a highly reproducible coupling topology across temperatures. LQBG8 combined substantial local conformational flexibility with persistent long-range coupling and retained the highest directed network density at 350 K. Across the three enzymes, the βα5–βα7 region repeatedly emerged as a shared structural and dynamic center. Coevolutionary couplings were also enriched in TIM-barrel-associated regions that spatially converged on this sector. These findings indicate that thermal adaptation in GH1 β-glucosidases is not adequately explained by uniform structural rigidification. Instead, enzymes with the same conserved fold may adopt distinct organizations of correlated motion, while greater thermal adaptation is associated with the persistence or reorganization of a βα5–βα7-centered dynamic coupling pattern under elevated temperature. The correspondence between dynamic coupling and coevolutionary enrichment is consistent with long-term evolutionary constraint on this structural sector, although it does not establish direct selection on the network as an independent functional unit. Our results therefore provide a testable framework in which thermostability reflects a balance among local stabilization, regional flexibility, and the resilience of higher-order dynamic organization.

title: In silico prediction of metabolic trait robustness in microbial cells
abstract: by Chunhao Gu, Ville Mustonen, Paula Jouhten Microbial strains undergo notable biomass expansion in industrial applications subjecting populations to Darwinian selection. The consequent adaptive evolution may threaten the often tediously developed desired metabolic traits of the strains, such as flavor or platform chemical production. Yet, it remains unresolved how to predict the evolutionary trait robustness. Here, we propose TRAEV (Trait Robustness Against EVolution), a computational framework for in silico prediction of evolutionary robustness of metabolic traits and trajectories of desired traits in application environments. TRAEV uses constraint-based metabolic models for predicting environment-dependent trait-fitness dependencies and accounts for the stochasticity of adaptive evolution by using Monte Carlo-based perturbation analysis. First, TRAEV predicts the immediate metabolic phenotype in the new environment, and then, the subsequent evolutionary trajectories of fitness and desired trait. Metabolic trait robustness is quantified from the evolutionary trajectories as two scores: Robustness Score (RS) and Trade-off Score (TS). RS represents trait robustness and the overall trait level during evolutionary adaptation, whereas TS captures trait–fitness trade-offs. We validated TRAEV by predicting relative evolutionary robustness of heterologous pigmentation of two engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains and two desired aroma generation traits by multiple wine strains of S. cerevisiae if they were developed via a laboratory selection process. Thus, we showed how TRAEV predictions could guide strain development. TRAEV can be integrated into computational strain design workflows across microbial strains, desired metabolic traits, and application environments. Ultimately, model-predicted evolutionary robustness of desired metabolic traits can guide both strain and process development and help enhancing the economic attractiveness of industrial applications using microbial cells.

title: KmerSignificance score: A discriminative and biologically informed framework for viral k -mer prioritization
abstract: by Dylan Lebatteux, Florian Corso, Hugo Soudeyns, Isabelle Boucoiran, Soren Gantt, Abdoulaye Baniré Diallo Distinguishing closely related viral strains requires identifying genomic regions where subtle sequence differences carry biological significance. While k -mer-based approaches offer computational efficiency for genome analysis, existing methods lack standardized frameworks for evaluating which k -mers are most informative. Current selection strategies focus primarily on statistical discriminative power without integrating biological context. We introduce KmerSignificance Score (KSS), a k -mer prioritization framework combining three components: an information-theoretic method measuring strain-distinguishing capacity, an optimized amino acid substitution matrix (MIYATA_EVO) for mutation impact assessment, and a protein characterization score derived from annotations and database cross-references retrieved through UniProt. All three component scores and the integrated KSS are bounded in [0,1] by construction, providing a common numerical scale for ranking positions within a dataset. The discriminative component achieved a mean F1 of 0.881, not significantly different from chi-squared (0.876), the strongest of eight baselines. Top-ranked selections from the discriminative component nonetheless differed from those produced by chi-squared, especially for SARS-CoV-2 and HIV-1. The MIYATA_EVO matrix, optimized using a genetic algorithm, increased the composite agreement score across eight amino acid characteristics by 28.4% over the original MIYATA matrix. Across 17,471 viral proteins, the protein characterization score tracked UniProt’s five-level annotation score closely (Kendall’s τ=0.775), as expected for measures drawing on overlapping annotation content. Within each level, the continuous score provided finer numerical resolution among proteins. Literature cross-referencing on SARS-CoV-2 (278,738 sequences, 19 Pango-derived lineage labels), HIV-1 (12,223 sequences, 15 subtype labels), and human cytomegalovirus (HCMV; 399–646 sequences, 4–8 locus-specific genotypes) found that the top-ranked k -mers reported here map to established variant-defining mutations, subtype-specific polymorphisms, and genotype markers. KSS provides a standardized framework for viral k -mer prioritization with potential applications in variant surveillance, molecular epidemiology, and functional annotation. The tool is available at https://github.com/bioinfoUQAM/KmerSignificanceScore.

title: Calsequestrin localization at RyR2 clusters enables calcium wave propagation in ventricular myocytes
abstract: by David Conesa, Blas Echebarria, Leif Hove-Madsen, Yohannes Shiferaw, Enrique Alvarez-Lacalle Intracellular calcium waves in cardiac myocytes propagate through a fire-diffuse-fire mechanism in which calcium released from one RyR2 cluster diffuses to neighboring clusters and triggers their activation. Yet propagation faces a fundamental physical difficulty: the calcium signal must cross distances of 1–2 μ m between Z-planes while being attenuated by cytosolic buffering and diffusion, and at the same time the release site depletes its local sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium store. How waves propagate efficiently despite these constraints has remained unclear. We developed a three-dimensional computational model of mouse ventricular myocytes at submicrometer resolution to address this question. Our central finding is that co-localization of calsequestrin2 (CASQ2) with RyR2 clusters is required for robust wave propagation. In a physiological model, where CASQ2 is concentrated at release sites as observed experimentally, calcium waves propagate reliably across the cell with velocities that match the experimental range. In contrast, when CASQ2 is distributed uniformly throughout the sarcoplasmic reticulum, keeping total CASQ2 unchanged, the wavefront stalls. These results identify CASQ2–RyR2 co-localization as a key structural requirement for effective calcium wave propagation in ventricular myocytes.

title: An integrative computational approach for obstacle avoidance during action selection
abstract: by Shan Zhong, Nader Pouratian, Paul Schrater, Vassilios Christopoulos Action selection in cluttered environments, where individuals must simultaneously pursue goals and avoid obstacles, presents a significant challenge for the brain. To understand the underlying mechanisms of action selection in such contexts, we propose a computational model that extends stochastic optimal control theory through a novel framework for obstacle avoidance. The model decomposes action selection into a weighted combination of individual control policies, each generated for either target approach or obstacle avoidance. By integrating value information from goals, obstacles, and actions into a unified measure of “relative desirability”, the model dynamically determines the contribution of each policy to the overall action selection process. We evaluated the framework using simulated target-reaching tasks in cluttered environments based on previous human studies. The results showed that the model qualitatively captures key features of human motor behavior, including the influence of obstacle properties on movement trajectories and the transient tendency to initiate movements toward obstacles before avoidance.This work offers new insights into the dynamic interaction between approach and avoidance behaviors, providing a basis for future studies of action selection in more complex and naturalistic settings.

title: A computational framework for modeling fluid and solid stressesin porous tissues with application to the trabeculated embryonic heart
abstract: by Christine Miller Buffinton, James W. Baish This study provides a framework for efficient solutions of computational fluid-solid interaction models of porous tissue, with a focus on blood flow through the developing heart wall in the critical chamber and valve formation stages, when trabeculation fills much of the ventricles. This porous, trabeculated tissue is the site of complex mechanotransduction processes, but accurately estimating solid and fluid stresses within such intricate geometries is difficult. We addressed this with three levels of modeling and verification. Images of E12.5 mouse ventricles were first obtained through confocal microscopy and 3D reconstruction. These guided creation of explicit pore-scale finite element simulations with fluid-solid interaction. Idealized and image-derived unit cells were analyzed to determine hydraulic permeability. Next, a multi-pore representation of the ventricular wall was solved with full fluid and solid equations. A continuum model based on Brinkman equations then replaced the explicit pore structure, and sensitivity to permeability was evaluated in terms of fluid flow in the open channel and porous region. Permeabilities obtained from unit cell simulations followed trends from Kozeny-Carman solid-pore and fiber theory for the rigid case, while simulations for hyperelastic unit-cell material quantified the effects of tissue elasticity. Comparison of continuum and explicit model results showed the Brinkman equation, which incorporates the diffusion of shear stress from flow in the free fluid into the porous media, but not explicitly inertial effects, could significantly improve the accuracy of continuum models compared to Darcy's law. A 3D model of blood flow through the ventricles of the developing mouse heart demonstrated the application of the technique to more realistic geometry, showed locations of peak solid and shear stress, and produced physiologically reasonable flow. Furthermore, we developed methodologies to estimate local wall shear and solid stress from continuum-based calculations. This approach can enable efficient, whole-organ parametric analyses of fluid flow, circumventing the need for computationally expensive explicit pore modeling.

title: Visuomotor coordination on the road: Low-dimensional representations reveal adaptive, context-dependent reductions in the dimensionality of natural driving behavior
abstract: by John Madrid-Carvajal, Shadi Derakhshan, Peter König The brain’s ability to transform complex, high-dimensional sensory and motor inputs into coordinated, goal-directed behavior remains a central challenge in neuroscience research. Current research suggests that behavior is generated through patterns within a low-dimensional structure. What visuomotor patterns underlie complex, unconstrained behaviors such as driving, and how stereotypical they are, remain poorly understood. Driving involves complex perception-action interactions, which we hypothesize are specific to the driver’s role and adapt to task demands. Here, we unfold these dynamics using an immersive virtual drive that recreates ten hazardous on-road events. We collected eye, head, and vehicle movements from participants assigned to either a manual or an automated driving condition. From the behavioral movements of 284 drivers, we constructed a common time-resolved behavioral state space based on collective variance, computed via principal component analysis across participants. The obtained low-dimensional representation thus captures generalized visuomotor coordination strategies. We then characterized the evolving low-dimensional structure with cosine similarity and various measures of effective dimensionality. We tested whether leading components contained condition-specific information using discriminant analysis. Throughout the entire drive, few components accounted for most of the variance in behavior, and effective dimensionality decreased reliably around critical events, indicating tighter coordination between perceptual and motor variables. During periods of low effective dimensionality, the contributions of eye, head, steering, and vehicle heading reorganized toward leading dimensions in a task-dependent manner. Across events, between-subject similarity was partially stable and stronger among manual drivers. This reorganization also made behaviors more distinct across driving conditions, enabling better classification of driving modes using only the first two components. These results show that naturalistic driving is supported by shared low-dimensional visuomotor coordination strategies that are flexibly reshaped by contextual demands, and provide a principled behavioral framework for linking neural manifolds, human driver models, and the design of adaptive automated vehicles.

title: Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation
abstract: by Susanne Dahle, Gaute T. Einevoll, Torbjørn V. Ness There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.

title: The evolutionary accessibility of cultural fitness landscapes
abstract: by Laurel Fogarty, Rebecca B. Hoyle Many human cultural and technological traits have a complex and peculiar structure. They are often characterized by multiple closely interacting parts that can form modules, and change as a result of innovation, collaboration, and social learning. A full understanding of the ways in which such cultural traits evolve requires a model that accounts for the close epistatic interaction of the constituent parts, and for the uniquely cultural processes that act on them. Here, we generalize the concept of ‘adaptive landscapes’, where populations search a landscape for optimal combinations of components. This generalization accounts for epistatic interactions, and includes processes such as modularization, communication, and collaboration, that are not features of genetic systems but may be quite common features of cultural systems. We show that modularization in combination with collaborative communication of search results is more successful, but sometimes more costly, than searching a full adaptive landscape. However, in many of the circumstances under which technology evolves, a full search of many thousands of possible modules may not be feasible since time, financial, energetic, and environmental constraints are likely to be strong. Under these conditions, our models suggest that there is a critical value for the number of modules to search below which the global optimum is more likely to be reached by searching the full landscape. The value of this threshold depends on the complexity of the technology. Overall, we suggest that analysis of cultural fitness landscapes is likely to be a fruitful avenue for research into technological change especially when combined with elements of human learning and interaction known to be important features of cultural evolution.

title: Proton transport drives allosteric conformational changes in the MmpL3 transporter
abstract: by Lixinhao Yang, E. Jeffrey North, Helen I. Zgurskaya, Mary Jackson, James C. Gumbart Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ), remains a global health crisis, further complicated by increasing drug resistance. The mycobacterial membrane protein MmpL3, which is essential for transporting cell wall precursors such as trehalose monomycolate (TMM), is a promising therapeutic target. However, the mechanistic link between proton-driven dynamics and substrate transport in MmpL3 is not fully understood. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how protonation of conserved Asp-Tyr dyads (Asp256-Tyr646 and Asp645-Tyr257) in Mycobacterium smegmatis ( Msmg ) MmpL3 regulates conformational changes and TMM binding. Protonation at Asp256 induces an open dyad conformation, increases local water accessibility, and is associated with a tendency toward more open configurations of the periplasmic binding pocket. In contrast, protonation at Asp645 stabilizes a closed dyad conformation, reduces water accessibility, and narrows the transmembrane binding pocket. These findings support a proposed sequential protonation model in which protonation-dependent conformational changes are allosterically coupled to substrate translocation.

title: The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts
abstract: by Milena Philomena Maria Musial, Sam Hall-McMaster, Kanji Shimomura, Ayaka Kato, Erik L. Bode, Clarissa C. Grundmann, Claudia Ebrahimi, Kenji Morita, Samuel J. Gershman, Tanja Endrass, Florian Schlagenhauf The successor representation (SR) is a reinforcement learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk ( n = 260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior ( n = 260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant, particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy in alcohol-related contexts – and instead more on model-free control. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.

title: SADRP: A structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction
abstract: by Ren Qi, Shujia Liu, Tianhong Quan, Tianru Wu, Alexey K. Shaytan, Bin Liu Motivation Predicting drug sensitivity across diverse cancer samples is a fundamental challenge in personalized therapy and drug discovery. This task requires comprehensive characterization of both drug and cancer cell line features. Current approaches often fail to fully capture the complex structural characteristics and interactions of drug compounds and struggle to integrate multi-omics features derived from the same sample, limiting their feature representation capacity. Consequently, there is a need for modeling frameworks that can jointly model molecular structural features and multi-modal cellular contexts in a unified manner. Results We present SADRP, a structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction, designed to model complex molecular structures and multi-omics data. For drug representation, SADRP incorporates Shortest Distance Path (SDP) encoding and edge encoding to capture both topological relationships and bond-type chemical semantics. For cell line profiling, a multi-view interactive encoder integrates gene expression and DNA methylation, capturing cross-omics synergistic complementarity. SADRP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, while also identifying potential therapeutic candidates and biomarkers, providing mechanistic insights and supporting applications in drug discovery and personalized medicine.

title: Multiscale modeling reveals non-linear dynamics of AKT-mediated NO-ROS crosstalk in shear stress-induced endothelial phenotype
abstract: by Yu-Yuan Zhang, Yi-Teng Wang, Yan Qiu, Yong-Jiang Li, Dong Chen, Kai-Rong Qin Endothelial dysfunction is a critical initiating event in atherosclerosis. The regulatory role of the AKT signaling pathway in the transition between injury and repair remains unclear. This study developed a multiscale model to elucidate how AKT signaling modulates endothelial repair under shear stress. The framework integrates hemodynamic stimuli, cellular behaviors, and nonlinear AKT/NO/ROS biochemical kinetics coupled with endothelial phenotypic transitions. Results demonstrate that endothelial dysfunction is driven by a spatial mismatch between NO production and ROS consumption rather than global deficiency. Phenotypic restoration is governed by the nonlinear interactions within the NO-ROS network. Systematic simulations identified a golden window, where Day 1 intervention and moderate AKT activation effectively restored endothelial cells and normalized redox status. Conversely, excessive activation caused supra-physiological over-suppression. These findings suggest that repair is determined by the tight coupling of redox homeostasis and immune dynamics, highlighting intervention timing and dosage as critical factors for precision vascular therapy.

title: Environmental volatility is associated with adaptive caution in visual search
abstract: by Nan Qiu, Fredrik Allenmark, Siyi Chen, Hermann J. Müller, Zhuanghua Shi Real-world distractors occur in environments whose states change at different rates. We asked whether such volatility alters initial overt oculomotor allocation, later target verification and response commitment, or both. Observers performed an additional-singleton search task with concurrent eye tracking while distractor presence followed high- or low-volatility sequences, with overall distractor prevalence held constant. Trial-pooled oculomotor capture was higher under high volatility, a pattern that appears to indicate altered filtering. Matching the same-location run position removed that difference, with no detectable difference in capture across volatility regimes at matched run position. The pooled capture effect was therefore consistent with a structural consequence of the volatility manipulation, which enriched high-volatility blocks with early-run positions where capture is intrinsically high. The volatility effect itself appeared on distractor-absent trials. Under high volatility, response times were longer, fixations more frequent, final-target dwell longer, and errors fewer, while target-acquisition latency itself was unchanged. Same-location repetition learning showed no detectable difference in slope across regimes. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model (DDM) and a complementary volatility Kalman-filter (VKF) comparison converged in showing that manual responses carried both boundary-related and drift-related structure. With distractor frequency held constant, the per-trial effect of volatility therefore emerged after the first saccade as an increase in response caution rather than in oculomotor capture. This pattern is consistent with precision-weighted adjustment to environmental uncertainty.

title: Computational deconvolution of drug sensitivity via single-cell–to–bulk transcriptome mapping
abstract: by Alexandre Coudray, Romain Forey, Benjamin Bejar Haro, Filipe Martins, Joana Carlevaro-Fita, Shaoline Sheppard, Sandra Eloise Offner, Gioele La Manno, Guillaume Obozinski, Didier Trono Analyses routinely conducted in both fundamental research and biomedical studies often report aggregate signals derived from heterogeneous mixtures of cells. These mixtures reflect the intrinsic anatomical and functional complexity of the tissues and organs from which they are derived. Such bulk measurements obscure cell-specific signals, thereby hindering accurate interpretation of the underlying biological processes. Here, we introduce CLIMB and CLIFF, a two-step machine-learning framework that deconvolves bulk RNA-seq into cell-type composition and expression, and then resolves bulk drug sensitivity measurements into cell subtype- and single-cell-specific profiles. We first validate CLIMB using in-vitro mixtures of leukemic cell lines with experimentally known cell-type proportions, then extend this validation to large-scale, cross-dataset pseudo-bulk analyses built from independent scRNA-seq references across two disease contexts and five cancer types — mimicking the reference-to-target mismatches encountered in real applications — and show that CLIMB accurately infers the cellular composition of bulk samples, outperforming state-of-the-art bulk deconvolution methods. We emphasize CLIMB’s effectiveness in acute myeloid leukemia, where it offers highly accurate estimation of leukemic stem cell fractions across three test datasets and three patient cohorts. We then validate CLIFF, our algorithm for estimating cell subtype- and single-cell-specific drug sensitivity, first on the same in-vitro cell line mixtures using experimentally measured drug responses, and then through in-depth, realistic-scale pseudo-bulk simulations. We applied our deconvolution strategy to the beatAML cohort dataset, currently the most extensive database of ex-vivo drug screening data. This analysis generated a cell subtype–resolved drug sensitivity landscape for 121 compounds, revealing multiple compounds putatively active against leukemic stem cells, including midostaurin, A-674563, SNS-032, and foretinib. Collectively, our work introduces a general computational framework for resolving bulk functional measurements at cell-type and single-cell resolution, providing an attractive new computational tool for drug development and precision medicine.

title: Ten simple rules for developing a reporting appraisal tool
abstract: by Kyle Morrison, Malgorzata Lagisz In an ideal world, authors would report clearly and transparently exactly what they conducted. In reality, reporting is often incomplete, and key elements of research conduct are frequently missing from manuscripts. Reporting guidelines were developed to address this problem by helping authors identify what should be reported. These guidelines have been highly valuable for authors, but they are not well suited for appraising reporting during peer review or editorial assessment despite common use. This is because authors and appraisers have different needs: authors require a comprehensive guide for writing, whereas appraisers need a tool that is concise, repeatable, and easy to use. We therefore propose the development of reporting appraisal tools: operationalised tools designed specifically to assess whether a paper has reported the minimum essential elements of a study. To support their development, we present 10 simple rules.

title: Weak dispersal and landscape size inevitably promote local biodiversity in heterogeneous metacommunities of competing species
abstract: by Frederik De Laender, Andrew Gonzalez, Olivia Bleeckx, Dieter Ebert, György Barabás We provide a general theoretical explanation for a longstanding result in spatial ecology: weak dispersal among habitat patches promotes local species richness. Using analytical approximations of spatial Lotka–Volterra competition models, we show that local species persistence in heterogeneous landscapes can be expressed as the balance between the total density across patches and the local exclusion rate. We further demonstrate that local multispecies coexistence is governed by the feasibility domain, linking spatial coexistence to a structural property of nonspatial competitive systems. Together, these results explain why weak dispersal increases local species richness and why this effect strengthens with the number of available patches, i.e., landscape size. We test these predictions using numerical simulations and find that the theory breaks down only when both dispersal and competitive interactions are very strong, in which case dispersal has a unimodal effect on coexistence. In contrast, landscape size retains a positive effect on coexistence whenever an effect is detectable. We then apply the theory to long-term data from a natural metacommunity of microcrustaceans. We detect strong competition among species and find no detectable effect of dispersal rate on local coexistence, whereas species co-occurrence increases with local landscape size, as predicted by theory. Together, our results identify how dispersal, interaction strength, and landscape size jointly regulate local species richness in competitive systems.

title: From prompts to genomes: A constraint-first framework for AI-driven sequence design across life and viruses
abstract: by Adhityo Wicaksono, Arli Aditya Parikesit A constraint-first framework for future ‘prompt-to-genome’ AI across Bacteria, Archaea, Eukaryota, and viruses is proposed. Genome-scale models can now generate long DNA sequences, and experimentally viable genome-scale designs have begun to appear, but sequence generation alone does not establish biological feasibility. Constraints should not require designs to remain within natural sequence space; rather, they should define testable boundaries for function, inheritance, lifecycle coherence and safe use, including new-to-nature designs. We propose a two-part system. First, a Constraint Compiler translates natural-language prompts into machine-checkable specifications defining scope, context, objectives, assumptions and governance requirements. Second, a modular Validator Stack (C1–C6) evaluates candidate designs for sequence integrity, gene and regulatory plausibility, genome completeness, comparative coherence, systems-level feasibility, and safety and governance. Extreme prompts serve as stress tests to expose hidden assumptions, conflicting objectives, and refusal points, complemented by adversarial testing and risk assessment. A phased roadmap and community benchmarks are proposed to measure specification accuracy, biological feasibility, robustness, and governance performance. The goal is to move prompt-to-genome systems from impressive generation toward reliable, auditable, and accountable biological design.

title: Ten simple rules to build genomics capacity for routine laboratory practice in the Global South
abstract: by Emilyn Costa Conceição, Abhinav Sharma, Davi Josué Marcon, Layana Rufino Ribeiro, Danna Karen Corrêa dos Santos, Lilian Eduarda de Oliveira Freitas, Alex Brito Souza, Hendor Neves Ribeiro de Jesus, Maria Cristina da Silva Lourenço, Valnete das Graças Dantas Andrade, Marco Aurélio Almeida de Oliveira, Tatyana Costa Amorim Ramos, Ítalo José Mesquita Cavalcante, Arabela Leal e Silva de Melo, Nabila Ismail, Tulio de Oliveira, Robin Mark Warren, Adriana Ayden Ferreira, Theolis Costa Barbosa Bessa, Cristiane Cunha Frota, Philip Noel Suffys, Karla Valéria Batista Lima, REVIGET Consortium Developing sustainable genomics capacity in the Global South requires more than technology transfer; it depends on human-centered approaches based on the workflows and existing expertise of laboratory personnel, institutional collaboration, and long-term integration into health systems. Drawing on lessons learned from regional capacity-building initiatives, this article proposes ten simple rules for implementing and sustaining genomics capacity within public health and clinical laboratory settings. These rules emphasize local context, strategic planning, continuous learning, and equitable collaboration. Together, they provide a roadmap for laboratories aiming to transform genomic technologies from research tools for diagnosis, surveillance and decision-making, into routine instruments for public health in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Leveraging spatial structure to design spatially-targeted malaria interventions at the community-scale
abstract: by Michelle V. Evans, Benjamin Roche, Vincent Herbreteau, Christophe Révillion, Thibault Catry, Matthew H. Bonds, Karen E. Finnegan, Ezra Mitsinjoniala, Felana A. Ihantamalala, Mauricianot Randriamihaja, Oméga Raobela, Andres Garchitorena Progress in malaria control has stagnated since the early 21st century in many countries, requiring new approaches such as the use of spatially-targeted interventions. However, evidence on the effectiveness of spatially-targeted interventions is mixed, depending on both the setting and intervention. In addition, the potential role of community health programs in implementing spatial targeting is underexplored, with models focusing on coarser spatial scales than those needed to guide programmatic activities. We developed a two-age-class, spatially-explicit model of malaria at the community-scale for a district in southeastern Madagascar, accounting for environmental heterogeneity and spatial structure, to explore spatially-targeted community health interventions. The model was fit to field-based case notifications and malaria prevalence data and then used to simulate three interventions: indoor residual spraying (IRS), supplemental coverage of long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLIN), and active case detection (ACD). We compared five scenarios, one with no spatial targeting and others targeting communities (i) nearest to clinics, (ii) furthest from clinics, (iii) with highest incidence, and (iv) that are spatially central. The non-targeted intervention was generally the most effective, but the least resource efficient. The second most effective intervention was based on spatial centrality, which reached a larger population while using fewer transportation resources than the non-targeted intervention. No combination of interventions was able to eliminate malaria in the district, although detecting symptomatic cases through ACD could avert 100% of severe malaria cases at high detection rates. These results highlight the potential for targeted malaria interventions, especially in low-income settings, that take into account spatial structure in the human population and transport networks to reduce malaria burdens using fewer resources than conventional district-wide interventions. [A French language abstract is available as Text A in S1 Appendix].

title: Computation-through-Dynamics Toolkit: Simulated datasets and quality metrics for dynamical models of neural activity
abstract: by Christopher Versteeg, Jonathan D. McCart, Mitchell Ostrow, David M. Zoltowski, Clayton B. Washington, Laura Driscoll, Olivier Codol, Jonathan A. Michaels, Scott W. Linderman, David Sussillo, Chethan Pandarinath A primary goal of systems neuroscience is to discover how ensembles of neurons transform inputs into goal-directed behavior, a process known as neural computation. A powerful framework for understanding neural computation uses neural dynamics – the rules that govern how neural activity evolves over time – to explain how goal-directed input-output transformations occur. As dynamical rules are not directly observable, we need computational models that can infer neural dynamics from recorded neural activity. We typically validate such models using synthetic datasets with known ground-truth dynamics, but unfortunately existing synthetic datasets don’t reflect fundamental features of neural computation and may therefore be poor proxies for neural systems. Further, the field lacks validated metrics for quantifying the accuracy of the dynamics inferred by models. The Computation-through-Dynamics Toolkit (CtDToolkit) addresses these critical gaps by providing: 1) synthetic datasets that reflect computational properties of biological neural circuits, 2) interpretable metrics for quantifying model performance, and 3) a standardized pipeline for training and evaluating models with or without known external inputs. In this manuscript, we demonstrate how CtDToolkit can help guide the development, tuning, and troubleshooting of neural dynamics models. In summary, CtDToolkit provides a necessary framework for model developers to better understand and characterize neural computation through the lens of dynamics.

title: How compartmentalization and proliferation shape the splenic T cell repertoire during an immune response to a complex antigen in mice
abstract: by Franka Buytenhuijs, Cornelia Tune, Thomas C. Smits, Andrea Schampel, Lisa-Kristin Schierloh, René Pagel, Jürgen Westermann, Johannes Textor The adaptive immune system recognizes billions of unique antigens using highly variable T cell receptors (TCRs). To what extent TCR features shape the spatial distribution of the TCR repertoire (TCR-R) within lymphoid organs remains unclear. Here, we compared the TCR-R composition in T cell zones (TCZ), B cell zones (BCZ), and germinal centers (GC) of the spleen by analyzing the complementarity-determining region 3 of the beta chain (CDR3β) in microdissected splenic compartments from naïve and immunized mice. While we found substantial differences in TCR-R composition between these compartments, these differences largely disappeared once the effects of compartment size and proliferation were accounted for: During steady state, the few T cells found in BCZs strongly resemble random subsets of those found in TCZs. After immunization, expanded clones started appearing in the TCZ at day 3 and later shifted to the BCZ. GCs harbored even further expanded clones that were grouped into clusters with high sequence similarity. TCR-R differences during the immune response were well explained by a Galton-Watson model of T cell proliferation, suggesting that this could be the central factor shaping the observed TCR-R differences. Similarly, while TCR length and closeness to germline initially showed more pronounced differences between the compartments, our models of random distribution and proliferation explained these differences almost entirely. Hence, our findings suggest that splenic TCR-Rs are shaped predominantly by compartment size and proliferation rates rather than TCR sequence features. This would imply that quantitative assessment of TCR-R dynamics across heterogeneous spatial compartments during an immune response is only possible when these effects are explicitly accounted for.

title: MEGH-DDI: MolT5-driven edge-aware graph learning with Hop2Token representation for drug–drug interaction prediction
abstract: by Li Zhou, Yun Zuo, Wenying He, Zhaohong Deng Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are critical in pharmacology, as synergistic or antagonistic effects between co-administered drugs can enhance therapeutic outcomes or cause toxicity, posing major challenges for drug safety assessment and new drug development. Current molecular representation methods often fail to capture dynamic substructure relationships or semantic interactions among functional groups. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes MEGH-DDI, a multimodal framework that integrates complementary molecular representation learning with graph-structure dynamic perception. The framework employs a dual-channel semantic module that combines Mol2vec-based substructure representations with MolT5 chemical language embeddings, while SHAP-based dynamic feature selection reduces redundancy. For fine-grained structural modeling, we introduce an edge-aware GCNII equipped with bond-level attention to distinguish different types of chemical bonds. Furthermore, the Hop2Token module converts multi-hop neighborhoods into token sequences, enabling Transformer-based modeling of high-order substructure dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that MEGH-DDI achieves competitive performance across both transductive and inductive settings. On the DrugBank dataset, MEGH-DDI attains an accuracy of 98.36% in the transductive task, outperforming earlier baselines and surpassing recent state-of-the-art methods, with both AUC and AP exceeding 99.7%. On the ChChMiner dataset, MEGH-DDI achieves an F1 score of 99.05%, improving over the best existing method by 2.74 percentage points. In the inductive settings, MEGH-DDI achieves competitive performance across most evaluation metrics on both datasets, showing advantages over competing methods on several key metrics. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MEGH-DDI in predicting DDI involving previously unseen drugs and its potential to generalize to complex DDI prediction scenarios. To enhance interpretability, MEGH-DDI incorporates a three-level mechanism spanning atoms, chemical bonds, and topological paths, highlighting key atoms and bond contributions. Overall, MEGH-DDI provides an efficient, accurate, and interpretable solution for drug safety assessment and new drug discovery. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Lilyjoys/MEGH-DDI, and a free web platform is provided at http://www.edgh-ddi.com.
authors: ["Li Zhou", "Yun Zuo", "Wenying He", "Zhaohong Deng"]

title: Diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence in early diagnosis of mosquito-borne viral infections: Systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: by Flavia Pennisi, Antonio Pinto, Claudia Cozzolino Cangiano, Giovanni Rezza, Carlo Signorelli, Vincenzo Baldo, Vincenza Gianfredi Early diagnosis of mosquito-borne viral infections is challenging because initial symptoms are often nonspecific and confirmatory testing may be delayed or unavailable. We synthesised evidence on artificial intelligence and machine learning models for the early diagnosis of dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. We conducted a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420251129670). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to 11 August 2025 for model-development or validation studies reporting diagnostic performance. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were pooled using random-effects models, while sensitivity and specificity were jointly synthesised using a bivariate random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Database searches identified 4,531 records, of which 43 studies met the inclusion criteria. The evidence was predominantly from Asia and overwhelmingly focused on dengue; no eligible studies evaluated West Nile virus, yellow fever, or Rift Valley fever. Pooled estimates were 0.954 (95% CI 0.936–0.968) for AUC, 0.904 (95% CI 0.888–0.918) for accuracy, 0.903 (95% CI 0.876–0.925) for PPV, and 0.882 (95% CI 0.859–0.902) for NPV. The bivariate pooled sensitivity was 0.861 (95% CI 0.809–0.900) and specificity was 0.902 (95% CI 0.871–0.927). Heterogeneity was substantial for the univariate outcomes (I 2 95.8%–97.7%). Most studies were at high overall risk of bias, while calibration and external validation were uncommon. Artificial intelligence models showed encouraging diagnostic performance in the published literature, but the pooled estimates should be interpreted as descriptive summaries of a highly heterogeneous evidence base rather than as definitive estimates of real-world performance. Prospective, externally validated, well-calibrated, and geographically diverse studies are needed before routine clinical implementation can be recommended.

title: Decision-making pathways for adopting, implementing, and scaling gamified physical activity interventions in municipal policy and practice in the Netherlands
abstract: by Ayla Schwarz, Maarten van Bottenburg, Monique Simons Municipalities increasingly pilot gamified physical activity (PA) interventions, yet few progress beyond pilots. This qualitative study examined decision-making pathways through which Dutch municipalities adopt, implement, and scale digital gamified PA interventions, using the case of ‘Missie Master’. A two-phase design was applied, combining exploratory interviews with policymakers, health professionals, and a company (phase 1), followed by two multi-stakeholder workshops and follow-up interviews with municipalities new to gamification (phase 2). Thematic analysis showed that adoption was driven by informal processes, enthusiastic individuals, trust in product reliability, and peer recommendations, while generic company outreach was ignored. Implementation relied on early preparatory capacity, such as designated coordinators, marketing plans, and timely app updates. Scaling was rare and cyclical, dependent on political support, cross-domain alignment, and short communication lines. The study offers a practical decision guide and highlights monitoring needs. Policy implications include transparent evaluation pathways, structured early implementation, and strengthened public-private co-development.
authors: ["Ayla Schwarz", "Maarten van Bottenburg", "Monique Simons"]

title: Structural limits of single-barrier reform in algorithmic recourse: A formal series-system model with implications for digital health
abstract: by A. C. Demidont Algorithmic decision systems mediate access to healthcare, credit, employment and housing, yet individuals who experience adverse decisions face multi-stage barriers when seeking recourse. We formalize these barriers as a series-structured system with 11 empirically parameterized stages across three layers (data integration, data accuracy and institutional access) and prove that single-barrier interventions are bounded by baseline system success. Under baseline parameterization derived from federal datasets and peer-reviewed algorithmic audit studies, end-to-end recourse probability is 0.0018%. Removing any single barrier yields negligible improvement (<0.02%). Factorial decomposition reveals that the three-way cross-layer interaction accounts for 87.6% of achievable improvement, illustrated by Shapley attribution, Sobol sensitivity analysis and bootstrap resampling (n = 1,000) within prespecified perturbation ranges. Introducing dependence among the stage pass-events with a Gaussian-copula analysis (latent correlation up to ρ = 0.5), while preserving each marginal pass probability, leaves the comparative conclusion—single-layer reform yields far less than coordinated reform—intact, while a repeated-attempt topology attenuates it, delimiting the model’s domain of validity. These findings are properties of the modeled system rather than empirical measurements of real recourse pathways; they yield testable hypotheses for digital-health governance—chiefly that single-layer fairness interventions are structurally unlikely to produce large absolute gains—pending validation against observed recourse data.
authors: ["A. C. Demidont"]

title: Quantitative assessment of collagen architecture from routine histopathological images shows concordance with Second Harmonic Generation microscopy
abstract: by Vedant Ingawale, Krishnendu Dandapat, Jyothsna Konkada Manattayil, Shashank Gupta, L. S. Shashidhara, Chaitanyanand Koppiker, Nameeta Shah, Varun Raghunathan, Madhura Kulkarni Collagen organization within the tumour microenvironment plays a critical role in tumour progression and has emerged as an important structural biomarker in cancer. Second Harmonic Generation (SHG) microscopy enables label-free visualization and quantitative assessment of fibrillar collagen architecture; however, its high cost, specialized instrumentation, and limited field-of-view restrict routine clinical application. In this study, we evaluated whether collagen features quantified from digitally scanned Masson–Goldner’s Trichrome-stained histopathological sections can approximate measurements obtained from SHG microscopy. Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded breast tumour tissues, including benign and invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) samples with varying collagen content, were analysed using SHG microscopy and whole-slide brightfield imaging. Matched regions of interest were analysed using two independent digital image analysis approaches: a conventional ImageJ-based workflow (TWOMBLI) and a machine learning–based computational pipeline. Collagen structural parameters including collagen deposition area, fibre number, and alignment metrics were quantified and compared across imaging modalities using correlation analysis. SHG signals were consistently detected from Trichrome-stained sections, confirming compatibility of SHG imaging. Quantitative comparison demonstrated significant concordance between SHG-derived collagen metrics and those obtained from digital image analysis pipelines, particularly for collagen area and fibre alignment. These findings demonstrate a proof-of-concept, that computational analysis of routine histopathological images can capture key spatial features of collagen organization comparable to SHG microscopy. Digital pathology–based collagen quantification therefore represents a potentially scalable and clinically accessible approach for assessing extracellular matrix architecture in tumour tissues.

title: Refocusing algorithmic fairness on feature-level bias: A diagnostic approach using dutch EHR data
abstract: by Cathleen S. Parsons, Shelley-Ann M. Girwar, Sepinoud Azimi, Marco R. Spruit, Marcel R. Haas While algorithmic fairness research in healthcare has predominantly focused on disparities in model performance, less attention has been given to the underlying data structures that may drive such disparities. High-level fairness metrics often obscure the deeper feature-level dynamics necessary for a critical and context-aware assessment of fairness. To address this gap, we propose and apply a diagnostic framework termed Feature-Level Bias Identification And Sensemaking (FL-BIAS). As a case study, we conducted a secondary analysis of a retrospective cross-sectional cohort study using electronic health record data from Dutch general practitioners, linked with sociodemographic data from Statistics Netherlands. The dataset included 112,872 patients, of whom 16.2% had a non-Western migration background. Hospitalization in the following year was modeled using Johns Hopkins Aggregated Diagnosis Groups (ADGs). We trained logistic regression and XGBoost models on different subgroup datasets to evaluate performance disparities using fairness metrics. To analyze feature-level contributions to predictions and errors, we applied Kernel Shapley Values and Cohort Shapley methods. Exploratory analysis revealed significant differences in socioeconomic status (SES) and ADG distributions between Dutch and non-Western groups, though Multiple Correspondence Analysis showed minimal structural variation. Mediation analysis indicated that the effect of migration background on hospitalization was largely mediated by SES, with potential unobserved confounding. While standard fairness metrics indicated modest bias in favor of non-Western patients, deeper feature-level analyses revealed subgroup-specific patterns of variable importance that suggest potentially less favorable underlying conditions. For instance, malignancy (ADG 32) had a stronger predictive impact among non-Western patients but contributed less to false negatives compared to Dutch patients, possibly reflecting structural disparities in cancer diagnosis and care. These findings highlight the need for contextual, multi-level evaluations of algorithmic bias. Fairness in healthcare algorithms must be approached as a socio-technical challenge, requiring multidisciplinary collaboration to uncover root causes in the processes that generate the data.
authors: ["Cathleen S. Parsons", "Shelley-Ann M. Girwar", "Sepinoud Azimi", "Marco R. Spruit", "Marcel R. Haas"]

title: External validation and adaptation of the Computational Barthel Index Tool in a large nursing home cohort
abstract: by Lemba Priscille Ngana, Janusz Wojtusiak, Atefehsadat Haghighathoseini, Bhumi Patel, Dharmi Desai The Computational Barthel Index Tool (CBIT), originally developed using U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) data, predicts future dependency in activities of daily living up to one year in advance. This study externally validated CBIT in a large non-VA nursing home population and evaluated whether population-specific adaptation could recover performance following external transport. We analyzed SEER-Medicare linked data, including 843,836 patients and over 8 million Minimum Data Set (MDS) assessments. The predictor and outcome structures of the original CBIT models were reconstructed in the SEER-Medicare cohort. Pretrained models were evaluated without modification for discrimination and calibration at current, 3-, 6-, and 12-month prediction timeframes. Population-specific adaptation was evaluated using progressively larger subsets of SEER-Medicare training data and compared with model reconstruction in the SEER-Medicare. Under strict external validation, discrimination declined relative to the original VA models, particularly for longer-term predictions. For evaluation models, mean AUC decreased from 0.795 in the original models to 0.693 at current prediction, 0.595 at 3 months, 0.595 at 6 months, and 0.592 at 12 months. Re-evaluation models showed stronger but similarly declining external performance. Calibration error increased, particularly for evaluation models at longer timeframes. Subgroup analyses showed modest variation in discrimination across demographic and clinical groups. Population-specific adaptation substantially recovered discrimination, with performance improving as more SEER-Medicare training data were incorporated. Using the adaptation training set, adapted models achieved performance comparable to SEER-Medicare model reconstruction. External validation revealed substantial performance degradation when CBIT was transported to a non-VA population. Population-specific adaptation recovered much of this performance loss, supporting a structured approach to clinical ML transportability in which pretrained models are externally validated first, followed by adaptation when performance degradation is observed. Full model reconstruction remains an alternative when sufficient local data are available.

title: An artificial intelligence-based audio recognition system for dysarthria home-based rehabilitation: A proof-of-concept study
abstract: by Vicente Sancenon, Pamela Y. S. Oh, Elvina K. W. Tay, Jarrod Z. X. Lee, Megan L. E. Soon, Han Leong Goh, Nicodemus Oey, Andy W. A. Ta Dysarthria is a common motor speech disorder affecting individuals with neurological conditions, with high prevalence among stroke survivors. Effective treatment of dysarthria requires accurate assessment of severity and the provision of speech exercises tailored to the degree of impairment. However, traditional speech intervention faces several limitations, including limited accessibility to therapists and low treatment adherence rates. AI-driven solutions have the potential to address these limitations by automating the detection of dysarthria severity and recommending personalized exercises. Although substantial progress has been made in the automated detection and classification of dysarthria severity, the performance of these approaches on less controlled, real-world speech remains insufficiently characterized. This proof-of-concept study describes the development and evaluation of Whisper-ST1, a novel framework for classifying dysarthric speech severity from audio files by fine-tuning a pretrained automatic speech recognition model. Our framework builds on previous studies by incorporating real-world data alongside traditional research datasets, adapting a model architecture pretrained on a large corpus of audio data, applying a progressive unfreezing strategy to prevent catastrophic forgetting of relevant speech features while promoting flexible adaptation to the new task, and implementing an ordinal regression loss to minimize the impact of misclassification errors. Ablation experiments demonstrate the performance contributions of individual pipeline components in isolation. Whisper-ST1 achieves 79% [67% – 100%] per-speaker F1 in the classification of dysarthria severity when tested on real-world samples, and shows strong agreement with two speech therapists’ ratings of dysarthria (Weighted Cohen’s kappa of 0.814 [0.400 – 1.000] and 0.878 [0.647 – 1.000]), comparable to inter-therapist agreement (0.851 [0.550 – 1.000]). Model errors are predominantly confined to adjacent severity levels, suggesting preservation of ordinal structure. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of leveraging pretrained speech models for dysarthria severity classification in heterogeneous audio conditions. and provide a foundational step toward AI-assisted tools for remote monitoring and support of dysarthria rehabilitation.

title: Assessment of change in drug-induced parkinsonism in daily-life gait using vision-based machine learning
abstract: by Benjamin Filtjens, Vida Adeli, Soroush Mehraban, Andrea Sabo, Babak Taati, Andrea Iaboni Drug-induced parkinsonism is a potentially reversible movement disorder that may be subtle and difficult to monitor in residential dementia care. Vision-based machine learning analysis of gait may provide unobtrusive longitudinal monitoring around medication changes. We conducted a two-center cohort study of 61 residents with dementia receiving psychotropic medication. Hallway gait sequences were recorded using ceiling-mounted cameras and converted to three-dimensional body pose. A TabPFN classifier estimated UPDRS-III item 29 gait severity for each walk. We evaluated associations between acute antipsychotic (AP) and antidepressant (AD) dose reduction/cessation (≥50% dose reduction or cessation, 0–21 days after change) and daily mean predicted gait severity using linear mixed-effects models in ever-exposed participants, with complementary equal-weight paired analyses among participants observed in both medication states. In mixed-effects models, acute AP dose reduction/cessation was associated with lower predicted gait severity (β=−0.127, p = 0.022), whereas AD dose reduction/cessation was not (β=−0.060, p = 0.210). Equal-weight paired analyses found no statistically significant participant-average within-person change among paired participants (AP mean change = 0.031, 95% CI [−0.114, 0.176], p = 0.653; AD mean change =−0.021, 95% CI [−0.098, 0.056], p = 0.575), consistent with heterogeneous individual responses. Vision-based monitoring captured within-participant gait variation around psychotropic dose-reduction periods, but findings are associative. Larger prospective studies with documented reasons for medication changes are needed before using such monitoring to guide medication decisions.

title: Identifying facilitators of and barriers to digital health literacy in pediatric rheumatic disease: A scoping review
abstract: by Craig Eling, Alan M. Rosenberg, Jennifer N. Stinson, Maryam Mehtar, Jasmin Bhawra, Roona Sinha, Donna Goodridge Digital health (DH) technologies have the potential to benefit pediatric patients with rheumatic diseases and their caregivers. Digital health literacy (DHL) refers to the knowledge and skills necessary to use technology and the internet to manage and communicate about health. The aim of this scoping review is to identify facilitators of and barriers to DHL and map them to the Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation Model of Behavior (COM-B Model) for children and adolescents with rheumatic diseases and their primary caregivers. We searched MEDLINE, CINAHL, Embase, Web of Science, and ProQuest for English full-text primary research studies. Facilitators of and barriers to DHL identified were codified and mapped to the COM-B Model. This review adhered to the JBI scoping review framework and conformed to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-Scoping Review guidelines. Of the 5789 unique records, 44 met inclusion criteria. All the included studies did not explicitly address the concept and impact of DHL. However, the studies identified promoting and detracting factors that matched the definition of DHL. Thus, these were coded as facilitators of and barriers to DHL. The COM-B Model domain of psychological capability emerged as a major determinant of DHL. The COM-B Model domain of psychological capability emerged as a prominent source of facilitators of and barriers to DHL. The design, function, language, and presentation of DH crafted to meet the developmental and educational needs of the user were essential to improving DHL. Likewise, providers fostering quality communication and answering medical and technical questions arising from DH use fostered DHL in the domain of physical opportunity. Addressing DHL requires consideration across clinical, administrative, design, and research contexts.
