title: Contribution of artificial intelligence research to the development of inclusive applications for people with disabilities: A scoping review (2015–2025)
abstract: by Soutongnoma Safiata Kaboré, Azadeh Bayani, Léandre Parfait Epoh Ewane, Davllyn Santos Oliveira dos Anjos, Jean Noel Nikiéma, Muriel Mac-Seing Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare. Yet people with disabilities (PWD), representing 16% of the global population, remain disproportionately excluded from these advances. This exclusion is driven by algorithmic bias, non-representative datasets, and limited involvement of PWD in the design, development, and evaluation of AI applications. This scoping review examines the extent to which AI research in health contributes to the development of inclusive technologies for PWD, focusing on equity considerations. It identifies current trends, methodological gaps, and opportunities for socially responsive innovation. We conducted a systematic search across MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL for the 2015–2025 period, following Arksey and O’Malley’s five-stage scoping review methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Data were extracted and synthesized thematically using the Population-Concept-Context approach. Of 4,233 references retrieved, 93 studies were included. Most studies originated from high-income countries, particularly in North America (45.2%) and Europe (26.9%). AI applications addressed motor, sensory, cognitive, communication-related, and psychosocial disabilities, with emphasis on prediction/diagnosis, assistive technologies, and personalized care. While about 60% of studies referenced equity, only 12 (12.9%) implemented concrete measures (e.g., adapting tools for vulnerable groups or ensuring sample diversity), and only six (6.5%) actively involved PWD through co-design or user validation. AI holds significant potential to enhance autonomy, access, and quality of life for PWD. Realizing this promise will require moving beyond technical optimization to embrace inclusive design, participatory methods, and equity-driven frameworks aligned with responsible AI development and use.

title: Demographic subgroup-aware analysis of blood pressure predictive models
abstract: by Blessing Kolawole, Sinuo Fan, Yingjie Lao, Valencia J. Koomson Blood pressure (BP) is an important cardiovascular health indicator, usually monitored non-invasively with a sphygmomanometer, which can be bulky and inconvenient for real-time monitoring. Blood pressure estimation using photoplethysmography (PPG) waveform analysis offers a promising alternative for intermittent or continuous cuff-less BP monitoring. However, changes in vascularization due to individual physiology and age can directly affect the morphology of the PPG waveform. Thus, prediction accuracy requires a demographic-aware approach. To address these challenges, we trained three conventional ML models for BP prediction and conducted a subgroup-aware analysis to evaluate model performance across individual and intersectional demographic groups. Additionally, we show that signal quality assessment is a pivotal step in the signal-processing pipeline before feature extraction to mitigate external perturbations (e.g., motion artifacts) in the PPG waveform. We achieve a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.36 mmHg for systolic blood pressure (SBP) and 1.76 mmHg for diastolic BP (DBP) with models trained when signal quality assessment is incorporated.

title: Perceptions, attitudes, and concerns of underrepresented groups regarding the use of big data in children and young people’s healthcare research – A systematic literature review
abstract: by Charlotte Burdge, Anne-Marie Burn, Lily Zhang, Sasha Menon, Karolina Kaminska, Sophie Wallace-Hanlon, Maria Fischer, Camille Evans, Peter Fonagy, Anna Wiedemann, Jessica Young, Anna Moore, Joanna K. Anderson Children and young people (CYP), and those from underserved groups, remain underrepresented in biomedical research. Understanding their perspectives on large-scale, data-driven healthcare research is essential to ensuring that such approaches are acceptable, ethically conducted, and equitable. This review is the first to systematically examine the perceptions, attitudes, and concerns of underrepresented groups regarding the use of big data in CYP healthcare research. Seven bibliographic databases, ASSIA, CINAHL, EMBASE, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science, were searched alongside grey literature sources. A mixed-methods systematic review design was used. Included studies captured the views of CYP, particularly those from underserved groups, as well as their parents or carers, acting as proxy decision-makers, regarding the use of big data in paediatric healthcare research. Study quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), and findings were integrated through narrative synthesis. Seventeen studies were included, capturing perspectives from 6,261 participants, including at least 4,710 CYP and 1,443 parents and carers; one study did not report participant numbers separately by group. Underrepresented groups expressed broadly favourable, but conditional, support for the use of big data in paediatric healthcare research. Willingness to share data was shaped by participant characteristics, lived experience, and trust in institutions. Perceived benefits included societal and public health gains, the opportunity to empower others with similar experiences, and the advancement of scientific progress. Concerns centred on privacy, the risk of re-identification, data misuse, commercial exploitation, and limited transparency in data governance. Conditions for acceptable data use included robust anonymisation, independent ethical oversight, and developmentally appropriate consent processes. Underrepresented groups hold broadly supportive, but conditional, views on the use of big data in paediatric healthcare research. Embedding inclusive governance practices and engaging these communities in research design will be essential to ensuring that data-driven paediatric research is both ethical and equitable.

title: Co-developing Georgia’s National Digital Health Strategy through a multistakeholder convergence workshop: An implementation case study from the WHO European Region
abstract: by Nato Gzirishili, Mehar Grover, Resham Sethi, Mariam Beridze, Tomas Roubal, Lela Sulaberidze, Karapet Davtyan, Silviu Domente, Karthik Adapa National digital health strategies (DHS) are widely recognized as essential for advancing universal health coverage. However, published evidence on operational, multi-stakeholder approaches to co-development—particularly beyond the Asian and African settings where convergence methodology has previously been applied—remains limited. This study details the application of a convergence-based methodology to validate and refine the draft National DHS of Georgia, an upper-middle-income country, aligning it with European Union frameworks. An implementation case study was conducted in Georgia from June to September 2025. Central to this was the Multistakeholder Convergence Workshop, adapted from the Asian Development Bank Digital Health Convergence Meeting Toolkit and a four-phase blueprint methodology. Forty-seven participants from diverse sectors (public, private, academia, and development partners) collaborated in five thematic working groups. They reviewed the draft DHS, generating recommendations that were synthesized against the seven WHO-ITU eHealth strategy building blocks using hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis by two independent coders with third-party arbitration. The revised strategy comprises six strategic goals and 38 priority activities. Key technical recommendations included adopting a federated data governance model, utilizing the existing national identification number instead of a separate Health ID, and establishing a national Health Information Exchange. The strategy endorses FHIR for data exchange, LOINC for laboratory data, and the WHO-FIC (including ICD-11) complemented by SNOMED CT. Governance recommendations emphasized enacting a stand-alone Digital Health Act, forming a dedicated Digital Health Unit within the MoIDPLHSA, integrating digital health into professional education, and extending the strategy horizon to 2030 with a mid-2026 review checkpoint. Structured convergence methodologies, initially developed for Asian settings, can be effectively adapted for upper-middle-income WHO European Region countries pursuing European Health Data Space alignment. This approach produced technically specific outputs, reinforced national ownership, and supported Georgia’s transition toward implementation, offering a highly transferable framework for similar contexts.

title: The ethical and regulatory framework of medical artificial intelligence (AI) system’s behavioral performance for image-based diagnostics: An ethical evaluation of the International and European Union Scope
abstract: by Nina Parchmann, Marcin Orzechowski, Daniel Braun, Florian Steger The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for image-based diagnostics is rising rapidly and enables new opportunities for improving clinical diagnostics through high precision and a quick identification of anomalies. However, a technology characterized by a high variability of image data and the opaqueness of AI models within patient care raises ethical challenges and requires protection by an appropriate ethical and regulatory framework. To identify ethical challenges of the ethical and regulatory framework of the behavioral performance of medical AI systems for image-based diagnostics on the international and European Union level, we searched and screened documents in April and May 2025. The documents were thematically evaluated before conducting an ethical analysis. We identified regulations and ethical recommendations that could be divided into five thematic categories: The (i) data basis is regulated by data standardization, data assessment, and data quality. (ii) Reliability considers assessments, the intended performance, robustness, accuracy, and compliance, whereas the (iii) comprehensibility centers on explainability, understandability, and traceability. The (iv) disclosure of the system considers transparency, operational disclosure, and collaborations, and the (v) usability is regulated on resources and competency. This framework could support the autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and (social) justice, however allows a wide range of compliant technical measures that vary in effectiveness. The insufficient technical feasibility to provide security measures against malicious data alteration as well as the dynamic development of attack and defense mechanisms severely challenge the maintenance of a compliant safe and secure diagnostic AI system. Thereby, the autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and (social) justice could be jeopardized. In conclusion, AI image-based diagnostic systems are regulated by a similar ethical and regulatory framework as general medical AI systems. To protect data and the intended performance, sufficient protection through a regulatory framework is necessary that responds to the challenges of image-based AI diagnostic systems.

title: Allostatic load, genetic susceptibility, and lung cancer risk: Evidence from a prospective cohort and integrative proteomic analyses
abstract: by Fan Yang, Wei Wang, Fangyi Chen, Zhichao Wang, Yifan Wang, Tianchen Qi, Zhazheng He, Shuang Liang, Qingyin Bu, Xirui Qiu, Dong Jiaqing, Shuai Ren, Juncheng Dai, Xiaoxiao Wang Allostatic load (AL), a composite measure of multisystem dysregulation associated with chronic stress, has been linked to lung cancer risk. However, its joint effects with genetic susceptibility and the biological pathways underlying this relationship remain unclear. We conducted a prospective cohort study of 336,945 UK Biobank participants to assess associations between AL and lung cancer incidence and its histological subtypes. A polygenic risk score was constructed to evaluate the joint associations of AL and genetic susceptibility. We further assessed whether AL provided incremental risk stratification beyond established low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening eligibility frameworks and integrated plasma proteomic data using machine learning, enrichment, and mediation analyses. We found that higher AL was associated with an increased risk of lung cancer (per-unit HR = 1.073, 95% CI: 1.053–1.094; Low vs. Normal HR = 1.284, 95% CI: 1.065–1.547; High vs. Normal HR = 1.629, 95% CI: 1.347–1.971). Subtype analyses revealed the strongest effect for small-cell lung cancer (SCLC), with significant associations also observed for lung adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. High AL combined with high genetic risk was associated with a 136.9% increased risk (HR = 2.369, 95% CI: 1.565–3.583), without evidence of interaction. AL provided additional risk discrimination beyond established LDCT screening eligibility criteria. Proteomic analyses identified 111 AL-associated proteins and 34 proteins with potential mediation signal, including HGF, RARRES2, and GDF15, implicating inflammatory, metabolic, and growth factor-related processes as biological correlates of the AL–lung cancer association. In conclusion, higher AL was independently associated with lung cancer risk, particularly SCLC. Integrative proteomic analyses provided exploratory evidence for biological pathways that may link cumulative physiological dysregulation to lung carcinogenesis. Incorporating AL, as a composite biomarker reflecting cumulative physiological burden, into risk models may improve risk stratification and help identify individuals at elevated risk.

title: Pathologies and technologies for digital therapeutics: An analysis of global clinical trials
abstract: by Paolo Rocco, Valentina Pagella, Umberto M. Musazzi, Sara Manellari, Elena Paola Lanati, Paola Minghetti CDigital therapeutics (DTx) are software-based medical devices that deliver evidence-based therapeutic interventions directly to patients. While the clinical use of DTx is expanding rapidly, regulatory fragmentation and the absence of harmonized legal definitions hinder their assessment and reimbursement policies, as well as their integration into healthcare systems. There is currently a lack of comprehensive overviews of DTx clinical development, which are essential for informing policy, research and regulatory priorities. This paper provides an updated overview of randomised clinical trials involving DTx. 254 eligible trials on DTx, (defined according to ISO/TR 11147:2023) registered through January 2025 were identified through a search on C linicalTrials.gov . Mobile applications represent the most prevalent technology (65%), followed by web-based tools and virtual reality (20%). Psychiatric disorders are the primary therapeutic target (52% of the studies) with insomnia, depression, and anxiety being the most addressed conditions. Trials were primarily conducted in North America (41%) and Europe (32%), where Germany, Spain, and Italy represent the most active countries. The analysis of clinical trials registrations on ClinicalTrials.gov reveals a heterogenous geographical distribution of DTx development but also a clear direction in the type of conditions for which they are mostly indicated, namely psychiatric and nervous system disorders. The fragmented policies on DTx reimbursement, even among EU countries, and the different capacity of governments to fund DTx research and development emerge as key factors, along with cultural and ethical issues, in determining the willingness of the industry to invest in these devices.

title: A longitudinal analysis of real world symptom tracking and patient-reported outcomes in Brisa, a German Digital Health App for multiple sclerosis
abstract: by Ann-Sophie Stratil, Steffeni Papukchieva, Julia Steinmetz-Späh, Natalie Joschko, Lars Masanneck, Benjamin Friedrich, Tjalf Ziemssen Brisa , a companion app designed for multiple sclerosis (MS) patients, can support the patient journey by collecting longitudinal real-world data. This study aimed to characterize the demographic and clinical profile of Brisa users and longitudinal trends in app engagement, self-reported symptoms and patient-reported outcomes (PROs). This retrospective analysis included Brisa users aged ≥18 years, reported use of category 1 (low), 2 (medium), or 3 (high efficacy) disease-modifying therapy (DMT) according to German DGN guidelines, and had no medication switching. Users diagnosed within 0–1 years were classified as newly diagnosed cases. App engagement was defined as any screen activity; disengagement was defined as >180 consecutive days without engagement and analysed using Cox proportional hazards regression. Symptoms were rated on a 1–5 emoticon-based scale (1 = poor, 5 = excellent). PROs included the MFIS, PDDS, PDQ-5, IVIS, and PES. Among 4,194 users, the majority were female (80.8%), aged 26–35 years (30.5%) and diagnosed with relapsing-remitting MS (77.4%), with 27.9% newly diagnosed. Consistent with a shift towards high-efficacy treatment, use of category 3 (high-efficacy) DMTs among newly diagnosed users significantly increased from 2023 to 2024/2025 (χ 2 , p < 0.0001). In engagement analyses, users receiving category 3 DMTs, those aged ≥36 years, and newly diagnosed users showed a significantly lower risk of disengagement compared with users on category 1 DMTs, aged 18–25 years or diagnosed ≥2 years prior. Overall, about 76.0% of users tracked at least one symptom or PRO. Longitudinally, among users with ≥1 year of tracking, symptom and PRO scores remained largely stable. A shift toward higher efficacy treatment in newly diagnosed users was observed, while symptom and PRO scores remained largely stable over time. These findings highlight the potential of digital health tools for tracking treatment patterns, patient engagement and self-reported symptom changes in MS.

title: A machine learning model for in-hospital mortality prediction in patients with sepsis-related myocardial injury
abstract: by Da-cheng Wang, Yan-pin Liu, Yu-ting Wang, Xiao-huan Zhuang, Xiao-peng Yin, Xin-yuan Zhang, Yan Zhuang Sepsis-related myocardial injury (SRMI) is associated with high mortality, but the transportability of prediction models across heterogeneous cohorts remains uncertain. We developed and externally validated a machine learning model for in-hospital mortality prediction in SRMI and evaluated its discrimination, calibration, interpretability, and distributional shift across cohorts. Using MIMIC-IV for development and MIMIC-III and a local cohort for external validation (n = 1,226, 962, and 280, respectively), we compared eight classification algorithms. A two-stage feature-selection strategy, recursive feature accumulation and sequential elimination with incremental feature evaluation, ranked 31 candidate variables to derive a parsimonious predictor set. The selected model was evaluated for discrimination, precision-recall performance, calibration, clinical utility, and risk stratification. Logistic recalibration, population stability index (PSI) analysis, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to assess probability alignment, cross-cohort distributional shift, and model interpretability. Feature selection reduced 31 candidate variables to 8 predictors with little loss of cross-validated performance (AUC, 0.819 with 31 variables versus 0.810 with 8 variables). The selected random forest model achieved an AUC of 0.819 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.787-0.848) and a PR-AUC of 0.702 (0.657-0.751) in MIMIC-III, and an AUC of 0.758 (0.693-0.816) and a PR-AUC of 0.525 (0.435-0.630) in the local cohort. Recalibration reduced the Brier score from 0.162 to 0.147 in MIMIC-III and from 0.233 to 0.196 in the local cohort. PSI indicated minimal distributional shift between MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-III but substantial shift in the local cohort, particularly for SOFA score, respiratory rate, and prothrombin time. SHAP identified prothrombin time, invasive ventilation, lactate, temperature, and urine output as major contributors to model predictions. In two external cohorts, an 8-variable random forest model showed moderate discrimination for mortality prediction in SRMI. The evaluation of external performance, calibration, distributional shift, and SHAP-based explanations provides an assessment of model transportability. Prospective validation is needed before clinical deployment.

title: The complexities and contradictions of online eating disorder content: A qualitative evidence synthesis of young people’s views and experiences
abstract: by Meena Khatwa, Rebecca Rees, Claire Stansfield, Vidhi Bassi, Ceri-Nicole Wilkins, Kelly Dickson Eating disorders (ED) continue to be a concern worldwide. There is a growing focus on problematic discourse around ideal bodies as well as on how exposure to related content and spaces online might influence disordered eating and other ED symptoms. A qualitative evidence synthesis using thematic synthesis methods was conducted to explore young people’s lived experiences of online ED content. Studies were included if they provided, from 2007 onwards, views about online content from young people from OECD countries aged 11–25 years old who identified as having had an eating disorder, disordered eating or eating difficulties. This article focuses on findings from 13 included studies whereby three key themes were identified: Comparing – how online content was used to evaluate others and oneself; Curating – how young people manage this content; and Community – spaces for connection over shared experience. Participants across the studies described the complex ‘double-edged’ nature of online spaces, which can offer inclusion but can also be experienced as harmful. The synthesis outlined a lack of supportive offline mental health-promoting spaces as part of the context of young people’s online content use.

title: Perceived value but persistent barriers: A qualitative study of healthcare worker experiences with the Impilo electronic health record system in rural Zimbabwe
abstract: by Shalom Rudorwashe Dube, Perez Livias Moyo, Methembe Yotamu Khozah Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are pivotal for improving healthcare data quality and service delivery. Despite the introduction of the Impilo EHR system at St Anne’s Mission Hospital in Brunapeg, utilisation remains low. This study aimed to explore healthcare workers’ (HCWs) experiences and identify the key barriers and facilitators to Impilo’s utilisation. A descriptive qualitative study was conducted at St Anne’s Mission Hospital. In-depth interviews were conducted with 20 HCWs authorised to use Impilo, selected via purposive sampling until thematic saturation was achieved. Thematic analysis, following the Braun and Clarke approach, was used to analyse the data. Trustworthiness was ensured through multi-coder analysis, the maintenance of an audit trail, and thick descriptive reporting. HCWs reported positive experiences related to ease of data access, improved communication, and better inventory management. However, significant barriers undermine utilisation. The analysis revealed three key themes: (1) Benefits of Impilo, (2) Multifaceted Challenges, and (3) Suggested Improvements. Challenges included pervasive technical and infrastructural issues (e.g., frequent network downtime, lack of offline functionality), human resource constraints leading to dual documentation and increased workload, and subsequent compromised data quality due to inconsistent entry. The underutilisation of the Impilo system is not due to a lack of perceived value but is primarily driven by remediable barriers related to infrastructure, training, and workflow design issues. For successful implementation, interventions must be multifaceted, addressing technical reliability (e.g., offline functionality), human capacity (continuous training and support), and organisational processes (dedicated data clerks and inclusive system redesign). This study provides a framework for improving EHR adoption in similar low-resource rural settings.

title: Monitoring influenza-like symptoms in the UK through participatory surveillance: Insights from FluSurvey over two winter seasons (2023-24 and 2024-25)
abstract: by Rebecca E. Green, Jonathon Mellor, Christopher Rawlinson, Elizabeth Waller, Nurin Abdul Aziz, Conall H. Watson, Gavin Dabrera FluSurvey is a participatory surveillance system used to monitor trends in influenza and other respiratory viruses through weekly symptom surveys among the UK population. We aimed to characterise the wider impact of “influenza-like illnesses” (ILI) among FluSurvey participants and assess correlations of ILI with other established influenza surveillance systems. We included data reported by FluSurvey participants over the 2023–24 and 2024–25 winter seasons. Using weekly symptoms surveys, we derived ILI episodes and estimated the proportion reporting healthcare service use, medication use, impact on daily life, absenteeism and use of tests. We applied existing methodologies (omitting first report and weighting to the age-sex structure of England) and assessed cross-correlations of weekly FluSurvey ILI rates with the national surveillance of GP ILI consultations, influenza hospital admissions, and influenza PCR test positivity at time lags of up to +/-2 weeks. There were 3057 participants over two winter seasons (N 2023-24 = 2540, 63% female, mean age 60 years; N 2024-25 = 2273, 64% female, mean age 61 years). Of 1868 ILI episodes, only a minority contacted healthcare services (14%, most frequently visiting the GP). A large proportion of episodes reported medication use (89%), impact on daily life (75%) and missing school or work (47%). Testing frequency notably declined in the 2024–25 season compared to 2023–24. FluSurvey ILI rates were strongly correlated with other influenza surveillance, predominantly leading GP ILI consultations (max r = 0.73), coinciding with influenza hospital admissions (max r = 0.88) and lagging influenza test positivity (max r = 0.88). The majority of ILI reported to FluSurvey do not contact healthcare due to symptoms but experienced wider impacts on daily life. FluSurvey ILI corresponds well with other national influenza surveillance and provides broader context on community illness, supplementing the monitoring of influenza activity for public health response.

title: An empirical benchmark of activation functions for medical image restoration networks
abstract: Activation functions (AFs) play a pivotal role in defining the representational power and learning dynamics of deep neural networks (DNNs). However, their influence on medical image restoration (MIR) remains insufficiently explored. This empirical study presents a comprehensive, multi-phase investigation into how different AFs affect spatial and frequency characteristics across MIR tasks, such as image deblurring, image deblocking, and image super-resolution, in three medical imaging modalities: computed tomography (CT), digital mammography (DM), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The study integrates a theoretical taxonomy of AFs, a fixed-weight analysis, and a full-scale empirical evaluation involving 15 representative AFs spanning classical, rectified, exponential, and modern smooth families, benchmarked across 3,000 medical images. These functions are implemented within two widely used state-of-the-art MIR architectures: U-Net and Enhanced Deep Super-Resolution (EDSR). Model performance is evaluated using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Edge Preservation Index (EPI), High-Frequency Energy Ratio (HFER), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS), with statistical validation performed using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) tests. Results reveal that while the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and its variants remain strong baselines due to their stability and efficiency, smoother and adaptive functions such as the Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU), Mish, and Funnel ReLU (FReLU) achieved superior performance in preserving fine spatial and frequency details. title: Health big data classification application based on collaborative training optimization algorithm
abstract: Health big data has complex structures, rich features, and scarce annotated data, posing challenges for conventional classification approaches to fully exploit the value of the data. To improve the accuracy and robustness of health big data classification, a graph structure fusion clustering algorithm is studied and designed to extract feature space and graph structure space information. An adaptive fusion network is used to achieve layer by layer bidirectional feature fusion, and a joint self supervision mechanism is used to guide end-to-end collaborative training. Meanwhile, a health big data classification model based on collaborative training is proposed, which achieves classification through data preprocessing, base classifier training, confidence screening, and iterative optimization. The results indicate that the graph structure fusion clustering algorithm has clustering accuracies of 0.789, 0.776, and 0.793 on three public datasets, respectively, all of which are superior to other comparative algorithms. The health big data classification model has outstanding advantages in classification tasks. When the annotation rate is 10%, the accuracy on the MIMIC-III dataset reaches 0.724, which is a relative improvement of 18.3% compared to support vector machines. When the annotation rate is 50%, the accuracy of Cochrane text classification reaches 0.834. The research results indicate that the fusion of multimodal features and collaborative training mechanisms can effectively improve the classification performance of health data, providing a new method for accurate analysis of medical data.

title: A complexity-aware adaptive hybrid AI–ML framework for redundancy-aware feature optimization in intrusion detection benchmarks
abstract: This study investigates whether a coordinated redundancy-reduction and resource-aware learning pipeline can improve predictive performance and computational efficiency for intrusion-detection benchmark datasets. The framework combines correlation-based feature pruning with a resource-aware learning-control layer. The pruning stage reduces redundant predictors before model training, while the adaptive layer uses the observed resource/complexity state to regulate learning behavior. The study evaluates the resulting pipeline against conventional and static feature-selection baselines. The reported aggregate results in the present manuscript are retained only as descriptive values; dataset-specific repeated-run statistics are not inferred where they were not recorded in the original study. Accordingly, the claims are restricted to the evaluated intrusion-detection benchmarks and computational conditions rather than generalized to all big-data domains.

title: AI and IoT-based training and evaluation system for college spoken English
abstract: Spoken English proficiency is essential for academic and professional communication however, learners often have limited opportunities for interactive practice and consistent feedback. Existing digital spoken English assessment systems lack adaptive evaluation mechanisms and fail to effectively handle diverse acoustic conditions and contextual learning environments, reducing assessment reliability. Therefore, this research aims to develop an Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT)-based training and evaluation system (IoT-TES) for accurate, adaptive, and intelligent spoken English assessment among college learners. Speech data are obtained from a publicly available Kaggle dataset using IoT-enabled microphones, mobile devices, and classroom sensors to capture diverse accents and environmental conditions. Pre-processing includes Wiener filtering for noise reduction, voice activity detection for speech segmentation, and normalization for signal consistency, followed by mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) for feature extraction. The novel contribution of this research is the proposed archimedes optimization algorithm-tuned random forest-extreme gradient boost (AOA-RXGBoost) model, which simultaneously performs optimal feature selection and hyperparameter tuning while integrating random forest for robust prediction and XGBoost for iterative error refinement, thereby improving evaluation accuracy and computational efficiency. The system is implemented using Python for effective model development and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves 95.47% accuracy, 95.12% precision, 94.86% recall, and 94.99% F1-score, consistently outperforming existing methods. The developed IoT-TES platform provides real-time feedback, personalized learning support, and adaptive evaluation, offering a scalable, reliable, and intelligent solution for spoken English training across diverse educational environments. title: Pose-guided spatio-temporal Mamba graph network for vision-based Taekwondo action recognition
abstract: Fine-grained Taekwondo action recognition is difficult because decisive cues are brief, visually similar, and concentrated in lower-limb joints. This paper proposes PG-STMGNet, a pose-guided spatio-temporal Mamba graph network that combines a lightweight RGB Vision Transformer, a bounded adaptive skeleton graph encoder, a selective state-space temporal module, and a pose-confidence-conditioned gate. The revision clarifies that the individual backbones are adopted from established architectures, whereas the substantive contribution is their reliability-aware coupling: lower-limb graph residuals are bounded and normalized, and the fusion gate uses pose confidence to suppress unreliable skeleton evidence while preserving RGB appearance cues. On the private eight-class Taekwondo dataset, the existing experiments report 94.3% accuracy, 93.1% macro-F1, 93.7% precision, 92.6% recall, and 97.0% macro-AUC. The revised evaluation protocol additionally specifies subject-independent data partitioning, repeated robustness trials, public-benchmark transfer, loss-weight sensitivity, modern RGB-skeleton baselines, and end-to-end edge-device profiling. The expanded evaluation reports detailed dataset statistics, five-run robustness estimates, public-benchmark validation, loss-weight sensitivity, comparisons with recent RGB-skeleton models, pose-noise analysis, and end-to-end edge-device profiling.

title: Capacity and competition aware machine learning for airline route passenger traffic forecasting and operational decision support
abstract: Accurate route-level realized passenger traffic forecasting is important for near-term airline operational monitoring, utilization assessment, and competitive decision support. This study develops a capacity- and competition-aware machine-learning framework at the carrier–route–month level. The methodological design combines exact calendar-month lag and target construction, training-only feature selection, chronological validation, temporal baselines, feature-family ablation, and multiple operational prediction tasks. Missing months and the excluded disruption period are not bridged when constructing predictors or targets. Using U.S. BTS T-100 records, linear, ensemble, boosting, and neural models were evaluated on chronologically later observations. XGBoost achieved the strongest primary one-month passenger-traffic performance, with a WMAPE of 11.91%, RMSE of 1,434.92 passengers, and R 2 of 0.9742, reducing WMAPE by 16.72% relative to the last-month naive benchmark. It also achieved 8.37% WMAPE and R 2 of 0.8309 for next-month load-factor forecasting. XGBoost and HistGradientBoosting produced nearly identical leading utilization-state classification results, with approximately 73.37% accuracy and a macro-F1 score of 0.7413. Capacity variables provided the largest improvement over traffic history, while competition and co-airport variables produced smaller, task-specific gains. Reviewer-requested robustness analyses showed a 9.39% relative WMAPE increase when contemporaneous information was removed, regime-dependent rolling-origin performance, monotonic degradation on a common multi-horizon sample, and near-nominal split-conformal marginal coverage of 89.58% and 94.79% for nominal 90% and 95% intervals. These findings support calendar-aligned gradient boosting primarily as a near-term passenger-traffic forecasting and utilization-screening tool.

title: Three decades of artificial intelligence in prostate cancer show technical progress while evidence of clinical benefit is still emerging
abstract: Artificial intelligence has been applied to prostate cancer for three decades, but evidence that it improves long-term patient outcomes remains limited. This narrative review traces the field chronologically from 1994 through 2025 and examines a recurring pattern of strong retrospective performance, reduced performance or uncertainty during external validation, and slow clinical adoption. Prospective studies have nevertheless reported clinically meaningful intermediate benefits, including more consistent grading, fewer unnecessary biopsies, more efficient workflows, higher detection of clinically significant cancer, and improved surgical margin status. Prostate cancer's long natural history means that survival and quality-of-life effects require longer follow-up, so their absence should not be interpreted as evidence of no clinical utility. We interpret the evidence as suggesting that translation depends on algorithm performance together with workflow fit, data standardization, infrastructure, regulation, and prospective evaluation.

title: Construction method of temporal deep learning model for aging assessment of power hard composite insulators
abstract: Hard composite insulators are essential for reliable power transmission, but aging caused by environmental and electrical stresses increases leakage current and failure risks. Existing assessment methods face challenges in prediction accuracy, adaptability, and temporal feature analysis. This research proposes a novel ModABi-LSTMO framework that integrates DWT-based feature extraction, BiLSTM temporal learning, and ModAO optimization for accurate and intelligent aging assessment of power hard composite insulators. The Power Hard Composite Insulator Aging Dataset (Kaggle, 9775 records) containing simulated operational and environmental sensor observations designed to emulate aging behaviour of high-voltage composite insulators under representative operating conditions. In the preprocessing step, missing sensor data was imputed and feature values standardized using Min–Max normalization to improve training stability. Feature extraction utilized Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) to obtain time-frequency features from leakage current signals, facilitating the detection of hidden aging patterns in the insulation system. A DL system named Modified Archimedes Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory Optimizer (ModABi-LSTMO) is created based on extracted temporal features. The model combines a Bi-directional LSTM (BiLSTM) network to efficiently represent forward and backward temporal relationships in the degradation process, and the modified Archimedes optimization (ModAO) strategy is employed to optimize the network parameters and enhance convergence behavior. Experimental analysis in Python demonstrates that the ModABi-LSTMO model achieves a 98.9% accuracy in predicting aging states, outperforming traditional methods. This model enhances the reliability and efficiency of power transmission systems through smart monitoring and predictive maintenance for power hard composite insulators.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence for label-free red blood cell morphometrics using brightfield microscopy towards clinical applications
abstract: Background For diagnosing certain hematological disorders, variations in the red blood cell (RBC) morphology are considered as a marker. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer the potential for automated, reproducible, label-free analysis of RBC morphology; however, most AI classifiers lack explainable, clinician-friendly outputs. Methods Single-cell RBC images of 17,781 across 10 morphological classes were acquired from three brightfield microscopes as a multicentric dataset. Mask R-CNN-based segmentation and 74 morphometric feature extractions were performed using the RedTell tool. Seven different machine learning classifiers were compared, and the best classifier was evaluated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis for interpretability and confidence calibration analysis for decision reliability. This led to the development of a comprehensive framework for evaluating the AI workflow through explainable AI in label-free RBC morphometric studies. Results The random forest classifier achieved an F1 score of 0.89. SHAP analysis indicated that intensity features strongly influenced the model predictions, followed by shape and texture features. These intensity-specific features were tested for PCA and were preserved across all three microscopes (0.49–0.88) with no meaningful device-driven confounding (silhouette ~ − 0.09). Expected calibration error was less (0.050), and the prediction confidence was good for clinically meaningful morphologies, supporting a practical reject-option strategy for flagging low-confidence predictions. Conclusion This fully explainable workflow, with feature-level interpretability and decision reliability, connects the AI and label-free RBC imaging domains, enabling trust and cost-effective adoption of label-free RBC morphology analysis, even in resource-limited clinical settings.

title: Open-domain image editing with FLUX and structural causal modeling
abstract: Open-domain image editing requires accurate semantic modification while preserving identity, structure, and non-target visual content. Existing diffusion- and rectified-flow-based editors often remain affected by attribute coupling, spurious correlations, and unintended changes to semantically related regions. This study presents a causal-structure-guided image editing framework built on FLUX rectified flow. A learnable hierarchical structural causal model (SCM) is introduced to represent directional dependencies among latent semantic attributes through an adaptive adjacency matrix constrained by acyclicity and sparsity. The resulting structural representation is integrated into the Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT) dual-stream attention through attribute-to-token projection. A counterfactual consistency objective based on the abduction–intervention–prediction formulation is further incorporated to align the intended semantic change with preservation of non-target information. Experiments on PIE-Bench, MagicBrush, CelebA-HQ, and a 20,000-sample LAION-derived editing subset demonstrate consistent improvements in editing fidelity and attribute specificity. On PIE-Bench, the proposed method improves Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) text alignment (CLIP-T) by approximately 1.7% and reduces Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) by 5.1% relative to FluxSpace. On CelebA-HQ, compared with FluxSpace, the Attribute Cross-Interference Rate (ACIR) decreases from 0.2074 to 0.1763, while identity similarity increases from 0.7692 to 0.7854. Ablation experiments further verify the complementary contributions of structural modeling, causal attention intervention, and counterfactual consistency. In the query, key, and value masking ablation study, full masking increases inference time by approximately 3.7% relative to the unmasked configuration. The framework provides a practical approach to controllable and identity-preserving open-domain image editing.

title: Hybrid transformer-based security risk classification for sports events using crowd flow and congestion analytics
abstract: Sports events are often held at large venues with complex movement patterns and different levels of congestion, making the job of security management and public safety difficult. Correct identification of security threats is significant to effective security prevention and good crowd control. This research proposes a fusion of transformer models for the classification of security risk in sports events based on indicators of crowd flow and crowd density in the stadium. The Sports Event Security Risk Classification dataset covers attendance, crowd density, congestion, security resources, emergency accessibility and infrastructure. In addition, several features have been derived from existing features to the system for security reasons to improve the predictive capability of the system. FT-Transformer based feature interaction learning combines with TabNet based feature selection, named TabFT-Net. The experimental results show that TabFT-Net surpasses all baseline models and obtains an accuracy of 99.53%, and an F1 score of 99.53%. Moreover, by using SHAP and LIME analysis, the interpretability of the model enhanced by enabling the identification of the most influential security indicators. The proposed framework is further validated under ten-fold cross-validation, extensive ablation studies and computational complexity analysis for robustness and practical efficiency.

title: Genetic algorithm-optimized state space neural operator for power plant data platforms
abstract: Modern power plant data platforms need to manage large-scale operational data, which are heterogeneous and high-speed and are not stationary. High-computational models like Recurrent and Attention-based often have high computational cost, sensitivity to noise and load variations, and, in the attention-based case, catastrophic forgetting. To overcome these difficulties, this paper introduces a novel framework of GA-SSNOOP (Genetic Algorithm–Optimized State Space Neural Operator) to efficiently model a power plant system in the time domain. The framework combines continuous-time state-space neural operators and multi-objective Genetic Algorithm optimization to enhance the prediction accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency. Approximately 50,000 data points with 15–20 sensor variables were tested under a variety of operating conditions for both the Steam Turbine and the Boiler datasets. GA-SSNOOP unites the advantages of state space learning with the hyperparameter optimization of evolution, enabling it to capture the complex dynamics of the system and automatically determine the optimal model configuration. Results show a better forecasting performance than the baseline models of LSTM and Transformer, with the models converging faster, making lower prediction errors and consuming less memory. These results indicate the potential of GA-SSNOOP to scalable, real-time industrial analytics, intelligent monitoring and decision support in modern power plant environments.

title: Text-level effects of artificial intelligence-mediated language refinement on author–reader alignment and comprehension in Chinese non-academic and academic texts
abstract: This study examined whether target-informed, author-guided large language model (LLM) refinement alters author-reader alignment and comprehension in Chinese texts. Two controlled experiments compared original texts with versions refined by GPT-4 accessed through ChatGPT, Claude 3 Opus, and, in Study 1, Gemini Advanced. Models received author-provided target ratings or answer-key information that was also used for outcome scoring, making the intervention criterion-linked rather than ordinary copyediting. Participants were recruited through Credamo and randomly allocated by the platform to text-version conditions. Study 1 ( N = 572) measured exact-match alignment with authors’ intended emotional-expression ratings and accuracy on 15 author-keyed comprehension items. Recruitment was extended after inspection of initial results; its inferential analyses are therefore exploratory. The GPT-4 condition showed higher emotional-expression alignment than the original-text condition ( p = .002, signed r = .18). Gemini Advanced reduced alignment at the unadjusted level ( p = .010, signed r = − .15) but did not meet the Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0083; Claude 3 Opus did not differ from original texts. No comprehension differences were detected. Study 2 ( N = 420) measured exact-match alignment on six textually conveyed scholarly attributes and author-keyed comprehension. Neither GPT-4 nor Claude 3 Opus produced detectable differences on either outcome. Results are conditional on the fixed materials, participant samples, prompts, single-output procedure, criterion-linked guidance, and scoring rules and do not establish preservation of all authorial meaning or objective scholarly quality.

title: Mitigating domain shift in cross-domain student performance prediction using a CORAL-based adaptation framework
abstract: Student performance prediction has become an important research area in educational data mining because it supports early academic interventions and decision-making processes. However, most previous studies assume that training and testing data originate from the same academic environment, which limits model generalization when applied to different academic programs. In practical educational settings, variations in student characteristics, academic behavior, and learning distributions across programs introduce substantial cross-domain distribution shifts that can significantly reduce prediction performance. This study proposes a CORAL-based cross-domain learning framework for student performance prediction under shifting distribution conditions. The framework applies CORrelation ALignment (CORAL) domain adaptation to align the feature covariance between the source and target programs before model training and evaluation. Four machine learning models, namely logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and extreme gradient boosting (XGB), were evaluated using three academic program datasets under within-domain, conventional cross-domain, and CORAL-based adaptation settings. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the curve (AUC), with the F1-score used as the primary evaluation metric. The experimental results demonstrate that baseline cross-domain learning consistently experiences performance degradation owing to distribution shifts. The proposed CORAL-based framework successfully improved the cross-domain prediction performance in most experimental scenarios and significantly reduced the performance gap toward within-domain learning. The highest improvement was achieved by the random forest model in the ASY target domain, where the F1-score increased from 0.737 to 0.802 after adaptation. Statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test further confirmed that most of the improvements were statistically significant. The findings indicate that CORAL-based domain adaptation provides an effective and computationally efficient solution for improving cross-domain student performance prediction under heterogeneous educational data distribution.

title: Target reindexing and residual reconstruction enable reliable retrieval augmented few shot recognition
abstract: Retrieval-augmented few-shot recognition supplements sparsely annotated target classes with external visual samples, but open retrieval results may exhibit unstable quality, semantic mismatch, and cross-domain feature shifts. Directly using query-derived labels or treating retrieved images as ordinary training data can therefore distort class representations and decision boundaries. We propose the Target Re-indexing and Residual Reconstruction Network (TRRN), which incorporates external samples under target-task constraints. TRRN first constructs class anchors from the few-shot support set and estimates the support of each retrieved sample for every target class, thereby remapping external samples into the current class space without directly inheriting their retrieval labels. It then models the components unexplained by the target-anchor projection as residuals and combines class-support weights, confidence gating, and residual magnitudes to estimate reliable sample contributions. The retained information supplements the few-shot anchors, while the class-wise mean residual direction is suppressed during classifier reconstruction. External images are retrieved from LAION-400 M through class-name-based text-to-image retrieval using a frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 encoder, with 20 valid images retained per class after deduplication and overlap removal. Experiments on FGVCAircraft and DTD under full-way 4-shot, 8-shot, and 16-shot protocols show that TRRN achieves the highest Mean Accuracy in all six settings and outperforms the strongest retrieval-augmented baseline by 1.11–1.78% points. title: A comprehensive review of attention-based multimodal deep learning techniques for lung cancer diagnosis
abstract: Lung cancer remains the deadliest cancer type worldwide, presenting a wide spectrum of subtypes, including several rare and difficult-to-diagnose types. Improving diagnostic accuracy and efficiency with technology seems promising, which helps medical experts to save many patients’ lives. Deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing several critical lung cancer diagnostic tasks, including early detection, subtype classification, survival prediction, and tumor segmentation. Most recent developments are multimodal deep learning (MMDL) techniques, which aggregate information from multiple data types, including medical imaging, genomic data, and clinical records, achieving superior performance over single-modality approaches. Fusion strategies are developed to integrate features from multiple modalities effectively, while attention mechanisms further enhance performance by identifying diagnostically relevant features and dynamically weighting modalities. The reviewed studies suggest that attention-based MMDL can enhance performance across several lung cancer diagnostic and prognostic tasks by leveraging complementary information from heterogeneous data sources. While some studies reported substantial gains, particularly in treatment response and survival prediction, direct quantitative comparison remains challenging because of variations in datasets, clinical objectives, baseline models, and validation protocols. This paper presents a comprehensive review of attention-based MMDL approaches for lung cancer diagnosis, analyzing studies published between 2020 and 2025, with a focus on clinical applications, data modalities, fusion strategies, and attention mechanisms.

title: Quantum-inspired context-aware adaptive federated edge intelligence for privacy-preserving healthcare analytics
abstract: Privacy-preserving healthcare analytics at the edge requires collaborative learning across distributed Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices while maintaining strict privacy guarantees, low inference latency, and high predictive accuracy. Existing federated learning frameworks employ static privacy budgets and fixed communication schedules, failing to adapt to heterogeneous clinical contexts, variable network conditions, and diverse device capabilities. Furthermore, conventional edge intelligence methods struggle to efficiently balance multi-objective trade-offs between privacy, utility, and latency under stringent resource constraints. This paper proposes Quantum-Inspired Context-Aware Adaptive Federated Edge Intelligence (QI-CAF-EI), a novel framework that dynamically co-optimizes privacy, utility, and latency through context-aware adaptive control and quantum-inspired optimization techniques while maintaining full compatibility with classical edge hardware. The framework integrates five tightly coupled functional modules: (1) data acquisition and edge preprocessing for privacy-preserving local analytics, (2) quantum-inspired edge intelligence leveraging tensor network decompositions for efficient model compression, (3) context-aware adaptive control that continuously monitors system state and clinical urgency to adjust privacy budgets and communication schedules, (4) secure federated learning employing differential privacy (DP) and homomorphic encryption for gradient aggregation, and (5) explainability and governance mechanisms ensuring regulatory compliance and clinical interpretability. Comprehensive experimental evaluation across five benchmark healthcare datasets MIMIC-III, PhysioNet, NIH ChestX-ray14, UCI Heart Disease, and WISDM IoMT demonstrates significant performance improvements. QI-CAF-EI achieves 3.7–4.5% accuracy improvement over differentially private federated learning, reduces inference latency by 25–36% compared to edge-only baselines, and decreases communication overhead by 40% while maintaining rigorous DP guarantees (ε ∈ [0.3, 2.0], δ = 10⁻ 5 ). Theoretical analysis provides formal convergence guarantees, DP proofs, and complexity bounds. The framework enables real-time, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient collaborative healthcare analytics, addressing critical requirements for safe AI deployment in modern healthcare ecosystems.

title: Developing a multi-level human-centered design framework for digital health implementation: a cross-project methodological synthesis
abstract: BackgroundDigital health interventions have considerable potential to improve healthcare access, quality, and efficiency. Despite increasing adoption, many interventions fail to achieve sustainable implementation or progress beyond pilot phases because they are insufficiently integrated with user needs, organizational workflows, and health system contexts. Although human-centered design (HCD) has improved the usability and acceptability of digital health technologies, its application frequently remains confined to early design activities and is rarely integrated with implementation science throughout the implementation lifecycle.ObjectiveThis study aimed to develop a multi-level, human-centered design framework informed by a cross-project methodological synthesis integrating participatory design and implementation science to support the design, implementation, evaluation, and scale-up of digital health interventions.MethodsA cross-project methodological synthesis was conducted using complementary digital health implementation studies undertaken in Kenya. The empirical corpus included studies spanning adolescent mental health, neonatal clinical decision support, digital health infrastructure, generative artificial intelligence, and frugal digital health innovation. Framework development followed an iterative analytical process combining thematic synthesis, constant comparative analysis, and abductive reasoning. The synthesis organized recurring methodological themes into an integrated framework spanning user, workflow, and system perspectives across the digital health implementation lifecycle.ResultsThe synthesis identified recurring methodological processes that consistently contributed to successful digital health implementation, including contextual understanding, participatory stakeholder engagement, iterative refinement, workflow integration, organizational readiness, governance, and sustainability. These findings informed the development of a multi-level framework structured around six iterative implementation phases: Understand, Co-design, Prototype, Evaluate, Implement, and Scale, and three interconnected analytical levels: user (micro), workflow (meso), and system (macro). The framework conceptualizes digital health implementation as a continuous sociotechnical process in which sustained adoption and scale-up depend upon coordinated alignment among these three levels throughout the implementation lifecycle.ConclusionsThis study advances human-centered design by integrating it with implementation science through an empirically derived, lifecycle-oriented methodological framework for digital health implementation. The proposed framework may provide researchers, developers, practitioners, and policymakers with a structured approach for designing, implementing, evaluating, and scaling digital health interventions while supporting sustainable, context-responsive, and equitable digital health transformation.

title: From continuous signals to accountable care: a trajectory-based framework for wearable monitoring in older adults
abstract: Wearable technologies can continuously measure cardiovascular, physiological, and behavioral signals outside clinical settings, but more measurement does not necessarily produce better care. This limitation is particularly important in older adults, in whom frailty, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, cognitive impairment, altered vascular physiology, and caregiver dependence modify both signal reliability and clinical meaning. We argue that wearable monitoring in later life should move from population thresholds toward individualized physiological trajectories and from automated alerts toward accountable clinical action. We propose a trajectory-to-action framework based on five elements: individual baseline, within-person deviation, multimodal concordance, geriatric contextualization, and predefined clinical response. The framework is conceptual and has not been prospectively validated; its clinical utility, safety, implementation feasibility, and impact on outcomes require prospective testing. In this model, an alert is not a diagnosis but a request for attention whose recipient, response time, confirmatory pathway, and escalation rules are established in advance. Evaluation should therefore extend beyond sensor accuracy to include actionability, alert burden, clinical utility, equity, and net benefit. We propose that wearable monitoring in older adults should be evaluated by whether continuous signals can be translated into proportionate, context-aware, and accountable care.

title: On the evolution of security and privacy in Android health APIs
abstract: IntroductionWith the rapid proliferation of mobile health technologies and smart devices, safeguarding sensitive personal health data has become critical. Android 14 introduced Health Connect as a centralized platform designed to optimize health data management, grant users granular control over their information, and enable secure, transparent inter-app communication. However, whether Health Connect represents an effective advance over earlier Android solutions remains to be evaluated.MethodsA structured, technology-agnostic evaluation framework was designed using a threat model grounded in European cybersecurity (NIS2 Directive, Cyber Resilience Act) and privacy (GDPR) standards. Across defined security and privacy criteria, Health Connect was comparatively evaluated against its predecessor solutions (Google Fit and the Android Sensors API) examining storage integration, encryption, operational models and permission granularity alongside empirical verification using the OWASP Mobile Application Security Testing Guide (MASTG).ResultsHealth Connect provides stronger native architectural support for security (availability, integrity and authenticity) and privacy (data minimisation, user consent management, transparency, accuracy and storage limitation) compared to the general-permission, cloud-dependent or developer-dependent models of Google Fit and the Android Sensors API. However, security support for confidentiality remains partial due to an empirical failure in runtime/database-level encryption within its local sandbox.DiscussionHealth Connect marks a significant step forward in Android health data protection, largely driven by fine-grained permissions and local container isolation. Nevertheless, the lack of database-level runtime encryption and sparse technical documentation represent key shortcomings. Addressing these issues and improving implementation transparency are essential to consolidate user and developer trust across the digital health ecosystem.

title: Considering the trade-offs of environmental, social, and governance risk in digital health
abstract: IntroductionDigital health innovations are increasingly recognized as cost-efficient and scalable solutions to improve healthcare delivery and accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, limited research has examined these technologies within broader socio-economic and sustainability contexts, particularly regarding Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) risks and potential trade-offs.MethodsThis narrative review integrates digital health within an environmental, social, and governance (ESG) framework. Literature on digital health, sustainability, and ESG-relevant risk was identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, supplemented by reference-list screening and purposive inclusion of policy and institutional reports; searches were last updated in May 2026. Eligible sources addressed digital health technologies and engaged with at least one ESG domain. Sources were synthesised thematically across the environmental, social, and governance domains, and a conceptual framework was developed to support evaluation of ESG-related trade-offs in digital health implementation.ResultsThe review highlights that digital health solutions, while offering significant benefits in accessibility and efficiency, may exacerbate health inequalities, increase environmental burdens through energy consumption and carbon emissions, and raise governance concerns related to ethics, data privacy, and regulation. The findings emphasize the interdependence of ESG factors and demonstrate that isolated evaluation of these dimensions can lead to incomplete or misleading conclusions. A preliminary framework is proposed to guide the systematic assessment of ESG trade-offs in digital health interventions.DiscussionIntegrating ESG considerations into digital health innovation is essential to ensure sustainable and equitable healthcare outcomes. The proposed framework provides a foundation for evaluating the broader impacts of digital health technologies, though further research is needed to develop standardized metrics and a comprehensive ESG taxonomy. Incorporating ESG principles into policy and implementation strategies will enhance the long-term effectiveness and societal value of digital health solutions.

title: Digital phenotyping for mental health monitoring and personalized prediction in people with diabetes: a Python-based scoping review
abstract: BackgroundDiabetes frequently co-occurs with depression, anxiety, and diabetes-related distress, and psychological status directly influences glycaemic control and the risk of complications. Traditional mental health assessment relies on subjective scales. With the growth of digital health, digital phenotyping offers a new paradigm for real-time, objective mental health monitoring and prediction. However, the pathways through which these technologies perform monitoring and prediction remain unclear.ObjectiveThis scoping review aimed to systematically map the application pathways of digital phenotyping for mental health monitoring and prediction in people with diabetes, and to use machine learning-assisted text mining to analyse the main research themes and hotspots, thereby informing the future development of individualised risk prediction models and monitoring systems.MethodsA scoping review search was conducted in six English databases (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library) and four Chinese databases (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and China Biomedical Literature Database[CBM]), covering studies published from database inception to 10 September 2026. The search strategy was built around terms related to diabetes, digital phenotyping, and mental health. Machine learning-assisted literature mining was used to identify thematic patterns in the included studies. The study selection process and overall workflow followed the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR).ResultsA total of 2,968 records were retrieved. After screening, 10 studies were included. The evidence indicated that digital phenotyping mainly enables real-time monitoring of mental health in people with diabetes through signals such as continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), passive smartphone sensing, voice, and ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Machine learning methods were widely used for risk prediction modelling, but most studies built models at the group level, with only a few adopting n-of-1 analysis or subgroup prediction to achieve individualised risk prediction. External validation of models was generally lacking, and no intervention studies were identified.ConclusionsPreliminary evidence suggests that digital phenotyping has exploratory potential for mental health monitoring and prediction in people with diabetes, but research that genuinely achieves individualised risk prediction remains limited. Closed-loop monitoring-intervention design and multicentre external validation are the main directions for future research.Systematic Review Registrationhttps://osf. io/6wsaj/.

title: CB-GFL: carbon-budgeted federated learning with blockchain auditing for healthcare applications
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare has made it harder to protect patient data, prediction performance, and environmental sustainability in federated learning (FL) systems. A single platform for sustainable healthcare applications, Carbon-Budgeted Green Federated Learning (CB-GFL), merges carbon-aware client selection, blockchain-based auditing, and energy-efficient collaborative learning. The framework integrates (i) a carbon-budget-aware client selection strategy formulated as a 0–1 knapsack optimisation problem with a greedy approximation guarantee of approximately 63.2%; (ii) a blockchain auditing layer consisting of three smart contracts, the Carbon Budget Ledger, Energy Verification Contract, and Incentive/Penalty Contract, secured using SHA-256 hash-based immutable records; and (iii) an ensemble learning model combining LightGBM, XGBoost, and Gradient Boosting with SMOTEENN resampling. All experiments are conducted in a simulated federated environment, with clients executed on a single machine. CB-GFL achieves AUC = 0.9113 on the UCI 4-site benchmark (4 hospitals, 3 countries, n = 920), exceeding the 0.90 threshold, and AUC = 0.7138 on Framingham, consistent with the clinical gold standard of 0.70 to 0.75. In the balanced operating point, experimental findings show 83.61% classification accuracy, 82.34% weighted F1-score, 0.7138 AUC-ROC, and 0.2771 MCC, and 72.07% sensitivity in the screening configuration. The proposed system ensures 100% carbon-budget compliance and a 74-block tamper-resistant blockchain audit trail for energy responsibility. Comparison to 11 benchmark algorithms shows that the dataset's realistic predictive qualities are 0.14–0.29. Additionally, five-fold cross-validation shows steady generalisation with an average accuracy of 84.25% ± 1.03%. The results show that CB-GFL supports sustainable AI adoption and privacy-preserving, carbon-aware, auditable federated healthcare intelligence.

title: Using secure WhatsApp-based digital recruitment as an intervention in prostate cancer research with black men
abstract: This paper describes the development and implementation of a secure, community-centred digital system as an intervention to share prostate cancer risk information among Black men in southeast Wales. In this study, the term Black men is used to refer to men of Somali and African Caribbean heritage. The system was designed to support culturally and linguistically appropriate participation. Recruitment was facilitated by two community co-applicants using project-funded smartphones and WhatsApp Business accounts to disseminate co-created prostate cancer risk messages, link to external prostate cancer risk checker and link to an evaluation survey, within closed community groups. Participants accessed the survey through a custom landing page that verified mobile numbers via CAPTCHA and unique access codes distributed using TextGlobal. After verification, participants selected their preferred language (English or Somali) to view participant information sheets and consent forms. Submitted consent data were encrypted and securely stored on university servers, with cross-referenced verification ensuring integrity. These measures upheld core digital security principles: protecting access to the WhatsApp groups to invited participants, controlling survey access, protecting the confidentiality and accuracy of consent data through encryption, and maintaining secure storage. A privacy risk assessment using the LINDDUN GO framework identified and mitigated vulnerabilities, including risks of data disclosure, unnecessary processing, and regulatory non-compliance. This paper presents a replicable approach for integrating community engagement with privacy-by-design principles in digital health research. It demonstrates how participatory digital systems can enhance inclusivity and trust while upholding data protection, offering practical guidance for researchers designing secure, culturally informed digital methodologies.

title: An interoperable and reusable research environment for digital medicine
abstract: Clinical research infrastructures remain fragmented and project-specific, with semantic inconsistency accumulating across studies and constantly increasing “interoperability debt”. Repeated transformations between heterogeneous standards cause semantic drift and information loss. Prospective studies require duplicate data entry across clinical and research systems, increasing workload and introducing inconsistencies. Project-driven data models accumulate technical debt that undermines the sustainability and maintainability of research infrastructure across studies and funding cycles. Here, we explore how a reusable research environment can be built, and whether governing data semantics at the persistence layer provides a foundation that outlasts individual projects. We present an environment addressing these deficiencies at the architectural level. An openEHR-based clinical data repository with governed archetypes serves as the canonical persistence layer, integrating retrospective EHR data, prospective study data, patient-reported outcomes, and wearable sensor streams under a shared semantic model. Prospective data is captured directly through openEHR-based forms, which removes the separate capture system for study variables, while duplicate documentation with a hospital information system that does not run on openEHR remains. Reusable transformation pipelines support bidirectional FHIR interoperability and OMOP-based analytics. Federation nodes at three institutions were tested with cohort count queries across sites and are not yet in routine use. Deployed at Charité university medical center across five studies covering approximately 16,000 patients and 7.9 million data points, the environment shows that one governed repository can be reused across successive studies from different clinical domains within an existing healthcare IT landscape. Of its 125 archetypes, 57 are shared between at least two studies. Sustainability beyond these five studies and scaling beyond one institution remain to be shown. All tooling is publicly available and provided as a deployable configuration for institutional adoption.

title: Oversight asymmetry in AI-assisted clinical documentation: a comparative-abductive study using neonatal discharge as a test context
abstract: BackgroundHuman oversight is widely treated as a safeguard for clinical artificial intelligence (AI), yet a reviewer may remain formally responsible without having the knowledge, time, or authority required to verify generated documentation. We develop “oversight asymmetry” as a prospective governance diagnosis and use neonatal discharge as a theoretical test context for responsible digital paediatrics, not as an observed setting of AI use.MethodsWe conducted a comparative-abductive, netnographically informed qualitative study of 64 public Reddit threads posted between 2021 and April 2026, with comment trees retrieved under pre-specified extraction parameters. The threads contained 2,848 comments and replies from 1,723 pseudonymised accounts in nursing, neonatal, paediatric, medicine, and health informatics communities, and 49 threads contributed to the final themes. A discharge and transition-home stream, drawn mainly from general nursing communities, and a smaller AI documentation and communication stream were analysed separately using reflexive thematic analysis before abductive comparison. Professional role was attributed only where contributors explicitly self-positioned.ResultsDischarge readiness was described as depending on knowledge distributed across records, professionals, bedside observation, and families, while responsibility for release could become concentrated. Frontline responsibility was separable from institutional authority, although several accounts described distributed oversight that worked because escalation was available. In four anchor threads from two communities, AI documentation discussions described faster drafting alongside residual source checking and correction, and a narrower set of accounts described reconstruction of missing clinical rationale. Workload accounts, together with AI-linked predictions in two threads, suggest that anticipated efficiency may be converted into higher workload before residual verification work is removed. We propose that oversight becomes vulnerable when verification responsibility and demand exceed epistemic access, protected time or consequential authority.ConclusionOversight asymmetry identifies a prospective mechanism through which nominal human review may fail to constitute meaningful oversight. Responsible paediatric artificial intelligence governance should measure residual verification work, preserve provenance and access to family and bedside context, protect review time, and provide effective output-level and system-level escalation authority before automation is treated as additional capacity. The study generates propositions for prospective evaluation and does not claim that artificial intelligence-assisted neonatal discharge was directly observed.
