title: Requirements and key factors for the successful implementation of AI in clinical practice: a qualitative study from the European CAIDX network
abstract: IntroductionArtificial intelligence (AI) is expected to become increasingly important in hospitals and clinical care. However, successful implementation depends on technical, organizational, and user-related factors. We aimed to identify the key requirements for equitable and effective adoption of AI-based applications in clinical practice.MethodsWithin the “Clinical AI-based Diagnostics” (CAIDX) project, we conducted systematic expert interviews with 55 stakeholders from four European countries working across the healthcare sector. Interviews explored the perceived added value of AI, barriers to implementation, usability requirements, and potential health-economic implications.ResultsStakeholder analysis revealed several recurrent sources of tension affecting implementation: limited physician involvement, differing perspectives between IT specialists and clinicians, unclear distribution of tasks and responsibilities, and low institutional commitment driven by concerns about inefficient use of time and resources. We also identified structural and workforce-related constraints that make implementation particularly challenging, including the large number of actors involved and the highly individual organizational setup of hospitals, which limits transferability of implementation models.DiscussionImplementation of clinical AI requires targeted action at hospital, vendor, and health-system levels. Compared with earlier healthcare technologies, AI adoption is shaped more strongly by AI literacy, professional attitudes, and perceptions of trust and responsibility. Based on these findings, we propose practical recommendations to support implementation of AI applications in routine care.

title: FHRFormer: a self-supervised masked transformer framework for fetal heart rate time-series inpainting and forecasting
abstract: IntroductionApproximately 10% of newborns require assistance to initiate breathing at birth, and around 5% need ventilation support. Continuous fetal heart rate (FHR) monitoring supports the assessment of fetal well-being and timely obstetric interventions. However, wearable FHR monitors are prone to signal dropout caused by maternal movement and sensor displacement, resulting in missing data that complicate automated analysis. Conventional interpolation methods often fail to preserve important temporal and spectral characteristics of FHR signals.MethodsWe developed FHRFormer, a self-supervised masked transformer-based autoencoder for reconstructing missing FHR signals and forecasting short-term FHR dynamics. The model was trained on 4,486 FHR recordings collected using the Moyo monitor during labor in Tanzanian hospitals. By combining temporal reconstruction with frequency-aware loss functions, the framework aims to preserve both local signal morphology and spectral characteristics. Performance was evaluated using independent validation and test datasets, different masking ratios, and varying input patch sizes.ResultsFHRFormer demonstrated the ability to reconstruct missing FHR segments while preserving temporal and spectral characteristics consistent with surrounding signals. Reconstruction performance was highest with an input patch size of 30 samples and a masking ratio of 15%, with decreasing accuracy at higher masking ratios. The framework also demonstrated short-term FHR forecasting using a 30-minute historical context and a 15-second prediction horizon.DiscussionFHRFormer offers a promising approach to improving the completeness of FHR recordings for retrospective research and AI-based analysis. Future integration into wearable FHR monitoring devices could support real-time risk detection. However, clinical benefits, including improved prediction of neonatal outcomes, remain to be established.

title: Physical activity phenotypes from volume-based versus intensity-based wearable metrics: discordant classification and divergent metabolomic, body composition, and cardiac magnetic resonance associations
abstract: BackgroundConsumer wearables report direct volume-based metrics (steps, distance, floors climbed) alongside device-derived metrics generated by manufacturer algorithms (activity-intensity minutes, energy expenditure). Both are widely used to characterize individuals into activity phenotypes, yet whether these representations yield concordant activity phenotypes and biological associations is unclear.ObjectiveTo compare activity phenotypes derived from direct accelerometry with those derived from device-derived intensity metrics, and to evaluate each against metabolomic, body composition, and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) phenotypes.MethodsUsing the SingHEART cohort, two hierarchical cluster analyses using Ward linkage yielded five phenotypes each for volume-based and intensity-based metrics. Agreement was quantified by the adjusted Rand index. For analyses, the two high-variability phenotypes were combined, giving four groups: sedentary, average movers, regular exercisers, and high-variability movers. Serum ¹H-NMR metabolomics was analyzed by PERMANOVA with Holm adjustment across pairwise contrasts. Body and CMR associations were assessed using linear regression with false discovery rate correction.ResultsIn total, 984 adults (mean age 45.6 years, 48.3% male) wore accelerometers for a mean of 7.1 valid days. The two classifications agreed poorly: adjusted Rand index was 0.18, with only 46.2% assigned identically. Volume-based phenotypes differed in metabolomic profiles (P < .001). Active participants (high-variability movers plus regular exercisers) differed from sedentary participants across 106 of 250 biomarkers (FDR q < 0.05), including higher HDL, lower VLDL, LDL and lower GlycA. Conversely, although intensity-based phenotypes showed a nominally significant omnibus metabolomic association (P = .003), no metabolomic difference was observed between active and sedentary groups defined by intensity-based phenotyping (P = .29). Across 16 body composition and CMR outcomes, volume-based phenotypes were associated with 11 and intensity-based phenotypes with 6, in divergent directions: volume-based high-variability movers showed lower body fat, higher skeletal muscle, and larger ventricular volumes and mass, whereas intensity-based high-variability movers showed higher body mass index and waist circumference.ConclusionsVolume-based metrics and intensity-based metrics assign the same individuals to discordant activity phenotypes. Volume-based phenotypes showed more consistent associations across metabolomic, body composition, and cardiac imaging measures. These findings suggest that the choice of wearable-derived metrics substantially influences digital activity phenotyping and its biological interpretation.

title: Effect of neurofeedback-assisted mindfulness training on migraine severity, associated disability, sleep quality, and emotional distress: protocol for a randomized controlled trial
abstract: BackgroundMigraine is a highly prevalent neurological disorder and a leading cause of worldwide disability, exerting significant clinical, social, and economic burdens. While pharmacological options exist, their efficacy is often limited by tolerability issues and risk of medication-overuse headache. Neurofeedback (NF) combined with mindfulness training has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological neuromodulation technique. However, clinical evidence in migraine management remains limited by methodological heterogeneity and small sample sizes. This study protocol aims to evaluate the efficacy of a Neurofeedback-Assisted Mindfulness Training Program (NAMTP) in adults with medium-to-high-frequency episodic migraine.Methods/designThis is a randomized, parallel-group, controlled clinical trial protocol. Sixty-six (N = 66) adults diagnosed with medium-to-high-frequency episodic migraine (5–14 monthly migraine days) will be recruited and randomized (1:1 ratio) into either the Intervention Group (IG: standard care plus NAMTP) or the Control Group (CG: standard routine care alone). The IG will undergo a 12-week home-based program consisting of 60 sessions (15–20 min each, 5 times per week) of mindfulness training assisted by the Muse® electroencephalography (EEG) headband. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, 12 weeks (post-intervention), and 24 weeks post-randomization. The powered primary outcome is the change in Monthly Migraine Days (MMDs). Secondary outcomes include migraine-associated disability (MIDAS), headache impact (HIT-6), sleep parameters (actigraphy and PSQI), quality of life (MSQ v.2), and mood symptoms (BDI-II and STAI-Y).DiscussionThis protocol addresses the urgent need for scalable, non-pharmacological therapies in migraine management. By combining objective neurophysiological monitoring with behavioral training within a rigorous randomized controlled framework, this trial will clarify whether NAMTP can reduce headache burden, optimize sleep patterns, and diminish affective distress. The findings are expected to provide standardized, actionable evidence regarding the integration of digital neurofeedback tools into routine clinical care for episodic migraine.Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07661888.

title: Common barriers and facilitators to the implementation of digital medicine in chronic respiratory diseases: a systematic review of reviews
abstract: Background and research questionDigital Medicine offers significant potential for improving care in Respiratory Medicine, yet its full uptake remains limited. Barriers and facilitators involve multiple stakeholders and are likely shared across diseases and technologies. This study had the following research question: What are the common barriers, facilitators, and transferable concepts for implementing Digital Medicine in respiratory diseases, exemplified by bronchial asthma, cystic fibrosis (CF), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and COVID-19?Study design and methodsSystematic review of reviews. Three electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science), as well as Cochrane Library were searched for review publications from September 2019 through May 2026. Nine included reviews were appraised using AMSTAR-2. Original publications referenced within these reviews were additionally screened for suitability for data extraction, leading to inclusion of 18 original publications. Extracted barriers and facilitators were visualized as disease- and actor-stratified co-occurrence networks and mapped to two implementation frameworks (CFIR and Chaudoir et al. 2013).ResultsNo COVID-19 publication met inclusion criteria. Asthma and, partially, CF evidence was rich and included institution-level data, while COPD evidence was less diverse. One CF program survey had structured its data according to the CFIR framework, enabling uniquely complete mapping of barriers and facilitators.ConclusionHigh-quality, framework-structured, network-visualizable evidence on barriers and facilitators to Digital Medicine exists in bronchial asthma and, partially, CF. In contrast, evidence on barriers and facilitators in COPD is not yet systematic. Future studies should be anchored in frameworks for sufficient comprehensiveness and facilitated knowledge translation into implementability.Systematic Review Registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251070944, PROSPERO, CRD420251070944.

title: Longitudinal DLQI trajectory patterns and early risk updating in telepharmacy-monitored psoriasis
abstract: BackgroundTelepharmacy platforms capture longitudinal patient-reported health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) data in psoriasis, but reports have emphasized average improvement, which may conceal a minority with persistent burden. Whether machine learning adds value beyond baseline severity, and whether the first follow-up sharpens risk estimation, remain unclear.ObjectiveTo characterize 12-month Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) trajectories in a telepharmacy psoriasis cohort, to identify a persistently impaired minority through trajectory-pattern analysis, and to determine where the added value of longitudinal monitoring lies.MethodsAfter curation of the NAVETA telepharmacy dataset, the analytic cohort consisted of 219 patients contributing a total of 831 observations. As the primary analysis, unsupervised Ward clustering of DLQI trajectories (a complete-case subset of 133 of the 219 patients with complete baseline-to-month-6 DLQI) identified exploratory trajectory patterns. A leakage-aware benchmark compared a null rule, a one-predictor baseline-DLQI logistic model, multivariable logistic regression and four ensemble learners for 6-month clinically meaningful improvement (≥4-point reduction) across 100 repeated stratified 80/20 splits, with calibration. For 6-month remission (DLQI ≤ 1), a baseline-DLQI-only comparator and a month-1 updating model were evaluated in the same dynamic cohort.ResultsMean DLQI improved from 7.78 to 2.89 over 12 months. Three exploratory trajectory patterns were identified—low-burden early control (n = 90), high-burden responder (n = 20) and persistent burden (n = 23; 17.3%); the retained three-cluster solution showed a silhouette of 0.43, and the last pattern remained impaired at 12 months (mean DLQI 7.31 vs. 1.91 and 1.80; p = 0.009). For improvement, a one-predictor baseline-DLQI logistic model matched the leading ensembles (AUROC 0.923 vs. XGBoost 0.903), and feature-attribution analysis confirmed the dominance of baseline DLQI. For DLQI remission, the baseline-DLQI-only model reached AUROC 0.641, whereas the month-1 DLQI updating model reached AUROC 0.753 with good calibration (intercept −0.02, slope 1.04, ECE 0.021).ConclusionsA favourable average conceals a clinically important minority with persistent HRQoL burden that trajectory-pattern analysis can identify. For outcomes anchored to baseline severity, machine learning adds little beyond a simple baseline-DLQI model; the added value of telepharmacy may instead emerge from longitudinal information, with the first follow-up providing an early, well-calibrated update to individual risk. External validation is required.

title: Multimodal prediction of documented 1-year asthma exacerbation risk incorporating a static baseline CT digital-twin framework: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: BackgroundTo develop and conditionally evaluate a multimodal prediction model incorporating a static baseline CT digital-twin framework for documented 1-year asthma exacerbation risk.MethodsThis retrospective single-center study analyzed 505 adults with asthma. Baseline three-dimensional CT reconstruction supplied quantitative features; the static baseline CT digital-twin framework did not simulate physiology or update dynamically. A LASSO-selected 10-variable logistic score was evaluated using nested domain comparisons, calibration, Brier score, and 1,000 bootstrap refits conditional on the selected predictor set. An available-variable clinical comparator was evaluated with and without CT features.ResultsSeventy-two patients (14.3%) had a documented exacerbation. The final score had apparent AUC 0.880 (conditional bootstrap 95% CI, 0.836–0.917) and Brier score 0.086. Fixed-predictor bootstrap correction yielded AUC 0.856, calibration slope 0.875, intercept −0.182, and Brier score 0.094, without accounting for the original variable-selection step. CT increased AUC from 0.880 to 0.894 in the fully nested comparison (likelihood-ratio P = 0.070), and from 0.725 to 0.774 in the available-variable comparator (P < 0.001). These were apparent, exploratory comparisons, not external validation.ConclusionThe multimodal score showed conditional internal performance, with a modest CT increment in the fully nested comparison and a larger apparent increment in the restricted available-variable comparator. The CT contribution remains exploratory and comparator-dependent. External validation, full selection-aware validation, quantitative CT repeatability assessment, and prospective impact evaluation are required before clinical use.

title: AI in Long-Term Care: A Closed-Loop Sociotechnical Reliability Framework
abstract: AI is increasingly used in long-term care (LTC), yet reliability is often judged at the level of individual models or devices. This is insufficient in LTC, where residents vary in capacity, autonomy, and preferences. Their ability to question AI outputs may fluctuate, and care delivery depends on distributed roles and finite operational capacity. We define sociotechnical reliability as the capacity of an AI-enabled care system to consistently translate resident-relevant information into appropriate and timely care actions under real-world LTC conditions, with failures that are detectable and correctable across the care pathway. In this Viewpoint, we draw on professional experience overseeing AI initiatives across LTC and hospital settings, examined in relation to a purposively mapped interdisciplinary literature, to inform the development of a reliability framework. Our aim is to reframe AI reliability in LTC as an end-to-end care system property and to provide a framework for identifying where reliability is gained, lost, and evaluated. We propose 5 reliability functions: sensing, inference, verification and contextualization, response and escalation, and learning and adaptation, with governance and accountability operating across all 5 functions. The framework highlights recurrent failures, including incomplete sensing, nonportable inference, overreliance on or dismissal of AI outputs during verification, unclear ownership or delayed response, and repeated failures without correction. The framework also makes reliability empirically examinable through questions about where the pathway fails, who has the authority to verify and act, whether response demands are sustainable within available capacity, and whether failures become visible to governance and inform learning and adaptation. Our central viewpoint is that AI in LTC should be judged not by model performance alone but by whether the surrounding care system can reliably translate AI-generated information into care.

title: Implementing Digital Care Pathways and Changes in Contact Volume, Contact Distribution, and Outpatient Costs in Specialized Health Care: Retrospective Longitudinal Observational Study
abstract: Background: Health care systems increasingly promote patient engagement and self-management through digital health services. Digital care pathways, which support coordinated care delivery across the patient journey, have emerged as a promising approach, although evidence regarding their impact on resource use and costs remains limited. Objective: The aim of this study was to examine the implementation and impact of digital care pathways specifically designed to reduce or replace physical contacts or phone consultations in specialized health care. Methods: We analyzed the 10 most widely used digital care pathways by user volume. The selection criteria were (1) more than 1500 users per digital care pathway and (2) the aim of replacing or reducing in-person contacts. Descriptive analyses quantified digital contact volumes, average contacts and costs per patient, and inflation-adjusted expenditures using the consumer price index, both overall and by patient group. Ecologic group-level correlations were examined to assess whether the 2024 proportion of digital contacts was associated with changes in physical contacts and total costs from 2018 to 2024. Results: Digital care pathways were progressively adopted between 2018 and 2024, increasing from no use to accounting for 19.1% (34,837/182,188) of all outpatient contacts among the studied patient groups. Physical visits declined from 74.8% (99,201/132,622) to 54.1% (98,642/182,188), while contacts per patient rose by 7.6% on average. Conditions with the highest uptake of digital pathways showed the strongest reductions in the share of physical visits per patient, with declines of up to 39.7% (0.73/0.44). Average outpatient costs per patient decreased by 18.2% (€421/€515; €1=US $1.12 as of Oct 16, 2026) in real terms, with a 39.3% (€233/€384) reduction in the costs of physical contacts and a 15.4% (€135/€117) increase in the costs of phone visits. Digital pathway contacts accounted for 12.6% (€53/€421 per patient) of total outpatient costs in 2024; however, only 8.8% of the variance in total cost levels was explained by digital pathway adoption, suggesting that the shift toward digital care pathways did not substantially drive overall cost changes. Conclusions: Digital care pathways expanded rapidly, reaching nearly one-fifth of all outpatient contacts by 2024 in the included patient groups and contributing to a notable reduction in physical visits. However, their overall cost impact remains uncertain, as there have also been other factors impacting the development of outpatient costs. Trial Registration:

title: Association of Screen Time With Physical and Mental Health in University Students: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background: Screen use is almost universal, and numerous studies have highlighted both the benefits and the risks of this digital integration. However, evidence on the association between screen time and health outcomes among university students remains inconsistent. Substantial methodological variation has limited the synthesis and interpretation of existing findings. Objective: This study aimed to (1) quantify the associations between screen time and health outcomes as primary analysis; (2) quantify the association between screen time and physical (sleep quality, eye health, weight-related) and mental health outcomes (depression, psychological distress/stress, combined mental health, and well-being); and (3) identify study-level characteristics that explain between-study heterogeneity by using subgroup and meta-regression analyses. Methods: PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched, with final searches conducted on July 11, 2026, and reference lists were additionally screened. Eligible studies included university students aged 17 years or older, assessed screen time as duration, and reported physical or mental health outcomes with sufficient statistical data for effect-size calculation. We followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) checklist. Data were synthesized in RStudio using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustments. Subgroup analyses and meta-regressions was examined. Small-study effects, leave-one-out, and influence diagnostics were also conducted. Results: A total of 82 studies (83 independent samples; 161,340 participants) were included. Longer screen time duration was significantly associated with poorer health outcomes overall (k=83; r =0.175, 95% CI 0.133-0.217; P I 2 =98.35%; Q 82 =4744.45; P r =0.176, 95% CI 0.124-0.227) and physical health outcomes (k=45; r =0.177, 95% CI 0.108-0.243) and broad health domain did not significantly moderate the association ( P =.96). Within mental health, outcome type significantly moderated the association ( P =.03). The association was the strongest for depression (k=21; r =0.230, 95% CI 0.167-0.291) and was weaker for well-being (k=7; r =0.040, 95% CI –0.146 to 0.223). Combined mental health outcomes were also significant (k=8; r =0.170, 95% CI 0.076-0.261), whereas stress was not (k=2; r =0.103, 95% CI –0.222 to 0.407). Within physical health, screen time was significantly associated with poorer sleep quality (k=26; r =0.120, 95% CI 0.083-0.158) and eye health outcomes (k=16; r =0.277, 95% CI 0.089-0.446), but not weight-related outcomes (k=3; r =0.071, 95% CI –0.222 to 0.351); differences across physical outcome types were not significant. Study-level moderators did not meaningfully explain the remaining heterogeneity. Conclusions: Greater screen time was associated with poorer health outcomes among university students, but the magnitude of association varied across specific outcomes and substantial unexplained heterogeneity remained. The predominance of cross-sectional designs, self-reported screen time, and sparse evidence for some outcomes limits causal inference and precision. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs and standardized measurement approaches. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD42024539034; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024539034

title: Real-Time Medical Record Quality Control System (MRQCS): Development and Retrospective Longitudinal Observational Study
abstract: Background: Medical record quality is a key focus of health care quality management. Traditional manual medical record quality control (QC) suffers from low efficiency, inability to achieve full-sample coverage, and poor consistency. Existing intelligent QC systems have significant deficiencies in real-time intervention and quantitative assessment of application effects. Objective: This study aimed to describe the design and development of the medical record quality control system (MRQCS) and to retrospectively evaluate its associations with medical record defect detection, medical record quality, and interreviewer consistency using 7-year longitudinal final-stage QC records (2019-2025). Methods: MRQCS implements a 2-level QC process for clinicians: nonblocking real-time prompting during documentation and blocking validation upon medical record completion. For QC reviewers, it provides AI-assisted defect detection and a 1-click write-back function. QC records from January 2019 to December 2025 were analyzed as 84 monthly discharge cohorts (43,324 sampled admissions), using interrupted time series (ITS) segmented regression with breakpoints aligned to the first discharge cohorts affected by each intervention (December 2020, July 2023, and May 2025). A stable‑rule‑set analysis was performed for genuine quality improvement. Linear mixed‑effects modeling with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) was applied to assess reviewer consistency, alongside multiple sensitivity analyses. Results: By 2025, the MRQCS QC rule library expanded from 41 rules initially to 597 rules. The sampled-case defect rate increased sharply after the January 2021 launch (trend change +0.06, 95% CI 0.03-0.08, P P =.007), and the residual defect rate showed an immediate decline at the May 2025 breakpoint (level change –0.44, 95% CI –0.85 to –0.03, P =.03). The AI-assisted write-back rate exceeded 97% after August 2023 and declined to 84%-87% after the May 2025 discharge blocking intervention (level change –2.14, 95% CI –3.08 to –1.21, P Conclusions: Through the collaborative model of 2-level real-time QC and AI-assisted final-stage QC, MRQCS was associated with improved defect detection, reduction of documentation defects, and substantially greater interreviewer consistency; the discharge-time blocking intervention further reduced the residual defect rate. These findings provide a practical reference for the construction of medical record quality management systems.

title: Beyond Time Saved: A Framework for Comprehensive Evaluation of AI Clinical Documentation
abstract: Ambient AI scribes have been rapidly adopted across health care organizations to mitigate documentation burden and burnout. Initial single-system reports described substantial time savings, but more recent multisite evaluations and meta-analyses describe modest, heterogeneous effects with generally low methodological quality. Most evaluations emphasize efficiency and satisfaction, leaving potential effects on communication quality, narrative preservation, cognitive performance, and equity largely unmeasured. This viewpoint aimed to characterize evaluation patterns in prominent ambient AI scribe implementations, explain why unmeasured domains warrant investigation for patient safety and care quality, and propose an expanded framework with feasible research priorities. This analytic viewpoint mapped evaluation domain coverage in a purposive, illustrative sample of prominent implementation reports published through April 2026, then synthesized findings with literature on clinical communication, narrative medicine, automation effects, and health equity. Reporting was guided by Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) principles for narrative reviews; PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) was not used because the work is a domain-coverage characterization rather than an evidence synthesis estimating effects. A single reviewer (VSME) performed selection and extraction, consistent with the viewpoint’s illustrative intent. Across the included implementations, evaluation consistently measured documentation time, after-hours work, and clinician satisfaction. Within this illustrative sample of 6 independently peer-reviewed real-world implementation evaluations, we did not identify any that reported systematic assessment of patient-clinician communication using validated instruments, structured comparison of AI-generated against human-generated notes for narrative fidelity, longitudinal evaluation of cognitive or educational effects, or equity analyses stratified by language and demographic group. The absence in this purposive sample reflects an absence of public reporting rather than proof that no organization has measured these dimensions internally. Limited error analyses found frequent omissions, with accuracy declining as encounter complexity increased. Evidence from multilingual and interpreter-mediated encounters was notably sparse. Current evidence supports continued implementation with quality safeguards in settings where benefits are demonstrated locally rather than universal adoption on the strength of early single-system reports. Organizations implementing ambient AI scribes should consider embedding prospective evaluation across 4 domains: validated communication quality measurement, structured narrative content comparison, longitudinal cognitive and training studies, and equity analyses across languages and demographics. Three near-term priorities offer immediate feasibility for organizations with evaluation capacity: (1) deploying validated communication instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool or Consumer Assessment of Health Care Providers and Systems (CAHPS) within ongoing rollouts; (2) launching multisite longitudinal trainee cohorts comparing programs with and without ambient AI exposure; and (3) oversampling multilingual and interpreter-mediated encounters for stratified equity analyses. Narrative preservation requires foundational methodological work before implementation-ready measures exist. Editors, implementers, and vendors can each act now: editors by requiring domain-coverage reporting; implementers by preregistering evaluation plans before rollout; vendors by publishing stratified performance data as a routine condition of deployment. The goal is to preserve documented efficiency gains while generating evidence about communication, narrative, reasoning, and equity dimensions that current evaluations leave unmeasured.

title: Real-World Applicability of Multiple International Terminology Systems in Oncology: Mapping Study of Clinical Terms for Cancer Diagnosis and Treatment
abstract: Background: With the rapid expansion of health care data, multiple international standardized terminology systems have been developed and refined to ensure semantic interoperability, which is a crucial factor in facilitating collaborative use. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the real-world use and applicability of standardized terminology systems by mapping clinical terms from routine cancer care and to propose guidelines that optimize mapping. Methods: Clinical terms generated during cancer care at the National Cancer Center Korea were extracted and mapped to multiple target terminology systems: the Korean Standard Classification of Diseases; ; Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes; RxNorm; Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification; and Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms (SNOMED CT). A multidisciplinary working group of health care information managers, data experts, and oncologists verified the mapping outcomes, calculated the cross-verification discordance rate, and compared the coverage across systems. Results: A total of 3472 source terms were identified across 7 domains: chief complaint, diagnosis, laboratory test, imaging test, surgery/procedure, medication, and radiation therapy. With postcoordination and predefined mapping guidelines, SNOMED CT achieved high overall mapping rates (98.3%‐100%) across domains. Applying postcoordination as needed substantially improved exact semantic match rates, which exceeded 90% in most domains. However, more than 40% of source terms were broadly mapped in the imaging test and radiation therapy domains because procedural details such as imaging technique and radiation field configuration could not be represented in SNOMED CT. The cross-verification discordance rate between mappers, defined as the proportion of source terms with disagreement, remained low (0.3%‐1.3%). RxNorm and Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes showed complementary strengths within their specialized domains, adding detail or specificity where SNOMED CT was less complete. Conclusions: Standardized terminology systems are feasible and effective in encoding clinical terms for cancer care. SNOMED CT was the most comprehensive, and predefined mapping guidelines provide a structured framework for mapping and consensus resolution. Domain-specific systems should be used alongside SNOMED CT, and all systems should be updated regularly to reflect evolving clinical practice.

title: Differential Diagnosis of Early-Stage Pulmonary Sarcoidosis With Normal Serum Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Activity Using Peripheral Blood Indicators: Machine Learning Models Development and Validation
abstract: Background: Early-stage pulmonary sarcoidosis with serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (sACE) activity within the normal range is difficult to distinguish from other pulmonary diseases with similar radiographic characteristics. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate machine learning (ML)–based diagnostic models for differentiating early-stage pulmonary sarcoidosis using indices from routine peripheral blood tests. Methods: From May 2014 to May 2021, a total of 1142 patients with atypical initial pulmonary imaging findings were enrolled. After applying strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, 420 cases were divided into sarcoidosis and nonsarcoidosis groups (including mediastinal lymph node tuberculosis [MLNT], lung cancer, lymphoma, and pneumoconiosis), then stratified by sex and randomly split (7:3) into training and validation sets. Features were selected via univariate analysis ( P F 1 -score, Brier score, calibration assessment, and decision curve analysis. Shapley Additive Explanations was used for interpretability. The selected models were deployed as an interactive Shiny web application. Results: After stratification, the male group comprised 224 cases (sarcoidosis n=42; MLNT: n=39; lung cancer: n=106; lymphoma: n=9; pneumoconiosis: n=28), and the female group comprised 196 cases (sarcoidosis: n=100; MLNT: n=39; lung cancer: n=49; lymphoma: n=4; pneumoconiosis: n=4). Models were selected based on comprehensive evaluation of multiple performance metrics, including AUC, accuracy, specificity, F 1 -score, and Brier score. The selected model for the male group was SVM, incorporating the following indices: age, lymphocyte count (Lym#), red cell distribution width standard deviation, D-dimer, sACE, cluster of differentiation 4-positive T cells to cluster of differentiation 8-positive T cells ratio (CD4 + /CD8 + ), erythrocyte sedimentation rate, triglyceride to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (TG/HDLC), basophil count, and total protein. The selected model for the female group was LR, using Lym#, sACE, total cholesterol, TG/HDLC, glucose, CD3 + %, and CD8 + %. The validation set results showed AUCs of 0.896 (95% CI 0.746-1.000) and 0.762 (95% CI 0.632-0.892), sensitivities of 0.700 (95% CI 0.397-0.892) and 0.679 (95% CI 0.493-0.821), and specificities of 0.942 (95% CI 0.844-0.980) and 0.815 (95% CI 0.633-0.918), respectively. Conclusions: Based on sex‑stratified strategies, the models demonstrated preliminary discriminative ability for differentiating early‑stage pulmonary sarcoidosis with normal sACE from other pulmonary diseases. However, the wide CIs preclude definitive conclusions about clinical performance, and external validation in larger cohorts is needed.

title: Early Prediction and Prognosis in Acute Kidney Injury Using a Biomarker-Aware Transformer: Retrospective Multicenter Study
abstract: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common, life-threatening complication among hospitalized patients. Timely prediction is crucial for prevention, while accurate prognosis following onset is essential for guiding care. Although electronic health records (EHRs) provide rich longitudinal data, their high dimensionality, heterogeneity, and temporal complexity pose challenges for traditional machine learning. Objective: The aim of this study was to develop and evaluate a transformer-based model for generalizable AKI prediction and prognosis by modeling long-range temporal dependencies and complex relationships in heterogeneous EHR data and to examine its interpretability. Methods: We developed the Biomarker-Aware Transformer for AKI (BAT-AKI), which integrates multidimensional embeddings capturing temporal dynamics, textual descriptions, hierarchical ontology structures, and semantic relationships in EHRs. To enhance sensitivity to AKI-related biomarker fluctuations, BAT-AKI combines masked language modeling with a novel biomarker abnormality-aware pretraining task. The model was pretrained and fine-tuned for 4 tasks: AKI onset, early reversal, recovery at discharge, and 90-day post-AKI mortality. Pretraining and internal validation used data from the National Patient-Centered Clinical Research Network (PCORnet) site, with external validation across 3 additional sites. Results: BAT-AKI achieved the strongest overall discrimination, outperforming baseline models in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) on most tasks. For AKI onset prediction, it achieved an AUROC of 0.8549 (95% CI 0.8433-0.8658) and an AUPRC of 0.6041 (95% CI 0.5786-0.6292), exceeding the second-best baseline by 2.8% in AUROC and 8.1% in AUPRC. Across prognostic tasks, BAT-AKI achieved AUROCs of 0.6006 (95% CI 0.5703-0.6318), 0.6080 (95% CI 0.5745-0.6397), and 0.8017 (95% CI 0.7708-0.8311) and AUPRCs of 0.7036 (95% CI 0.6690-0.7388), 0.7417 (95% CI 0.7082-0.7765), and 0.5063 (95% CI 0.4422-0.5684) for early reversal, recovery at discharge, and 90-day post-AKI mortality, respectively, corresponding to relative gains of 2.4% to 6% in AUROC and 3.7% to 4.1% in AUPRC over the second-best baseline. Performance remained stable across external cohorts, with AKI onset AUROCs ranging from 0.7754 (95% CI 0.7677-0.7827) to 0.7989 (95% CI 0.7885-0.8092) and AUPRCs ranging from 0.4777 (95% CI 0.4631-0.4924) to 0.5687 (95% CI 0.5495-0.5871), corresponding to relative improvements of 3.7% to 5.3% in AUROC and 16.8% to 25.3% in AUPRC over the transformer baseline. In a low-resource setting using only 2% of the fine-tuning data, BAT-AKI achieved an AUROC of 0.7898 (95% CI 0.7759-0.8036) and an AUPRC of 0.4903 (95% CI 0.4640-0.5178) for AKI onset prediction, exceeding the second-best baseline by 4.2% in AUROC and 10.9% in AUPRC. Visualization of embeddings, attention patterns, and integrated-gradient feature attributions highlighted clinically meaningful relationships and patient-specific trajectories. Conclusions: BAT-AKI provides generalizable AKI prediction and prognosis with consistent discrimination across institutions, while offering interpretability insights into its predictions, supporting its potential for early warning and AKI care optimization. title: Integrating Natural Language Processing in Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services Research Using Normalization Process Theory: Implementation Report
abstract: Background: Anxiety problems are prevalent among autistic children and adolescents and those with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Natural language processing (NLP) is increasingly used to structure information from electronic health records (EHRs), but its implementation within secure child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) research environments is less frequently reported. Objective: This study documented the specification, governance, integration, and evaluation of an NLP-enabled information extraction workflow within the Oxford Health National Health Service (NHS) Foundation Trust CAMHS research setting for extracting documented anxiety treatment information and outcome-related text from the EHRs of autistic young people and those with ADHD and examined implementation using normalization process theory (NPT). Methods: A multidisciplinary team developed a locally deployed NLP pipeline to identify labeled text spans describing presenting problems, medication attributes, psychological therapies, and treatment outcomes in pseudonymized EHR notes. Implementation followed an iterative seven-phase road map: (1) defining research questions, (2) identifying key constructs, (3) codeveloping an annotation schema, (4) training human annotators, (5) resolving annotation discrepancies, (6) large-scale annotation of EHR data, and (7) developing and evaluating the NLP model. NPT was applied throughout to guide implementation and evaluate progress. Quantitative outcomes (data volume processed, annotation reliability, and model performance) and qualitative feedback were collected to assess implementation success. Results: The source cohort comprised 454,127 notes from 5906 patients; 697 (0.2%) randomly selected, manually annotated notes from 302 (5.1%) patients were used for model development and held-out evaluation. Category-specific position-based Krippendorff α values ranged from 0.325 to 0.579 for problem, psychological therapy, and outcome spans and from 0.665 to 0.967 for medication spans. Agreement was highest for medication names, doses, and frequencies and lowest for cognitive problems and treatment outcomes. Held-out macroaveraged F1-score was 0.87 (95% CI 0.86-0.89) across the 4 medication labels and 0.71 (95% CI 0.68-0.73) across the 5 problem labels, psychological therapy labels, and outcome labels; label-specific F1-score ranged from 0.60 to 0.98. Team-generated implementation records indicated that multidisciplinary schema development and clear protocols supported shared understanding and engagement, whereas annotation burden, documentation variability, data access delays, and computing constraints impeded implementation. No major adverse events or harms were reported. Conclusions: This report demonstrates the feasibility of integrating NLP tools into NHS CAMHS research workflows to extract structured information on anxiety treatments from routine clinical records. The NPT framework provided a structured approach for documenting the organizational work, barriers, and adaptations involved. External validation, refinement of less reliable labels, and further evaluation are required before broader use.

title: Condition-Aware Trajectory Prediction via Velocity-Aware Model Selection
abstract: Safe and proactive decision-making in autonomous driving systems depends on predicting the future locations of vehicles, pedestrians, and other dynamic actors in traffic with high precision. However, trajectory prediction is an extremely challenging problem due to the existence of multimodal possible futures, the random nature of human behavior, and the complexity of densely interactive urban scenes. The previous trajectories of the actors are essential in future prediction. Usually, interactions between actors, map information, and environmental context are also considered. In this study, we focus on the velocity of the ego-vehicle for trajectory prediction as an additional factor. Our approach estimates future trajectories by selecting an appropriate velocity-aware model, which learns behavioral patterns from past experiences. The effectiveness of the proposed approach, the results of extensive experiments carried out on large-scale autonomous driving datasets covering different traffic scenarios and driving contexts, demonstrate that the proposed design reduces prediction error relative to the corresponding generalist baselines. The code and dataset splits generated for this study will be released on GitHub and can be accessed at https://github.com/mltmnrgz/velocity_aware_trajectory_prediction

title: Adaptive Hybrid Transformer Framework With Dynamic Convolution, Confidence-Aware Learning, and Cross-Domain Feature Alignment for Automated Steel Surface Defect Recognition
abstract: Accurate steel surface defect recognition is essential for intelligent manufacturing systems, yet reliable inspection remains challenging because of complex texture variations, high intra-class similarity, heterogeneous imaging conditions, and distribution shifts across industrial environments. Although recent convolutional neural networks and transformer-based architectures have achieved promising classification performance, they often provide limited prediction reliability and reduced robustness under heterogeneous data distributions. This paper presents an adaptive hybrid framework that integrates Dynamic Convolution, Efficient Channel Attention (ECA)-based feature refinement, Vision Transformer (ViT) encoding, evidential uncertainty learning, and domain-adaptive feature calibration into a unified architecture for automated steel surface defect classification. Dynamic Convolution enhances local feature extraction through input-adaptive kernels, while attention-guided refinement improves discriminative feature representation before transformer-based global context modeling. An evidential learning strategy based on Dirichlet distributions enables uncertainty-aware prediction, and a lightweight domain-adaptive calibration module promotes feature consistency across heterogeneous datasets using unlabeled target-domain samples within a leakage-controlled adaptation protocol. The proposed framework is evaluated on the publicly available NEU and XSDD benchmark datasets using a comprehensive experimental protocol that includes quantitative performance evaluation, confusion matrix analysis, convergence analysis, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, uncertainty calibration, explainability assessment, and systematic ablation studies. Experimental results demonstrate classification accuracies of 98.9% and 94.1% on the NEU and XSDD datasets, respectively. In addition, the proposed framework achieves improved confidence calibration, yielding an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.041, a Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) of 0.214, and a Brier Score of 0.057, outperforming representative CNN-based, transformer-based, and ablated architectures. The experimental results indicate that integrating adaptive local feature extraction, global contextual representation learning, uncertainty-aware prediction, and domain-adaptive feature calibration improves classification performance, predictive reliability, and cross-domain robustness while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time industrial inspection.

title: Robustness in AI-Based Power System Forecasting: A Structured Review and Unified Evaluation Framework
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced load, solar PV, wind, and net-load forecasting, yet evaluation remains largely accuracy-centric, with limited assessment of reliability under missing data, measurement perturbations, distribution shifts, extreme events, and training variability. This paper presents a structured review and a proposed standardized robustness evaluation framework for AI-based power-system forecasting. Robustness failures are organized into four dimensions: data imperfections, distributional non-stationarity, extreme/out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, and intrinsic model instability. The resulting failure-mode-driven framework integrates tail-error and regime-aware analysis, probabilistic calibration, controlled stress testing, cross-domain validation, and retraining-stability assessment. A preliminary benchmark across three datasets, two forecasting tasks, three model families, two forecast horizons, and five independent training runs per configuration demonstrates that nominal accuracy and robustness criteria can favor different models. Robustness-enhancing methods are further organized at the data, model, and training levels, and their implications for reserve scheduling, risk-aware operation, and economic performance are examined. The review highlights persistent gaps in calibration assessment, systematic stress testing, cross-domain evaluation, and reproducible benchmarking. These findings motivate a shift from accuracy-centric evaluation toward multidimensional, deployment-oriented robustness assessment for trustworthy AI-based power-system forecasting.

title: A Feasibility Study Comparing Body-Powered and Myoelectric Prostheses Using Plug-and-Play Module
abstract: Two types of widely used prostheses are the body-powered prosthesis actuated with the shoulder/trunk movement and the myoelectric prosthesis actuated with a motor using sEMG signals. Even though these devices have been used for several decades, controlled quantitative comparisons that isolate the effects of prosthetic actuation strategy under identical mechanical interfaces remain limited. The challenges of the comparison studies stem from factors including different interfaces of these devices, different shape/length of the residual limb, the cause of amputation, or frequency of the prosthesis use during daily life. In this study, we designed a plug-and-play module that can change the body-powered prosthesis easily to a myoelectric prosthesis while keeping the interface structure of the body-powered prosthesis offering a cost-effective and personalized solution. Ten non-amputee participants were recruited to conduct three daily living tasks by wearing two different prostheses with a bypass of their own forearm. These participants were assumed to be novice users of both body-powered and myoelectric prostheses. The myoelectric prosthesis reduced compensatory ipsilateral elbow motion by approximately 30%, with significant reductions observed in two of the three tasks ( $p\lt 0.001$ ), and contralateral shoulder motion by about 40%, with significant reductions observed across all three tasks ( $p\lt 0.01$ ), compared to the body-powered prosthesis. Muscle activation in the biceps, triceps, and deltoids was substantially lower with the myoelectric prosthesis, showing reductions ranging from 50% to 60% ( $p\lt 0.001$ ). Additionally, pressure exerted on the users back by the harness was drastically reduced due to the lack of straps in the myoelectric application ( $p\lt 0.001$ ) when using the myoelectric prosthesis.

title: Distributed Adaptive Dual-Channel Fault-Tolerant Cooperative Control for Radar Networks Under Persistent Disturbances
abstract: Radar networks in contested electromagnetic environments suffer from node faults, clock desynchronization, communication delays, and interference, causing cooperative chain disruption and tracking collapse. This paper proposes a distributed adaptive dual-channel fault-tolerant cooperative control method. First, a unified electromechanical hybrid beam control model is established, decomposing the beam pointing angle into mechanical and electronic channels with second- and first-order dynamics. The detection performance constraint is formulated as bounded convergence of the beam pointing error. Second, a task-oriented integral sliding surface is designed to directly map the sliding motion to the desired tracking accuracy convergence. Damping-modified adaptive sliding-mode and adaptive compensation laws are developed for the two channels, achieving coordinated large-range coarse and small-range fine pointing. Feedforward and delay-dependent compensation suppress clock and delay disturbances. Furthermore, a dual-layer fault-tolerant mechanism integrating node-level actuator reconfiguration and network-level event-driven topology reconstruction is constructed, coupled with event-triggered communication based on beam pointing error to reduce communication load while preserving accuracy. Based on the Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional and average dwell-time method, the uniform ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop system is derived via cascaded synthesis. The necessary condition of average dwell time and the degradation law under violated condition are established, and the UUB property under infeasible actuator reconfiguration is proved. Explicit relationships between steady-state error bound, fault-damage factor, and delay upper bound are derived, and Zeno behavior is ruled out. Simulation results show that under the nominal model, the proposed method reduces position RMSE by about 32% compared with standard adaptive sliding-mode control. Under compound scenarios, it reduces communication load by about 63% compared with continuous communication, while maintaining effective detection even when 25% of nodes suffer severe faults. Hardware-in-the-loop experiments further verify real-time feasibility.

title: A Novel Design Method for Multi-Band Wilkinson Power Dividers With Distinct Power Split Ratios Based on Non-Uniform Transmission Lines
abstract: This paper introduces a novel design for a multi-band Wilkinson power divider (WPD) featuring a frequency-dependent power division ratio based on non-uniform transmission lines (NTLs). The proposed design procedure results in a simplified and modular structure. To derive the necessary design constraints for a WPD, a comprehensive analysis based on $ABCD$ parameters is employed. Furthermore, the characteristic impedance of each NTL is expressed using its own truncated Fourier series, from which the corresponding $ABCD$ matrix is derived. To demonstrate the scalability of the method, multiple design examples are presented, including dual-band, triple-band, and quad-band WPDs. The dual-band and triple-band devices are verified through simulation, while the quad-band device is both simulated and fabricated. Both simulations and measurements validate the design approach, demonstrating excellent port matching, high isolation between the output ports, and accurate power division at each operating band. The proposed method is general and can be extended to an arbitrary number of operating bands.

title: Algorithms on Imperfect Graphs: A Framework for Optimization on Digital Twin Networks
abstract: Classical graph optimization algorithms are analyzed under the assumption that the input graph accurately represents the underlying system. In digital twin environments, however, optimization is often performed on a model graph that only approximates the real network. Structural discrepancies between the model graph and the real graph may arise from incomplete observations, delayed updates, or estimation errors. Consequently, a solution computed on the model graph may become suboptimal or infeasible when evaluated on the real system. This work studies graph optimization under such structural discrepancy. A framework is introduced in which algorithms compute solutions on a digital twin graph $\hat {G}$ , while solution quality is evaluated on a real graph $G$ , in a single model–deployment–repair cycle. To quantify the effect of this separation, the Graph Discrepancy Ratio (GDR) is introduced. The ratio compares the cost of the repaired feasible solution on the real graph with the cost of an optimal solution on that graph. A distortion model based on edge discrepancies between $\hat {G}$ and $G$ is further developed. The framework is analyzed quantitatively through the vertex cover problem, where the objective is to compute a minimum-cardinality subset of vertices that covers all edges of a graph. The analysis shows that structural discrepancy introduces an additional additive loss term that is not captured by classical approximation guarantees. The standard assumption that computation and evaluation take place on the same graph is thereby shown to be oversimplified for digital twins: an approximation guarantee established on the model graph transfers to the real graph only with an additive term that grows linearly with the edge discrepancy, and this dependence is unavoidable in general. In particular, a solution that is feasible on the digital twin graph may become infeasible on the real graph. More generally, a transfer theorem is established for graph optimization problems that admit bounded repair under edge discrepancies. The vertex-cover analysis and the bounded-repair transfer theorem characterize how structural discrepancy affects feasibility and approximation quality when optimization is performed on imperfect graph representations. Additional examples for dominating set and matching illustrate problem-dependent feasibility-repair mechanisms. The framework is complemented by an empirical evaluation on road networks from Dubai and Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, obtained from OpenStreetMap, and on two synthetic benchmark networks with markedly different degree structure. Digital twin graphs are generated using controlled edge perturbations, including a spatially localized distortion model. The experiments report matching-based upper estimates of the Graph Discrepancy Ratio and the repair costs of two classical vertex-cover algorithms, and examine their behavior relative to the theoretical bounds. They show that the observed repair cost remains far below the worst-case bound and is governed not only by the number of mismatched edges but also by their spatial concentration and deletion–addition composition.
