title: A Compact, Uniplanar, Quasi-Isotropic Antenna for 2.4-GHz Bluetooth Low Energy Data Link in Neural Interface Devices
abstract: The antenna in neural interface devices should exhibit a near-isotropic radiation pattern, minimizing null spots that could cause connection dropouts. The design must also be compact to integrate into limited space. Here we present a uniplanar antenna design with a quasi-isotropic pattern for 2.4 GHz Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) communication. The design uses two crossed dipoles with meandered arms and nine individually optimizable parameters. The design philosophy follows the redundant sensing architecture, where information redundancy is achieved through a large number of interdependent parameter configurations that yield near-isotropic radiation. The Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm or Genetic Algorithm (GA) is then applied to search for a heuristic solution that minimizes gain deviation. The proposed antenna has uniplanar dimensions of $21\times 21$ mm. It achieves a gain deviation of 5.5 dB at 2.44 GHz over the full space. The antenna maintains a -10 dB bandwidth across the BLE frequency range of 2.402–2.480 GHz. The proposed antenna is integrated into a prototype neural interface device. It enables reliable, real-time streaming of neural data from the device to a host computer via a BLE data link.
authors: ["Anh Tuan Nguyen;Byeongchan Jeong;Markus W. Drealan;Brian Zhe Hui Lim;Maral Daneshyan;Wei Wang;Zhi Yang;"]

title: A Unified Deep Learning Framework for Motion Correction in Medical Imaging
abstract: Deep learning has shown significant value in medical image registration for motion correction. However, current techniques are either limited by the type and range of motion they can handle or require iterative inference and/or retraining for new imaging data. To address these limitations, we introduce UniMo, a Unified Motion Correction framework that leverages deep neural networks to correct for various types of motion in medical imaging. UniMo exploits an alternating optimization scheme for a unified loss function to train an integrated model of 1) an equivariant neural network for global rigid motion correction and 2) an encoder-decoder network to correct local deformations. To this end, it features a geometric deformation augmenter that 1) enhances the robustness of global motion correction by addressing any local deformations, whether they are caused by non-rigid motion or geometric distortions, and 2) generates augmented data to improve the training process. UniMo is a hybrid model that uses both image intensities and shapes to achieve robust performance amid image appearance variations; therefore, it generalizes well to various medical imaging modalities without a need for network retraining. We trained and tested UniMo to track motion in fetal magnetic resonance imaging, which is a very challenging application due to 1) the presence of both large rigid and non-rigid motion, and 2) large variations in image appearance. Then we tested the trained model, without retraining, on various image modalities from three public datasets, including MedMNIST, lung CT, and BraTS. The results show that UniMo surpassed existing motion correction methods in terms of accuracy; notably, it enabled one-time training on a single modality while maintaining high stability and adaptability for inference across multiple unseen imaging datasets. By offering a unified solution to motion correction, UniMo marks a significant advantage in challenging applications with a mixture of bulk motion and local deformations. The code is available at: https://github.com/IntelligentImaging/UNIMO
authors: ["Jian Wang;Razieh Faghihpirayesh;Danny Joca;Polina Golland;Ali Gholipour;"]

title: SC-SAE-RAG: Bounded Section-Chain Evidence Recovery for Scientific Literature Question Answering
abstract: Scientific literature question answering (QA) requires precise evidence from long documents whose section organization provides strong but underexploited retrieval signals. Existing hierarchical retrievers commonly use coarse section retrieval as a hard filter, making evidence irrecoverable when an evidence-bearing section is missed. We propose SC-SAE-RAG, a bounded section-chain evidence recovery framework for individual documents that combines structure-aware chunking, expandable section anchors, protected multi-view fusion, and source-paragraph calibration. The framework expands structurally plausible evidence regions while preserving a fixed final evidence budget and explicit paragraph provenance. We evaluate the frozen method on all 927 evidence-bearing questions and all 1,005 answer questions from the 281-paper QASPER development split, then test it zero-shot on PeerQA. On QASPER, SC-SAE-RAG reaches Recall@10 of 0.9752 and exact paragraph Evidence F1 of 0.2824, exceeding SAC flat by 0.0709 with a 95% paired-bootstrap interval of [0.0612, 0.0806] and Holm-adjusted $p=0.00040$ . On zero-shot PeerQA, paragraph F1 improves over SAC flat by 0.0598 [0.0355, 0.0838]. The improved evidence sets also yield consistent mean official QASPER Answer F1 gains across two generator families and a significant gain over the SAE-RAG baseline. Evidence-identity-preserving context enrichment further improves automated completeness scores without changing cited paragraph identities. Stage tracing shows that seed retrieval omits 300 of 1,424 gold-section instances and that bounded SC-Chain expansion recovers 202 (67.3%), with 39 recovered sections supplying exact gold paragraphs to the final evidence set. These results establish SC-SAE-RAG as an effective, efficient, and auditable evidence-construction layer for scientific document question answering.
authors: ["Qi Zhang;Xucheng Liu;Huan Wang;Zixuan Wang;Jiguang Liu;Jiangke Cheng;"]

title: Very Low-Profile, Small-Size, MIMO Four-Antenna Module Covering 7.125-8.4 GHz for 6G Upper Mid-Band Mobile Devices
abstract: This article presents a very low-profile, small-size, four-antenna module covering 7.125-8.4 GHz in the upper mid-band for multi-input multi-output (MIMO) operation for future sixth generation (6G) mobile devices. The MIMO four-antenna (M4A) module has a thickness of only 0.6 mm (about $0.014\lambda $ with respect to the wavelength at 7.125 GHz), much lower than those of the reported ones with 1 mm thickness to cover the same spectrum. Additionally, the M4A module has a small size of $0.31\lambda ^{2}$ , also smaller than the reported ones. Notice that the 7.125-8.4 GHz band is a promising new international mobile telecommunication (IMT) spectrum to be determined at upcoming World Radiocommunication Conference 2027 (WRC-27); and it is an attractive 6G mobile spectrum for its large contiguous spectrum for wider channel bandwidths. To demonstrate its practical application, we fabricated two M4A modules for a smartphone-like mobile device application to provide 8 antennas for MIMO operations. Furthermore, based on applying the fabricated M4A modules, we conducted an $8\times 4$ MIMO communication trial with only 4 transmitted spatial streams to achieve a large data throughput of about 3.2 Gbps with only 100 MHz bandwidth in the module’s operating bandwidth; and the corresponding spectral efficiency is as large as about 32 bps/Hz. Details of the proposed M4A module and its $8\times 4$ MIMO application for 6G mobile devices are presented.
authors: ["Kin-Lu Wong;Han-Hsin Ko;I-Chan Huang;Wei-Cheng Li;"]

title: Evaluating Static Security Gates and Learned Detectors on LLM-Generated Code in CI/CD Pipelines
abstract: Automated security gates in Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines assess software security by matching source code against predefined rules. However, this approach is challenged when the code is generated by Large Language Models (LLMs), whose outputs may contain vulnerabilities that are not represented by existing detection rules. The aim of this study is to examine this limitation and to establish an appropriate framework for its evaluation. To this end, we conducted a controlled experiment using 21 adversarial conditions covering three vulnerability scenarios, three programming languages and four generative models within an ERP CI/CD pipeline. Each artefact was analysed by its industrial scanner, with exploitability confirmed by proof-of-concept exploits, then by deep learning detectors against 25 template-written safe controls and 34 generated by the same model as the vulnerable artefacts. Scanners reported no finding in 13 of 21 conditions; under a controlled registry, scanners resolved five of six dependencies and reported nothing. Zero-shot detection was unusable (AUC = 0.466). Fine-tuning reached 0.982 and 0.947 against the template-written controls, 0.841 and 0.773 against LLM-generated ones, a gap that reverses when the corpus is itself LLM-generated, and 0.791 and 0.698 once malformed artefacts are excluded. On an untrained fourth class the ranking transfers (AUC 0.604–0.913), the threshold does not (recall 0.000–0.722). Compliance with CI/CD security gates does not reflect the security of LLM-generated artefacts; semantic detection requires supervision and holds only within the trained classes. Detectors should be validated against negative controls, whose provenance determines what they are measured to have learned.
authors: ["Mohammed Bedjaoui;Mohammed Yassine Kazi Tani;Sidi Mohammed Benslimane;"]

title: NeuroFormer: A Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Transformers for Transdiagnostic Mental Health Classification
abstract: Multimodal mental health classification is promising, but small clinical cohorts make it hard to distinguish apparent model gains from demographic confounding and evaluation effects. We evaluate NeuroFormer, a hierarchical multimodal Transformer integrating Electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking, and behavioural features, on a complete-case Multimodal Resource for Studying Information Processing in the Developing Brain (MIPDB) cohort of 100 participants (19 with a reported history of at least one psychiatric diagnosis and 81 with no reported diagnosis history). Under stratified five-fold cross-validation repeated five times, NeuroFormer achieved the highest descriptive mean fold-level Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC-AUC) among 17 evaluated models (0.677), with balanced accuracy of 64.1% and F1-score of 39.9%. However, dependence-aware pairwise inference did not establish statistically reliable superiority over the evaluated baselines. At the participant level, repetition-averaged out-of-fold NeuroFormer predictions yielded an ROC-AUC of 0.635, compared with 0.748 for an age-only logistic regression model. In the fold-local confound analysis, NeuroFormer ROC-AUC decreased from 0.686 to 0.502 after age/sex residualization, while age-matched evaluation yielded an ROC-AUC of 0.546 ( $p=0.329$ ). Threshold selection and test-informed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) further demonstrated sensitivity to evaluation choices, and repetition-averaged probabilities were poorly calibrated (Brier score 0.192 versus 0.154 for a prevalence-only reference). These findings indicate that developmental age and evaluation design materially influence apparent performance in this small cohort. NeuroFormer is therefore best interpreted as a controlled research benchmark; it is not suitable for clinical screening or deployment.
authors: ["Ayesha Anzer;Abdul Bais;"]

title: A Comparative Small-Signal Stability Assessment ofSequence-Extraction Methods for Positive- and Negative-Sequence-Controlled Grid-Connected Inverters
abstract: The operation of grid-connected inverters under unbalanced grid conditions is increasingly common due to asymmetrical faults and growing penetration of distributed energy resources in asymmetrical distribution networks. In such conditions, negative-sequence voltage components induce inherent double-frequency ( $2\omega _{\mathrm {g}}$ ) oscillations in conventional $dq$ -frame controllers, leading to pronounced active-power ripple, dc-link voltage stress, and degraded phase-locked loop (PLL) synchronization. These effects are further exacerbated in weak grids, where control–grid interaction becomes highly sensitive to system dynamics. To address these issues, positive–negative-sequence control (PNSC) is a widely adopted solution which enables independent regulation of sequence currents. However, the effectiveness, control performance, and stability of PNSC are fundamentally constrained by the sequence-extraction stage, which determines how grid quantities are decomposed into positive and negative components. Despite its critical role, most existing studies select a specific sequence-extraction method a priori and treat it as a fixed preprocessing stage, without justification or systematic investigation of how different extraction principles influence PNSC closed-loop stability and inverter–grid interaction. Consequently, the impact of sequence-extraction dynamics has not been consistently evaluated across different methods within a unified framework. Therefore, this paper investigates the impact of four sequence-extraction methods on the small-signal stability of a three-phase PNSC grid-connected inverter. Four common sequence-extraction methods are considered: matrix-based symmetrical-component extraction, $\tfrac {1}{4}T$ -delay extraction, notch-filter-based extraction, and decoupled double synchronous reference frame (DDSRF) extraction. The assessment is performed under balanced and unbalanced grid voltages over a range of short-circuit ratios (SCRs), considering both inner current-control (CC) and open-loop power-control (OLPC) operation with $K\in \{0,1,-1\}$ for sequence-current reference shaping. Frequency-domain impedance characteristics and inverter-grid stability margins are evaluated using Bode plots and the generalized Nyquist criterion, while EMT simulations are used to validate the predicted dynamic behaviour under weak and unbalanced grid conditions. In addition, the influence of PLL dynamics on each sequence-extraction method is systematically examined. The results show that DDSRF provides the most effective balance among stability margin, dynamic response, and robustness under unbalanced and low-SCR conditions.
authors: ["Muhammad Ajmal Khan;Foad Taghizadeh;Mohammad Javad Sanjari;Yong Zhu;Junwei Lu;Nabil Mohammed;"]

title: Dual-Perspective Reparameterized Convolutional Network for Single Image Deraining
abstract: The core challenge of single image deraining is to effectively model the complex spatial distribution of rain streaks while retaining rich background details. Existing Transformer-based deraining methods excel in capturing long-range feature dependencies, but the quadratic complexity of self-attention leads to excessive computational overhead, which makes it hard to satisfy real-time application demands. In comparison, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) enjoy the merit of linear complexity, yet they are restricted by insufficient deep feature representation and weak cross-layer feature interaction. To address these issues and fully exploit the advantages of CNNs, this paper proposes a Dual-Perspective Reparameterized Convolutional Network for single image deraining. From the feature reuse perspective, the network integrates Stage-wise Feature Aggregation (SFA) and Initial Feature Injection (IFI) to achieve fast cross-network feature aggregation and transmission, constructing an efficient information flow to strengthen feature interaction and boost deraining performance. From the feature enhancement perspective, a multi-directional Gaussian reparameterized convolution fusion module is designed, which embeds the Gaussian blur prior into standard convolution. Through multi-branch learning in the training phase and structural reparameterization in the inference phase, this module enhances the rain streak removal ability of convolutional layers and reduces parameter redundancy simultaneously. Extensive experiments on public deraining datasets (Rain100L and Rain100H) show that the proposed method obtains state-of-the-art PSNR and SSIM values. Overall, our network balances deraining performance and computational efficiency effectively, providing a practical and high-performance solution for real-world single image deraining tasks.
authors: ["Xiaolong Shi;Wei Zhang;Kelei Yao;Fan Wang;Tianming Wang;"]

title: State-Transition Instrumentation in AI-Mediated Block-Based Programming: Replay Consistency and Provenance Preservation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated block-based programming requires process records connecting direct editing, generated proposals, and checking to observable workspace states. This article presents a state-transition instrumentation framework combining structural normalization, SHA-256 identifiers, task-specific checker linkage, proposal provenance, and self-loop retention in a shared schema. The architecture separates online capture from offline reconstruction. Controlled synthetic traces exercise schema-level invariants, and a frozen export from five sixth-grade classes provides 31,168 source records, including 12,513 snapshots. Offline recomputation reproduced all stored canonical representations and state hashes under the specified normalization rules. Canonical hashing consolidated 10,857 raw-snapshot identifiers into 5,345 identifiers. Reconstruction yielded 11,954 transitions, including 5,822 self-loops (48.7%), reported by snapshot-triggering label and mode. In 1,021 state-changing observations at checking, session-end, or generation triggers marked as unapplied, the trigger alone did not identify the operation responsible for the difference. By recording convention, each of the 441 generation events was paired with a provenance entry. Across 1,122 checked task–state pairs, no pair had conflicting recorded outcomes. A stratified 100-pair comparison with adjudicated task judgments reported 93.0% checker–reference agreement (Cohen’s $\kappa =0.86$ ), with seven disagreements in two rule-coverage categories. The contribution is a source-linked representation for direct and AI-mediated programming that supports deterministic replay and inspection of retained process evidence.
authors: ["Jaecheon Jeon;"]

title: Deterministic Kinematic Extraction From Diffusion Models for Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Physical Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) data scarcity is a critical bottleneck for deploying lightweight Human Activity Recognition (HAR) models on edge devices. We propose a direct kinematic augmentation framework that uses foundational video diffusion models as a scalable surrogate for physical sensor deployment, completely bypassing probabilistic cross-modal distillation. We extract continuous 3D spatial trajectories via monocular human mesh recovery fused with Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), anchoring the simulated kinematics to a gravity-aligned coordinate system. A deterministic Savitzky-Golay Digital Signal Processing (DSP) stage smooths these trajectories while retaining high-frequency biomechanical impacts (e.g., $10g$ falls). The resulting synthetic acceleration tensors are statistically calibrated against physical datasets (PAMAP2, SisFall) via Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Jensen-Shannon alignment, preventing metric exploitation. Systematic evaluation across six edge architectures, using a subject-independent partition and repeated over multiple random seeds, localizes precisely where the synthetic prior pays. Under extreme data starvation (1% availability) it prevents majority-class collapse, yielding Macro F1-Score gains of + 20.66 points for the spatial 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), + 12.64 for the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and + 8.50 for the Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM); these gains survive Holm correction and are reproduced by exhaustive subject-grouped cross-validation. As the availability of physical training data expands, this performance advantage narrows, establishing direct kinematic augmentation as a specialized intervention rather than a universal substitute. Ultimately, deterministic kinematic extraction converts freely available generative video data into inertial training signals exactly where physical data is hardest to obtain, without introducing inference-time overhead.
authors: ["Marcos Eduardo Pivaro Monteiro;Jamil De Araujo Farhat;João Alberto Fabro;Bogdan Tomoyuki Nassu;"]

title: 3D Photogrammetric Scanner for Pediatric Head Acquisition
abstract: Accurate three-dimensional assessment of cranial morphology is central to pediatric clinical practice, including the diagnosis and monitoring of congenital deformities. Conventional imaging modalities, while effective, expose patients to ionizing radiation or require sedation, making repeated acquisitions impractical in neonatal settings. Existing optical scanning solutions overcome these limitations but remain largely confined to specialized centers due to their cost and size. This work proposes the development and pre-clinical validation of a low-cost, compact photogrammetric scanner for pediatric cranial surface acquisition, utilizing physical mannequins in both static conditions and with simulated motion to mimic the involuntary movements of infants. The system integrates 20 Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 units mounted on a 3D-printed modular frame and driven by five Raspberry Pi 4B computers. Synchronized software management ensures short sequential acquisition capture, while fiducial markers provide real-time alignment feedback during reconstruction. The resulting structure has a diameter of 780 mm, weighs 2.5 kg and completes a full acquisition in 1.6 seconds. Geometric accuracy, evaluated against a Revopoint Miraco structured light scanner, yielded a surface deviation RMS of 0.359 mm (Std = 0.290 mm), with comparable results maintained under the simulated movement conditions. The proposed system offers a radiation-free and affordable solution for longitudinal cranial morphology monitoring in pediatric patients. Its modular construction and open software architecture further support reproducibility and ease of clinical integration. While these preliminary pre-clinical results demonstrate adequate geometric accuracy, future clinical trial on pediatric patients is required to validate its performance under real operative conditions across the full clinical pathway.
authors: ["Aurora Magnani;Federico Mussa;Michaela Servi;Francesco Dalle Mura;Monica Carfagni;Mirko Scagnet;Rina Agushi;Yary Volpe;"]

title: Private Discrete Fourier Transform With Applications to Linear Convolution
abstract: We study the problem of computing the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) on data secret-shared to two non-colluding cloud servers. While DFT in plaintext is typically computed using floating-point arithmetic, secure computation of DFT requires the use of fixed-point representation. A central challenge in this mode of computation is that fixed-point multiplication causes intermediate values to grow, necessitating secure truncation to ensure that the underlying integer representation remains within the secure computation domain. While secure truncation typically requires interaction, shares can also be truncated locally when there is a sufficiently large gap between the plaintext input range and the secure computation domain. However, local truncation introduces a probabilistic risk of failure. In this work, we demonstrate a secure DFT protocol based on local truncation and empirically validate the derived truncation-failure bounds. Since local truncation introduces a downward-biased truncation offset, we also evaluate its impact on numerical accuracy by comparing it against two variants: a secure DFT protocol based on interactive truncation and a fixed-point DFT with deterministic rounding. Our results show that all truncation strategies have similar effects on fixed-point rounding error, as measured by signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and root-mean-square error (RMSE). Owing to its non-interactive nature, local truncation achieves substantially better performance—up to two orders of magnitude faster in our evaluation of the online phase under the client-aided setup—due to minimal communication. Extending our DFT protocol, we construct an inverse discrete Fourier transform (IDFT) protocol and leverage these constructions to compose a secure linear convolution protocol for fixed-point arithmetic. Our results show that the DFT-based protocol scales efficiently for large input sizes compared with direct and matrix-based baselines, owing to its superior asymptotic complexity, and is an order of magnitude faster in our online evaluation. We further demonstrate the practical usability of our protocol by applying it to an image-denoising task.
authors: ["Mohammad Nabil Ahmed;Kana Shimizu;"]

title: BR-PVGen—The Brazilian Photovoltaic Generation Dataset
abstract: Solar energy plays a pivotal role in Brazil’s evolving energy matrix, particularly in the distributed generation (DG) sector. Despite the rapid expansion of PV installations, publicly accessible datasets that accurately reflect the operational realities of Brazilian photovoltaic systems remain limited. This study introduces BR-PVGen, a comprehensive and curated dataset derived from inverter-level measurements of 51 PV plants distributed across diverse climatic regions in Brazil. The dataset integrates synchronized, high-resolution meteorological and power generation data, processed through a structured pipeline including anomaly detection, temporal alignment, missing-data treatment, and normalization. Theoretical generation was computed following IEC 61724-2 guidelines, enabling the systematic estimation of performance gaps and loss components such as bifacial gain, temperature losses, inverter clipping, and system unavailability. To demonstrate its applicability for forecasting and benchmarking tasks, multiple machine learning models were evaluated for daily and 15-minute-ahead generation prediction using standardized preprocessing and lag-based feature selection. Performance was assessed using complementary scale-independent and normalized error metrics. The results confirm the dataset’s consistency, robustness, and suitability for comparative evaluation across heterogeneous PV systems. BR-PVGen establishes a reliable foundation for PV performance analysis, forecasting research, and data-driven methodological development.
authors: ["Caian D. de Jesus;Rhuan N. Ferreira;Eduardo Pestana de Aguiar;"]

title: Toward Personalized SSVEP-Based Brain–Computer Interfaces: A Human Factor-Aware Framework for Visual Stimulation and Information Transfer Rate Evaluation
abstract: Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP)-based brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) commonly use checkerboard stimuli for reliable command selection; however, prolonged visual stimulation can lead to irritation and fatigue. This study investigates flickering-dot stimuli as an alternative visual stimulation approach, focusing on classification performance and user comfort. We evaluated a conventional checkerboard and two flickering-dot stimuli under single- and mixed-frequency conditions using five stimulus classes associated with 6, 7, 8, 13, and 15 Hz. The electroencephalography (EEG) signals were analyzed using spectral- and correlation-based methods with different sampling rates, stimulus-window lengths, and EEG channel configurations. Flickering-dot stimuli achieved classification performance approaching that of the conventional checkerboard stimulus and were generally associated with lower self-reported visual irritation and fatigue. Mixed-frequency stimulation generally achieved higher classification accuracy than the corresponding single-frequency stimulation. Participant-specific analysis using a three-fold held-out personalization procedure yielded mean classification accuracies of 82.2% for the common configuration and 83.1% for the personalized configuration, while the selected stimulus and EEG channel configurations varied across participants. To incorporate user experience into communication-performance assessment, we evaluated an exploratory Human-Factor Information Transfer Rate (HF-ITR), which integrates visual irritation and fatigue into conventional Information Transfer Rate (ITR). The results suggest that the evaluated flickering-dot configurations are promising alternatives to the conventional checkerboard configuration and highlight the importance of considering human factors when evaluating SSVEP-based BCI systems. The proposed framework provides a foundation for the future development of predictive tools for estimating user fatigue and expected BCI performance.
authors: ["Natjamee Tohkhwan;Dollaporn Anopas;Si Thu Aung;Yunyong Punsawad;"]

title: Uncertainty-Aware Paw-Tip Localization in Animal Pose Estimation via Gaussian Regression
abstract: Animal pose estimation methods predict keypoint locations without quantifying localization uncertainty, limiting their use in applications where prediction reliability matters. We focus on paw-tip keypoints, the most ambiguous and biomechanically distinctive joints in AP-10K, and validate the method on all body keypoints. We show that a simple modification to standard pose regressors, replacing $L_{2}$ loss with a 2D Gaussian negative log-likelihood (NLL) head, yields interpretable uncertainty at a modest 5.2% accuracy difference relative to the $L_{2}$ baseline. Without any explicit supervision, the model learns structured uncertainty consistent with biomechanical motion patterns: back-paw predictions exhibit horizontally-elongated covariance ( $\sigma _{x}/\sigma _{y} \approx 1.8$ ), while front paws are near-isotropic. The learned uncertainty enables single-pass selective prediction that outperforms multi-pass MC Dropout, achieving roughly 22% lower RMSE on the retained predictions at half retention. We further evaluate held-out-species generalization (Felidae), hybrid $L_{2}$ /NLL losses, and isotropic-covariance variants on CNN and transformer backbones, characterizing where each is appropriate.
authors: ["Zy Li;"]

title: Multiobjective Optimization of PWM for Multilevel Inverter in PMSM Applications
abstract: Permanent magnet motors and multilevel converters are promising technologies for electrifying transportation. However, power converters do not produce sinusoidal voltage waveforms, which introduces harmonic content into the voltage applied to the PMSM. This work proposes an offline PWM optimization for multilevel converters that minimizes the total harmonic distortion of the line voltage ( $THD_{V_{line}}$ ) while tracking a target RMS voltage, using the multiobjective NSGA-II algorithm, which also determines the number of switching angles. Additionally, the formulation includes a set of priority rules that select the switching-angle set with the lowest phase-voltage distortion ( $THD_{V_{phase}}$ ), together with the constraints that make the resulting modulation implementable. The proposed method has been implemented on an FPGA Nexys A7 programmed in VHDL and experimentally evaluated on a Surface Mounted Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor with an NdFeB core. Altogether, this work includes detailed explanations of the cascaded H-Bridge inverter implemented, the PMSM model, and the NSGA-II multiobjective optimization algorithm. Experimental test bench was implemented in a laboratory scale prototype suited to analyze the harmonic suppression optimization strategy under the proposed methodology. Under no-load operating conditions, the $THD_{V_{line}}$ remains below 0.3% across the 22 modulations evaluated; under load with the PMSM this figure increases to 1.9% due to coupling and the machine’s nonlinear behavior. Both values remain below the 8% voltage THD limit that IEEE Std 519-2022, by more than one order of magnitude at no load and by a factor of four under load. The measured RMS voltage follows the computed value to within 0.1 V. Current THD reaches 7.3% in open-loop operation, dominated by the fifth and seventh harmonics inherent to the machine; requiring closed-loop current control to achieve harmonic compensation.
authors: ["Edison Caicedo;Aldo M. Rizo;Abdoulaye Bodian;Alben Cardenas;Aldo Pardo Garcia;María Alejandra Mantilla Villalobos;"]

title: A Comparative HMI Design Framework for Direct and Indirect Remote Operation of Automated Public Transport Vehicles
abstract: Remote operation centers (ROCs) are expected to play a critical role in deploying highly automated vehicles (HAVs) in public transport; however, evidence-based guidance for designing Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) across remote-operation modes remains fragmented. This study developed a comparative HMI design framework for direct (remote driving) and indirect (remote assistance) operations, identifying the interface capabilities experts consider necessary for supporting operator situational awareness, workload management, safety, and fleet scalability. An online survey of 19 questions was administered to an international panel of experts with direct experience in remote-operation projects, yielding 31 valid responses (item-level n = 20–30). Open-ended responses were analysed using thematic and content analysis, while closed-ended items were analysed descriptively using a 70% agreement threshold. HMI emerged as a critical cross-cutting enabler of ROC performance, identified by 77% of respondents; situational awareness was rated the most challenging contributor to safe operation (4.63/5), followed by mental workload (4.43/5). Findings are synthesized into a comparative design matrix spanning eleven HMI dimensions, distinguishing essential and optional capabilities for direct and indirect operation, including multimodal feedback, warning systems, AI-supported decision support, communication functions, and multi-vehicle supervision. The framework extends existing mode-specific guidance by explicitly linking HMI design choices to operator performance and fleet-level scalability. HMI complexity was identified as a training barrier by 67% of experts, while 76% supported continuous physiological monitoring to mitigate workload-related risks. The results offer a practical reference for ROC specification and underscore the importance of human-centered, mode-specific interface strategies for safe, scalable deployment of automated public transport.
authors: ["Nikoo Razavi;Heikki Liimatainen;"]

title: Study of Probe Marking in Medical Ultrasound Imaging Using Infrared Thermography
abstract: During medical ultrasound examinations, sonographers are required to mark the examination position and the ultrasound probe orientation. The manual marking is time-consuming for imaging practitioners, and inaccurate markings can reduce clinical efficiency. In this study, we propose a novel ultrasound probe surface marking method based on infrared thermography. Since thermal images capture only temperature distributions and do not record any recognizable visual information, this method is inherently designed to protect patient privacy. Specifically, we attach heating elements to the ultrasound probe using a custom fixture, and use a thermal imaging camera mounted on the ceiling to capture the ultrasound examination process from a top-down perspective. We use template matching and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to determine the human body contour and the probe orientation. Furthermore, we propose a Temperature-controlled Memory-guided Tracking (TMGT) algorithm that leverages temporal correlations in thermal image sequences to maintain robust probe tracking even when thermal features are partially lost. The proposed method was evaluated through controlled experiments, achieving an overall positioning accuracy of 99.36%, with an average distance error of 10 mm and an average angular error of $1.05\pm ~0.6$ . These results demonstrate that the proposed approach offers a robust, privacy-preserving solution for ultrasound probe surface marking, showing strong potential for clinical adoption in standardized examination documentation and longitudinal analysis.
authors: ["Hao Luo;Dian-Xun Li;Shu-Yi Lyu;Bin Chen;Jia-Lei He;Jie Yuan;"]

title: LYCO: Learning to Yield for Decentralized Multi-Agent Path Finding in Congested Environments
abstract: Leveraging its flexibility and scalability, decentralized reinforcement learning (RL) has been widely applied to multi-agent path finding (MAPF). However, existing methods often exhibit a decline in success rate as agent density increases. For example, agents that reach their goals early may remain there and block other agents. To maintain a high success rate as the number of agents grows, we propose Learning to Yield for Decentralized MAPF in Congested Environments (LYCO), a decentralized policy that explicitly learns localized yielding behaviors. LYCO is trained by imitation learning from Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT), a lightweight heuristic solver, and adds two components that promote yielding: (i) an observation channel encoding the estimated next positions of higher-priority neighboring agents, and (ii) a local cooperative reward that discourages waiting at a goal unless nearby agents have also reached theirs. Crucially, PIBT serves only as a source of imitation targets during training; during both RL training and inference, each agent selects actions solely from its local observations using the learned policy. LYCO thus maintains decentralized action selection without performing priority inheritance or backtracking at inference time. In grid-world settings, LYCO consistently outperformed representative decentralized RL baselines in high-density environments, achieving a success rate above 0.7 at an agent density of 0.3 on a $20\times 20$ map with obstacle density 0.1 while maintaining a competitive makespan. These findings show that LYCO is an effective decentralized approach for congested MAPF.
authors: ["Hiroya Makino;Koji Noshiro;Koji Hasebe;Seigo Ito;"]

title: A Multi-Dimensional HID Fingerprinting Framework for Detecting Malicious HID Devices
abstract: Human Interface Device (HID) attacks pose significant security threats by exploiting the inherent protocol-level trust in Universal Serial Bus (USB) peripherals. While traditional endpoint defenses are frequently circumvented by hardware-level identity spoofing of static metadata such as Vendor and Product IDs, this paper proposes a multi-dimensional HID fingerprinting framework that integrates deep structural hardware characteristics with real-time behavioral timing dynamics. Operating entirely in user space via the Windows Raw Input API, the framework extracts firmware-level features—including interface topology, report descriptor hierarchies, and usage mappings—to establish a robust, hardware-grounded identity. These structural fingerprints provide a complementary hardware-grounded signal alongside behavioral models based on clicks-per-second (CPS), inter-key interval (IKI) variance, and burst pattern stability, reducing reliance on timing-only detection when adversarial timing perturbations are present. Formally, we cast this decision task as supervised binary classification between Legitimate and Attack HID sessions, treating the deviation and anomaly scores produced during fusion as intermediate risk indicators within the inference pipeline rather than as the final output, preceded by an optional Zero-Trust Perimeter Mode that defaults to denying any device not already registered as trusted, independent of its behavioral or structural profile. Experimental evaluation on a 100% synthetic, parameterized corpus of 1,610 interaction sessions representing wired, wireless, and integrated keyboard profiles as well as Flipper Zero and USB Rubber Ducky attack-device profiles demonstrates that the proposed fused model achieves a classification accuracy of 100%, a precision of 100%, and an F1-score of 100% on this synthetic baseline corpus, a result preserved even under a supplementary adversarial evaluation with spoofed device identity and interface topology. The system maintains a lightweight computational profile with an average processing latency of 1.93 ms and low average CPU usage on the evaluated host, with brief transient CPU peaks reported separately, facilitating practical, real-time deployment on commodity endpoints without requiring privileged kernel-level instrumentation. This dual-layered approach provides complementary structural and behavioral evidence for proactive defense at the HID input boundary.

title: A Systematic Literature Review of Single-Cell Foundation Models for Transcriptomics: Design, Adaptation, Benchmarks, and Future Directions
abstract: Large single-cell atlases have enabled reusable representation learning across tissues, diseases, platforms, and species. Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) build on these resources by learning cell- and gene-level representations from large-scale transcriptomic data. However, current scFMs vary substantially in input encoding, tokenization, backbone architecture, pre-training objective, biological prior knowledge, adaptation strategy, and evaluation protocol. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, this review synthesizes 166 unique studies represented by 175 eligible reports published between 1 January 2022 and 9 June 2026. It addresses five research questions covering architecture, gene-expression representation, pre-training, downstream adaptation, generalization and robustness. The evidence is organized into four technical lineages: scale- and architecture-driven modeling, knowledge-enhanced modeling, adaptation and representation reuse, spatial, multimodal, multiscale, and contextual extension. The review also distinguishes claims reported in original model studies from evidence provided by independent benchmark and re-evaluation studies. The findings provide stronger support for supervised or fine-tuned annotation-like tasks than for zero-shot embedding reuse, while perturbation-response prediction remains more sensitive to data splitting, overlap between pre-training and test data, comparator strength, and metric choice. Independent benchmarks also provide limited support for treating model scale as a proxy for biological understanding or robust transfer. Study-level appraisal judged 10 studies to be at low risk of bias, 140 to have some concerns, and 16 to be at high risk; 78 studies had strong reproducibility support. Future work should prioritize leakage-resistant out-of-distribution evaluation, stronger biological grounding and interpretability, context-aware modeling, and reproducible and secure deployment.

title: SecureNAS-IDS: Resource-Aware Neural Architecture Search and Model-Stealing Defence for Intrusion Detection Systems on IoT Microcontrollers
abstract: Integrating Machine Learning (ML) based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) into Internet of Things (IoT) microcontrollers involves three mutually dependent issues that have not been addressed collectively in prior literature: 1) automatic discovery of a compact neural architecture suitable for effectively handling heterogeneous tabular network traffic data, 2) compression of the resulting architecture under the extremely limited flash and memory resources available on embedded devices, and 3) safeguarding the deployed model’s intellectual property against black-box model-stealing attacks. To address these challenges, Secure Neural Architecture Search for Intrusion Detection Systems (SecureNAS-IDS) is proposed as an end-to-end framework that integrates differentiable architecture search, sensitivity-aware quantisation, and an inference-time model-stealing defence, and that is demonstrated through the first physical deployment of such a combined pipeline on an IoT microcontroller. The framework introduces a neural architecture search strategy based on Differentiable Architecture Search (DARTS) and a custom tabular operation set, enabling the automatic discovery of compact multi-cell classifiers for highly imbalanced intrusion detection datasets. To facilitate deployment efficiency on resource-constrained IoT microcontrollers, a Selective-Layer Dynamic Quantisation (SLDQ) scheme is developed, preserving 32-bit floating-point (FP32) precision only in the most sensitivity-critical layer while quantising all remaining layers to 8-bit integers (INT8), thereby substantially reducing memory and storage requirements with minimal impact on detection performance. Furthermore, model security is enhanced through the proposed Locality-Sensitive Hashing Tabular Guard (LSH-TabularGuard), an inference-time defence mechanism against black-box model-stealing attacks. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that SecureNAS-IDS achieves competitive intrusion detection performance while significantly reducing resource consumption and improving resilience against model extraction attempts by a single-identity attacker. The defence is evaded when the same query budget is distributed across a sufficient number of synthetic identities. The on-device query counter, shared by all queries reaching the device, defines an operating envelope of approximately 50,000 queries, corresponding to about one hour of continuous scoring at the measured throughput, which suits intermittent, event-driven deployments. The framework is therefore presented as a practical solution for IoT edge environments within this single-identity, intermittent-querying scope.
authors: ["Ashwin Ramesh;Michael Schukat;Priyanka Verma;"]

title: Adaptive Multi-Factor Component Tree Loss Function for Topology-Preserving Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: In recent years, numerous medical image segmentation models have been proposed with notable improvements in performance. Several widely adopted approaches have consistently delivered robust results across diverse medical imaging modalities. Despite their strong performance on conventional evaluation metrics, such as the Dice similarity coefficient, these methods often fail to preserve topological structures accurately. For example, disconnections are a common issue in various segmentation tasks and are often accompanied by a large number of false positive connected components (FPCCs). Such anatomically inconsistent outputs produced by diagnostic support systems can undermine clinicians’ confidence and diminish the perceived reliability of these systems. In this study, a new component tree-based loss function is proposed to improve topological correctness by reconnecting the desired connected components and removing undesired connected components. This loss design ensures smooth loss transitions during optimization. In addition, adaptive parameter settings tailored to each image are introduced, thereby improving the differentiation of anatomically relevant structures. Experiments were conducted on several publicly available datasets in which segmentation networks are prone to topological errors, including DRIVE, LES-AV, and CREMI. The results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively reconnects true positive connected components and significantly reduces both the number and size of FPCCs, with the most statistically significant improvements and the fewest statistically significant degradations in both pixel-wise and topological metrics in the majority of experiments. Code is available at https://github.com/nguyenqanh/MultiCTree
authors: ["Anh Q. Nguyen;Jean Cousty;Yukiko Kenmochi;Akinobu Shimizu;"]

title: UAV-YOLO: A Resolution-Guided Feature Fusion and Attention Network for Small Object Detection in Aerial Imagery
abstract: Small and densely distributed objects in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery are difficult to detect because deep feature extraction progressively removes the spatial evidence needed to separate and localize neighboring targets. This paper presents UAV-YOLO, a resolution-guided multi-scale detector that couples spatial-detail preservation with adaptive feature refinement. First, a stride-4 P2 pathway extends both the top-down and bottom-up necks, providing a high-resolution prediction surface for fine object boundaries. Second, Bidirectional Feature Pyramid Network (BiFPN)-style weighted bidirectional fusion learns the relative contribution of each scale and prevents shallow detail from being diluted by coarse semantic features. Third, Efficient Multi-Scale Attention (EMA) captures grouped cross-spatial dependencies to strengthen discriminative responses with limited parameter overhead. The resulting P2–P5 architecture forms a continuous information pathway from fine spatial evidence to deep semantic context. A complete five-seed factorial study characterizes the effects of the architectural factors and identifies resolution preservation as the principal performance mechanism. On a deterministic held-out subset of VisDrone2019, UAV-YOLO achieves $49.19~\pm ~0.15$ % mAP50 and $30.22~\pm ~0.06$ % mAP50-95, exceeding YOLO11s by 2.97 and 2.35 percentage points, respectively. COCO-style evaluation further increases small-object AP from $11.84~\pm ~0.22$ % to $15.06~\pm ~0.16$ % and small-object recall from $19.59~\pm ~0.35$ % to $25.33~\pm ~0.14$ %, without a statistically detectable reduction in large-object AP. These results demonstrate that resolution-guided feature refinement provides an effective and compact 9.70M-parameter solution for dense aerial small-object detection.
authors: ["Junhao Xu;Zenghui Li;"]

title: Theoretical Data Rate Limits in Future Wireless Networks: A Simplified Cellular Model
abstract: Advances in wireless communication technologies from first generation (1G) to fifth generation (5G) have been so rapid that it is essential to establish a rigorous theoretical framework to analyze progress toward future generations. In this paper, the growth of the next generation wireless technologies is examined in terms of data rate. Primarily, this work focuses on whether the present trend of advancements can be sustained indefinitely in the future generations or not. The relationship between physical constraints, spectral efficiency, power limitations, and network densification is formalized, and theoretical upper bounds are formulated on achievable data rate. Overall, the analysis indicates that the fundamental physical limitations of current wireless communication systems may present significant challenges for maintaining historical growth patterns. Further, we investigate whether a hypothetical system requiring data rates consistent with historical growth patterns can be realized under electromagnetic wave propagation constraints, finite spectrum availability, etc. Further, analysis is conducted to assess the impact of emerging technologies such as millimeter wave communications, ultra-massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO), intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS), artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum communications on data rate. The studies reveal that paradigmatic technological shifts, rather than incremental improvements, will be required for future generations.
authors: ["Sanjana T.;Amrita Mishra;Shrisha Rao;"]

title: An Empirical Framework for Evaluating the Evolving Risk of Compounding Power Outages and Heatwaves Under Climate Change
abstract: Electric power systems are increasingly exposed to compound heatwave hazards, where extreme heat coincides with weather drivers such as high wind and precipitation that can intensify outage conditions. In this study, we define outage risk during extreme heat as the human exposure-relevant burden of power disruption under high heat conditions, because loss of electricity in such periods can increase exposure to dangerous indoor and outdoor thermal environments. We develop an empirical, data-driven framework to quantify how wind-precipitation outage fragility, evaluated under extreme-heat conditions, changes between historical (CTRL) and pseudo-global warming (PGW) thermodynamic scenarios. The analysis focuses on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) service region at the county scale, integrating daily outage observations from the EAGLE-I platform with high-resolution meteorological forcing from the CONUS404 dataset and its PGW counterpart. Hazard-impact relationships are constructed as empirical fragility surfaces in joint wind-precipitation space and stratified by settlement class, then applied to climate-conditioned scenarios to estimate a heat-duration-weighted relative outage burden, defined as the expected daily maximum outage fraction multiplied by the number of hours above the heat-index threshold. This metric is an exposure-relevant outage-burden proxy, not an observed time-integrated outage-duration measure and is evaluated using extreme value theory. Results show that warming produces a structural shift in outage risk during extreme heat rather than a proportional increase across space and system types. Across settlement classes, annual maxima of the heat-duration-weighted relative outage burden increase while historical return-period benchmarks contract sharply. Conditional on the matched PGW-selected event pool and fixed present-day empirical fragility, historical 5-year and 10-year CTRL burden thresholds shift toward approximately annual to low-multiple-year recurrence under PGW, with transformed median return periods ranging from 1.03 to 1.49 years across settlement classes. Rural systems exhibit the largest increases in heat-duration-weighted relative outage burden, whereas urban systems dominate the heat-duration-weighted customer-outage burden proxy because of higher customer exposure.
authors: ["Shah Afzal Saki;Giulia Sofia;Emmanouil Anagnostou;"]

title: Diversity-Oriented Interaction Augmentation for Multimodal Recommendation
abstract: Multimodal recommendation has attracted increasing attention because user preferences in real-world platforms are often reflected not only in historical interactions but also in item images and textual descriptions. Existing multimodal recommender systems mainly exploit such information to improve accuracy-oriented performance, while the diversity of recommendation results is often less emphasized. However, directly increasing diversity by adding dissimilar items may introduce noisy interactions and weaken the modeling of user preferences. To address this problem, we propose a user-aware diversity-oriented interaction augmentation framework for multimodal recommendation. The proposed method first constructs relevance-preserving candidate items based on multimodal item representations derived from visual and textual features. It then builds user preference profiles by aggregating the multimodal representations of historical items and selectively generates augmented user-item interactions under user-aware diversity constraints. The framework uses multimodal information to construct relevance-preserving candidates and category-directed selection to expand category-level exposure. Experiments on Sports, Clothing, and Yelp with four recommendation backbones show consistent gains in category coverage together with lower Recall and NDCG. Feature-space ILD results vary across dataset-backbone settings. These results distinguish category breadth from content-space dissimilarity.
authors: ["Jiajie Lu;Haruka Yamashita;"]

title: Picogrid: A Low-Cost, Remotely Accessible Hardware Platform for Power Systems Education and Research
abstract: Hardware validation of power engineering paradigms is crucial for bridging the gap between simulation-based research and real-world applications. However, there are significant barriers to using hardware experimental platforms including high costs, lab space requirements, and maintenance challenges. Additionally, users must typically be present on-site to effectively conduct experiments. This paper presents a low-cost low-power hardware experimental platform for power systems research and education, and a cloud dashboard designed for conducting remote virtual experiments using the platform. This enables researchers and educators to provide virtual laboratory exercises and remote experimentation through a hardware-as-a-service model. We present five experiments using the platform that demonstrate diverse power systems concepts: smart solar home systems, load aggregation, demand response schemes, electricity markets, and load forecasting. Our experiments demonstrate successful concurrent access by multiple users and validate the platform’s effectiveness for remote collaborative research and education. Additionally, we validate the platform’s accessibility through deployment in a university workshop and a community-based research meeting with non-expert participants.
authors: ["Varun Balan;James Dolle;Maitreyee Marathe;"]

title: Reliable Navigation-Assisted Grasping on Resource-Constrained Mobile Robots
abstract: Mobile robots can fail at navigation-assisted grasping even when the individual navigation, perception, and manipulation components are available, because failures may occur during cross-module execution and stage transitions. This paper presents a rule-driven execution-reliability framework for navigation-assisted grasping on a Jetson Nano-based ROS2 mobile robot. The framework coordinates existing components through staged module activation and bounded recovery actions for observation, local approach, grasp verification, and localization–navigation anomalies. The evaluated task begins with system initialization and navigation to the target area and ends with post-grasp verification; object transport, return navigation, and placement are outside the experimental scope. Staged launch increased pure-navigation arrival from 25.00–40.00% under the two legacy launch conditions to 78.00%. Complete recovery increased final Approach+Grasp success from 35/63 trials (55.56%) to 65/66 trials (98.48%), while approach-stage recovery increased the separate /approach_ready endpoint from 45/62 trials (72.58%) to 58/60 trials (96.67%). System-level navigation recovery increased arrival from 78.00% to 90.00% but increased mean task time from 58.15 s to 404.20 s. The results support a reliability–time trade-off for interpretable execution orchestration on the tested platform; they do not establish a new detector, SLAM method, grasp-pose model, or measured resource-optimization algorithm.
authors: ["Shan Zhao;Lianen Qu;Yunlong Luo;Jinlin Xie;Mengjie Xu;Jiabo Xu;Chuanjun Liang;"]

title: A Closed-Loop Enterprise Warehouse Execution Framework Integrating SAP EWM, SAP BTP, Mobile Robotics, and QR-Based Destination Validation
abstract: Traditionally, warehouse operations rely on warehouse operators using radio frequency (RF) scanner devices to execute and confirm warehouse tasks generated by warehouse management systems. In this process, operators physically travel to designated destination bins, scan storage locations, and manually confirm task completion. Although effective, this approach introduces labour dependency, operational delays, and an increased risk of human error. This paper presents an Industry 4.0 framework for automated warehouse-task integration using SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM), SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP), mobile robotics, and QR-based destination bin validation. The proposed framework establishes a closed-loop integration between enterprise warehouse management and physical warehouse execution. Warehouse tasks generated in SAP EWM are transmitted through SAP BTP Integration Suite to a mobile robotic platform. The robot receives execution instructions, executes scripted movement along a predefined route, and performs QR-code scanning to verify the target storage bin. Upon successful destination validation, the robot communicates the verification result back through SAP BTP, enabling automatic warehouse task confirmation within SAP EWM. This approach replicates and automates the destination verification and confirmation activities traditionally performed by warehouse operators using RF devices. A proof-of-concept implementation was developed using SAP EWM on SAP S/4HANA On-Premise, SAP BTP Integration Suite, a Raspberry Pi–based mobile robotic platform, HTTPS-based communication through a Cloudflare tunnel, and computer vision–based QR recognition. Experimental validation using real warehouse tasks demonstrated successful end-to-end execution, including warehouse task processing, destination verification, and automated warehouse task confirmation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of linking SAP EWM warehouse-task transmission, scripted robot movement, QR-based destination-code validation, and automatic task confirmation under the tested prototype conditions. Comparative improvements in accuracy, manual effort, or execution time were not measured. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future autonomous warehouse operations involving multi-robot coordination, intelligent navigation, and advanced warehouse automation capabilities.
authors: ["Naveen Chandra Sharma;Kunal Sharma;"]

title: ShipCrawler: Agentic Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) Platform for Maritime Cybersecurity - Implementation and Empirical Validation
abstract: The maritime industry’s increasing digitalization has expanded the cyber attack surface of vessels and ports, yet systematic monitoring of vessel internet exposure and behavioral patterns remains limited. Port authorities lack automated tools to track vessels calling at their terminals for indicators of sanctions evasion, shadow fleet activity, or long-term behavioral anomalies, while fleet operators face challenges in assessing what information about their own vessels is publicly accessible and exploitable by adversaries. This paper presents ShipCrawler, an agentic open-source intelligence (OSINT) platform addressing both operational use cases. ShipCrawler integrates automatic identification system (AIS) feeds, internet scanning datasets (Shodan), shipping registries (Equasis), and web intelligence into an autonomous agent-driven investigation pipeline. The platform enables port authorities to conduct sustained monitoring of vessel AIS histories, ownership structures, and flag-state patterns to identify vessels operating within shadow fleet or sanctions-evasion networks, while helping fleet operators systematically enumerate their publicly visible attack surface, including exposed Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT) communications, bridge systems, and unsecured operational technology interfaces. A key architectural contribution is the agent-driven queue-based pipeline, where an artificial intelligence (AI) agent processes OSINT tasks asynchronously with real-time Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming to a web dashboard. ShipCrawler has been validated on 63 crude oil tankers spanning Aframax/LR2, Suezmax, and VLCC classes within shadow fleet networks, demonstrating that sustained OSINT monitoring can successfully detect shadow fleet operational patterns, quantify vessel internet exposure, and generate structured intelligence products automatically. A discrimination test on 15 non-sanctioned control tankers drawn by a fixed-seed random sample from a non-sanctioned eligible pool exhibited zero shadow-fleet signatures, confirming the specificity of the detected indicators. The platform is released as open-source software under the MIT license.
authors: ["Ahmed Nagi Nasr;Inga Zaitseva-Pärnaste;Pentti Kujala;"]

title: Video-Based Remote Photoplethysmography for Atrial Fibrillation Detection: A Systematic Review
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common cardiac arrhythmia associated with increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular complications. Although electrocardiography (ECG) remains the diagnostic gold standard, remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has emerged as a promising non-contact approach for extracting pulse-related information from facial videos and enabling unobtrusive rhythm screening. This systematic review investigates the current evidence on facial-video-based rPPG methods for AF detection. Following a PRISMA-based workflow, records were identified from PubMed, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and additional search sources. After removing 151 duplicates, 358 records were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 36 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility. Two additional studies, not retrieved by the database search, were identified through reference-list screening, resulting in 19 studies being included in the review. The reviewed literature shows that recent computer-vision and deep learning approaches have improved robustness to motion artifacts, illumination changes, and acquisition noise, often achieving promising detection performance in controlled settings. However, the field remains limited by the small number of available studies, heterogeneous datasets, and scarce clinical validation. Moreover, within the reviewed literature, widespread regulatory-cleared clinical deployment of camera-based rPPG systems for remote AF detection was not identified, indicating that further methodological standardization, larger clinical studies, and regulatory-oriented validation are needed before this technology can become a reliable tool for real-world AF screening.

title: A Systematic Review of Learning-Based Control: Theory and Applications
abstract: Learning-based control is an important advancement in intelligent control theory, integrating data-driven learning, feedback optimization, and complex system control. In modern industrial applications, it is widely deployed in robotic manipulation, autonomous driving, power electronics, and process industries. Given that real-world systems are frequently subject to unknown dynamics, strong nonlinearities, and external disturbances, traditional model-based approaches often fail to ensure high precision, robustness, and adaptive optimization, leading to performance degradation or even instability. Learning-based control has received significant attention, as it can overcome the challenges faced by model-based control. This paper presents a review of learning-based control techniques. First, learning-based control problems are formulated for nonlinear dynamic systems. Second, this paper overviews three typical categories of learning-based control methods including model-informed learning-based control, model-free learning-based control, and integrated learning-based control, with particular attention to their theoretical foundations and algorithmic implementations. Third, the applications of each learning-based control method across different engineering domains are discussed. Finally, this paper concludes by outlining future research directions.
authors: ["Weinan Gao;Kaiyue He;Zhong-Ping Jiang;"]

title: Interpretable Fault Diagnosis for Industrial Processes: A Unified Perspective
abstract: With the continuous advancement of industrial automation, informatization, and intelligent manufacturing, modern industrial process systems have become increasingly large-scale and complex. Such systems are typically characterized by strong multivariable coupling, nonlinearity, and frequently changing operating conditions. Fault diagnosis plays a critical and irreplaceable role in ensuring the safe and reliable operation of industrial systems. Beyond achieving high diagnostic accuracy, industrial fault diagnosis systems are increasingly required to provide interpretable results, as diagnostic decisions are closely tied to operational actions, safety assessment, and engineering trust. This paper presents a systematic review of fault diagnosis methods for industrial processes from the perspective of interpretability. The evolution of major diagnostic paradigms and recent research advances are reviewed, with an emphasis on how different methods achieve interpretability in practical industrial applications. The strengths and limitations of representative approaches are analyzed in terms of both diagnostic performance and explanatory capability. Furthermore, key challenges related to real-world industrial deployment are discussed, and potential future research directions toward reliable and interpretable industrial fault diagnosis systems are outlined.
authors: ["Mingyi Huo;Shen Yin;"]

title: A Comprehensive Survey on Control of Structured Nonlinear Systems Under Network Transmission Constraints: Advances, Prospects and Challenges
abstract: The control problem of nonlinear systems under network transmission constraints has become a central research topic in networked control systems (NCSs). While communication networks introduce flexibility and scalability, their inherent limitations disrupt the information conditions and structural assumptions required by traditional nonlinear control methods, thereby posing significant challenges to system stability and performance. These issues have led to extensive efforts to develop nonlinear robust control frameworks tailored for networked environments. This survey reviews the main progress in this area by examining three representative classes of nonlinear systems with distinct structural features: strict-feedback/pure-feedback systems, nonlinear systems with matched uncertainties, and feedback-linearizable systems. The specific ways in which network-induced phenomena destroy the structural premises of these control approaches are clarified, including interruptions of recursive chains in backstepping, violations of arrival and sliding conditions in sliding mode control, and distortions of state transformations in feedback linearization. The solution strategies proposed to address these challenges are then grouped and summarized according to their underlying mechanisms. Finally, key conclusions are drawn, and several potential research directions are outlined to guide future work on nonlinear control under network transmission constraints.
authors: ["Ning Li;Zidong Wang;Lei Zou;Guhui Li;Weihao Song;"]

title: Complex Evolutionary Games: Problem, Method, and Future
abstract: Evolutionary game theory (EGT) is a complex and emerging research area. In recent years, the rapid development of evolutionary games has driven extensive research across multiple interdisciplinary domains. However, existing surveys remain scenario-specific and lack a comprehensive overview of complex evolutionary games. To address this research gap, this survey aims to provide a comprehensive review of existing studies in the field of complex evolutionary games, thereby offering a clear reference framework for future researchers. First, a novel 5C taxonomy framework is proposed to systematically characterize the core complexities in complex evolutionary games from five complementary dimensions, namely complex structures, contingent strategies, changing environments, coupled players, and compound payoffs. This framework provides a unified taxonomy for organizing fragmented studies and revealing the intrinsic relationships among different categories of complex evolutionary games. Second, based on the proposed 5C taxonomy framework, this survey systematically investigates and analyzes state-of-the-art studies, comprehensively summarizing their advantages and limitations. Finally, potential future research directions are discussed with the aim of promoting further advancements in complex evolutionary games. This survey seeks to provide researchers with a comprehensive reference and valuable research insights, thereby facilitating the continued development and prosperity of the evolutionary games field.
authors: ["Zhou-Zhi Lu;Yi Jiang;Zhi-Fan Tang;Liu-Yue Luo;Chun-Hua Chen;Jun Zhang;Zhi-Hui Zhan;"]

title: ResBi-Mamba Plus: Deep Bidirectional Mamba with Spatiotemporal Attention for Robust Interpretable Hourly Runoff Forecasting
abstract: As runoff forecasting shifts from single-step to multi-step, stakeholders in the hydrological field have placed higher demands on the multilead-time forecasting performance of models. In this paper, we propose a novel interpretable fine-grained runoff forecasting framework: Residual Bidirectional Mamba Plus (ResBi-Mamba Plus). The backbone of the proposed model is our redesigned bidirectional Mamba (Bi-Mamba) architecture that captures more contextual information through parallelized forward and backward sequence traversals. For multivariate long-sequence inputs, we further integrate a dual-path spatiotemporal attention (STA) module after each Bi-Mamba branch. Based on the channel-dependence (CD) and channel-independence (CI) strategies, the STA module adaptively recalibrates the original features in the temporal and spatial dimensions, so that the important information in each unidirectional branch can be highlighted during the branch fusion process. In addition, the overall framework adopts the ResNet Plus architecture, which improves information flow in the network through two parallel residual block paths and dense shortcut connections. This design allows the model to obtain clear benefits from increased depth that are difficult for conventional models to achieve. Ablation and comparative experiments on the hourly runoff dataset from the Columbia River in the United States fully verify the effectiveness of the components in ResBi-Mamba Plus. The results also show that the proposed model performs better than current state-of-the-art time series forecasting models across various forecasting horizons.
