title: Creating order in the uncertainty of childbirth: A qualitative study of obstetric admission and triage practices in rural Malawi
abstract: by Emily Bundy, Bianca Kandeya, Wanangwa Chimwaza, Claudia Hanson, Effie Chipeta, Helle Mölsted Alvesson Maternal and neonatal mortality continues to be a concern in sub-Saharan Africa. Although standardized obstetric triage improves clinical outcomes, little is known about how locally developed admission practices function in low-resource settings where national obstetric triage guidelines are absent. This study explored how hospital-based obstetric admission procedures in rural Malawi were experienced by maternity care providers, laboring women, and companions. We used qualitative methods including in-depth interviews with mothers and maternity care providers, focus group discussions with companions and maternity care providers, and observations of two labor wards. Study participants were chosen purposively to represent diverse birth outcomes and professionals. Data analysis followed reflexive thematic analysis, concentrating on obstetric admissions. Mary Douglas’ concepts of purity, danger, and risk informed interpretation during theme development. Obstetric admissions were organized through standardized admission forms that structured assessment and enabled providers to classify women according to visible danger signs and labor progression. Although the forms were not formal triage tools, they functioned as the primary mechanism for prioritizing care, organizing patient movement through maternity spaces, and managing high patient volumes. Shared recognition of danger signs among providers, women, and companions reinforced the legitimacy of risk-based decision making. At the same time, communication was selectively restricted, limiting patient and companion participation while reinforcing professional authority and hierarchical relationships. Standardized admission procedures created order by classifying obstetric risk and prioritizing clinical efficiency, but they also reinforced hierarchical relationships that limited communication and patient participation. Efforts to strengthen obstetric admissions should preserve the benefits of standardized risk assessment while incorporating more person-centered communication and companion engagement.

title: The science of child and adolescent mental health in Mozambique: A systematic review of prevalence estimates, measurement tools, and interventions
abstract: by Helena Mutede Cutótua Daniel, Lauro Estivalete Marchionatti, Jessica Azevedo Veronesi, André Cardoso Campello, Luis Augusto Rohde, Caio Borba Casella, Peter Raucci, Afonso Mazine Tiago Fumo, Jair Mari, Giovanni Abrahão Salum, Lidia Gouveia, Zeina Mneimneh Mozambique is home to 18 million children and adolescents largely underrepresented in mental health research. We conducted a systematic review of evidence-based resources (prevalence estimates, assessment instruments, and interventions) on mental health-related outcomes addressing individuals aged 0–19 years in Mozambique. We searched PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Google Scholar, African Index Medicus, and local catalogues. Extraction followed COSMIN and Cochrane manuals (PROSPERO registration: CRD420251016208). The search yielded 81 unique publications, including 61 reports presenting prevalence estimates from 25 studies, 29 reports providing data on 42 assessment instruments, and 9 intervention reports describing 8 intervention trials. The clinical prevalence of mental disorders were estimated in two surveys, conducted in Nampula (ADHD: 13·4%; N = 748, 6–18 years) and Maputo (any mental diagnosis: 23%, anxiety disorders: 17·5%; major depression episode: 8·5%; disruptive behavior disorder: 6·6%; substance use disorders: 4·5%; ADHD: 3·3%; PTSD: 1·2%; N = 486, 12–19 years). Most research focused on psychosocial adversities, with nationally representative adolescent surveys reporting significant exposure to violence (physical/emotional violence annually: 24·86%; girls suffering intimate partner violence: 21·11%; lifetime sexual abuse: 16·55%). National suicide rates were highest among 15–19-year-olds (1·53 per 100,000). Only four instruments were cross-culturally adapted and showed reliable psychometrics (MINI-KID, GAD-7, PHQ-A, and SDQ), whilst unadapted tools performed poorly. There was a single randomized clinical trial which reported a cost-effective intervention for neurodevelopment among high-poverty preschoolers. Children and adolescents in Mozambique face significant psychosocial adversity, and available evidence suggests a substantial burden of mental disorders according to limited clinical data. There are few available instruments assessing mental conditions, and culturally sensitive approaches are warranted for strengthening local research.

title: Changes in attitudes toward the HPV vaccine in Kenya
abstract: by Corrina Moucheraud, Jinghong Miao, Eric Ochieng, Suyanpeng Zhang, George Ganda, Ginger Golub, Risa M. Hoffman, Peter G. Szilagyi, Sze-Chuan Suen Globally, attitudes about vaccines and vaccination are changing rapidly, but few studies have examined within-person shifts over time. We use a longitudinal survey in Kenya to assess how respondents’ attitudes about the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine changed between 2022 and 2024. In 2022, we conducted a random digit-dialed phone survey of 1405 Kenyan parents/caregivers of girls age-eligible for the HPV vaccine; respondents were re-contacted in 2024, and 1093 people (78%) were successfully re-surveyed. Each survey included identical questions about HPV vaccine and vaccination attitudes (adapted from the Vaccine Hesitancy Scale-HPV). We estimate direction and degree of each person’s change in attitude, overall and by construct/question, and explore associations between these changes and respondent demographics, and baseline knowledge about HPV and HPV vaccination. Attitudes about the HPV vaccine changed substantially from 2022 to 2024. Although perceptions of the vaccine’s importance and effectiveness were relatively stable (only 25% of respondents reported any attitude change), there were significantly more changes among respondents with lower educational attainment and who were unemployed. Safety perceptions changed substantially over this period: two-thirds of respondents changed their beliefs around the vaccine’s side effects and riskiness. Approximately one-quarter of respondents developed a worse safety attitudes, while 18.9% of respondents improved their safety attitude. Among individuals with lower socioeconomic status, attitudes about following a clinician’s HPV vaccination recommendation and riskiness of the HPV vaccine significantly worsened over this period. We found that, in this population of Kenyan adults and over a two-year period, attitudes about the HPV vaccine have changed both positively and negatively. Targeted interventions may be needed, particularly with less socioeconomically-advantaged groups, to reinforce messages about the vaccine’s importance, effectiveness, and safety. Further research is needed about reasons for the large changes in safety perceptions, both toward more and less favorable views.

title: Common mental health problems experienced by adolescents living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa: A scoping review
abstract: by Celumusa Ndlangamandla, Musa Mamba Adolescents living with HIV (ALWH) carry a substantial burden of mental health problems, yet summary data remain limited. Previous reviews, particularly systematic reviews, have focused mainly on diagnosed disorders among adults or broader populations of young people living with HIV, while substance use and emotional and behavioural symptoms remain understudied and often underreported. This scoping review synthesized existing evidence on common mental health problems among ALWH aged 10–19 years in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). We searched five electronic databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Embase, and Open Access for Africa) and Google Scholar, and screened the bibliographic references of selected articles for additional studies. Search terms were combined using Boolean operators and organized into four concept categories: HIV, age, mental health, and region. Eligible studies were original, peer-reviewed research published in English between 2020 and 2026, conducted in SSA, and reporting on mental health among ALWH aged 10–19 years. The search yielded 427 records, of which 29 duplicates were removed. Of the 398 articles screened, 317 were excluded at the abstract stage and a further 57 after full-text review, leaving 24 articles for inclusion. The review identified six common mental health problems among ALWH in SSA: depressive disorders and symptoms, generalized anxiety, suicidality, emotional and behavioural problems, posttraumatic stress, and substance use problems. Depression and suicidality were the most frequently reported, whereas substance use, generalized anxiety, posttraumatic stress, and emotional and behavioural problems were less frequently reported. ALWH in SSA experience a range of mental health problems that may affect their well-being and engagement in HIV care. Routine mental health screening, prevention, and psychosocial support should be integrated into HIV care for this population. Strengthening integrated mental health and HIV services may help address unmet needs and improve health outcomes among ALWH in SSA.

title: Impact of a phased transition model on Advanced HIV Disease outcomes: A pre- and post-implementation evaluation study in Malawi
abstract: by Thulani Maphosa, Rhoderick Machekano, Lise Denoeud Ndam, Lucky Makonokaya, Lloyd Chilikutali, Louiser Upile Kalitera, Eddington Matiya, Allan Mayi, Reuben Musarandega, Bilal Wilson Matola, Aida Yemane Berhan, Allan Ahimbisibwe, Appolinaire Tiam To promote sustainability and strengthen national ownership of Advanced HIV Disease (AHD) services, a transition was implemented across 22 health facilities in Central Malawi. This transition involved shifting responsibility for key AHD program elements from partner-led implementation to full Ministry of Health (MoH) leadership. This evaluation assessed the impact of this transition on diagnostic coverage, TB preventive therapy (TPT) uptake, and 12-month survival outcomes. A retrospective cohort study included all children and adults enrolled in AHD care during the pre-MoH transition (January 2020–December 2021) and post-MoH transition (January 2023–December 2024) periods. Eligibility was defined by national AHD criteria: CD4 count <200 cells/mm³, WHO stage 3 or 4 disease, or age < 5 years. Data were abstracted from clinical records and routine facility registers. Kaplan–Meier survival curves, Cox proportional hazards, and Fine and Gray competing risk models were used to evaluate 6 and 12-month mortality and retention as primary outcomes. A total of 1,044 AHD clients were included (553 pre-transition; 491 post-transition). Median age increased post-transition (35.9 to 38.5 years, p < 0.001). CD4 testing uptake declined (80.7% to 46.0%, p < 0.001), while WHO staging and TB diagnostic coverage improved. TB diagnoses decreased (44.5% to 31.2%, p = 0.002). TPT uptake dropped from 46.4% to 31.6% (p < 0.001). Twelve-month mortality declined significantly from 9.4% to 5.5% (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] = 0.59, 95% CI: 0.37–0.94, p = 0.026). Retention in care remained stable (HR = 0.86, 95% CI: 0.62–1.20, p = 0.384). Transitioning AHD services to MoH leadership was associated with sustained key program outcomes and a significant reduction in mortality. Continued mentorship and government ownership appeared to support these outcomes, although the pre-post design precludes causal inference. Declines in CD4 testing and TPT coverage highlight the need to strengthen diagnostics and integrate preventive care. These findings support scaling nationally led AHD models in high-burden HIV settings.

title: Microscopically detectable maternal schistosomiasis at delivery in Eastern Uganda: Prevalence, microscopy-based species distribution and associated household WASH characteristics in a hospital-based cross-sectional study
abstract: by George Binna Sande, Musa Kasujja, Emmanuel Okurut, Maxwell Okello, Marie Pascaline Sabine Ishimwe, Theodore Nteziyaremye, John Yaweh, Daniel Mugabi, Sara Liban, Geoffrey Okot, G. R. Neel, Bot Yakubu Sunday, Matthew Chibunna Igwe, Amos Muhumuza, Theoneste Hakizimana Schistosomiasis remains an important but neglected public health problem in Uganda. We estimated its prevalence, microscopy-based species distribution and associated factors among women delivering at Jinja Regional Referral Hospital. A hospital-based analytical cross-sectional study included 392 women from 1 September to 30 December 2025. One stool and one urine specimen per participant were examined microscopically for Schistosoma mansoni and S. haematobium, respectively. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associated factors; parsimonious conventional and Firth penalized models were used in sensitivity analyses. Microscopically detectable schistosomiasis was present in 44/392 women (11.2%; 95% CI: 8.5–14.8). Among microscopy-positive women, S. haematobium accounted for 63.6% of infections (95% CI: 48.2–76.7), S. mansoni for 29.5% (95% CI: 17.7–45.0), and mixed infection for 6.8% (95% CI: 2.1–19.6). Unimproved main water source (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 3.11; 95% CI: 1.46–6.64; p = 0.003), unimproved toilet facility (aOR = 4.40; 95% CI: 2.01–9.67; p < 0.001) and absence of a handwashing facility (aOR = 2.12; 95% CI: 1.02–4.41; p = 0.043) remained associated with microscopy-detected infection after adjustment. Women reporting fewer than four antenatal care contacts had higher adjusted odds than those reporting four to seven contacts (aOR = 8.43; 95% CI: 3.21–22.18; p < 0.001). The principal WASH associations remained consistent in sensitivity analyses. S. haematobium predominated among microscopy-classified infections. Household WASH characteristics remained associated with microscopy-detected infection, while the antenatal care association requires cautious interpretation. These cross-sectional findings do not establish causality but support further evaluation of context-appropriate schistosomiasis risk assessment within maternal health services and coordinated WASH and schistosomiasis-control strategies in endemic settings.

title: Smart Paper Technology for maternal and newborn health data in The Gambia: A qualitative study of early implementation
abstract: by Oluwatosin Nkereuwem, Jana Prauseová, Rachel Ford, Alpha Omar Jallow, Musa Marena, Gibril Jarju, Sidat Fofana, Mamady Cham, Buba Manjang, Beate Kampmann, Joanna Busza Many low- and middle-income countries rely on paper-based maternal and child health records that are often incomplete, fragmented, and difficult to use for continuity of care and decision-making. Smart Paper Technology (SPT), a hybrid paper–digital documentation system, has been proposed as a practical alternative to fully electronic medical records in resource-constrained settings. This study explored the early implementation of SPT in maternal and infant health services in The Gambia, focusing on feasibility and acceptability. We conducted a qualitative descriptive implementation evaluation guided by Rapid Assessment Procedures (RAP) in two pilot facilities in the Western Region of The Gambia between September and December 2024. Data were collected through 30 semi-structured interviews; four focus group discussions with 30 participants spanning facility-level clinical, management, and administrative staff, Ministry of Health staff, and technical and implementing partners; and non-participant observations across key service delivery areas. Data were analysed thematically using NVivo 14. Participants described SPT as feasible and broadly acceptable because it built on familiar paper-based workflows, was introduced through a participatory process, and offered advantages in reporting, information retrieval, and maternal–infant record linkage. However, these benefits were contingent on the implementation context. Key challenges included uneven training coverage, dual documentation, limited internet connectivity, scanning and data capture errors, storage constraints, and concerns about data governance. Staff adapted through peer mentoring, remote troubleshooting, and local workarounds. Participants emphasised that successful scale-up would require sustained training, clear governance arrangements, adequate human and technical resources, and a phased transition to government ownership. SPT offers a practical pathway towards digitisation in maternal and infant health services in LMICs, but its success depends on strong organisational systems, workforce support, and implementation processes that are responsive to routine service realities.

title: The intention to use Kangaroo Mother Care among first-time mothers 15-24 years in Kinshasa, DRC: An application of the integrated behavioral model
abstract: by Madeline Woo, Anastasia J. Gage, Julie H. Hernandez, Pierre Z. Akilimali, Jane T. Bertrand Kangaroo mother care (KMC) is a low-cost, safe, and simple method that has proven efficacious at improving neonatal health outcomes, including mortality, in low-income countries. While beneficial for all newborns, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends KMC specifically for low birthweight (LBW) and premature infants. This study examined the applicability of a modified Integrated Behavioral Model (IBM) framework for predicting KMC intentions among first-time mothers (FTMs) 15–24 years old in Kinshasa, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This study used secondary cross-sectional data from the 2020 Momentum Project endline survey, a quasi-experimental study in three intervention and three comparison health zones in Kinshasa, DRC. The association between IBM components and KMC intentions was tested using multivariate logistic regression. The total sample consisted of 1,918 adolescent and young first-time mothers (FTMs). About half of the respondents stated that they were “very likely” to practice KMC if they had a LBW or preterm baby. Approval of KMC, normative expectations, descriptive norms, self-efficacy, and autonomy were all positively associated with the intent to practice KMC. Age was also found to be a significant predictor; the odds of KMC intentions were 90% higher (95% CI= (1.11-3.24)) for FTMs 20–24 years compared to FTMs 15–19 years. The association between autonomy and KMC intentions was moderated by age. Marginal effects of the interaction found that the probability of intending to practice KMC for respondents 20–24 years was constant regardless of autonomy level, while autonomy significantly increased the probability of KMC intentions for younger women aged 15–19 years. Results suggest that KMC intentions among first-time mothers 15–24 years are associated with multiple factors simultaneously. Programs seeking to improve KMC intentions among this population should consider implementing age-specific empowering and norms-based strategies.

title: Community mobilization and policy demands in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic: A transnational dialogic non-extractive research approach
abstract: by Ruth Iguiñiz-Romero, Pamella Liz Nunes Pereira, Christiane Falge, Stephanie Mayell, Mylène Fauvel, Theresa Martens, Luiza Witzel Farias, Lucero Diaz Gomez, Paulo Trivellato, Franziska Satzinger, Deisy de Freitas Lima Ventura, Michael Knipper, Laurence Monnais, Anne-Emanuelle Birn This essay discusses the interplay of epistemological-methodological approaches and research practices developed within a global health study that aims to understand and strengthen community actions and organizing by – and preserve the memories of – made-marginalized places and people during the COVID-19 pandemic. The project has brought together community actors and social justice scholar-advocates in two Global South countries (Brazil and Peru) and two Global North countries (Canada and Germany) to explore and dialogue around how community mobilization efforts during the pandemic sought to influence policymaking toward health equity and social justice. Rather than emphasizing our research results per se, we relay our experiences of countering dominant, asymmetrical approaches to global health research, both in theory and practice, based on a shared belief that community engagement is central to societal transformation. We provide an in-depth account of how we have carried out our project – through what we aspirationally name Dialogical and Non-extractivist Approaches (DNA) – using an analytic narration of the possibilities of global health research anchored in an ethical dialogic praxis, guided by principles of non-extractivism and Freirean action research.

title: Voices from the front line: Community health workers’ perspectives on effectiveness and needs in Madagascar’s tuberculosis response
abstract: by Onja Gabrielle Ravololohanitra, Alphonsine Razanamiarana, Michel Tiaray Harison, Justine Nafeno, Lydia Raveloarisoa, Harizaka Emmanuel Andriamasy, Haingotiana Razafimanantsoa, Anne Neumann, Nadine Muller Community health workers (CHWs) are central to primary health care delivery in Madagascar, yet their perspectives on what enables effective work are rarely centered in program design and implementation. This study aims to examine the lived experiences of Malagasy CHWs engaged in tuberculosis (TB) program activities and to develop context-specific recommendations to strengthen their effectiveness in Madagascar’s TB response. We conducted a qualitative study nested within the formative phase of a participatory action research initiative aimed at strengthening Madagascar’s community health workforce. TB program support was used as a tracer condition for universal health coverage-relevant service delivery. Five focus group discussions were held with 26 CHWs in August-September 2024 in two contrasting regions (Analamanga and Atsimo-Andrefana). Discussions were conducted in Malagasy and its dialects, audio-recorded, transcribed, translated into French, and analyzed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. CHWs articulated five interlinked priorities for effectiveness in the TB response: (1) stable and equitable socio-economic protection; (2) standardized, continuous, and practical training; (3) formative and collaborative supervision; (4) reliable provision of tools, equipment, transport, and personal protective equipment; and (5) recognition and integration within communities and the health system. CHWs emphasized reliability and fulfillment of promised entitlements and described fragmentation across implementing partners as a key source of inequity, uncertainty, and demotivation. CHWs’ accounts point to a persistent implementation gap between policy commitments and the reliability of day-to-day support. Addressing fragmentation and strengthening coordinated national stewardship and partner accountability will be essential to ensure predictable, equitable support for CHWs - a prerequisite for advancing equitable progress toward universal health coverage in Madagascar.

title: Strategies and approaches to vector control effectiveness toward the elimination of malaria in mainland Tanzania: An implementation case study analysis
abstract: by Mponeja Peter Gitanya, Matt Worges, Hannah Koenker, Samson Kiware, Samwel Lazaro, Jovin Kitau, William Kisinza, Naomi Serbantez, Benjamin Kamala, Charles Dismas, Johnson Matowo Effective malaria control and elimination require continuous monitoring of vector control interventions, entomological indicators, and their relationship with malaria case incidence. This implementation case study describes data fragmentation and develops a unified, granular profile of malaria burden and vector control at the district level in mainland Tanzania. By integrating data on malaria burden, vector control interventions, and intervention coverage, the study complements existing stratification approaches and generates actionable insights to inform policy and strategic decision-making on effective interventions at the council level. We extracted monthly council-level malaria incidence data (2018–2022) from DHIS2. Insecticide-treated net (ITN) access was estimated using ITN distribution and population data through a stock-and-flow model, assuming a Tanzania-specific median net lifespan of 2.15 years. Data on indoor residual spraying (IRS) implementation and entomological monitoring reports (2011–2022) were reviewed. Rainfall data were summarized and visualized as overlapping monthly time series. According to the annual vector control report (AVCR) for 2021 and 2022, the mean modeled council-level population access to ITNs was 63.9% in 2021 and 65.2% in 2022. Across 184 councils, 17.4% had low ITN access ( 80%). Councils with ITN access above 80% consistently reported lower malaria incidence rates, whereas those with access below 50% were generally associated with higher malaria burden. Higher ITN access was associated with lower malaria incidence, underscoring the importance of accurate quantification and timely distribution of insecticide-treated nets. In areas where Anopheles arabiensis predominates, complementary outdoor vector control interventions may be needed to address residual outdoor transmission. District-level vector control profiling can enhance the effectiveness of malaria programmes by supporting evidence-based resource allocation and adaptive intervention strategies.

title: A narrative systematic review of snakebite risk factors in Kenya, incorporating grey and academic literature
abstract: by Eleanor Collinson, Rikki Gumbs, Shelley Lees, Alex Bowmer Snakebite is a neglected tropical disease, the drivers of which remain poorly understood and controlled in many countries. Incorporating grey literature has been recommended by previous academic publications on snakebite, due to the limited studies available globally, to provide a more accurate understanding of burden. In this review we aimed to identify and better understand risk factors that are associated with increased risk of snakebite, specifically across Kenya, using both grey and academic literature sources. We appraised academic studies using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, while grey literature was assessed using the Authority, Accuracy, Coverage, Date and Significance guidelines. This systematic review synthesised evidence from 16 eligible peer-reviewed studies and 4 grey literature sources (1994–2025) examining determinants of snakebite risk and outcomes across Kenya. Given the limited number of eligible studies and heterogeneity of study types we conducted a thematic narrative synthesis. A total of 25 variables clustered into four domains were assessed, spanning human demographic factors, and environmental exposures. This study concurred with established literature on factors such as rurality, poverty and farming increasing snakebite risk, but also highlights discrepancies with global data. Several studies reported no seasonal variation or more bites in the dry season; bites were reported to occur equally in the day and the night in some studies; and no significant gender difference was observed in several reports. Overall findings converged on a consistent picture, snakebite envenoming in Kenya is concentrated among poorer, rural populations, and is more consistently linked to livelihoods and housing conditions, than seasonality or temporality. Actual burden and species responsible for bites remain poorly understood.

title: The impact and cost of reaching the UNAIDS global HIV targets
abstract: by John Stover, Deepak Mattur, Mariana Siapka, Triantafyllos Pliakas, Ricardo Valladares-Cardona HIV funding has been declining in the past decade creating a large gap in required funding. In 2024, UNAIDS (Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS) convened a Global Task Team in 2024 to recommend new targets and approaches for 2030 for key HIV interventions. This paper describes the approach to estimate the impact and cost of achieving those targets. We calibrated an HIV simulation model, Goals, to the historical HIV epidemic in 134 countries and used the model to project the impact of achieving the UNAIDS targets by 2030. Resource needs were estimated for 118 low-, lower-middle and upper-middle income countries (LMIC). To estimate the cost of achieving the targets we compiled a database of the unit costs for each intervention from published studies, country reports and commodity costs. Achieving the UNAIDS 2030 targets would reduce the annual number of new HIV infections globally by 77% from 2023 to 2030, from 1.3 million to 300,000. The number of AIDS deaths would decline by 50% over the same period. Resources needed to achieve the targets in all LMIC would rise to US$21.9 billion by 2030. Of this amount, 17% is needed in low-income countries, 38% in lower-middle income countries and 45% in upper-middle income countries. Achieving the UNAIDS targets for 2030 would reduce the annual number of new HIV infections to just 9% of the peak value in 1995 and AIDS deaths to 13% of the peak value in 2004. The resources required to achieve these targets are substantial but $7 billion less than previous estimates of $29.3 billion.

title: Assessing a local vaccination initiative: Eight years of “Immuniser Lyon” in France
abstract: by Juliette Dessemon, Romain Saux, Christelle Elias, Anne-Sophie Ronnaux-Baron, Anne Sophie Malachane, Sophie Pamies-Jeantet, Benoit Soubeyrand, Pascal Roy, Philippe Vanhems “Immuniser Lyon” (IL) is a French city-level initiative launched in 2015 to promote vaccination through coordinated, locally tailored actions. The objective of this study is to describe and compare temporal trends in vaccine coverage for HPV and influenza in the Rhône area versus the neighboring Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes (ARA) region, and to explore whether observed patterns are consistent with a potential contribution of the IL initiative. A comparative analysis of vaccine coverage was performed for HPV (2010–2022) and influenza (2016–2020) between different areas within the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes (ARA) region versus the ARA region, using binomial log-linear models. HPV vaccine coverage in Rhône and ARA followed similar patterns, increasing from 2015 to 2022 after a nationwide decline. For influenza, vaccine coverage among adults aged ≥65 was significantly higher in Lyon in 2020 (64.5%) than in the rest of ARA (59.2%, OR=1.25, 95% CI [1.24–1.26], p < 0.001). While HPV trends reflected broader national dynamics, the observed pattern may be consistent with a potential contribution of IL to the accelerated uptake of influenza vaccines in older adults. These findings highlight the potential of sustained local action to complement national immunization strategies.

title: Mental health and psychosocial wellbeing among beneficiaries of a community-based intervention in Nepal: Findings from a cross-sectional endline evaluation of the PARBARDHAN project
abstract: by Himal Gaire, Ganesh Bhandari, Rima Mishra, Ram Lal Shrestha, Aishwarya Prasad Dhakal, Pashupati Mahat Mental health and psychosocial wellbeing among migrant workers and their families are important public health concerns in Nepal. The PARBARDHAN project used a community-based approach to strengthen mental health and psychosocial support, community participation, and local service capacity in migration-affected communities. This study describes psychosocial wellbeing at endline evaluation and compares findings descriptively with baseline and midline. A cross-sectional, mixed-methods endline evaluation was conducted in Salyan and Kailali districts of Nepal. The quantitative component included 245 project beneficiaries aged 16–80 yearsincluding20 (8.2%) migrant/returnee workers and 225 (91.8%) family/community respondents; 216 (88.2%) reported having a family member currently abroad. Psychological distress was assessed using the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12), and anxiety and depression the Hopkins Symptom Checklist (HSCL-25). Life satisfaction and subjective happiness were assessed. Qualitative interviews and focus group discussions provided contextual information on project implementation and perceived effects. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics while qualitative data were analysed using framework analysis. Data were collected from3-26 February, 2026. At endline, 34.7% screened positive for psychological distress, while 8.2% screened positive for anxiety and 5.3% for depression (5.3%). Compared with baseline and midline assessment rounds, anxiety and depression screening positivity was lower at endline, whereas probable psychological distress was higher. Qualitative findings indicated increased mental health awareness, greater willingness to seek support, perceived reductions in stigma, and support through self-help groups, peer groups counselling, and community activities. However, substantial dissatisfaction with life was also reported. Because the evaluation rounds used independent cross-sectional samples, the observed differences cannot be interpreted as within-person changes or attributed causally to the PARBARDHAN intervention. The findings indicate the perceived value of community-based mental health and psychosocial support while highlighting continuing economic insecurity, family separation, and other structural factors affecting psychosocial wellbeing.

title: 5-year survival rate and determinants of decreased survival among patients with breast cancer in Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Introduction Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Survival varies across regions, with most deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries due to limited early detection and treatment access. This study aimed to estimate the 5-year survival rate and identify determinants of decreased survival among patients with breast cancer in Africa. Methods A systematic review of only retrospective cohort studies was conducted using PubMed, Hinari, EMBASE, Google Scholar, African Journals Online, African Index Medicus and Web of Science. The literature search was conducted for a 1-month duration (1–30 November 2024). We included all available articles without restriction on publication date to ensure a comprehensive review. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa 2016 Critical Appraisal Checklist. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s test, and heterogeneity was assessed with the I 2 test. Data were analysed with Stata V.17. Results 55 articles with 19 577 participants from 19 countries were included; 37 studies (4622 participants) were used to estimate pooled 5-year survival. The pooled 5-year survival rate of patients with breast cancer in Africa was 40.38% (95% CI 33.92 to 46.83%). Reduced survival was strongly associated with tumour characteristics, including tumour stage >2 (HR 3.06, 95% CI 2.02 to 4.09), negative oestrogen receptor status (HR 2.52, 95% CI 1.89 to 3.15), tumour size >5 cm (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.48 to 1.76), positive nodal status (HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.58 to 1.70) and higher histological grade (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.29). Treatment-related factors such as single-agent chemotherapy (HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.53) and patient-related factors, including comorbidities (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.40 to 1.50) and illiteracy (HR 6.54, 95% CI 4.39 to 8.69), were also associated with reduced survival. Conclusion This study reveals a critically low 5-year survival rate of 40.4% for breast cancer in Africa. Poor survival is linked to advanced tumour features, suboptimal treatment and patient-related factors, with comorbidities and illiteracy being the strongest patient-related factors. These results highlight the urgent need for integrated strategies focused on early diagnosis, public education, equitable access to multimodal therapies and systematic management of comorbidities across the continent. title: Formalising remote consulting in primary care services for underserved populations with long-term conditions in sub-Saharan Africa: a process evaluation and stakeholder engagement
abstract: Introduction Remote consulting can improve healthcare access and equity. When delivered by trained health workers, it is safe, trustworthy and efficient. Alongside two independent clinical trials, we studied the implementation of a cascaded health worker training intervention (REaCH), plus airtime, on remote consulting in primary healthcare facilities in Nigeria (n=35) and Tanzania (n=21). Additionally, we assessed health service readiness for sustainable remote consulting in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Malawi, Sierra Leone, Tanzania and Uganda. Methods We explored what worked for whom, how, and why in both health worker training in Nigeria (n=115) and Tanzania (n=136), and the implementation of remote consulting for patients with long-term conditions. We assessed REaCH training for talent, resources, alignment, implementation and nurture. We analysed system readiness with WHO’s Digital Investment Guide. We undertook 82 semi-structured interviews with health workers and patients (n=40: Nigeria, n=42: Tanzania), collected text produced, engaged with stakeholders and reviewed key policies/guidelines. Data were analysed thematically. Results Health workers were already doing informal remote consulting. REaCH training helped facilities to plan and implement remote consulting. It addressed concerns about delivering a safe and ethical service. Provision of airtime was critical. Health workers used remote consulting for patient follow-up and patients sought advice, test results, prescriptions, referrals and emergency help. Patients and health workers trusted and appreciated remote consulting as it saved time. Patients felt cared for, but some received calls at inconvenient times. Health workers reported reduced stress but noted off-duty calls could be burdensome. Stakeholders were aware of informal remote consulting and were concerned about quality. None of the study countries provided airtime for remote consulting or had guidance or recording systems for remote consulting. Conclusion There is an appetite for remote consulting in primary healthcare. However, health systems in seven countries of sub-Saharan Africa are not yet fully prepared for this.

title: Precision immunisation: reaching zero-dose children in underserved communities in Niger State, Nigeria
abstract: Nigeria has one of the highest burdens of zero-dose children globally, particularly in underserved and hard-to-reach communities where routine immunisation systems face persistent barriers. In Niger state, these challenges are compounded by insecurity, seasonal flooding and dispersed populations, limiting the effectiveness of conventional facility-based approaches. We describe the implementation of the Strengthening Routine Immunization in Consequential Areas of Niger State (STRICAN) initiative, which applied a precision immunisation approach to identify and reach previously unreached children. The model combined household-level enumeration, geographical information system-enabled microplanning through a digital Micro Coverage Tracking Tool and community-based mobilisation using Community Health Influencers, Promoters, and Services agents and local leadership structures. Across 10 local government areas, the initiative generated granular data on settlements and under-five children, enabling targeted service delivery through a mix of outreach, mobile and facility-based strategies. Vaccination activities were adapted in real time to contextual challenges, including insecurity, poor network connectivity and population displacement. This implementation experience highlights the importance of integrating digital tools with trusted community systems to improve identification, tracking and service delivery for zero-dose populations. Key lessons include the value of data-driven microplanning, flexible delivery strategies in fragile settings and strong partnerships between government and implementing actors. The STRICAN model offers practical insights for policymakers and programme implementers seeking to strengthen routine immunisation systems and reach underserved populations in similar contexts.

title: Assessment of the performance of primary healthcare in eight African countries: based on the Composite Fuzzy Index
abstract: Background African countries face a dual burden of infectious and non-communicable diseases, placing substantial pressure on primary healthcare (PHC) systems. Existing indicator-weighting approaches are limited in addressing redundancy and non-linear relationships. In addition, conventional composite indices often rely on linear aggregation assumptions that may not adequately reflect complex relationships among PHC performance indicators. This study proposes a novel weighting method and composite index to improve facility-level assessment of PHC performance. Methods We analysed nationally representative healthcare facility data from Service Provision Assessments conducted in eight African countries (Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, Malawi, Kenya, Namibia, Rwanda and Uganda). Based on the Primary Health Care Performance Initiative framework, we constructed an indicator system comprising 34 indicators across five subdomains within the Service Delivery domain. Two composite indices were calculated: the Arithmetic Mean Index (AMI) and the Composite Fuzzy Index (CFI). AMI was derived using a simple arithmetic mean, while CFI employed a distance-based aggregation approach with indicator weights estimated using Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines. The associations between the composite indices and patient-reported satisfaction were examined, with patient satisfaction calculated as a weighted average across surveyed patients. Findings A total of 6921 facilities were included. Overall performance across indicators was low, with particularly poor scores observed in community engagement within the population health management subdomain (mean=0.08). AMI ranged from 0.238 to 0.806, and CFI ranged from 0.237 to 0.705. Facility-level CFI scores showed a positive association with patient satisfaction (Spearman’s =0.039, p Conclusion PHC performance in African countries remains suboptimal across multiple dimensions. The proposed weighting and aggregation approach better captures inter-relationships among indicators and provides a more plausible assessment of PHC performance than traditional composite indices.

title: Associations between Mediterranean lifestyle and its components with cardiovascular outcomes among community-dwelling older adults
abstract: AimThe present study examined the cross-sectional and longitudinal associations of adherence to the Mediterranean lifestyle (MEDLS) and its individual components with cardiovascular outcomes among older adults in England.MethodsData from 565 adults aged ≥65 years participating in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing were analyzed. MEDLS adherence (score range: 0–24) comprised six domains: Mediterranean diet adherence, physical activity, water intake, sleep, social isolation, and cooking activities. The outcomes of interest were hypertension, heart attack (myocardial infarction/coronary thrombosis), and stroke. Logistic regression models were used to examine cross-sectional and longitudinal associations, with analyses adjusted for age and sex.ResultsAmong 565 participants, 96 had hypertension, 14 had experienced a heart attack, and 10 had experienced a stroke at baseline; 42, 16, and 13 incident cases, respectively, were identified during follow-up. Higher MEDLS adherence was cross-sectionally associated with lower odds of hypertension (OR 0.849, 95% CI 0.722–0.999). No statistically significant longitudinal associations were observed between MEDLS and hypertension (OR 0.990, 95% CI 0.902–1.085), heart attack (OR 0.919, 95% CI 0.707–1.195), or stroke (OR 1.053, 95% CI 0.827–1.341), although the small number of events limited precision. At the component level, Mediterranean diet adherence was associated with lower odds of incident heart attack (OR 0.670, 95% CI 0.454–0.988); However, this finding was considered exploratory.ConclusionHigher adherence to the MEDLS was associated with lower odds of prevalent hypertension but not with incident cardiovascular outcomes among communitydwelling older adults. At the component level, greater adherence to the Mediterranean diet was prospectively associated with lower odds of heart attack; however, given the absence of adjustment for multiple comparisons, this finding should be considered exploratory and requires confirmation in adequately powered studies.

title: Socioeconomic gradients in diabetes prevalence across Israeli municipalities: the role of population density
abstract: BackgroundHealth policies often prioritize the most socioeconomically disadvantaged populations, implicitly assuming that health outcomes improve monotonically with socioeconomic status. However, this assumption may obscure important patterns in disease distribution and lead to suboptimal targeting of interventions.MethodsThis study uses municipality-level data covering 127 Israeli municipalities to examine the relationship between municipal socioeconomic rank and diabetes prevalence and whether this relationship varies with population density. A quadratic specification interacted with population density is used to allow for non-linear gradients in health outcomes across different levels of density.ResultsDiabetes prevalence is strongly negatively associated with socioeconomic rank at the municipal level, but the relationship between population density and diabetes prevalence varies across the socioeconomic distribution. Higher population density is associated with significantly lower diabetes prevalence among municipalities at SES ranks 1–3, whereas this association is not statistically significant at higher SES ranks. The quadratic SES component also becomes more negative as population density increases and is statistically significant at the 75th-percentile density, although this evidence of density-dependent curvature should be interpreted cautiously.ConclusionsThese findings challenge the common assumption of a uniform socioeconomic gradient in health across different urban contexts. In the Israeli context, policies that focus primarily on socioeconomic status without considering population density may overlook important differences in disease burden. Incorporating interactions between socioeconomic gradients and population density, together with outcome-based indicators, may provide useful additional information for identifying heterogeneity in diabetes burden and informing the targeting of prevention strategies.

title: From menarche to menopause: a lifespan perspective on women's health in sickle cell disease
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) has long been associated with high childhood mortality and reduced life expectancy; however, advances in newborn screening, disease-modifying therapies, and comprehensive care have substantially improved survival. As increasing numbers of women with SCD reach midlife, new challenges are emerging that extend beyond the traditional focus on fertility and pregnancy. Despite growing recognition of reproductive health issues in SCD, menopause remains an underexplored and underrecognized phase of the disease trajectory. In this Perspective, we propose a lifespan framework for women's health in SCD that extends from menarche through menopause and healthy aging. We discuss how the underlying pathophysiology of SCD—including chronic hemolysis, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and progressive organ injury—intersects with reproductive transitions across the female life course. We highlight emerging evidence suggesting earlier menopause in women with SCD and examine the potential implications for pain burden, cognitive health, bone health, cardiovascular risk, iron overload, and quality of life. We further explore how symptom overlap between menopause and SCD may contribute to underdiagnosis and undertreatment during midlife. At the same time, we highlight the role of protective factors—including comprehensive multidisciplinary care, the development and evaluation of menopause-specific interventions through dedicated clinical trials in individuals with SCD, reproductive health services, and coordinated lifespan care models—in supporting healthy aging and improving long-term outcomes. Finally, we argue that menopause should be recognized as a critical component of comprehensive SCD care and research. Integrating reproductive aging into clinical practice, research agendas, and health policy represents an important opportunity to improve lifelong health outcomes, strengthen women-centered care, and advance health equity for women living with SCD worldwide.

title: Red blood cell distribution width and all-cause mortality in low-income populations: a NHANES-based cohort study
abstract: BackgroundRed blood cell distribution width (RDW) may be associated with all-cause mortality. This study aimed to evaluate the relationship between RDW and all-cause mortality in low-income populations. Low-income status was defined as a Family Income to Poverty Ratio (PIR) < 1, consistent with previous studies. All analyses were weighted to account for the complex sampling design.MethodsThis study included 92,062 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999–2016 database, with survival follow-up through December 31, 2016. Analyses were restricted to the low-income subgroup and weighted according to the NHANES sampling design to ensure national representativeness. Linear and nonlinear multivariable Cox regression models were used to evaluate the association between RDW and all-cause mortality. Participants with missing data were excluded through complete-case analysis. Statistical analyses were performed using EmpowerStats and R software.ResultsA total of 17,412 participants were included in the final analysis. In the low-income population, RDW showed a nonlinear association with all-cause mortality, characterized by a threshold at 15.9%. Below this threshold, each 1% increase in RDW was associated with a 29% higher risk of mortality (HR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.20–1.38, P < 0.0001), while above 15.9%, the association was no longer statistically significant. Multivariable Cox regression analysis demonstrated that RDW remained significantly associated with mortality after adjustment for potential confounding factors (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.11, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.08–1.15, P < 0.0001). Specifically, each 1% increase in RDW was associated with an 11% increase in the risk of all-cause mortality.ConclusionElevated RDW was associated with increased all-cause mortality among low-income adults and may indicate a potential prognostic marker for mortality risk in this vulnerable population. However, further studies are needed to validate its clinical predictive utility.

title: Practical guidance for collecting reproducible time-to-event endpoints in retrospective observational oncology studies
abstract: Time-to-event endpoints such as progression-free survival, overall survival, and recurrence-free survival are among the most commonly reported outcomes in cancer research, yet the practical decisions required to collect and structure these data appropriately in retrospective observational studies remain poorly described in the literature. While substantial regulatory and methodological guidance exists for prospective clinical trials, investigators working with data collated retrospectively must navigate consequential decisions about index date selection, event definition, censoring, and follow-up time without equivalent support. Decisions at the data extraction stage can bias results and undermine reproducibility regardless of the rigor of the statistical analysis that follows. In this paper, we provide a practical, decision-focused guide to collating and updating time-to-event endpoints in retrospective oncology studies. Specific topics include how to define the index date, event date, and follow-up end date for different endpoints; what counts as an event and how competing events should be handled; how to manage missing and interval-censored data; how to update outcomes over time; and how to identify potential data quality issues through exploratory analysis and sensitivity testing. We illustrate key concepts using a publicly available lung cancer dataset and a worked example that follows endpoint creation from source records to analysis-ready variables, and we provide a practical checklist that researchers can apply directly to their own work. Our goal is to help epidemiologists, clinicians, and statisticians build time-to-event analyses on a foundation of rigorously collected data, resulting in more reliable and reproducible inference.

title: Cancer prevention and interception studies registered in ClinicalTrials.gov: a landscape analysis of trial characteristics and reporting gaps
abstract: BackgroundCancer interception has emerged as a prevention-oriented approach that seeks to intervene during early stages of carcinogenesis, before the development of clinically manifest invasive disease. However, the extent to which prevention and interception research is represented and classified in clinical trial registries remains unclear.MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional, registry-based analysis of cancer prevention and interception-related studies registered in ClinicalTrials.gov through September 2025. Records identified using terms related to cancer prevention, interception, chemoprevention, risk reduction, premalignant lesions, precursor lesions, and minimal residual disease were screened for eligibility. Study characteristics, including study type, recruitment status, participant eligibility, enrollment, intervention model, allocation, masking, cancer localization, study phase, and funding category, were summarized descriptively. Associations between categorical variables were assessed using exact tests when appropriate.ResultsAmong 209 eligible studies, 157 (75.1%) were interventional and 52 (24.9%) were observational. Most studies included adults and older adults, and 52.6% were classified as completed. Among interventional studies, randomized allocation and parallel-group designs predominated, while most studies were unmasked. Gynecological and gastrointestinal malignancies were the most frequently represented cancer localizations. Funding was classified as ‘Other’ in most records, reflecting a heterogeneous registry category that could not be further disaggregated. Study type was associated with funding category (p = 0.028), whereas the association between study type and cancer localization was not statistically significant (p = 0.09, with a Cramér's V of 0.32). Among interventional studies, 54 (34.4%) focused on early detection and diagnosis, aligning with the registry's ’Screening’ and ‘Diagnostic’ fields. Cancer interception and post-treatment disease control accounted for 52 studies (33.1%) but lacked distinct registry designations, while 51 (32.5%) addressed primary prevention and chemoprevention, corresponding to the ‘Prevention’ category.ConclusionsCancer prevention and interception research registered in ClinicalTrials.gov is heterogeneous and encompasses distinct clinical objectives. Our findings highlight the need for explicit operational definitions and more granular, standardized reporting fields to improve the visibility, interpretability, and comparability of preventive oncology.

title: β-lactam infusion strategies in critical illness: is continuous superior to extended infusion? A systematic review and network meta-analysis
abstract: BackgroundProlonged β-lactam infusion is common in critical care, but whether continuous infusion (CI) improves outcomes more than extended infusion (EI) is unclear.MethodsWe conducted a systematic review and random-effects Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in critically ill adults comparing intravenous β-lactam administration by continuous infusion (24-hour infusion), extended infusion (≥3 h per dose), and intermittent infusion (≤1 h per dose). We searched PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from January 1, 2000, to July 25, 2025. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Relative risks (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) were synthesized using random-effects models. Network meta-analysis used Markov chain Monte Carlo methods in R, with complementary pairwise analyses in Stata. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE for network meta-analysis.ResultsTwenty-five randomized trials (N = 9,915) were included; no direct CI vs. EI trials were identified. Versus II, CI reduced mortality (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.66–0.98; moderate certainty); EI had uncertain mortality effects (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.60–1.10; low certainty). Clinical cure improved versus II for CI (RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.03–1.20) and EI (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.07–1.55). ICU length of stay was uncertain (CI vs. II: MD −0.47 days, 95% CI −2.10–1.28; EI vs. II: MD −1.32 days, 95% CI −4.65–2.52). Indirect CI vs. EI comparisons showed no significant differences in mortality (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.73–1.44), clinical cure (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.70–1.05), or ICU length of stay (MD 0.86 days, 95% CI −3.32–4.54). Bayesian posterior probability analysis suggested a 93.2% probability that EI is superior to CI for clinical cure.ConclusionsCI did not demonstrate greater clinical benefit than EI. CI can reduce patient mortality, and both CI and EI appear to improve clinical cure rates compared with II. CI conferred no additional benefit over EI, suggesting that EI may be sufficient as a prolonged-infusion strategy in clinical practice. However, this finding is based on indirect evidence. The apparent advantage of EI should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in adequately powered head-to-head randomized controlled trials.Systematic Review Registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42023452814, PROSPERO CRD42023452814.

title: Low prevalence of Plasmodium falciparum pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 gene deletions in archived samples collected before and after nationwide malaria-RDT rollout in Kenya
abstract: Rapid and accurate malaria diagnosis is essential for effective treatment and malaria control. In Kenya, most malaria testing relies on P. falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2)-based rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). However, deletions in the pfhrp2/pfhrp3 genes can lead to false-negative RDT results, which can sustain transmission and worsen clinical outcomes. This study assessed the prevalence and pattern of pfhrp2, pfhrp3 and their respective flanking genes in archived samples collected before and after the nationwide rollout of PfHRP2-based RDTs in Kenya in 2012. A total of 350 archived whole-blood samples were analysed, comprising 95 pre-RDT samples (collected before the nationwide rollout of RDTs in Kenya) from 2003 to 2005 and 255 post-RDT samples (collected after the nationwide rollout of RDTs in Kenya) from 2013 to 2017 from multiple malaria-endemic regions of Kenya. Samples were first screened by quantitative Real-Time PCR to identify those with adequate parasite density for genotyping. Nested PCR assays were then used to genotype pfhrp2, pfhrp3 and their flanking genes. Where available, PfHRP2-based RDT results were compared with molecular genotyping outcomes to investigate potential causes of false-negative RDT results. The overall prevalence of single pfhrp2 or pfhrp3 deletions was low, at 0.3% (1/317) and 1.3% (4/317), respectively. All pre-RDT samples carried intact pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 genes. Among post-RDT samples, deletions were rare 0.4% (1/224) for pfhrp2 gene only and 1.8% (4/224) for pfhrp3 gene only. No sample exhibited a triple deletion of pfhrp2 and both of its flanking genes or triple deletion of pfhrp3 and both of its flanking genes. The sensitivity of the PfHRP2-based RDT was 89.2% (174/195). Notably, 95.2% of false-negative RDT results occurred in samples with intact pfhrp2 and pfhrp3, suggesting that low parasitemia or other factors, rather than gene deletions, were the primary cause of diagnostic failure. Overall, pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions remained rare in the samples collected up to five years after the nationwide rollout of PfHRP2-RDTs in Kenya. However, continuous molecular surveillance is essential to identify emerging deletion hotspots and to ensure the sustained reliability of PfHRP2-based diagnostics as testing practices and parasites continue to evolve.

title: Predicting disease progression under a “treatment-naive” counterfactual scenario in a competing risks framework
abstract: PurposePrognostic models aim to estimate the individual risk of developing a specific health outcome based on patient characteristics and prognostic factors. A key factor affecting performance over time and across different populations is evolving treatment strategies. These shifts can alter the relationship between predictors and outcome, as well as occurrence of competing events. Counterfactual risk models may yield more reliable estimates across different time periods and treatment regimens than traditional approaches like ignoring treatment, restricting analysis to untreated patients, stratifying, or adjusting for treatment.Patients and methodsIn the Turin Prostate Cancer Prognostication cohort study, which includes patients diagnosed with non-metastatic prostate cancer and followed longitudinally, the performance of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center prediction model was evaluated in predicting metastatic progression up to 5 years after diagnosis in the presence of competing mortality risk. Using the g-formula, time to the two competing events was generated under a counterfactual scenario in which no patients received prostatectomy. The performance of the MSKCC model developed in the TPCP cohort and applied to the counterfactual cohort (applied model) and the model updated under this counterfactual scenario (updated model) were compared.ResultsAt 5 years post-diagnosis, the updated model had an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.82; 0.85) and the applied model had an AUC of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.81, 0.85). The calibration slope for the updated model was 1.02 (95% CI: 0.99, 1.12) compared to 1.07 (95% CI: 0.97, 1.17) for the applied model. Calibration intercepts were 0.00 (95% CI: −0.10, 0.10) and 0.05 (95% CI: −0.04, 0.15) respectively. The predicted probabilities of the outcome of interest under counterfactual treatment strategy varied not only because of the treatment itself, but also due to its impact on competing risks.ConclusionWhen a prediction model cannot be validated in a new population due to treatment shifts, counterfactual risks under hypothetical regimens can still be cautiously estimated. In particular, counterfactual modeling should be considered as a useful complementary assessment of model transportability and calibration under clinically relevant treatment scenarios.

title: Factors associated with common mental disorder symptoms and lived experiences among adults with hypertension in Nepal: a mixed-methods study
abstract: BackgroundIn hypertension care, common mental disorder (CMD) symptoms such as depression and anxiety shape adherence, self-management, and outcomes. Evidence from low- and middle-income settings on factors associated with CMD symptom severity and patients’ lived experiences remains limited. This study aimed to examine factors associated with depressive and anxiety symptom severity among adults with hypertension in Nepal and to explore how patients’ lived experiences contextualize the quantitative findings.MethodsWe conducted a community-based, explanatory sequential mixed-methods study in Budhanilkantha Municipality (Kathmandu, Nepal). Quantitatively, 327 adults with hypertension were selected via systematic random sampling. Depressive and anxiety symptom severity were measured with Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) and modeled as continuous outcomes using linear regression in prespecified blocks (socio-demographic; health/medication; lifestyle) and a fully adjusted model. Qualitatively, we conducted in-depth interviews with 16 purposively selected participants (with and without depressive/anxiety symptoms). Transcripts were thematically analyzed and interpreted using a Biopsychosocial framework. We integrated quantitative and qualitative findings across conceptually related domains to identify areas of convergence, complementarity, and contextual elaboration.ResultsIn fully adjusted models, sleeping ≥6 h per day was associated with lower depressive and anxiety symptom scores. Non-high-caste group was associated with higher depressive symptom scores, whereas older age was associated with lower anxiety symptom scores. Consumption of >2 servings of fruits and vegetables per day was associated with lower depressive symptom scores. Higher household income and controlled blood pressure showed borderline inverse associations with anxiety symptom scores. Qualitatively, hypertensive patients with CMD symptoms reported persistent insomnia, bothersome medication side-effects, activity restriction, loneliness/stigma, anger/fear, low confidence, and financial strain, whereas those without symptoms described adaptation to medicines, stronger family support, and greater self-efficacy. Mixed-methods integration showed strong convergence for sleep, while qualitative findings complemented quantitative patterns related to financial burden and medication experiences and provided contextual elaboration of perceived hypertension symptoms.DiscussionSleep duration, social position, age, diet, and socioeconomic circumstances were associated with CMD symptom severity among adults with hypertension in Nepal. The integrated findings highlight the importance of considering sleep, treatment experiences, financial circumstances, and social support within hypertension care.

title: Epidemiological trends of reported syphilis incidence in Xihu district, Hangzhou, China, 2005–2025
abstract: BackgroundSyphilis remains a critical global public health concern. The reported incidence of syphilis in Zhejiang Province has long stayed at a high level nationwide, with Xihu District of Hangzhou identified as a hyperendemic area for local syphilis transmission. This study used 2005–2025 surveillance data of Xihu District, Hangzhou to analyze syphilis trends for precise prevention evidence.MethodsSyphilis surveillance data (2005–2025) for Xihu District were retrieved from China's National Notifiable Infectious Disease Reporting System. We calculated crude reported incidence rate for overall, primary, secondary, tertiary, and latent syphilis (per 100,000 population), and notification rate for congenital syphilis (per 100,000 live births). Joinpoint Regression 6.0.1 identified trend inflection points and computed period-specific annual percentage change (APC) and overall average annual percentage change (AAPC) across the 21-year span.ResultsTotal syphilis reported incidence rate presented an inverted U-shaped trajectory: rising rapidly from 68.71/100,000 in 2005 to the peak of 155.16/100,000 in 2010, followed by sustained sharp decline down to 13.17/100,000 in 2025, with the overall AAPC = −8.18% (p < 0.05). Four trends phases were identified: rapid growth (2005–2008, APC = 25.23%), mild decline (2008–2019, APC = −5.00%), accelerated decline (2019–2023, APC = −18.69%), and apparent reduction (2023–2025, APC = −39.01%). Latent syphilis dominated all stages throughout the study period. Primary and secondary syphilis shared long-term descending trends (AAPC = −14.76% and −12.19%, respectively). Tertiary syphilis remained at extremely low absolute levels with sparse case counts. Congenital syphilis surged in 2006–2007 and no notified congenital syphilis cases have been recorded since 2017. Gender disparity existed: females exhibited a faster overall descending rate (AAPC = −10.23%) than males (AAPC = −5.54%). The 20–39 age group consistently bore the highest reported incidence burden, with a long-term AAPC of −10.47%; the elderly (≥60 years) also showed prominent high reported incidence before 2019 and then dropped sharply (AAPC = −9.53%).ConclusionsSyphilis control achieved substantial progress in Xihu District over two decades. Still, epidemiological challenges remain, including persistent vulnerability among young and older adults and hidden undiagnosed latent infections. Tailored interventions for high-risk groups, standardised latent-syphilis care, and sustained prevention of mother-to-child transmission are needed to lower residual disease burden.
authors: ["Jing Li", "Luyang He", "Tingting Wu", "Jiajia Meng", "Taoran Wang", "Fei Sun", "Bangma Wang"]

title: A survey of self-reported varicose veins with prior clinical diagnosis among adults residing in the United Arab Emirates: a cross-sectional study examining associated factors
abstract: BackgroundVaricose veins are a common manifestation of chronic venous diseases. Despite their clinical and occupational relevance, epidemiological data from the United Arab Emirates remains limited. This study estimated the prevalence of self-reported clinically-diagnosed varicose veins and examined the associated factors among adults residing in the UAE.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted across all seven emirates of the UAE between June 2025 and April 2026. A total of 1,043 eligible participants residing in the UAE were recruited through non-probability convenience sampling technique, and findings should be interpreted as preliminary and non-generalizable. The prevalence of varicose veins was estimated based on self-reported prior clinical diagnosis. Data was analyzed using SPSS (v29), associations with demographic, lifestyle, and medical factors were assessed using Pearson's chi-square tests and logistic regression models.ResultsAmong surveyed adults in the UAE, 15.05% self-reported a prior clinical diagnosis of varicose veins; this figure reflects the study sample only and should not be interpreted as a population-representative prevalence. Most participants correctly identified varicose veins. Advancing age, body mass index, prolonged standing, and positive family history of the disease were significantly associated with higher odds (p < .001).ConclusionThese findings provide preliminary, non-generalizable evidence on self-reported previously diagnosed varicose veins among the surveyed convenience sample of adults in the UAE. The condition represents a notable concern within the study population, and the results are hypothesis-generating, emphasizing the need for targeted early diagnosis among high-risk individuals, while also highlighting the need for clinically validated, probability-based population studies in the UAE.
authors: ["Riya Inder Sevhani", "Vivek Vasudevan", "Diya Harish Vanjani", "Prasanna AP", "Aashna Anuraag Mewada", "Dhyan Ashish Shah", "Kashish Doulatram Mohandas Devnani", "Shahnaz Mohammad Wazil", "Anusha Sreejith"]

title: Climate-informed surveillance for climate-sensitive infectious diseases in Somalia: early warning systems, policy gaps, and preparedness priorities
abstract: Climate variability is reshaping infectious disease risk through ecological, environmental, social, and health-system pathways. However, its operational implications remain insufficiently defined in fragile and conflict-affected settings. Somalia is a critical case because recurrent droughts and floods intersect with displacement, food insecurity, weak water and sanitation infrastructure, disrupted immunisation, livestock dependence, and constrained health-system capacity. This narrative review synthesises evidence on climate-sensitive infectious disease risks in Somalia, examines existing surveillance and early warning systems, identifies policy and implementation gaps, and proposes priorities for a climate-informed surveillance-to-action model for infectious disease control. The review distinguishes directly climate-sensitive infections, including cholera, malaria, dengue, and Rift Valley fever, from indirectly climate-amplified vaccine-preventable diseases, including measles, diphtheria, and polio. While Somalia has important surveillance and early warning assets, including EWARN, IDSRS/DHIS2, FEWS NET, FSNAU intelligence, WASH monitoring, livestock signals, and community-based reporting, these streams remain insufficiently integrated into district-level risk assessment and pre-financed preparedness action. Therefore, the central challenge is not the absence of warning signals but the failure to convert them into timely, disease-specific, and accountable responses. We propose a surveillance-to-action framework based on multisource signal detection, integrated district risk assessment, disease-specific trigger decisions, early preparedness actions, and feedback, accountability, and learning. Closing Somalia's warning-to-action gap requires pre-agreed disease-specific triggers, One Health coordination, flexible anticipatory financing, strengthened district surveillance capacity, and equity-centred outreach to internally displaced persons, pastoralist and nomadic communities, zero-dose children, malnourished populations, and hard-to-reach areas. Climate-informed surveillance should be understood not merely as better data collection but as an anticipatory public health function designed to act before climate shocks become infectious disease emergencies.
authors: ["Abdikadir Ahmed Hassan", "Liibaan Abdulahi Sudi", "Mohamed Daud Mohamed", "Iqro Omar Ibrahim", "Yakub Burhan Abdullahi"]

title: Donor type dynamics and associated factors among blood donors in northern Ghana: a six-year retrospective analysis
abstract: BackgroundRepeat blood donors have lower transfusion-transmissible infection (TTI) rates, making donor type distribution critical for blood safety. This study characterised donor type patterns, factors associated with first-time donation, and TTI prevalence differences in Northern Ghana.MethodsA retrospective cross-sectional analysis of 3,546 donor records (2017–2022) from seven health facilities in Upper West, Northern, and Oti regions. Donor type (first-time vs. repeat) was the primary outcome. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression were used. TTI prevalence, defined as positivity for at least one of HIV, HBV, HCV, or syphilis (“any TTI”), was compared between donor types. Significance was set at α = 0.05.ResultsFirst-time donors constituted 82.0% (2,907) and repeat donors 18.0% (639). Repeat donation increased from 12.3% (2020) to 22.6% (2022). Rural donors (93.1% first-time) and non-volunteer donors (82.5% first-time) showed higher proportions of first-time donation (both p < 0.001). In adjusted analysis, older age (AOR 0.97 per year) and urban residence (AOR 0.69) were associated with lower odds of being first-time. The Oti region had markedly higher odds (AOR 491.65). First-time donors had significantly higher TTI prevalence: any TTI (16.06% vs. 5.48%), HBV (5.64% vs. 1.88%), HCV (2.51% vs. 0.16%), and syphilis (8.67% vs. 3.60%).ConclusionsThe predominance of first-time donors (82%) and low repeat donation rates represent a blood safety vulnerability that would benefit from targeted donor retention programs, particularly in rural areas and the Oti region.
authors: ["Yula Salifu", "Prosper Gyebuni", "Torjim Salifu", "Eleonora B. Wobi", "Joseph Lasong"]

title: Local thermal anomalies and the altitudinal rise of dengue hospitalisation rates in Ecuador, 2011–2024: a national ecological study
abstract: IntroductionDengue is expanding beyond its traditional lowland range as rising temperatures may enable Aedes aegypti establishment at progressively higher altitudes. Ecuador, spanning sea level to above 4500 m, offers a natural altitudinal experiment, yet hospital-based evidence on the thermal drivers of Andean dengue is lacking.MethodsWe conducted a national ecological time-series analysis at the canton level using Ecuador's hospital discharge registry (INEC) for 2011–2024, the period with standardised canton coding, identifying dengue hospitalisations by ICD-10 codes A90, A91 and A97. Monthly land surface temperature, precipitation and vegetation index were derived from MODIS and GPM products. A distributed lag non-linear model estimated the temperature–hospitalisation association; a quasi-Poisson model restricted to Andean cantons (≥1500 m), with canton, calendar-month and year fixed effects, tested whether thermal anomalies above each canton's 2007–2015 baseline were associated with hospitalisation rates.ResultsAmong 74,601 dengue hospitalisations with a resolvable canton of residence (232 deaths; case fatality 0.31%), dengue was recorded in 68 cantons above 1500 m, including altitudes exceeding 3000 m. The national hospitalisation rate rose from 29.7 to 77.0 per 100,000 and the Andean rate approximately 7-fold (1.9 to 12.8). The minimum hospitalisation temperature was 18.4°C nationally and 18.9°C in Andean cantons. A +1°C anomaly versus zero was associated with a 1.07-fold increase in hospitalisation rates (95% CI 1.02–1.13; p = 0.012). Without canton fixed effects, the same contrast yielded 1.21 (1.07–1.36); the within-canton association fell to 1.04 (1.00–1.08) when the 2024 epidemic year was excluded.DiscussionPositive deviations from local historical baselines, rather than absolute temperature, were associated with rising dengue hospitalisation rates among Andean residents, by a modest margin that depends materially on the 2023–2024 epidemic. In-hospital case fatality was nearly twice as high in low Andean cantons (0.62%, 95% CI 0.20–1.45; five deaths) as on the coast (0.33%), a non-significant difference that nonetheless supports strengthening dengue recognition in highland facilities.
authors: ["Jaime Angamarca-Iguago", "Jaen Cagua-Ordoñez", "Juan Marcos Parise-Vasco", "Daniel Simancas-Racines"]

title: Insights on United States cumulative measles cases during the 2026 outbreak using ARIMA and generalized linear models
abstract: To understand the nature of the current measles outbreaks taking place across the United States in 2026, we analyzed historical surveillance data dating back to 1997 using four distinct forecasting models. By withholding data from the first four months of 2026 for out-of-sample validation, we evaluated how well traditional trend tracking and temporal dependence could anticipate this year's trajectory. While models incorporating short-term patterns performed best overall, every single model underestimated the cumulative cases recorded by May 1, 2026. This systematic underprediction reveals that the ongoing resurgence cannot be explained merely as a continuation of past trends or 2025 outbreak effects. Instead, 2026 represents a distinct, more severe outbreak regime, as the projected annual burden was already reached by May. These findings indicate that public health tracking must adapt to this heightened risk environment, and warn that the final 2026 case burden will substantially exceed that of previous years.
authors: ["Antonio Gondim", "Chidozie W. Chukwu", "Folashade B. Agusto", "Joshua Ologbonyo"]

title: Adverse childhood experiences, psychological distress, and the role of locus of control
