title: Cell-type-specific explainable spatial features extracted from digitized H&E slides explain gene expression variability beyond cell-type composition
abstract: Cell-type composition and tissue architecture jointly influence gene expression patterns. Although single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies can characterize both factors, their cost limits widespread use. Bulk RNA deconvolution estimates cell-type composition but lacks spatial context. In contrast, routine H&E whole-slide images provide a scalable source of explainable cell-type-specific spatial features describing tissue architecture. However, the extent to which the spatial features explain gene expression variability beyond cell-type composition remains largely unknown, and in this study, we aim to address this gap. The study leveraged a dataset of 471 normal prostate tissue samples with bulk RNA gene expression and paired WSIs. The WSIs are processed for nuclei segmentation and cell-type classification to extract cell-type-specific proportions ( n = 7) and spatial features ( n = 38) reflective of local neighborhood and tissue architecture. We model the gene expression as a function of cell-type-specific features to assess their contribution to gene expression variability, and evaluate the incremental explanatory effect of spatial features over the cell type compositions. Likelihood ratio testing comparing the full model (cell-type-specific spatial and proportion features, with the proportions-only model serving as the null model) to the proportions-only model identified 2330 of 24,075 genes with significantly improved model fit after adjustment for multiple testing (FDR-adjusted p-value

title: Attentive interpretable tabular learning (TabNet) for miRNA expression classification in cervical cancer and Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Background and Objective The classification of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data presents a fundamental challenge in computational biomedicine: raw read counts are high-dimensional, over-dispersed, and heteroscedastic, requiring careful preprocessing before machine learning models can be applied. Existing deep learning approaches for RNA-seq classification have largely overlooked the tabular nature of genomic expression data and have offered limited embedded interpretability. This study proposes TabNet, an attentive interpretable tabular learning architecture, as a framework for miRNA-based disease classification and evaluates its performance and interpretability against three established baseline models. Methods Two publicly available miRNA expression datasets were examined: a cervical cancer cohort (58 samples, 714 miRNAs) and an Alzheimer's disease cohort (70 samples, 503 miRNAs). Raw count data were preprocessed following the MLSeq framework, encompassing DESeq median-ratio normalisation, near-zero variance filtering, supervised gene ranking based on DESeq differential expression analysis, and the DESeq variance-stabilising transformation (vst). Gene subsets corresponding to 5%, 10%, and 30% of the post-filtering feature space were evaluated. TabNet was benchmarked against eight baselines spanning four learning paradigms: a 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a Long Short-Term Memory network (LSTM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest, ElasticNet-regularised logistic regression, a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), the prior-fitted transformer TabPFN, and the inherently interpretable Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM). Each configuration was assessed over 50 independent random train/test splits (70%/30%) under a strict leakage-free protocol in which all preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, and early stopping relied exclusively on inner validation subsets of the training partitions; all metrics are reported as mean $$\pm $$ SD. Results Under the leakage-free protocol, a group of four methods reached a statistically indistinguishable accuracy ceiling: on the cervical cancer dataset, ElasticNet (95.06% $$\pm $$ 4.66), EBM (94.94% $$\pm $$ 4.60), TabPFN (94.71% $$\pm $$ 4.64), and Random Forest (94.35% $$\pm $$ 5.82); on the Alzheimer's disease dataset, TabPFN (70.86% $$\pm $$ 10.26), EBM (70.67% $$\pm $$ 12.67), and ElasticNet (70.48% $$\pm $$ 9.76) led. TabNet reached 85.18% $$\pm $$ 11.10 (cervical) and 64.38% $$\pm $$ 11.23 (Alzheimer's) at its respective best levels -- below the top tier, but with the distinctive property of producing sparse, instance-level attention explanations as part of its forward computation. Supplementary analyses showed that self-supervised pre-training conferred no significant benefit at these cohort sizes, that results were robust to the choice between supervised differential-expression and unsupervised variance feature ranking, and that instance-level attention patterns varied substantially across splits, supporting their use as illustrative rather than confirmatory evidence. Conclusions In rigorously leakage-controlled small-cohort miRNA classification, strongly regularised classical models, glass-box additive models, and prior-fitted transformers converge to the same accuracy ceiling, and no evaluated method -- including attention-based deep learning -- surpasses it. Within this landscape, TabNet remains distinctive as the only evaluated deep architecture whose sequential attention mechanism produces sparse instance-level miRNA attributions as an inherent part of prediction, offering a trade-off between embedded interpretability and a moderate accuracy cost that we quantify precisely. These results argue for protocol-first evaluation and calibrated claims when deep tabular models are applied to small transcriptomic cohorts.

title: RFhap: accurate alignment-free long-read phasing for improved diploid de novo assembly
abstract: Background Haplotype-resolved de novo assemblies enable genome-wide separation of maternal and paternal variation, improving the interpretation of complex variants relevant to human disease. Trio-aware assemblers such as Hifiasm-Trio leverage parental short reads by deriving parent-specific k-mers to guide phasing within the long-read assembly graph; however, fixed k-mer length and heuristics cannot be optimal in the presence of sequencing errors and graph complexity in repetitive regions, contributing to phasing errors and reduced haplotype-resolved contiguity. Results Here we present RFhap, a trio-based long-read phasing method that integrates multi-k-mer parent-specific markers with an alignment-free k-mer lookup engine and a random forest classifier to assign long reads to maternal, paternal, or unknown haplotypes prior to de novo assembly. We benchmarked RFhap on four human trio datasets from the Human Pangenome project spanning two ONT chemistries (R10.4 and R9.4.1). Using Merqury to evaluate downstream assemblies, RFhap nearly doubled corrected haplotype NG50 (mean 24.3 Mb vs. 13.1 Mb) and halved switch error rates (mean 0.111% vs. 0.236%) relative to Hifiasm-Trio, while remaining competitive in consensus QV and parental k-mer completeness. Consistent with improved phasing, RFhap reduced long-switch errors by ~ 3-fold across datasets, particularly within interspersed repeats. Conclusions RFhap improves phasing accuracy from standard trio data, representing a step toward accurate and automated diploid human de novo assembly from long reads.

title: Extracting candidate motif patterns for multiple RNA modifications using direct RNA sequencing
abstract: RNA modifications have emerged as key regulators of virtually all aspects of RNA biology, driving growing interest in computational approaches for their transcriptome-wide detection. For some RNA modifications, the search space can be reduced by exploiting characteristic sequence motifs, as exemplified by the canonical DRACH motif associated with m⁶A. However, comparable sequence preferences remain largely unknown for most other RNA modifications, making systematic motif discovery considerably more challenging. Here, we applied exponential population analysis to direct RNA sequencing data from HEK293T cells and peripheral human blood to identify candidate motif patterns for pseudouridine (Ψ), inosine (I), and 5-methylcytosine (m⁵C). Our results demonstrate that exponential population analysis provides a systematic framework for identifying candidate motif patterns from nanopore-derived RNA modification predictions, thereby prioritizing sequence contexts for future biological validation.

title: CORE clonotypes: a reproducible structural component of the peripheral TCR repertoire revealed through variation in blood processing times
abstract: Background High-throughput T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire sequencing is widely used for immune profiling, yet repertoire measurements remain sensitive to pre-analytical variables that can affect reproducibility and downstream interpretation. Among these variables, delays between blood collection and sample processing may alter detectable repertoire composition, particularly among low-frequency clonotypes. Here, we use processing-delay variability as a structured technical perturbation to examine organizational features of the peripheral TCR repertoire. We analyzed peripheral blood TCRβ repertoires from 211 patients with newly diagnosed colorectal cancer, comparing samples processed shortly after blood collection with samples subjected to extended processing delays. Delayed processing was associated with reduced clonotype richness, depletion of singleton clonotypes, and altered diversity distributions, indicating preferential loss of low-frequency repertoire elements under prolonged handling conditions. Within this framework, we defined CORE clonotypes (COnsistent Repertoire Elements) operationally as amino-acid-identical CDR3β sequences detected in both processing groups. Results We characterized CORE clonotypes across multiple analytical levels, including abundance distributions, V/J gene usage, amino-acid composition, nucleotide redundancy, codon usage, biochemical properties, and correlation-network structure. CORE clonotypes were largely distinct from abundance-matched clonotype sets, indicating that reproducible detection across perturbation conditions is not explained solely by clonotype abundance. At the nucleotide level, CORE clonotypes exhibited elevated synonymous sequence diversity while maintaining conserved amino-acid composition across processing conditions. Following sequencing-depth normalization, CORE clonotypes showed reduced codon-usage divergence and narrower distributions across multiple biochemical properties relative to group-unique clonotypes. Correlation-network analysis further identified a small CORE-associated subnetwork enriched for previously annotated antigen associations compared with randomized controls. Conclusion These findings suggest that technical perturbations can reveal reproducibly detected, non-random repertoire elements with distinct organizational properties across multiple molecular levels. More broadly, this work highlights the value of pre-analytical variability as a tool for characterizing reproducible repertoire structure in immune repertoire sequencing studies.

title: Alignment of RNA secondary structures with arbitrary pseudoknots using structural sequences
abstract: Background Comparison of RNA secondary structures is fundamental for RNA classification, motif analysis, and evolutionary studies. While efficient methods exist for pseudoknot-free structures, the comparison of RNA secondary structures with arbitrary pseudoknots remains computationally challenging. The aim of this study is to introduce a novel sequence-based representation and an associated alignment distance for efficiently comparing RNA secondary structures with arbitrary pseudoknots. Results We introduce a novel representation of RNA secondary structures with arbitrary pseudoknots based on integer sequences, called structural sequences. On this representation, we define the SERNA distance, an extension of the classical edit distance with structural correctness constraints, and prove that it is a metric. We present SERNAlign, an open-source tool that computes the SERNA distance using dynamic programming with quadratic time complexity. To evaluate the proposed distance, we conduct two complementary experiments within a clustering-based evaluation framework: classification of experimentally validated pseudoknot motifs, which directly targets the design goal of SERNA, and phylogenetic clustering of ribosomal RNAs as a robustness check against existing structural distances. Across both tasks, SERNA demonstrates competitive clustering performance with respect to state-of-the-art comparison methods, while providing improved discrimination in complex motif settings and significantly lower computational cost compared to structure-based approaches.

title: PELICAN: a new bacteriophage genome annotation tool
abstract: Background Bacteriophages, or simply phages, are viruses that infect bacteria. They can serve as antibacterial agents, particularly against important bacterial pathogens. Accurate gene identification in phage genomes is essential for research and therapeutic applications. Detecting genes linked to lytic or lysogenic lifestyles, toxins, or bacterial fitness helps guide phage selection. Results We present PELICAN, a command-line tool for bacteriophage genome annotation. The PELICAN pipeline has four stages: (i) integration of multi-tool predictions; (ii) probabilistic and machine learning-based evaluation of non-consensus genes; (iii) resolution of overlapping predictions; and (iv) codon bias check of overlapped positions to produce a final annotation. For validation, we used reference phage genome annotations validated by transcriptomics and compared the results to those of other phage genome annotation tools. PELICAN had the best recall, but a higher false positive rate than some of the other tools. We present evidence that most of these false positives may be in fact true positives. Our evidence is primarily based on protein folding scores of the putative proteins coded in the predicted coding regions. Conclusions PELICAN is a novel tool for bacteriophage genome annotation that provides improved gene recall and competitive F1 values compared to an existing similar tool.

title: scDIG: an R Shiny application for interactive density-based gating of single-cell proteomic and transcriptomic data
abstract: Background Delineating biologically meaningful cell populations within single-cell embedding spaces requires methods that balance expert guidance with reproducibility. Current approaches range from subjective manual selection to fully automated algorithms that may obscure rare but biologically significant populations. Results We present scDIG, a Shiny-based tool that integrates bimodal index-driven feature selection, feature-weighted kernel density estimation, and interactive contour-based gating to define cell populations directly within two-dimensional projections of scRNA-seq and CITE-seq data. Applied to CITE-seq PBMC data from subjects in the Cardiovascular Assessment Virginia (CAVA) cohort, scDIG resolved transcriptionally distinct CD4⁺ T cell subpopulations within continuous embeddings not readily captured by conventional clustering and identified GZMB -enriched cytotoxic lymphocyte subsets from RNA expression data. Sensitivity analysis confirmed that defined gates correspond to coherent cell populations in high-dimensional feature space. Conclusions s cDIG provides a robust, reproducible framework for density-based gating of single-cell data, bridging the interpretability of manual expert gating with the rigor of algorithmic population definition. The app is freely available for non-commercial use at https://au-cbgm-shiny.augusta.edu/gating , with source code at https://gitlab.com/pbombina/scdig .

title: A kinematic interpretation of spatial expression gradients from single-snapshot spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Background Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression across tissue position, but temporal or mechanistic interpretation of a spatial gradient requires an explicit model. We derive a kinematic interpretation for tissues with a stationary position-conditioned expression field and positive mean cell displacement along an anatomical axis. Under these assumptions, a gene’s gradient sign equals its net-production sign. The measured statistic remains a spatial gradient, and without an independent velocity estimate the framework does not recover absolute rates. Results We evaluate the framework on a human liver atlas with 16 standard-Visium sections, three matched Visium HD sections and companion single-nucleus RNA-seq; the primary cross-donor analysis uses eight live-donor sections. Gradient direction is reproducible: mean cross-donor correlation is 0.87 on a strict 66-gene panel and 0.67 on a broad 15,192-gene panel. On prespecified top-quartile subsets, cross-platform sign agreement is 14/14 genes for M2 and 13/14 for M6 ( n = 14 per donor); cross-pipeline agreement is 76%. Four diagnostics and a geometric argument show that the gene-gene coupling matrix is not stably identifiable or interpretable as a regulatory Jacobian from one sampled trajectory. In graded steatosis across four donors, GLUL , LYZ and ORM1 show consistent spatial-gradient responses to lipid, but wild-cluster calibration finds cluster-robust significance anticonservative; we report directional observations, not significant discoveries. On the mouse crypt-villus axis, all 15 canonical markers recover their expected directions on an anatomy-derived coordinate. Conclusion The framework provides a reproducible, splicing-free estimator of spatial expression gradients applicable to imaging-based platforms. Under explicit steady-state and positive-flow assumptions, gradient direction has a kinematic interpretation as net-production direction; cross-sectional data establish gradient reproducibility, not time-resolved dynamics. Separating the observable from its conditional interpretation, and diagnosing the coupling matrix’s identification failure, defines both the method and its inferential boundary.

title: HGACL-DRP: Heterogeneous graph attention dual-perturbation contrastive learning network for drug response prediction
abstract: Background The marked heterogeneity of cancer poses a substantial challenge to precision drug therapy, resulting in considerable variability in patient responses to identical treatments. Accurately predicting drug sensitivity thus represents an urgent and critical challenge in the field of pharmacology and personalized medicine. Existing methods have limitations in addressing the complexity of multi-modal biological data and heterogeneous graphs. Additionally, their heavy reliance on labeled data hinders model generalization. Results In this work, we propose the Heterogeneous Graph Attention Dual-Perturbation Contrastive Learning Network for Drug Response Prediction (HGACL-DRP). This framework constructs an optimized heterogeneous graph structure by integrating multi-omics features and implementing a robust neighbor filtering mechanism. HGACL-DRP innovatively introduces a Dual-Perturbation contrastive learning paradigm that incorporates both feature and structural perturbations specifically designed for drug response prediction, thereby enabling the self-supervised learning of more robust heterogeneous graph node embeddings. On two major public datasets, the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) and the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE), HGACL-DRP exhibits exceptional performance across multiple classification metrics, achieving a mean AUC of 95.48% on CCLE and 98.99% on GDSC. Compared to existing state-of-the-art drug response prediction algorithms, HGACL-DRP demonstrates statistically significant improvements in predictive accuracy. Conclusions The innovative multi-view graph augmentation strategy and attention mechanism are designed to enhance personalized drug selection and facilitate novel drug discovery. HGACL-DRP is anticipated to address the challenges posed by drug response heterogeneity, thereby providing reliable support for clinical decision-making. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: ENflorA: a flexible tool for the bulk submission of next generation sequencing data to the European Nucleotide Archive
abstract: Background With the advancement of sequencing technologies and increasing quality of assembly and annotation tools, the amount of biological sequence data produced by research grows rapidly. To keep this data accessible for potential re-analysis, it is typically stored in public online databases, such as the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA). However, the increase in data entails an increase in time needed for metadata curation and upload. We propose a tool to simplify and automatize the upload of experimental and metadata to public repositories. Results We developed ENflorA, a set of scripts by which sample, sequence read and (annotated) assembly data can be uploaded to ENA in a simple and standardized manner. Our software allows easy metadata entry via spreadsheets, is suitable for batch upload of data from different sources, and can be fully integrated in bioinformatic workflows. It is platform independent and can be run natively on High Performance Computers, integrates an lftp upload option for big files and a test upload option. Conclusions By easing the ENA submission process, ENflorA contributes to making high-throughput sequencing data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable.

title: A new explainable AI pipeline for cancer cell segmentation and classification for microscopy images
abstract: Background The development of novel therapeutic approaches to cancers requires significant time and labour, especially for uncommon cancers (e.g. of mesenchymal origin). In addition, these rare cancers typically receive less research attention but still need sufficient analysis. For example, a trustworthy analysis of tissue samples to identify cancer progression and cell response to candidate therapies is a task to develop certain treatments and drugs. Thus, this research work develops a new explainable Deep Learning pipeline for accurate, high-throughput and autonomous recognition of metastasising cells from large-scale fluorescence microscopy images, which can be used to evaluate cell response with low cost and high trustworthiness, and facilitate the therapeutic approaches development. Results The pipeline includes pre-trained and domain-generalised segmentation to identify single cells, training the latest self-supervised transformers: DINO-based models to provide normal or metastasising classification, and leveraging Explainable AI methods to produce biologically meaningful model explanations towards the trustworthiness of model predictions; this is crucial in future clinical applications. Compared to supervised learning-based models, DINO achieves the best predictability (over 97% F1-weighted score) when only training the classifier, and the most efficient downstream adaptation. Besides, all DINO-based models can classify successfully when finetuning the entire model (DINOv3 achieves the highest F1-weighted score with 98.35%). We have also used an additional cross-magnification test and a self- / weakly-supervised model comparison to discuss the generalisation ability and superiority of DINO-based models. Biologically accurate model explanations are produced via heatmaps and analysed through quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation; the important cell regions in the model decision-making process align well with biological consensus. We also demonstrate that biologically meaningful cytoskeletal features can be detected and exploited by the developed pipeline for cancer cell classification, which facilitates the development of cytoskeleton-based diagnosis. Conclusion We develop a precise, efficient, and trustworthy pipeline that can facilitate the development of effective and bespoke cancer treatments via AI-assisted testing of the response of cancer cells to various treatments and drugs.

title: PROBE: a multi-organism benchmark for evaluating general-purpose large language models on Gene Ontology protein function annotation
abstract: Background One of the most important unresolved issues in computational biology is systematic protein function annotation. Despite decades of curation by the Gene Ontology Consortium and UniProt Swiss-Prot, most sequenced proteins lack experimentally validated functional annotations. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on scientific literature raises the question of whether they can map natural-language descriptions of experimentally characterized protein function to the correct Gene Ontology (GO) terms without task-specific training. Answering this question requires a benchmark with gold-standard experimental annotations and multi-organism coverage, which existing benchmarks lack. Results We introduce PROBE ( PR otein functi O n B enchmark E valuation): 1,000 UniProt Swiss-Prot proteins from five organisms, experimental-evidence-only annotations. We evaluate 10 open-source LLMs across five prompt formats, zero-shot and inference-only, yielding 150,000 predictions. The best model (Mistral Large 123B) achieves macro-F1 of 9.3%, yet a most-frequent-5 heuristic outperforms four of the ten LLMs. 41.3% of predicted GO terms were unmatched to the benchmark’s annotations; a temporal-holdout check against current UniProt records found only 1.25% newly supported, suggesting most are genuine errors rather than incomplete ground truth. Performance varied by organism— Saccharomyces cerevisiae unexpectedly scored highest (F1 = 8.6%), but with only five organisms this does not track evolutionary distance, and neither literature density nor annotation-pool size reaches significance, so the finding remains exploratory. Candidate-selection prompting (P5) reduces the unmatched-prediction rate by 33.5 percentage points relative to P1 while achieving the highest F1 (8.2%). GO semantic similarity analysis shows LLM predictions exceed a random baseline by 2.1–2.6× across all namespaces, indicating biologically meaningful semantic alignment despite exact-match failures. A preliminary 50-protein comparison of four closed-source models against the best open-source model found F1 of 0.081–0.127 versus 0.099 (0.028-point gap), suggesting but not establishing that current limitations extend beyond open-source models. Conclusions PROBE shows that general-purpose LLMs can map some natural-language descriptions of protein function to GO terms, but performance is often insufficient and unreliable for autonomous annotation. Unmatched predictions are common, and organism-level performance differences remain an open question rather than explained by training data or evolutionary relationships. The benchmark, evaluation pipeline, and all 150,000 experimental response records are publicly available to ensure reproducibility.

title: Taxonomic, predicted functional, and network-based characterization of the breast cancer-associated gut microbiome
abstract: Background Gut microbiome dysbiosis has emerged as a non-genetic risk factor in breast cancer (BC), yet the taxonomic, predicted functional, and microbial association patterns of the gut microbiome in BC remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to provide a combined taxonomic, predicted functional, and network-based characterization of the gut microbiome in BC using publicly available 16 S rRNA sequencing data. Methods Publicly available 16 S rRNA V4 sequencing data from PRJNA658160 were analyzed with 804 fecal samples, including 386 BC samples and 418 healthy controls. Taxonomic profiling was performed, and predicted pathway profiling was conducted with PICRUSt2. Diversity, differential abundance, and network analyses were performed at both the genus and predicted pathway levels. Taxonomic differential abundance was evaluated using ANCOM-BC2, pathway differences using LinDA, taxonomic networks using SPIEC-EASI, and predicted pathway association networks using Spearman correlation. Results BC samples exhibited significantly reduced taxonomic alpha diversity, whereas genus-level beta diversity showed no strong global separation between groups. 13 genera were differentially abundant; Bacteroides , Erysipelatoclostridium , Parabacteroides , and Fusobacterium were enriched in BC, whereas Prevotella , Alloprevotella , and Coprococcus were more abundant in healthy controls. Exploratory network analysis identified Bacteroides as a prominent hub-like taxon and Erysipelatoclostridium as a bridge-like taxon in the BC inferred association network. Predicted functional analysis indicated reduced pathway alpha diversity and identified 130 differentially abundant predicted pathways. BC-enriched predicted pathways were mainly associated with carbohydrate degradation, the glyoxylate cycle, fatty acid β-oxidation, and stress-related metabolism, whereas control-enriched predicted pathways were associated with menaquinone biosynthesis, biotin biosynthesis, fermentation, and broader biosynthetic functions. Predicted pathway beta diversity also differed significantly between groups (PERMANOVA R² = 0.013, p = 0.001); however, beta-dispersion was significantly greater in BC samples, indicating that this difference may partly reflect increased within-group heterogeneity rather than only a shift in group centroids. Because PICRUSt2 infers pathway abundance from 16 S rRNA gene profiles, these pathway-level findings represent predicted functional potential rather than confirmed functional activity. Conclusion BC-associated gut microbiome dysbiosis appears to involve selective genus-level alterations, descriptive differences in inferred microbial association patterns, and broader predicted pathway-level shifts rather than complete community replacement. These findings highlight candidate microbial and pathway-level signatures that require validation using shotgun metagenomics, metabolomics, and independent cohorts. Graphical abstract

title: ParaDISM : precise mapping of short reads to genes with highly homologous regions
abstract: Background Genes with highly similar genomic copies (paralogs, tandem duplications and pseudogenes) pose a major challenge for Short-Read High Throughput Sequencing (srHTS). High sequence similarity makes it difficult to unambiguously identify the sequences of origin of short reads. This results in misalignment artifacts which can propagate through bioinformatic pipelines and increase error rates in subsequent steps such as single nucleotide variant calling. Results We present ParaDISM , a pipeline that refines standard alignments to improve read placement and reduce misalignment-driven false variant calls in highly homologous sequences. The pipeline uses a multiple sequence alignment of reference sequences to identify disambiguating positions and assign a read/read pair to a sequence only when supported by unambiguous sequence-specific evidence. ParaDISM focuses on specificity and precision (positive predictive value) rather than sensitivity by adopting a conservative strategy of read placement and reporting reads with insufficient evidence for the gene of origin as unassigned. An optional iterative refinement procedure calls variants from confidently assigned reads, updates the reference sequences to gain sample-specific evidence for read placement, and re-processes remaining non-assigned reads to mitigate the loss of sensitivity caused by the stringent criteria for read placement. We evaluated the performance of ParaDISM both in terms of read alignment and the resulting short variant calls using extensive computational simulation experiments and the Genome in a Bottle HG002 benchmark. We applied ParaDISM to reanalyze two case studies: five public tumour exomes at the GNAQ/GNAQP1 locus, and 18 short-read sequencing datasets of patients diagnosed with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (15 exomes and 3 panel sequencing datasets). Compared to Bowtie2, BWA-MEM2 and minimap2, ParaDISM reduced the number of misalignment artifacts, thus increasing specificity and precision of subsequent single nucleotide variant calls. Conclusions ParaDISM refines BAM files to improve the precision of read placement and downstream analyses in highly homologous sequences. The pipeline can be used as a precision-focused add-on to standard bioinformatic pipelines before the variant calling step to provide a stronger level of evidence for variants called in regions of high homology. This approach is useful for applications where false positive variant calls have more severe consequences than false negative ones, such as identifying causal mutations for genetic disorders. In applications where experimental wet-lab confirmation of shortlisted variants is necessary, ParaDISM can be used to prioritise variants with strong support to reduce cost and effort spent on attempting to confirm false positive calls. ParaDISM can be used alongside the results of standard mappers to cross-check results and identify unreliable read placement and variants potentially caused by misalignment artifacts. The pipeline is open source and available under the MIT license at github.com/BioGeMT/ParaDISM.

title: Genes2Reg: Constructing a biologically-faithful gene coupling prior via deep adaptive fusion of heterogeneous knowledge sources
abstract: Genomic association and predictive modeling often operate in high-dimensional regimes where the number of candidate genes far exceeds the number of study subjects, making inference prone to instability and sensitive to missing values, batch effects, and sparse signals. Meanwhile, biology provides rich relational context (protein interactions, pathway co-membership, regulatory targeting, and more) that encodes functional relationships between genes. The recent success of deep learning has demonstrated effective model designs for integrating heterogeneous directed and symmetric relationships into a compact unified representation. Existing methods that leverage graph-based representations of biological knowledge fall along several axes: some use them as input for deep learning models with predictive modules that generate outcome predictions for supervised tasks; others learn general-purpose numerical representation (embeddings) of genes for use in downstream analysis; and a separate line of research constructs regularization priors from the biological sources tailored to a specific application. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has trained a model to integrate multiple biological sources by learning their relative reliability to build a task-agnostic Laplacian-based smoothness prior for epidemiological inference. We introduce a framework that fuses complementary biological networks into a single symmetric gene-gene coupling matrix via a Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network (HGAT), creating a reusable prior that can regularize any model with gene-indexed parameters. We first perform an intrinsic methodological validation of the approach against multiple benchmark models to assess the embeddings and output graph quality. Through controlled simulation we establish that a faithful prior must capture multi-hop functional coherence rather than direct edges alone, and that the value of learning lies specifically in the adaptive, reliability-weighted fusion of incomplete, heterogeneous sources, where fixed kernels and uniformly-weighted linear baselines fall short. We further validate that the learned prior generalizes by preserving graded biological similarity on regulatory sources held out from training, maintains competitive performance in downstream cancer prediction, and demonstrates a concrete practical advantage in a niche, under-annotated regulatory application where generalization matters. The resulting prior offers transparent biological provenance and proven generalization by integrating fragmented biological knowledge into convex inference without sacrificing predictive performance.

title: Metacontextify: automated environmental annotation of marine metagenomic samples
abstract: Background Environmental metadata is essential for using metagenomic and microbiome data to gain relevant biological insights like relations between the environment and microbial communities, genome content and protein-level adaptations. Unfortunately, obtaining standardized environmental context for those samples remains difficult. One possible solution is to use Earth observation data to retrieve the missing metadata. However, using such data requires spatiotemporal coordinate matching and handling large environmental datasets in specialized file formats, creating a barrier for its applicability. Results Metacontextify addresses this gap by automatically retrieving environmental properties (e.g., temperature, salinity, pH, nutrients) for marine metagenomic samples using Copernicus Marine Service data. The tool connects ENA and MGnify identifiers or sampling coordinates and dates to historical environmental observations, enabling large-scale ecological, genomic, and functional analyses. The tool is used to study the difference in environmental context between cold-shock proteins, involved in adaptation to temperature decreases, and antifreeze proteins, which prevent ice formation in the cell. We show that cold-shock proteins are present across the full range of marine temperatures observed in the dataset, while antifreeze proteins are predominantly found below 5 ∘ C (83% of matched proteins). However, we observe a negative association between temperature and the number of cold-shock proteins per sample (Spearman correlation of -0.439, p -value 1.2 × 10 −70 ). After a genome-level analysis, we find a negative correlation between genome length and temperature ( ρ = − 0.28, p = 4.2 × 10 −65 ) and a positive correlation between genome length and the count of cold-shock proteins in a genome ( ρ = 0.41, p = 1.5 × 10 −144 ). Conclusion Metacontextify enables researchers to integrate environmental context into large-scale metagenomic analyses, even when original datasets lack environmental metadata. This is shown for a collection of marine samples where the number of samples with temperature annotations increased 1.45-fold. For the use case, we identified distinct temperature-associated distributions of cold-shock and antifreeze proteins and demonstrated how environmental contextualization can reveal biologically meaningful patterns in large metagenomic datasets. Metacontextify is implemented in Python and is freely available under an MIT license. It can be installed via pip, conda or a container image and is accessible as a Python library and command-line tool with source code available on GitHub.

title: A hybrid beam search framework with deep representation learning for the multiple longest common subsequence problem
abstract: Background The Multiple Longest Common Subsequence (MLCS) problem is a classical computational challenge in biological sequence analysis and comparative genomics. Existing approximate methods often lack effective mechanisms for incorporating contextual information from local sequence fragments when processing complex multi-sequence biological data, which may cause promising candidate paths to be overlooked in the search space and make it difficult to achieve a good balance between computational efficiency and solution quality. Methods We propose a hybrid beam search framework enhanced by deep representation learning, which consists of three core modules. First, a lightweight Transformer encoder is combined with contrastive learning to perform representation learning on local sequence fragments. Second, a non-dominated filtering strategy and a dual-criterion evaluation mechanism are introduced during candidate-path expansion to screen and evaluate search branches. Finally, a multidimensional scoring model is constructed to rank candidate paths and guide beam-search pruning. Results Experiments were conducted on randomly simulated DNA datasets and real biological sequence fragments obtained from NCBI. The real datasets include bacteriophage sequences with relatively concentrated host backgrounds, as well as heterogeneous viral sequences from different viral taxa and sources. The experimental results show that, under different sequence-length and sequence-number settings, the proposed method generally obtains longer common subsequences than representative approximate algorithms while maintaining good computational efficiency. In addition, on small-scale instances for which exact solutions can be obtained, the approximate solutions produced by the proposed method remain close to the exact optima. Conclusions By combining the context-based sequential representation information with heuristic search strategies, this study proposes a hybrid search framework for solving the MLCS problem. Experimental results show that the proposed method can obtain high-quality approximate solutions across different sequence scales and characteristics while maintaining good computational efficiency.

title: GenPerturb: sequence-grounded interpretation of perturbation transcriptomes using pretrained genomic models
abstract: Background Perturb-seq captures transcriptional responses to thousands of genetic and chemical perturbations, but does not directly resolve the cis-regulatory elements or transcription factor motifs underlying those responses. Existing approaches rely on indirect post hoc analyses or external epigenomic annotations, making it difficult to connect gene-level responses to specific regulatory elements. Results We present GenPerturb, a model-based interpretation workflow that fits condition-specific linear readouts of pretrained sequence embeddings to observed Perturb-seq pseudobulk expression. Because control and perturbation readouts operate on one gene-centred sequence representation, control-subtracted attribution ranks candidate regions and motif instances as computational hypotheses associated with each fitted contrast. The fitted readouts recover much of the observed expression variation between genes, whereas recovery of variation across perturbation conditions within each gene is more modest. On the single available erythroid Perturb-multiome benchmark, region rankings showed agreement with accessibility labels comparable to annotation-based scores, with slightly closer agreement in the 1–10 and 10–100 kb strata, while the perturbed transcription factor’s motif family was recovered at comparable frequencies from attribution-derived and chromatin-derived regions. Selected lineage and compound examples illustrate motif associations that can differ from those of the corresponding transcription factor mRNA. Conclusions GenPerturb transfers regulatory priors learned during external pretraining to observed RNA-only Perturb-seq profiles, producing ranked, locus-anchored cis-regulatory hypotheses without a matched chromatin assay in the target experiment. Scoped to observed responses rather than prediction of unseen perturbations or cell types, the workflow offers computational candidates for experimental assessment of enhancer and transcription-factor activity.

title: A Conditional GAN for Tabular Data Generation With Probabilistic Sampling of Latent Subspaces
abstract: The tabular form constitutes the standard way of representing data in relational database systems and spreadsheets. But, similarly to other forms, tabular data suffers from class imbalance, a problem that causes serious performance degradation in a wide variety of machine learning tasks. One of the most effective solutions dictates the usage of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in order to synthesize artificial data instances for the under-represented classes. Despite their good performance, most of the proposed GAN models do not take into account the vector subspaces of the input samples in the real data space, leading to data generation in arbitrary locations. In addition, the class labels are handled in the same manner as the other categorical variables, so conditional sampling by class is rendered less effective. To overcome these problems, this study presents ctdGAN, a conditional GAN for alleviating class imbalance in tabular datasets. Initially, ctdGAN executes a space partitioning step to assign cluster labels to the input samples. Subsequently, it utilizes these labels to synthesize samples via a novel probabilistic sampling strategy and a new loss function that penalizes both cluster and class mis-predictions. In this way, ctdGAN generates samples in subspaces that resemble those of the original data distribution. We also introduce several other improvements, including a simple, yet effective cluster-wise scaling technique that captures multiple feature modes without affecting data dimensionality. The evaluation of ctdGAN with 14 imbalanced datasets demonstrated its strong ability in generating high fidelity samples and improving classification accuracy.

title: A Contrastive Paradigm for Representation Learning in Interactive Recommendation
abstract: Interactive Recommendation (IR) has attracted considerable attention in recent years. IR agents commonly utilize Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to capture users’ unique dynamic interests and demands. However, it’s challenging to train DRL agents in online recommender systems due to the large action space and the sample inefficiency problem. We discover that the principle of tackling this challenge is to integrate neighborhood collaborative information into the representation. To implement this idea and address the challenge, we propose CPIR (Contrastive Paradigm for Representation Learning in Interactive Recommendation), which comprises three Contrastive Learning (CL) approaches, a data sampling mechanism, and an agent training mechanism. The CL methods start from the perspectives of sequence alignment, interest partial order, and interest community collaborative filtering separately. The recommender agent can optimize itself more efficiently on top of the extracted representations. The data sampling and agent training mechanism ensure the stability and consistency of the multi-task training in IR. Moreover, we have explained the effectiveness of the CPIR both theoretically and experimentally. Extensive experiments conducted on Virtual-Taobao and ML-1 M have demonstrated superior improvements in sample efficiency during the training of the DRL-based IR agent.

title: A Memory-Efficient SubGraph Learning Method for Urban Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
abstract: Spatio-temporal graph learning has been widely applied to urban spatio-temporal forecasting tasks, analyzing the relationships between data to achieve accurate predictions. However, in recent years, model structures have become increasingly complex in pursuit of higher performance, resulting in greater computational complexity and GPU memory consumption during execution. In addition, urban expansion requires models to cover larger areas, further increasing memory demands. These factors collectively limit the applicability of existing models in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose a plug-and-play SubGraph Learning (SGL) method to reduce the memory overhead without compromising performance. Specifically, we introduce a SubGraph Partition Module (SGPM), which leverages a set of learnable memory vectors to select node groups with similar features from the graph, effectively partitioning the graph into smaller subgraphs. Noting that partitioning the graph may lead to feature redundancy, as overlapping information across subgraphs can occur. To overcome this, we design a SubGraph Feature Aggregation Module (SGFAM), which mitigates redundancy by averaging node features from different subgraphs. In addition, we propose a SubGraph Distributed Computation (SGDC) method that divides subgraphs into multiple groups and distributes them across different GPUs for feature extraction, thereby reducing the load on any single GPU during the subgraph processing phase. Experiments on four traffic network datasets of various scales demonstrate that SGL can significantly reduce memory overhead, achieving up to a 56.4% reduction in average GPU memory overhead, while maintaining robust prediction performance.

title: A Survey on Tensor-Based Spatiotemporal Data Imputation: Knowledge Engineering Perspectives and Modeling Strategies
abstract: Missing spatiotemporal data is prevalent in domains like traffic forecasting, meteorological analysis, and urban management. Tensor decomposition has emerged as a prominent technique for spatiotemporal data imputation due to its capability to model multi-dimensional interactions. Recent research demonstrates that incorporating structured prior knowledge—such as spatiotemporal correlation, spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and geographical similarity—is key to enhancing imputation performance. However, a systematic framework for integrating these priors with data-driven models remains underdeveloped. To bridge this gap, this survey adopts a knowledge engineering perspective to systematically review strategies for modeling spatiotemporal effects in tensor-based imputation. We propose a taxonomy centered on the mechanisms for representing spatiotemporal effects, which comprises three primary modeling pathways: spatiotemporal correlation, spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and geographical similarity. We further summarize representative methods in terms of their modeling mechanisms, optimization objectives, and algorithmic implementations. Applications and resources across domains like transportation, meteorology, and environmental science are also reviewed. Finally, we discuss challenges and future research directions, focusing on issues such as model generalization, uncertainty quantification, and the integration of causal mechanisms. This survey provides a comprehensive methodological foundation for modeling spatiotemporal knowledge in tensor imputation, laying the theoretical groundwork for developing more generalizable, interpretable, and geographically adaptive intelligent imputation models.

title: A Trust-Aware Data Collection and Inference Framework for Sparse Mobile Crowdsensing
abstract: Sparse Mobile Crowdsensing (SMCS) has emerged as a prominent data engineering paradigm for large-scale, trust-aware environmental data acquisition, enabling diverse data-driven cyber-physical applications. However, the sparsity of the collected sensing data and the presence of untrustworthy workers present key challenges for optimizing data collection and inference accuracy. In particular, malicious workers may submit falsified data, significantly compromising system reliability and the accuracy of data-driven inference. To address these challenges, we propose a Trustworthy Worker Recruitment framework based on Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO-TWR) for trust-aware data collection and inference. The framework evaluates the trustworthiness of workers and leverages high-trust contributions to enhance both data acquisition and inference accuracy in sparse sensing scenarios. The main contributions are threefold: 1) We develop a trust evaluation algorithm that incorporates behavioral scoring to quantitatively evaluate each worker’s reliability and contribution. 2) We design a multi-dimensional trust-aware data collection and inference strategy that jointly optimizes data coverage, inference accuracy, trust evaluation, and acquisition cost. 3) To improve the efficiency of PPO training, an action masking mechanism is introduced to mask invalid actions during training, thereby accelerating policy convergence. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly improves both data quality and inference accuracy while reducing the cost of data acquisition. Compared to baseline methods, our approach achieves a reduction of 22.23%–57.22% in collection cost and a 12.79%–56.45% improvement in inference accuracy, highlighting its effectiveness in trust-sensitive mobile crowdsensing scenarios.

title: Achieving Efficient, Privacy-Preserving and Secure Verifiable Outsourced Database
abstract: A verifiable database (VDB) is a key technology, enabling query users of an outsourced database to verify the correctness and integrity of query results. Although various VDB solutions exist, most fail to achieve data security and query privacy, and are rendered impractical due to low query efficiency. This paper introduces the Merkle-vector matrix commitment (MVMC), which integrates Merkle hash trees with vector commitments to significantly improve verification performance. Building on this, we propose PSVDB, an efficient, privacy-preserving and secure verifiable outsourced database. Specifically, the data owner encrypts the database, generates MVMC-based commitments and proofs, and outsources them to the server, while creating proxy re-encryption keys for query users. During the query, the user sends a homomorphically encrypted query index, and the server performs homomorphic operations on the encrypted database and row Merkle tree to produce encrypted query results and verification proofs. The user then uses the homomorphic key to recover the proof and the encrypted query results, verifies the correctness and integrity of the query results, and decrypts the data via proxy re-encryption. Security analysis demonstrates that PSVDB guarantees both data security and query privacy while enabling verifiable query results. Performance evaluation shows that PSVDB outperforms existing schemes, achieving an online query time of 10.20 s for a $2^{20}$220-entry database and improving query efficiency by $61 \, \times$61× (618.50s), $124 \, \times$124× (1271.37s) and $24889 \, \times$24889× (253871.49 s), respectively.

title: AdaPrompt: Adaptive Prompt Learning to Alleviate Semantic Inconsistency for Conversational Recommendation
abstract: Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) aim to proactively elicit user preferences through natural language conversations. However, CRSs usually face the challenge of semantic inconsistency between the conversation module and recommendation module. Many existing methods strive to leverage prompt learning to unify these two modules, but the prompt templates they designed are still manually created and weakly correlated. To address these issues, we propose a novel paradigm, Adaptive Prompt Learning to Alleviate Semantic Inconsistency for Conversational Recommendation (AdaPrompt), which consists of Adaptive Prompt Learning (APL) and Prompt-Enhanced CRS (PECRS). First, APL focuses on the adaptive learning of both task-agnostic and task-oriented tokens by utilizing knowledge-aware prompt tuning on large-scale Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs). Then, PECRS aims to utilize these two types of tokens to dynamically construct conversation-oriented and recommendation-oriented prompt templates, to proactively elicit the highly-consistent knowledge from the base PLMs to generate responses and predict items, respectively, thereby alleviating semantic inconsistency between both modules. Extensive experiments on four public CRS-based datasets show that our AdaPrompt achieves new state-of-the-art performance and exhibits its superiority of addressing semantic inconsistency in the CRS.

title: Amplification in Locality-Sensitive Hashing for Webshop Product Deduplication
abstract: The aggregation of highly heterogeneous product listings across online webshops suffers from severe scalability limitations and high false positive rates, as identifying duplicates without universal product identifiers typically requires computationally expensive pairwise comparisons. To resolve these specific challenges, this paper introduces two concrete enhancements to Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) within the Multi-component Similarity Method with Pre-selection+ (MSMP+) that significantly improve both overall scalability and duplicate detection precision. First, we substitute the conventional MinHash sketching technique with Fast Similarity Sketching (FSS). FSS provides faster and more precise Jaccard similarity estimates, inherently reducing the time complexity of the initial hashing process. Second, we develop a parametrized amplification strategy leveraging iterative AND/OR operations on LSH functions to substantially minimize both false positive and false negative rates. Crucially, this amplification strategy improves scalability by allowing the algorithm to achieve higher accuracy while using fewer underlying hash functions, thereby directly decreasing the computational overhead of generating candidate pairs. We develop a comprehensive framework for these amplified LSH schemes, deriving optimal parameter configurations by minimizing a weighted error function that balances the trade-off between false positives and false negatives. Empirical evaluations, based on data collected from four webshops, including extensive bootstrap experiments, confirm that combining FSS with amplification consistently outperforms baseline, non-amplified MinHash configurations. To further validate the robustness and generalizability of our approach, we conducted an additional empirical analysis using the established Walmart-Amazon dataset. These supplementary experiments demonstrate that our optimized LSH framework maintains good deduplication precision across different, widely-used product domains. Ultimately, these targeted enhancements enable highly scalable duplicate detection, reflected in improved performance metrics such as pair completeness and pair quality, as well as an increased F1 score.

title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Over Temporal Vector Data
abstract: Unstructured data, such as images and texts, are increasingly represented as high-dimensional vectors for emerging AI applications like retrieval-augmented generation. A key operation in these applications is querying for vectors that are both semantically similar and temporally relevant. This operation can be formulated as Timestamp Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (TANNS), where both the vectors and the query incorporate temporal attributes, aiming to retrieve the approximate nearest neighbors valid at the given timestamp. A naive solution is to create separate indexes for each timestamp, which enables accurate and fast searches but incurs high update latency and excessive storage demands. In this paper, we introduce the timestamp graph, a novel structure that supports rapid index updates while minimizing storage costs. Exploiting the temporal locality of changes in valid vectors, our timestamp graph effectively manages a unified index across all historical timestamps, thereby substantially reducing storage overhead. Moreover, we design the historic neighbor tree, which further compresses the space complexity to that of a single-timestamp index. In addition, we extend the Timestamp Graph and Compressed Timestamp Graph to support Interval Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (IANNS) queries—a generalized form of TANNS queries that specify a time interval and retrieve the nearest vectors valid during that interval. Extensive evaluations on five datasets show that our method achieves over 99% accuracy while improving the query efficiency by 3.3× to 138.1× than existing solutions.

title: C3-Predictor: An Efficient Framework for Performance Prediction of Concurrent Queries
abstract: Query performance prediction is a challenging task in AI-enabled database (DB) research because prediction capability is crucial to optimizing DB operations (e.g., parameter optimization) and resource allocation in modern DB systems. However, existing methods often struggle to meet the flexible requirements for both prediction accuracy and query latency in real-world applications, and focus on predicting the performance of individual queries instead of concurrent queries, which is very universal in large and complex DB tasks. To address these limitations, we propose an efficient prediction model called $C^{3}$C3-Predictor (Concurrency, Cost factor, and Confidence), which integrates a cost factor model into a graph neural network (GNN) model to reduce the latency of prediction with guaranty of accuracy. First, the cost factor is used to achieve the performance prediction of concurrent queries through a concurrent adjustment mechanism. Second, a confidence estimation algorithm is applied to evaluate the cost factor model, while the confidence mechanism evaluates the reliability of initial predictions to determine whether to activate the GNN model. Third, the GNN model is used to calibrate prediction deviations from the cost factor model, which retains only those features that impact the prediction of concurrent queries to construct graphs, and applies the GNN model to predict query performance in an accurate fashion. Extensive experiments are conducted on varying types of workload. The results demonstrate that $C^{3}$C3-Predictor outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) models, that is, for different levels of concurrent queries, $C^{3}$C3-Predictor achieves the lowest prediction error and the lowest prediction latency.

title: CFANet: Channel-Frequency Adaptive Network for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Frequency domain modeling methods have emerged as a promising research direction for long-term series forecasting, owing to their natural advantages in capturing global dependencies and reducing computational complexity. However, existing methods overlook the heterogeneity and dynamic characteristics of frequency properties across different channels. These methods adopt a unified frequency-domain processing strategy and static filtering approaches for all channels, which limits the model’s ability to capture long-term temporal dependencies. To address this issue, this paper proposes a Channel Frequency Adaptive Network (CFANet) for long-term time series forecasting. CFANet designs a dual adaptive mechanism: (i) a channel adaptive mechanism that enables each channel to learn optimal frequency response patterns through channel-specific frequency filters; (ii) a frequency adaptive mechanism that allows filters to dynamically adjust frequency weights through end-to-end learning, thereby adapting to evolving frequency patterns. Unlike existing models with channel-shared and static filtering strategies, CFANet achieves channel-level adaptive enhancement in the frequency domain. In extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets encompassing 72 test scenarios, CFANet achieves optimal performance in 50 scenarios, reducing prediction errors by 9.8% on average compared to state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating consistently superior performance across diverse forecasting tasks. Notably, on heterogeneous datasets where channel spectral characteristics diverge significantly, CFANet delivers 10%–15% error reductions, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed channel frequency adaptive mechanism.
