title: Real-world performance of large-scale propensity score adjustment strategies: matching, weighting, and stratification
abstract: Objective Propensity score (PS) models are commonly used for addressing confounding in observational studies. Researchers are increasingly incorporating large numbers of covariates into PS models, using techniques like large-scale propensity score (LSPS) adjustment. It remains unclear if the inclusion of many covariates affects the subsequent choice of adjustment strategy. Methods In this paper, we evaluate commonly used adjustment strategies using large-scale models, including matching, stratification, and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), to estimate treatment effects under a new-user cohort design. Evaluations employ real-world data across four national healthcare databases and incorporate 3,840 treatment effect estimates per model specification for 24 different treatment cohort comparisons against 160 negative control outcomes. We assess adjustment strategies for covariate balance between treatment cohorts and type-I and type-II error, mean-squared error, and precision of the adjusted effect estimate. Results Across all model specifications, IPTW with symmetric Crump trimming and 1:1 matching perform best overall, achieving strong balance and low type-I error. Additionally, empirical calibration of effect estimates can substantially reduce differences between strategies. Discussion No single strategy is clearly superior in all settings. We recommend incorporating the top-performing strategies at least as sensitivity analyses in studies even if researchers anticipate that some other strategy may excel due to expectation of their study’s operating characteristics. We also recommend use of diagnostics like covariate balance to check strategy performance. Conclusion IPTW with Crump trimming and 1:1 matching are strong default choices for large-scale PS adjustment, but strategy selection should be guided by study context and validated with balance and error diagnostics. We broadly recommend empirical calibration to reduce sensitivity to model choice.

title: Performance of different algorithms in dealing with missing data in the presence of structural bias: a simulation study
abstract: Background Missing data can compromise causal effect estimation by introducing bias, reducing precision, and distorting statistical uncertainty. In addition to complete case analysis (CCA), we evaluated three commonly used imputation methods in R: multiple imputation by chained equations (mice); additive regression, bootstrapping, and predictive mean matching (aregImpute); and single imputation by chained random forests (missRanger). Methods We simulated two datasets under three missing mechanisms: missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and missing not at random mechanisms (MNAR). For each scenario, we generated three missing proportions (10%, 25%, 50%) and four sample sizes ( n = 300, 600, 1200, 5000). We estimated effects using the three imputation methods and CCA. Performance was evaluated using relative bias and root-mean-square error on the log odds-ratio scale, confidence-interval coverage and width, standard-error calibration, and computation time. Results Bias and root mean squared error (RMSE) increased with higher missingness and decreased with larger sample sizes. CCA and mice generally showed lower bias and RMSE than aregImpute and missRanger. aregImpute achieved the highest coverage overall but had wider CIs and higher RMSE. missRanger performed worse than the other methods. Conclusion Although no missing-data handling strategy consistently outperformed others, mice provided more balanced performance across the evaluated scenarios. These findings suggest that researchers should carefully consider bias-variance trade-offs when choosing an imputation strategy when dealing with missing data in the presence of structural bias.

title: Beyond regulatory compliance: strengthening reporting quality and transparency in ClinicalTrials.gov
abstract: Background ClinicalTrials.gov is the world’s largest clinical trial registry and a cornerstone of transparency in research involving human beings. Since its launch in 2000, the registry has undergone several regulatory and technical updates. However, important challenges remain regarding data quality, usability and adherence to international reporting standards. In this article we critically assessed the current content and structure of ClinicalTrials.gov and identified areas where targeted modifications and further developments beyond regulatory requirements could improve reporting quality, transparency, and usability for key stakeholders. Methods We conducted a critical review of the current version of ClinicalTrials.gov. We examined the different sections of the registry in light of relevant meta-research and methodological literature, including the SPIRIT 2025 and CONSORT 2025 statements. We sought to identify limitations in the registry’s content and structure and formulate pragmatic recommendations for improvement. Results We identified six major domains in which ClinicalTrials.gov could be strengthened: (1) study identification data, including a clearer characterisation of the connections between trials and researchers; (2) methodological data, including the creation of new dedicated sections, improved structuring of eligibility criteria and outcome measures, as well as the ability to pre-specify the statistical methods; (3) trial results, through more detailed reporting of participant flow and an explicit description of causes of death; (4) search engine, including the option to search by any eligibility criterion; (5) patient-centred features, through the creation of a specific section explaining what participation in the trial entails; and (6) transparency and quality indicators, summarised in a dashboard presenting key information with visual flags. Conclusions We propose several approaches to improve ClinicalTrials.gov, including structural changes to the way data are captured and to the website interface. These improvements could increase the registry’s utility for patients, researchers and policymakers, thereby strengthening transparency and accountability in clinical research.

title: Structuring evidence in air pollution and cognitive impairment research using a role-analysis framework built on LLM-based entity extraction
abstract: Background Rapid growth in biomedical literature has increased the need for auditable methods that convert article-level text into structured evidence data. Air pollution is increasingly framed as a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline and dementia, but publication growth alone does not indicate a structurally diverse evidence base. We aimed to develop and apply a human-validated large language model (LLM)-assisted role-analysis framework based on structured entity extraction to characterize recent air pollution–cognition evidence. Operationally, role-analysis retains pollutant and cognition-related entities as multi-label fields while assigning a single predominant study-level analytical role to each domain. Methods We conducted an abstract-level evidence-structure analysis of PubMed-indexed human original studies published from 1 January 2020 through 22 March 2026. PubMed formed the primary analytic corpus, and Web of Science was used as a supplementary coverage check. A predefined coding schema was used to extract pollutants, cognitive outcomes, study designs, statistical methods, populations, data sources, geographic settings, and analytical roles from titles and abstracts. LLM-assisted screening, extraction, and role coding were constrained by field definitions, conservative coding rules, and consistency checks. Human validation evaluated screening, extraction, and role-coding outputs. Results Of the 1,061 PubMed records that entered the four-domain eligibility screening, 406 eligible studies were included. In the screening-validation sample ( n = 106), precision was 1.000, recall was 0.881, accuracy was 0.953, F1 score was 0.937, and Cohen’s κ was 0.899. In the structured-extraction and role-coding validation sample ( n = 81), field-level agreement ranged from 0.765 to 1.000; agreement was 0.926 for pollutant roles and 0.901 for cognition roles. The structured evidence dataset showed concentration around particulate matter and gaseous pollutants, older-adult populations, and cognitive outcomes including global cognitive performance, domain-specific cognition, and dementia-related outcomes. Direct pollutant exposure–cognitive outcome analyses dominated the role structure, whereas mediation, effect modification, and alternative role configurations were uncommon. Evidence sparsity reflected overlapping limitations in pollutant characterization, cognitive domain coverage, analytical role diversity, population representation, geographic distribution, and data-source dependence. Conclusions The post-2020 air pollution–cognition literature is volume-rich but structurally uneven. A human-validated LLM-assisted role-analysis framework can convert biomedical abstracts into auditable evidence data that preserve multi-label study entities together with study-level analytical-role summaries and help distinguish growth in study volume from structural diversity of the evidence base.

title: Correction: How have contemporary research studies used social media to recruit to digital self-help intervention research for young people’s mental health?: a mapping review
Investigating the instability of variable selection in Lasso-penalized Cox proportional hazards models: a simulation study on low-dimensional real-world medical data
abstract: Background This study examined the stability of Lasso-penalized Cox proportional hazards models in low-dimensional clinical data. While Lasso is a popular method for simultaneous variable selection and regularization, its performance is known to vary across cross-validation (CV) runs due to random fold assignments. We aim to quantify the effects of the number of folds, stratification procedures, and elastic net mixing parameters on variable selection consistency. Methods We analyzed real-world data from the Berlin Initiative Study in older adults, focusing on a subcohort with measurements of a novel biomarker ( n = 930) and assessing two time-dependent outcomes: all-cause mortality ( n = 882) and a cardiovascular composite endpoint (CE, n = 638). We applied Lasso to identify prognostic variables among 20 medically preselected predictors. In simulation studies, we systematically varied the number of CV folds, implemented stratification by nonproportional covariates, and adjusted the elastic net’s mixing parameter. We evaluated model stability by examining variability in the number of selected predictors and predictive performance via the C-index. Results In our datasets, the number of CV folds substantially influenced model size and selection stability across random seeds, with higher fold numbers generally yielding more consistent results (optimal: 10-fold for mortality, 15 for CE). Stratifying by covariates, which violated the proportional hazards assumption, enhanced stability in some cases. The elastic net did not consistently outperform Lasso in terms of stability or predictive accuracy; mixing parameters below 0.6 led to greater variability. Conclusions The stability of Lasso-penalized Cox models is strongly affected by CV design. Higher fold numbers and appropriate stratification can improve stability, but at a computational cost. Elastic net offers no clear benefit in this setting. These findings highlight how routine modelling choices, including default cross-validation settings, may influence variable selection stability in low-dimensional clinical survival analyses.

title: Exact divide-and-recombine estimation for negative binomial regression: a simulation study and application to SPARCS hospital length-of-stay data
abstract: Background Hospital length of stay (LOS) is a right-skewed count outcome markedly overdispersed relative to the Poisson benchmark, rendering ordinary least-squares and Poisson regression inappropriate at scale. Methods This paper develops a divide-and-recombine (D&R) framework for negative binomial (NB) regression that enables full-data maximum likelihood inference on datasets exceeding available memory by partitioning observations into sequential chunks and accumulating asymptotically lossless compressed representations (ALCRs) at each pass. We prove the resulting estimator is algebraically identical, not merely asymptotically equivalent, to a fully specified centralised alternating Fisher-scoring/IRLS algorithm at every iteration; conditions for recovering the full-data MLE are stated separately, and we derive the dispersion parameter’s pooled asymptotic variance. Results Relative to MASS::glm.nb, active memory falls from O ( n p ) to O ( n S p + p 2 ) per iteration. A Monte Carlo study ( n = 5,000,000, 1,000 replications) confirms agreement with MASS::glm.nb, the empirical reference, to within 1.8 × 10 −10 for the coefficients and 8.0 × 10 −10 for the dispersion, leaving relative efficiency indistinguishable from 1.000. Peak memory falls by 96% and computation time by a factor of 3.75, of which partitioning contributes 2.35 (1.15 of 2.58 on the SPARCS data). A forced 50-iteration trace confirms the identity at every iterate, and the plug-in standard error for the dispersion attains 0.947 coverage in a separate study at n = 200, 000. Supplementary experiments show this exactness holds an order of magnitude below the recommended chunk-size floor and that D&R remains faster than a direct fit from n = 10,000 to 5,000,000. In the 2024 New York SPARCS inpatient discharge dataset ( n = 2,196,737), the estimated dispersion $$\widetilde{\theta }=1.797$$ confirms severe overdispersion (variance-to-mean ratio = 13.4); APR severity dominates, with incidence rate ratios (IRRs) of 4.26, 2.16 and 1.55 for Extreme, Major and Moderate versus Minor admissions. Because discharges cluster within facilities, we report facility-clustered robust standard errors, which inflate model-based errors by a mean factor of 17.8 and move eleven of twenty-nine terms out of nominal significance, while the severity and mortality-risk gradients remain robust. Conclusions These results establish D&R as a principled, interpretable, and computationally tractable foundation for large-scale count regression in health services research.

title: A joint extreme value and mixed copula framework for modeling blood pressure extremes and BMI association
abstract: Background Overweight and hypertension are two critical cardiovascular risk factors, making the relationship between body mass index (BMI) and blood pressure (BP) particularly important for early prevention. Existing approaches that model systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) separately, or reduce BP to a binary hypertension indicator, either ignore their inherent physiological correlation or discard clinically relevant continuous information. Furthermore, reliance on mean-based regression fails to capture the extreme elevations most critical for cardiovascular risk assessment. Methods We propose a framework combining extreme value theory and mixed copula modeling to construct a joint, continuous BP index. Marginal distributions of SBP and DBP were fitted using a Lognormal-Generalized Pareto distribution composite model, and their dependence structure was captured via mixed copulas. The resulting BP index was regressed on BMI using weighted least squares. The framework was applied to 41,451 health examination records from Suzhou, China (2021-2023), stratified by age and sex, with 39,740 from 2011-2013 and 114,096 records from 2016–2018 serving as a temporal reference. Results The Lognormal–Generalized Pareto distribution composite model provided a superior fit to the empirical SBP and DBP distributions compared with single parametric distributions across all age and sex subgroups. Mixed copulas outperformed single copulas in capturing dependence structure in all subgroups. In the most recent 2021–2023 cohort, younger and middle-aged adults exhibited strong upper-tail dependence (indicating substantial co-movement of extreme SBP and DBP), whereas older adults demonstrated a progressive decoupling of the two measurements. Within this same period, BMI was positively associated with the BP index in nearly all subgroups. Across the three study periods, both the dependence structures and BMI coefficients showed heterogeneous and non-monotonic patterns, with significant reductions in the BMI coefficients in 2021–2023 concentrated primarily among several male age groups. Conclusion The proposed framework captures marginal tail behavior and joint SBP–DBP dependence and provides a continuous summary of concurrent BP elevation. The age–sex-specific results revealed heterogeneous dependence structures and BMI associations across demographic groups and study periods. These findings highlight the potential value of incorporating tail and dependence modeling into epidemiological analyses, and future research should validate the framework in independent prospective cohorts.

title: Improved classification of agricultural injuries from free-text analysis of pre-hospital care reports under temporal drift
abstract: Background Agriculture, Forestry, and Fishing occupations have the highest fatality rate of any US sector, yet nonfatal injuries remain poorly captured. Machine learning can identify agricultural injury cases from free-text pre-hospital care records (PCRs), but surveillance systems operate for years, and data distribution shifts with time. We benchmark four classifiers for case detection, show how their accuracy declines under this temporal drift, and evaluate ways to manage it. Methods Using a manually coded dataset of PCRs from Maine, 2008–2022 ( n = 60,010), we benchmarked Naïve Bayes, penalized logistic regression (elastic net), a support vector machine (SVM), and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) under a temporal design (train 2008–2016, test 2018–2022). Discrimination was summarized by AUC (with 95% confidence intervals) and by the false-positive rate needed to capture 90% of cases (FPR*). Drift was quantified with the population stability index. We evaluated three ways to counter it: re-estimating the decision threshold on the most recent labeled year, retraining on all data to date, and fine-tuning the existing model on recent data (transfer learning). Results On stable-period data (2008–2016), XGBoost, elastic net, and SVM performed almost identically (test AUC ≈ 0.94), while Naïve Bayes matched them on discrimination but needed a higher false-positive rate to reach 90% capture. Trained on 2008–2016 and tested on each later year, performance held through 2019, then declined across 2020–2022 as feature distributions shifted and the labeled case fraction rose, the latter driven substantially by how records were selected for labeling. A decision threshold set to the year prior to test year could not hold the 90% target, over-capturing review burden in some years and missing cases in others as the score distribution shifted relative to the carried-over cutoff. Retraining and transfer learning gave only modest recovery, indicating genuine drift on sparse recent data. The three leading classifiers were statistically indistinguishable year to year. Conclusions Temporal drift substantially degrades free-text injury classification and is not fully reversed by retraining on limited recent data. For deployment, pairing a fast-to-retrain classifier with continuous drift monitoring and threshold re-estimation on more recently coded data is more robust than a fixed model and threshold. We propose a practical protocol for detecting and managing drift in surveillance machine learning. Trial registration Not applicable.

title: Pragmatic strategies to improve reach and representativeness in a hybrid type 1 hypertension trial in older adults
abstract: Background Results of clinical trials are often not generalizable as the trial cohort often does not represent older and real-world populations. In a hybrid type 1 effectiveness-implementation study of remote monitoring and management of hypertension, we used pragmatic enrollment and intervention strategies to improve reach and enroll a trial cohort similar to the older primary care clinic population with uncontrolled hypertension. Methods We evaluated whether prespecified pragmatic strategies — including broad inclusion criteria, automated identification, an opt-out approach to initial contact, low study burden, phone-based study visits, and stakeholder engagement — were associated with improved source-population reach and reduced enrollment bias. We performed a cross-sectional analysis of enrollment data from a multicenter randomized controlled hybrid type 1 trial enrolling adults 65 years or older with inadequately controlled hypertension from primary care clinics within two large health systems. We compared characteristics of enrolled patients with those of all eligible primary care patients meeting criteria for guideline directed blood pressure lowering. Results Among 64,671 patients 65 years or older who had primary care visits during the enrollment period, 6,006 were potentially eligible and 1,000 were enrolled and randomized, yielding a source-population reach of 16.7%. Compared with eligible non-enrolled patients, enrolled patients were slightly younger (73 ± 6 vs. 75 ± 7 years) and had a lower prevalence of stroke (5.9% vs. 8.9%). The groups were otherwise similar with respect to sex, Black race, Charlson comorbidity index, diabetes, coronary artery disease, and estimated glomerular filtration rate. Conclusion Logically integrated, prespecified, pragmatic enrollment strategies supported enrollment of a cohort of older adults with hypertension that was similar to the eligible primary care population across key measured characteristics. These strategies may serve as a framework for trials seeking to improve external validation. Trial registration This trial is registered in clinicaltrials.org as “Remote Monitoring and Virtual Collaborative Care for Hypertension Control to Prevent Cognitive Decline Phase II (vCCC 2)” NCT05138601 with a registration date of 12-01-2021. Trial registration NCT5138601.

title: ShapleyHALE: an R package for ordering-free decomposition of health-adjusted life expectancy change with population-level interaction indices, demonstrated using Global Burden of Disease Study data
abstract: Background Conventional decompositions of health‑adjusted life expectancy (HALE) change assume that diseases act independently and produce results that depend on the order in which causes are evaluated. They also cannot quantify whether the combined effect of two causes is larger or smaller than the sum of their separate effects. The Shapley value from cooperative game theory provides an ordering‑free and additive attribution that can quantify population‑level complementarities among causes. Its adoption in population health has been hindered by computational complexity and the absence of reusable software. Methods We developed shapleyHALE , an open‑source R package that performs a complete Shapley decomposition of HALE change. The package treats each disease as a player and averages its marginal contribution over 5,000 randomly sampled cause orderings by default. It yields a unique and additive attribution with no residual. Mortality‑driven and disability‑driven components are separated. Second‑order Shapley interaction indices are computed to quantify pairwise synergies and antagonisms. A parametric bootstrap with 1,000 iterations propagates input data uncertainty to all outputs by default. The package accepts standard age‑cause matrices of mortality and morbidity rates. It is compatible with any population‑based surveillance data. Results We used Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 data for 22 causes across five Socio‑demographic Index (SDI) quintiles over 1990–2023. The decomposition ranked cause contributions, separated mortality from disability effects, and quantified pairwise interactions. Mental disorders appeared among the 10 leading causes in the Low, Middle, and High SDI groups. They were a negative contributor in each group, with values of −0.336 years (95% UIs : −0.482 to −0.252), −0.295 years (−0.440 to −0.213), and −0.342 years (−0.518 to −0.234), respectively. The separation of mortality and disability effects showed that mental disorders and diabetes and kidney diseases contributed negatively primarily through disability. The interaction analysis revealed predominantly positive complementarities among major causes. Mental disorders exhibited systematic antagonism with other major causes in every group where they appeared among the top 10. Conclusions shapleyHALE provides an open‑source and ordering‑free decomposition tool for HALE with population‑level interaction indices. It offers a standardised and reproducible platform to generate evidence for integrated and multi‑disease health strategies in an era of rising multimorbidity. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Matrix tools to identify and evaluate quantitative bias analysis methods for summary-level epidemiologic data
abstract: Background Quantitative bias analysis (QBA) methods can be used to estimate the potential impact of systematic biases on effect estimates from observational studies. However, QBA methods remain underused in applied health research, partly due to difficulties in selecting methods that are suitable for specific study designs. Therefore, we developed structured applicability matrices to help identify and evaluate QBA methods suitable for use with summary-level data across diverse study settings. Methods We identified summary-level data QBA methods through a systematic review of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, and classified each method by bias type: unmeasured confounding, information bias, or selection bias. For each bias type, we developed an applicability matrix that categorized methods as “Applicable”, “Maybe Applicable”, or “Not Applicable”, based on study design, required bias parameters, data format for the exposure, confounder, and outcome, type of effect estimate, output produced, and any stated assumptions or implementation requirements. To demonstrate use of the matrices, we applied them to three published observational studies, each presenting a distinct bias challenge. Results We developed a set of three QBA applicability matrices based on 55 QBA methods for summary-level data (unmeasured confounding [ n = 28], information bias [ n = 21], and selection bias [ n = 6]). Across the three QBA applicability matrices, most methods were classified as “Applicable” for cohort studies ( n = 35) and case-control studies ( n = 40), while only four methods were “Applicable” for meta-analyses of observational studies. QBA methods were consistently classified as “Applicable” for studies with binary exposures ( n = 51) or outcomes ( n = 51). However, fewer methods were “Applicable” for studies with polytomous exposures ( n = 13) or outcomes ( n = 6), as well as continuous exposures ( n = 7) or outcomes ( n = 7). Most QBA methods were classified as “Applicable” for studies reporting risk ratios ( n = 35) or odds ratios ( n = 41); in contrast, only 11 methods were “Applicable” for studies with rate ratios, and 9 methods were “Applicable” for those using hazard ratios for time-to-event outcomes. In the applied examples, the matrices successfully narrowed the set of potentially relevant methods and provided structured guidance for method evaluation and selection. Conclusions The QBA applicability matrices offer a systematic framework for identifying methods suitable for summary-level data across diverse study contexts. By reducing barriers to method selection and implementation, they aim to enhance the rigor of causal inference in observational research. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Estimating hypothetical estimands with time-to-event intercurrent events using controlled direct effect under semi-competing risk framework
abstract: Background Estimating the effect of clinical trials when there are time-to-event intercurrent events (ICEs) is an unresolved methodological issue. Hypothetical strategy is one of the five approaches proposed by the ICH E9 (R1) addendum for handling ICEs, and its estimands align with the controlled direct effect (CDE) in causal mediation. But no current study shows how to estimate the CDE given time-to-event ICEs. This study aims to propose an estimator unifying hypothetical strategy and causal mediation under a semi-competing framework and evaluate its accuracy targeting the hypothetical estimands. Methods The effect of treatment under a hypothetical scenario in which the ICE does not occur was defined as the controlled direct effect (CDE) within a semi-competing risks framework. A generalized Nelson–Aalen estimator was developed, and its performance on the cumulative-hazard, survival, and restricted mean survival time (RMST) scales was evaluated in a structured simulation study based on a cardiovascular trial setting. The hypothetical, treatment-policy, and composite-variable estimators were evaluated, and differences between the treatment-policy or composite-variable estimates and the CDE estimand were summarized as estimand discrepancies. Results In 760 simulation replicates, the proposed estimator showed small bias across the prespecified follow-up times. Relative bias ranged from − 4.54% to 2.83% on the cumulative-hazard scale, from − 5.13% to 1.60% on the survival scale, and from − 8.84% to − 2.79% on the RMST scale. The three estimators closely tracked the true values of their corresponding estimands, with coverage probabilities ranging from 93.42% to 95.79% on the cumulative-hazard scale. The treatment-policy and composite-variable estimands showed different degrees of discrepancy from the CDE estimand over follow-up. In the case study, the three estimand strategies produced different estimates of the contrast in treatment-related death between the ALL and AML groups. Conclusion The proposed estimator showed unbiased estimation for the hypothetical CDE under the simulation settings considered. The treatment-policy and composite-variable strategies produced different degrees of discrepancy for the CDE.

title: Adaptive platform trials: A revolution or a fleeting trend? A review of the strengths and limitations
abstract: Platform trials have gained significant attention in recent years, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, for their potential to deliver efficient and flexible clinical research. Designed to evaluate multiple interventions within a single, ongoing infrastructure, platform trials allow for dynamic trial modifications, such as adding or removing treatment arms. These features offer potential advantages over conventional randomised controlled trials, including resource optimisation, reduced participant numbers, and faster evaluation of new therapies. Despite these potential strengths, the design and implementation of platform trials are associated with several methodological and logistical challenges that may undermine their validity. This review critically evaluates the platform trial methodology, exploring its potential to revolutionise clinical research or serve merely as a transient innovation. We discuss key advantages such as infrastructure reusability, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency in comparative effectiveness research. However, we also highlight significant limitations. These include a frequent lack of blinding, reliance on non-concurrent control groups, and the use of response-adaptive randomisation, all of which may introduce bias, reduce statistical power, and compromise internal validity. Additional issues such as increased ethical and regulatory complexity, underreporting of negative results, and insufficient realisation of theoretical efficiencies further temper the enthusiasm for this design. Evidence from recent systematic reviews reveals that many platform trials do not fully exploit their potential—40% have not added new arms, and only a minority conduct appropriate statistical adjustments for multiple testing. Nevertheless, simulations suggest long-term cost and time savings compared to traditional randomised controlled trials, assuming adequate implementation. We conclude that platform trials are not inherently flawed, although must be designed and conducted with rigorous methodological standards. Their success depends on maintaining core principles of trial integrity—especially reducing the risks of systematic, random, and design errors—while navigating operational and regulatory challenges. Platform trials are likely to become an integral part of the clinical trial landscape, provided they supplement, rather than compromise, the foundations of evidence-based medicine.

title: A unified likelihood approach for progressive multistate frailty models under double censoring: application to retinopathy of prematurity
abstract: Background In multistate survival studies, transition times may exhibit within-subject dependence and be simultaneously subject to left and right censoring. Existing approaches typically address these features separately. The joint analysis of progressive multistate transitions, shared frailty dependence, and double censoring within a unified likelihood framework has received limited attention. This study proposes a parametric progressive multistate survival model that simultaneously accommodates shared frailty and double censoring. Methods Transition intensities are modeled using Weibull distributions. Parameters are estimated via maximum likelihood with log-stabilized numerical integration over the gamma frailty distribution to ensure computational stability. Simulations were conducted under varying sample sizes (100, 200, and 600), frailty variances (0.5, 1, and 1.5), and proportions of left censoring (20%, 40%, and 60%), with performance assessed using bias, root mean square error (RMSE), and coverage probability of 95% confidence intervals. Results Under the simulation settings examined, the proposed model showed reduced bias and improved estimation accuracy and confidence-interval coverage compared with models that ignore frailty and/or left censoring, with gains becoming more pronounced under higher frailty variance and higher left-censoring proportions. Conclusions The proposed framework provides a practical approach for progressive multistate data with correlated transition times and double censoring. The method is illustrated using data on retinal vascular development in premature infants with retinopathy of prematurity, demonstrating its utility for correlated multistate processes in biomedical studies.

title: Optimizing parametric survival model selection: an analysis using constructed individual patient data extracted from oncology trials from 2014 to 2023
abstract: Background Parametric survival models are widely used in oncology for long-term extrapolation of survival data. We aimed to evaluate fitting and extrapolation performance of parametric survival models and to examine correlation between Akaike and Bayesian Information Criteria (AIC/BIC) and extrapolation accuracy. Methods We included oncology trials supporting Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved indications with updated Kaplan-Meier survival curves from 2014 to 2023. Individual patient data (IPD) were reconstructed from survival curves. Standard Parametric Models (SPM), Fractional Polynomials (FP), Restricted Cubic Splines (RCS), Royston-Parmar models (RPM), Generalized Additive Models (GAM), and Parametric Mixture Models (PMM) were evaluated. Goodness-of-fit assessments (extrapolation [GoF-e], a combination of within-sample fit and extrapolation [GoF-fe]) were measured by Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Restricted Mean Survival Time Difference (RMSD) between parametrically extrapolated and updated Kaplan-Meier curves. Models were compared for their performance in both direct goodness-of-fit and relative goodness-of-fit in preserving treatment effect differences between treatment regimens. Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for model comparisons. Subgroup analyses by clinical characteristics, and regression analyses were conducted to verify the robustness of results. Spearman tests were used to assess the correlations between within-sample fit and GoF-e. Results 109 trials providing 346 survival curves were included. AIC and BIC showed no correlations to model extrapolation performance, with Spearman correlations between GoF-f and GoF-e near zero (ρ Conclusions Relying solely on AIC/BIC appears insufficient for reliable extrapolation, especially across different classes of parametric models or flexible parametric models. Less-utilized RPM offers the best extrapolation accuracy, has potential for long-term survival predictions.

title: A pragmatic workflow for handling missing PROM data in registry studies: a methodological scoping review and simulated worked example
abstract: Background Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical quality registries. Registry-based PROM data frequently exhibit structural non-response, including patients who never return PROMs (“never-responders”), and longitudinal attrition, making missing-not-at-random (MNAR) mechanisms plausible. Although MNAR sensitivity methods such as delta adjustment and tipping-point analysis are methodologically well-described, their uptake in registry-PROM practice is unknown. Methods A structured search of PubMed (Nordic-specific terms), PubMed (global terms), Embase and CINAHL was conducted (2018–2024), yielding 425 records. After deduplication and screening, 61 registry-based observational PROM studies with explicit missing-data methods discussion were included as the primary analytic sample (17 Nordic, 44 global). The audit was conducted as a methodological scoping review and reported in accordance with the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A three-step pragmatic workflow is proposed and demonstrated: (1) non-response diagnostics separating never-responders from dropout, with standardized mean differences (SMD); (2) inverse probability weighting (IPW) as a default primary analysis strategy; and (3) MNAR sensitivity via delta adjustment with explicit tipping-point identification and a simple robustness classification. The workflow is demonstrated in a simulated registry-like cohort ( N = 8,000). Results In the primary analytic sample ( n = 61), 24 studies (39%) stated no missing-data strategy. MNAR sensitivity analysis was reported in 18/61 (30%), but formal MNAR models were used in only 5/61 (8%). Critically, tipping-point analysis was not reported in any of the 61 included studies (0%); delta adjustment was reported in only 1/61 (2%). Never-responders were distinguished from dropout in only 17/61 (28%). In the simulated cohort, non-response was substantial and selective. In the primary scenario, the complete-case estimate was 1.21 PROM points (95% CI: 0.69–1.72), the single-stage IPW estimate was 1.22 (95% CI: 0.69–1.74), and the two-stage IPW estimate was 1.23 (95% CI: 0.67–1.79). The tipping point was δ* = 7.2 points (classified as sensitive under the illustrative thresholds). In the secondary scenario, the corresponding tipping point was δ* = 30.5 points (classified as stable). Conclusions Tipping-point analysis was not reported in the accessible methods or supplementary material of any of the 61 included registry-PROM studies; delta adjustment was reported in only one study as a sensitivity check. The five formal MNAR analyses identified used methods that typically require specialist expertise and stronger modeling assumptions than are routinely feasible in many registry settings. A pragmatic workflow using IPW and tipping-point analysis can close this gap without specialist infrastructure.

title: Loss of power by degree of heaping in covariables
abstract: Heaping or digit preference is frequently occurring in health research data as well as in deliberate data masking. We investigate the associated loss of power associated by degree of heaping by simulation and illustrate the effect with a real dataset. Moderate heaping leads to little power loss and may be tolerable. However, heaping in broad categories induces major power loss and should be avoided.

title: Methodological issues relating to case study site selection for a study of emergency department waiting
abstract: This paper examines the purposive selection of case study sites in health services and medical research. It describes different data that can inform case selection, and considers some of the challenges encountered when choosing cases for a study of waiting in English NHS emergency departments (EDs). Case study is a well-established naturalistic research design that can generate a rich, multi-faceted understanding of complex healthcare environments. While the method does not seek to produce statistically predictive results it does aim to produce findings that are transferable to other settings and contexts. The methods literature outlines a number of ways of selecting cases, all broadly purposive, but little practical detail is provided on using data to inform selection. Research papers typically report that purposive sampling was used, and sometimes that ‘maximum variation’, or typical or unique cases were sought. Few reports provide detail about how data or other evidence was used to inform case selection. This paper describes the different kinds of publicly available statistics and information, and local health service data which is available only to researchers, that can inform case selection for a study of a health service or facility. We examine the different understandings these different data provide and discuss the particular challenges these pose when the unit of analysis is an ED. Throughout the paper, we illustrate our arguments by focusing on data available for the area of Luton, England and the ED associated with this area. We hope to address the gap in the methods literature about case study sampling, encourage more discussion of case selection decisions and indicate the particular problems when sampling EDs for case study research.

title: Sequential randomization tests using e-values for clinical trial monitoring across endpoint types
abstract: Background In randomized trials, repeated interim analyses of accumulating data must keep the Type I error controlled. Sequential analyses that use e-values allow continuous assessment of evidence while controlling their own Type I error. We present e-RT, a randomization-based e-value method for continuous trial monitoring, intended mainly as a non-binding ancillary review trigger for data safety monitoring boards, used alongside prespecified primary stopping boundaries. Methods At each update, the endpoint data are reviewed before the current randomized assignment enters the betting-martingale wealth calculation. Under the null hypothesis, the assignment cannot be predicted from the observed data, so the wealth process is a nonnegative martingale and Ville’s inequality controls the monitor’s Type I error at any time. We describe variants for binary, event-only, and continuous endpoints. A charter prespecifies the alert’s role: process-only review, standalone stopping rule, or path to an efficacy stop. We evaluated operating characteristics in simulations against calibrated group-sequential designs matched on sidedness and Type I error, and illustrate the method by reanalyzing two completed mechanical ventilation trials. Results The calibrated one-sided design showed 11.6 percentage points higher power than the design-calibrated binary e-RT variant, although e-RT signaled earlier, at a null crossing rate below the nominal 5%. Under a treatment effect, an e-RT alert occurred before 91.8% of scheduled stops, at a median lead of 776 patients (in the process-only role, an alert that leaves the primary analysis’s Type I error unchanged). Letting every crossing stop the trial raised the null stop rate to 7.2%; a confirmation-bar repair returned it to 5.6% while preserving power, and an alpha-partition repair is bounded by construction at a modest power cost. Conclusions e-RT offers a transparent surveillance method for randomized trials that remains valid at any time, whatever the wager policy, as long as wagers stay predictable. Under a prespecified charter, it can alert data safety monitoring boards to accumulating evidence between scheduled interim analyses. Trial registration Not applicable: this manuscript describes a statistical monitoring method; reanalyses used deidentified completed-trial data from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute biorepository (BioLINCC).

title: Validation of EUCAST 2026 breakpoints for Brucella species using routine laboratory methods: A comprehensive French National Reference Centre study
abstract: by Marie Gaillard, Théo Pastre, Chloé Magnan, Albert Sotto, David O’Callaghan, Anne Keriel, Jean-Philippe Lavigne Brucellosis, caused by various species of the bacterial genus Brucella , represents a significant global health burden in many parts of the world. The European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) recently established standardized clinical breakpoints (version 16.1, 2026) for Brucella to support global surveillance and evidence-based treatment. This study validates EUCAST 2026 breakpoints using routine laboratory methods in a large national reference collection. We retrospectively analyzed 234 Brucella isolates from the French National Reference Centre between January 2017 and June 2026, using MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and multiplex PCR for species identification, and E-test strips and disk diffusion for antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) according to EUCAST guidelines. Brucella melitensis predominated (n = 210, 89.7%), with smaller numbers of B. suis , B. abortus , and B. amazoniensis . Universal susceptibility was observed across all 234 isolates for eight tested antibiotics. Notably, 49.6% of isolates displayed rifampicin minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) within two doubling dilutions of the EUCAST epidemiological cut-off (ECOFF) value, highlighting the need for continued surveillance of rifampicin susceptibility in this genus. A critical methodological finding emerged regarding streptomycin assessment. E-test strips indicated elevated streptomycin MICs in a substantial proportion of isolates, with results consistent across different lots. However, disk diffusion performed on identical isolates demonstrated universal susceptibility for all 234 isolates, with inhibition zone diameters ranging from 21–35 mm. This study validates that EUCAST 2026 breakpoints are clinically appropriate and epidemiologically sound when applied using appropriate routine laboratory methods. Disk diffusion should be considered the reference method for streptomycin susceptibility determination in Brucella species. These findings provide essential practical guidance for clinical microbiology laboratories, demonstrate that France remains free from antimicrobial resistance, and support standardized AST testing for optimized management of human brucellosis in both endemic and non-endemic regions worldwide.

title: From first contact to challenge: Lung immune modulation by single-sex Schistosoma mansoni infections
abstract: by Miriam Bischofsberger, Tim A. Dannenhaus, Sanja U. Schönberger, Emil C. Reisinger, Micha Löbermann, Martina Sombetzki Background Schistosomiasis is a chronic parasitic disease caused by blood flukes of the genus Schistosoma and remains a major public health concern in endemic regions. Following skin penetration, schistosomula migrate through multiple host tissues before maturing into adult worm within the mesenteric vasculature. Immunological priming critically influences host responses during secondary infections, yet the importance of prior single-sex Schistosoma mansoni infection on pulmonary recall immunity remains largely unknown. Since the lungs serve as an important immunological checkpoint during schistosomula migration, we herein investigated how single-sex and bisexual priming influence the pulmonary immune landscape upon reinfection. Methodology Using a murine reinfection model, mice were infected with male, female or mixed-sex S. mansoni cercariae and subsequently challenged with a bisexual infection. Pulmonary immune responses were analyzed by expression of key-regulatory genes, high-dimensional flow cytometry, tSNE/FlowSOM clustering and immune cell phenotyping. Conclusions Single-sex priming resulted in distinct immune responses compared to bisexual infection. Male priming was associated with reduced pulmonary worm burden and a preferential enrichment of circulating CD4 + central and effector memory T cells, whereas female priming promoted the accumulation of CD4 + resident memory T cells together with broader alterations in pulmonary myeloid cell populations. Our findings demonstrate that the sex of primary Schistosoma mansoni infection differently programs pulmonary immune recall responses, particularly through distinct organization of the CD4 + memory T cell compartment. The association between male priming, enrichment of circulating memory T cell subsets and reduced pulmonary worm burden identifies pulmonary memory T cell organization as a potential correlate of protection during reinfection.

title: Occupational brucellosis among livestock farmers in Northeastern Thailand: A cross-sectional study of knowledge, attitudes, and practices from a One Health perspective
abstract: by Savek Kiatsomphob, Karunasinee Suphaphiphat, Bopit Puyati, Kan Kledmanee Brucellosis remains a significant occupational zoonotic disease among livestock farmers, with substantial implications for animal health, worker safety, and public health in endemic regions. Effective control at the livestock-human interface depends on understanding farmers’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding disease prevention. This study aimed to assess determinants of occupational brucellosis prevention behaviors among ruminant farmers in Northeastern Thailand through comprehensive KAP analysis to inform targeted One Health strategies. A cross-sectional survey was conducted from October 2024 to July 2025 across three provinces (Nakhon Ratchasima, Buriram, and Surin) in lower Northeastern Thailand. Structured questionnaires were administered to 385 livestock farmers managing ruminants (beef cattle, dairy cattle, buffalo, goats, or sheep). Knowledge, attitude, and practice domains were scored and analyzed using logistic regression to identify behavioral determinants. Although 65.5% of farmers demonstrated satisfactory knowledge, only 20.0% reported comprehensive favorable preventive practices across personal and farm-level measures. Notably, farmers exhibited selective engagement with prevention: while all avoided raw milk and placental product consumption, only 38.7% used gloves during high-risk activities compared to 61.6% wearing boots. Multivariate analysis identified farm certification, including Good Farm Management as shown by adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR) 2.60 (95% CI: 1.06-6.39), and brucellosis-free certification as shown by aOR 5.35 (95% CI: 1.63–17.54). Awareness of having heard regarding the scientific term “brucellosis” was associated with favorable practices (aOR 2.74, 95% CI: 1.00–7.46). In conclusion, knowledge alone was insufficient to drive consistent preventive behaviors, instead, farm certification, targeted education on transmission routes, and perceived occupational susceptibility emerged as key drivers of practice adoption. Our findings highlight the necessity for integrated interventions combining domain-specific training, formal disease alerts, and structural supports such as certification programs to enhance occupational safety and brucellosis control aligned with One Health principles in Thailand.

title: Integrating MaxEnt and copula models to assess plague-associated ecological suitability under climate change in Northern Tianshan, China
abstract: by Fang Li, Guoyu Zhao, Abulimiti Moming, Xiaobo Liu, Ping Ma, Shang Zhan, Huiqian Wang, Jianhui Chen, Wuliken Tuerdali, Qiguo Wang, Tao Luo, Haiyan Wu, Yujiang Zhang Background Plague, a paradigmatic zoonotic disease, depends on the intricate interplay among ecological environments, climatic conditions, and host-vector-pathogen interactions for its transmission. Climate change is reshaping the ecological distribution and transmission risks of plague. However, a systematic understanding of the future epidemiological trends for the Northern Tianshan Natural Plague Focus in Xinjiang remains limited. Methods By employing an optimized maximum entropy model (MaxEnt) integrated with joint distribution Copula functions, the spatiotemporal dynamics of Marmota baibacina , Yersinia pestis , and plague transmission risk under both current and future climate change scenarios were evaluated. Results The results revealed that the high-suitability habitats for both M. baibacina and Y. pestis within the focus were projected to exhibit trends of contraction and expansion in the future. These patterns could be attributed to the distinct environmental factors shaping their distributions. Specifically, the distribution of M. baibacina was primarily determined by temperature (Bio6 and Bio7) and precipitation (Bio15), whereas the distribution of Y. pestis was predominantly influenced by Bio15 and elevation. The spatial distribution of high-risk areas for plague transmission was projected to undergo dynamic changes, characterized by phases of stability, contraction, and expansion. Furthermore, the centroid of these high-risk regions may shift from Wusu City to Nileke County. Conclusions Under future climate scenarios, the distribution and transmission risk of plague in the focus may be influenced by environmental factors, resulting in scenario- and period-dependent spatial changes. The western region of the focus is anticipated to experience the most pronounced shifts and is projected to remain at elevated risk of epizootic plague.

title: Genomic microdiversity of Mycobacterium africanum in Sénégal
abstract: by A. Ba Diallo, J. Badiane, M. Beye, K. Gueye, S. Cortaredona, S. Lo, M. Drancourt, G. Grine, M. Camara Introduction Mycobacterium africanum is responsible for up to half of tuberculosis cases in West Africa and comprises four sub lineages. Its genomic diversity remains undescribed in Sénégal where M. africanum was first described and where the present study was conducted. Results Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) identified one M. africanum lineage L5 isolate and 50 M. africanum lineage L6 isolates, with a predominance of sub lineage L6.1.1 (24/50, 43.7%) across seven of eight regions of Sénégal. The Dakar region gathered all the sub lineages (L5.3, L6.1, L6.1.1, L6.1.3, L6.2.3, L6.3.1, L6.3.2, L6.3.3, unclassified L6), except for sub lineage L6.2. Further Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) analysis revealed substantial genetic diversity among the lineage L6 isolates with mean value of 668.54 (±239.61), while themedian was 465 SNPs (interquartile range = 400, median absolute deviation:163.09). According to the World health Organization Catalogue of mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and their association with drug resistance, WGS predicted antibiotic resistance in 16 strains. Comparing Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST) and WGS results showed complete concordance across 19 DST tested strains. Conclusion This study highlights the diversity of M. africanum in Sénégal, with intra-lineage genomic variability and predicted antimicrobial resistance. The presence of synonymous mutations in the absence of resistance-associated variants suggests that WGS–based predictions of drug resistance should be interpreted with caution.

title: A new semi-automated, motility-based screening assay for discovery of compounds with activity against the juvenile stage of Fasciola hepatica
abstract: by Alice Bernal, Diana S. Gliga, Giulia Colangeli, Matías Preza, Rossitza N. Irobalieva, Caroline F. Frey, Andrew Hemphill, Britta Lundström-Stadelmann, Natalie Wiedemar Fasciola hepatica is a trematode parasite responsible for fasciolosis, a liver disease that affects humans and livestock worldwide. Together with other food-borne trematode infections, fasciolosis is considered a neglected tropical disease. Further, it imposes substantial agricultural losses due to infections in ruminants. No vaccine is currently available, and control heavily relies on drug treatment, especially with triclabendazole (TCBZ). However, the intensive use of TCBZ over the past four decades has led to increasing rates of treatment failures and the emergence of drug-resistant parasites. Therefore, the identification of new treatment options is an urgent priority. The currently available toolset for drug screening, however, is limited. To address this need, we established a novel, semi-automated, standardized, and objective screening assay based on motility monitoring of newly excysted juveniles using microscopic live imaging. The assay was validated by testing a panel of ten compounds with known anthelmintic properties, amongst them TCBZ (IC 50 : 1.5 µM) and the new activator of the F. hepatica transient receptor potential melastatin (TRPM PZQ ) ion channel, benzamidoquinazolinone (IC 50 : 1.05 µM). In addition to these two compounds with known activity against F. hepatica , three compounds were identified as particularly promising with a fast onset of action and IC 50 values in the nanomolar range: the salicylanilides MMV665807 (IC 50 : 44 nM), niclosamide (IC 50 : 32 nM), and its ethanolamine salt, niclosamide ethanolamine (IC 50 : 9 nM). Complementary live/dead staining revealed that only TCBZ displayed parasiticidal activity, while the other compounds, although leading to parasite paralysis, did not lead to parasite death within 72 hours. Scanning electron microscopy of drug treated parasites did not reveal any significant damage at concentrations corresponding to the IC 50 s, but strong phenotypes were visible at 20 µM. The presented motility assay provides a robust method for the discovery of novel anthelmintic compounds and facilitates the ongoing effort to combat fasciolosis.

title: Contact in context: How land use histories, sociocultural practices, and animal profiles shape human-animal contact and zoonotic pathogen exposure in a fragmented forest of the Democratic Republic of Congo
abstract: by Romain Duda, Victor Narat, Thibaut Langlois, Robert Monfura, Marc Allassonnière Tang, Placide Mbala, Claude Monghiemo, Tamara Giles-Vernick Pathogenic spillovers from animals into humans have catalyzed epidemics throughout history. They result from multiple factors. One such factor, human-animal contact, remains poorly understood. Current studies often neglect variability in human-animal engagements across ecological zones and the broader processes bringing people, animals, and pathogens into engagement. We investigated factors and longer-term processes shaping human-animal contacts and indirectly, potential exposures to zoonotic pathogens in a fragmentated forest. We conducted our mixed-methods investigation in three villages along an ecological gradient of forest fragmentation in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), a hotspot of biodiversity and disease emergence. Twenty-four village participants recorded their daily activities and contacts with animal species over five months. We developed a cluster analysis to categorize classes of animals according to type and frequency of contact and conducted transects to estimate animal species abundance according to village proximity. We then tested the influence of species abundance, human activities, gender, and village on contact frequency. We also undertook ethnographic and ethnohistorical interviews and observations to explore changing human-animal relations. Participants had physical and environmental contact with 61 animal species, which clustered into three classes according to their contact profiles. Relative abundance of animal species was associated with contact frequency, but its effects were weak. Our ethnohistorical and anthropological analyses, however, situated these contacts within their longer-term processes and sociocultural practices that our models could not capture. The animals with which participants had most frequent contact were those whose abundance and accessibility resulted from decades of land use change and hunting intensification. Several abundant species were rarely contacted because local categorizations of animals as ngeyi (“disgusting”) suppressed contacts that proximity alone would have predicted. Human-animal contact profiles are thus historically produced and socioculturally mediated; they cannot be derived exclusively from species ecology, land cover, or demographic variables.

title: Massive envenomations by bees in French Guiana: A ten-year retrospective study (2014–2023)
abstract: by Rémy Blaud, Rémi Mutricy, Florian Negrello, Marie Eeckhout, Loïc Epelboin, Maylis Douine, Hatem Kallel, Alexis Fremery Background Massive bee stings can cause systemic manifestations and life-threatening complications. In French Guiana, data on such envenomations are scarce. This study aimed to describe the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and management of patients presenting to the emergency department. Methods We retrospectively reviewed medical records of all patients admitted for bee stings over the period 2014–2023 at Cayenne Hospital. A composite variable of systemic involvement was created (neurological, respiratory, hemodynamic and digestive). All analyses were descriptive. An exploratory two-graph receiver operating characteristic (TG-ROC) analysis was used to describe the sensitivity and specificity of sting-count cut-offs for four binary indicators of systemic involvement. Results Among 143 patients included, 40% (n = 57) presented at least one systemic manifestation. The median number of stings was 50 [20–150]. In the exploratory TG-ROC analysis, the cut-offs maximizing the Youden index were approximately 72 stings for digestive and hemodynamic manifestations and 99 stings for neurological and respiratory manifestations, with modest sensitivity (0.50–0.76) and specificity (0.68–0.76). Overall mortality was low (0.7%, n = 1/143). Conclusions This study provides the first detailed epidemiological and clinical description of massive bee envenomations in French Guiana. Exploratory analyses suggested that systemic manifestations may occur at sting counts below the conventional 200-sting threshold. These findings should not be interpreted as a validated clinical cutoff and require confirmation in prospective multicenter studies.

title: Vector competence of Aedes albopictus and Culex quinquefasciatus for Oropouche virus
abstract: by Angel Elma I. Abu, Xinyi Hua, Rachel Sattler, Margaret V. Becker, Julia Forato, Shirlene T. S. de Lima, Ingra M. Claro, Gabriel C. Scachetti, Leda M. Simões Mello, Maria Anice M. Sallum, Kenneth S. Plante, Scott C. Weaver, José Luiz Proenca-Modena, William M. de Souza, Laura B. Dickson Oropouche virus (OROV) is an arthropod-borne virus transmitted mainly by Culicoides paraensis midges in Latin America and the Caribbean, though evidence suggests occasional transmission by mosquitoes. Oropouche fever has been reported primarily in the Amazon Basin since the 1950s. In 2024, the number of Oropouche fever cases rose sharply and spread beyond the Amazon region, which has been associated with the emergence of a new reassortant OROV strain. We assessed whether increased case numbers could be explained by enhanced replication or transmission of the reassortant strain in peri-urban Culex quinquefasciatus and Aedes albopictus . Laboratory colonies established from Salvador, Brazil were orally exposed to the ancestral OROV strain BeAn 19991 or the contemporary strain 240023 (10⁴–10⁶ PFU/mL), and viral replication was quantified in bodies, legs, and saliva. To evaluate the influence of mosquito genotype on infection outcomes, infection rates were compared between Ae. albopictus from Salvador City (Brazil) and Houston (USA). In Cx. quinquefasciatus , the outbreak strain replicated less efficiently than the historical strain at low viral doses but not at high infection doses. Regardless of strain or dose, vector competence was extremely low, with only 0–1% of mosquitoes exhibiting infectious OROV particles in their saliva after extrinsic incubation. Conversely, Ae. albopictus showed consistently higher body infection rates for the 240023 strain than for BeAn 19991 at both low and high doses. However, overall transmission potential remained limited: only 0–6.4% of leg or saliva samples were positive across OROV strains and doses. The higher infection rates of the 240023 strain was consistent across both Ae. albopictus genotypes, but infectious saliva was detected only in mosquitoes from the Salvador line (up to 20%) and not in the Houston line (0%). Taken together, this suggests that the recent geographic expansion of OROV is unlikely to be driven by a vector shift from midges to these mosquitoes. Importantly, our findings do indicate higher infectivity of the 240023 strain in Ae. albopictus across different mosquito lines which may have future implications for further adaptation to OROV.

title: Epidemiological, clinical, and diagnostic characteristics of a large-scale upsurge of dengue in the rohingya refugee camps and host communities in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, 2021 to 2024: A retrospective study
abstract: by Charls Erik Halder, Md Abeed Hasan, Emmanuel Roba Soma, James Charles Okello, Md Mostafizur Rahman, Partha Pratim Das, U. Maung Prue, Dickson Wafula Barasa, Md Atiquzzaman, Md Sobuz Hosen, Saddam Hossain Shagar, Elizabeth Yie Chuen Chong, Debashish Paul, S. M. Niaz Mowla, Mohammadul Hoque, Abu Toha MHR Bhuiyan, Md Farhad Hussain Background Dengue emerged as a new public health threat in the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, in 2021 and expanded into large-scale upsurges in subsequent years. Evidence on dengue epidemiology and clinical presentation in protracted refugee settings remains limited, despite the need for stronger outbreak preparedness and case management in these contexts. Objectives To describe the epidemiological, clinical, and diagnostic characteristics of the dengue upsurge among Rohingya refugees and surrounding host communities in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, and to identify predictors of inpatient admission and diagnostic positivity patterns. Methods This retrospective observational study used anonymized surveillance data from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) dengue patient database. Rapid diagnostic test (RDT)–confirmed dengue cases identified across 36 IOM-supported health facilities in Ukhiya and Teknaf between 1 October 2021 and 31 December 2024 were included. Demographic, epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory variables were summarized using descriptive statistics. Weekly case counts were aggregated by epidemiological week and calendar year, and epidemic growth and decay phases were modelled using phase-specific Poisson regression. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with inpatient admission, while separate models examined associations between delay in presentation and RDT positivity patterns, adjusting for age and sex. Results A total of 35,581 RDT-confirmed dengue cases were reported, of which 90.2% occurred among Rohingya refugees. The median age was 17 years (IQR 7–30), and 46.0% of cases were among children aged 0–14 years. Annual caseload increased from 1,011 in 2021–11,752 in 2022, 10,669 in 2023 and 12,149 in 2024, with seasonal peaks during the monsoon period and progressively later peaks and longer epidemic tails over time. Poisson models showed decreasing growth rates across years (r = 0.449 in 2021 to r = 0.091 in 2024) with increasing doubling times, while decay rates remained broadly comparable (halving time ~4.4–6.0 weeks). Overall, 8.0% of cases required inpatient admission, 1.3% were referred, and four deaths were reported (case fatality Conclusion Sustained dengue preparedness is required in Cox’s Bazar, including strengthened surveillance, community-based early referral, targeted monitoring of high-risk groups, environmental vector control, and phase-appropriate use of NS1 and IgM/IgG diagnostics to reduce missed diagnoses and prevent progression to severe disease. These findings highlight the need for a policy shift from episodic outbreak response toward sustained dengue preparedness in humanitarian settings, including strengthened surveillance systems, integrated diagnostic strategies, community-based early referral, and coordinated vector control interventions.

title: Efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolones in the treatment of human brucellosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: by Mohsen Mohammadi-Sartang, Nastaran Rafieipour, Shahla Afrasiabian, Roya Mahmoudi, Yousef Moradi, Medi Karimi, Karo Servatyari Introduction Brucellosis is a major zoonotic infection worldwide, with the highest burden reported in the Mediterranean region. The therapeutic role of fluoroquinolones in this disease continues to be controversial. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens compared with standard non-fluoroquinolone regimens for the treatment of human brucellosis. Methods In accordance with PRISMA recommendations, this systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-based regimens for treating brucellosis. It was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251142019). A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library was carried out, including studies published through August 2025. Randomized controlled trials comparing fluoroquinolones with conventional therapies (such as doxycycline with streptomycin or rifampicin) were included. Therapeutic failure, relapse, adverse events, and time to defervescence were the main outcomes. To compute pooled risk ratios and mean differences with 95%CIs, data were analyzed using STATA v18. The GRADE method and the RoB 2 tool were used to evaluate the risk of bias and the certainty of the evidence. Results The analysis comprised 9 clinical studies with 602 brucellosis patients. When compared to standard regimens, fluoroquinolone-based regimens were linked to a significantly higher risk of therapeutic failure (RR = 2.11, 95% CI: 1.26–3.51; P = 0.004) and a higher, though not statistically significant, risk of relapse (RR = 1.88, 95% CI: 0.94–3.74; P = 0.07). No statistically significant between-study heterogeneity was observed for either outcome (I² = 0%). Subgroup analyses showed a significantly increased risk of therapeutic failure in patients with uncomplicated brucellosis and in studies with treatment durations >8 weeks, although between-subgroup differences were not statistically significant. On the other hand, no statistically significant difference in adverse events was observed between fluoroquinolone-based and standard regimens under the random-effects model (RR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.29–1.33; P = 0.22). Although the point estimate favored fluoroquinolone-based regimens, the confidence interval included the null effect. Fluoroquinolone-based regimens were also associated with a significantly longer time to defervescence compared with standard regimens (MD = 1.20 days, 95% CI: 0.66–1.74; P Conclusion Compared with conventional doxycycline-based combinations, fluoroquinolone-based regimens were associated with a higher risk of therapeutic failure and longer time to defervescence, while the overall risk of relapse did not differ significantly. No significant difference in adverse events was observed with the random-effects model, although the point estimate favored fluoroquinolone-based regimens. Overall, these findings do not support the routine use of fluoroquinolones as first-line therapy for adult brucellosis. Further well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed.

title: Schistosomiasis as an urban disease: 13 years of studies in the neighborhoods of Salvador, BA, Brazil

Blanton Background Rapid urbanization in Brazil has shifted the epidemiological landscape of parasitic diseases, such as schistosomiasis and malaria. Although typically considered a rural infection, Schistosoma mansoni transmission persists in urban settings where sanitation and water access remain uneven. This study investigates the persistence and dynamics of urban schistosomiasis across neighborhoods of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil. Methods Between 2011 and 2024 cross-sectional surveys were conducted to identify neighborhoods with the highest prevalence in the major metropolitan area of Salvador, Bahia. A total of 6,863 residents provided demographic information and Kato-Katz examination of at least one stool sample. We conducted demographic surveys and stool examination on 3,964 individuals who were re-examined on up to three occasions at intervals ranging from 1-5 years. Findings The overall prevalence of initial examination was 7%. Regardless of treatment intervals, the community-wide prevalence declined by more than half and did not rebound. These findings indicate that schistosomiasis transmission in Salvador is largely local rather than imported. The decline in prevalence coincides with observed community-level improvements in sanitation and reduced contact with surface water. f prevalence rates were applied across the population of Salvador, this city could be considered one of the state’s most important endemic areas.

title: Transgenic Plasmodium berghei expressing P. vivax pre-erythrocytic antigens SSP3 and SPECT1 to elucidate their efficacy towards vaccine development
abstract: by Surendra Kumar Kolli, Pradeep Annamalai Subramani, Jai Ramesar, Justin Nicholas, Madison M. Ogbondah, Samantha J. Barnes, Pooya Mahdavi, Ahmed M. Salman, Francis Babila Ntumngia, Chris J. Janse, John H. Adams The development of an efficacious vaccine against Plasmodium vivax malaria remains a top global health priority. P. vivax forms hypnozoites, dormant forms of the parasite in the liver that can become reactivated after a few months or even years, causing relapse malaria and enhancing transmission. Therefore, targeting antigens expressed during the pre-erythrocytic stages offers the potential to prevent clinical malaria from both primary and relapse infections. The circumsporozoite protein (CSP) is the leading pre-erythrocytic vaccine candidate and forms the basis for the current P. falciparum malaria vaccines RTS, S and R21/Matrix M. Studies have shown that in P. vivax , CSP attributes limited protection, highlighting the need to identify additional pre-erythrocytic antigens to improve vaccine efficacy. Evaluation of new candidates often requires human volunteers, making initial screening complex and highlighting the need for robust preclinical models. In this study, we generated transgenic P. berghei parasite lines as research tools to investigate the potential efficacy of two P. vivax pre-erythrocytic vaccine candidates, SSP3 and SPECT1. The chimeric Pb-Pv SSP3 and Pb-Pv SPECT1 lines showed normal development throughout the parasite life cycle, in both mice and mosquitoes. Antisera raised against recombinant Pv SSP3 and Pv SPECT1 using TitreMax Gold adjuvant exhibited reduction in sporozoite invasion of hepatocytes in vitro , with mean inhibitions of 27% and 14%, respectively. In vivo sporozoite challenge studies showed sterile protection in 10% of mice immunized with r Pv SPECT1, whereas r Pv SSP3 provided no detectable protection. Although substantial protection was not observed for either antigen under the conditions tested, the transgenic P. berghei lines generated in this study serve as useful platforms for evaluating the efficacy of these antigens as vaccine candidates across different delivery systems and adjuvanted formulations.

title: Cost-effectiveness of end-game strategies against sleeping sickness across the Democratic Republic of Congo
abstract: by Marina Antillon, Ching-I Huang, Samuel A. Sutherland, Ronald E. Crump, Paul E. Brown, Paul R. Bessell, Emily H. Crowley, Rian Snijders, Andrew Hope, Iñaki Tirados, Sophie Dunkley, Paul Verle, Junior Lebuki, Chansy Shampa, Erick Mwamba Miaka, Fabrizio Tediosi, Kat S. Rock Background Gambiense human African trypanosomiasis (gHAT) is marked for elimination of transmission (EoT) by 2030. We examined the cost-effectiveness (CE) of EoT in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the country with the highest burden. Methods In 165 health zones (HZs), we modelled the transmission dynamics, health outcomes, and economic costs of six strategies during 2026–40, including cessation activities once reported cases reach zero. Uncertainty in CE was assessed within the net monetary framework, presenting optimal strategies across willingness-to-pay (WTP) values, in costs per disability-adjusted life-year averted. We assessed the optimal strategy for CE and EoT in each health zone separately, but present results by health zone, by coordination, and for the whole country. Results Status quo strategies, CE strategies (WTP = $500), and strategies with a high probability of EoT by 2030 are predicted to yield EoT by 2030 in 118 HZs, 123 HZs, and 134 HZs respectively, at a cost by 2040 of $67.8M [95% PI: $36.7M–113M], $93.3M [95% PI: $51.6M–153M], $185M [95% PI: $111M–309M]. A more lenient timeline of EoT by 2040 would lead to EoT in 152 HZs at a cost of $158M [95% PI: $91.6-265M], leaving 13 HZs shy of the goal. Costs would have to be front-loaded; in 2026, while status quo strategies would cost $8.75M [95% PI: $7.01M–11.2M], elimination strategies would cost $27.0 [95% PI: $21.0M–35.2M]. Investing in EoT by 2030 is predicted to reduce 68% of gHAT deaths from 7979 [95% PI: 770–27,868] with status quo strategies to 2576 [95% PI: 255–9133]. Conclusions Current tools could make considerable progress to maximise the probability of EoT by 2030, but novel tools could help in select health zones are facing a low probability of EoT even with more ambitious strategies.
