title: The impacts of host community composition, clustering and vector host choice on zoonotic mosquito-borne virus transmission
abstract: by Jennifer S. Lord, Michael B. Bonsall, Tijani A. Sulaimon Zoonotic mosquito-borne viruses, including West Nile, Rift Valley fever and Japanese encephalitis viruses, present a substantial public health burden in some countries, with transmission involving complex interactions between multiple vector and host species, making control difficult. While host community composition is known to affect transmission, the role of host community structure coupled with mosquito aggregation behaviour remains poorly understood. Motivated by furthering understanding of potential Japanese encephalitis virus transmission routes and persistence in contexts where cattle – dead-end hosts – are dominant in the community, we developed a patch model in which host distributions and the resulting mosquito biting allocation among patches are fixed within each simulation. This framework represents mosquito host-seeking across two scales: long-range aggregation toward host-dense patches and short-range host species choice determined by local host availability and innate vector preference. Using this model, assuming that vectors prefer dead-end hosts (choosing them 90% of the time if given an equal choice of other hosts), we explored the potential effect of host clustering, patch fragmentation, and the strength of mosquito aggregation on the basic reproduction number. Our results show that identical host communities can yield very different transmission outcomes depending on how they are distributed and the level of mosquito aggregation. Under circumstances where dead-end hosts are preferred by vectors, if competent hosts are clustered and mosquitoes aggregate strongly, transmission may be amplified compared with uniformly distributed hosts and vectors. If dead-end hosts are clustered, transmission may be diluted as mosquitoes aggregate in patches where dead-end hosts are dominant in the host community. Fragmentation effects are context-dependent: when competent hosts are clustered and mosquitoes aggregate, increasing patches increases transmission. When dead-end hosts are clustered, transmission decreases under strong mosquito aggregation with increasing number of patches. These findings highlight that variations in the local spatial context of host-vector interactions can lead to variations in disease risk. Locally-informed surveillance and targeted interventions may therefore be important in attempts to prevent outbreaks of zoonotic mosquito-borne viruses.

title: “I will not accept to bury my pig”: Taenia solium, WASH, and gender roles in the smallholder pork value chain in Southern Province, Rwanda
abstract: by Janna M. Schurer, Ruth Zihiga Uwase, Prince Rwagasore, Kristen Rodrigues, Anselme Shyaka, Tayechalem Moges Taenia solium is a zoonotic cestode and the causative agent of human taeniasis/cysticercosis and porcine cysticercosis. The burden in Rwanda is significant, including death and disability in people and income losses across the pork sector. Despite widespread recognition on the need for multi-sectoral and inclusive T. solium control programming, little is known about water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) access and gendered disease exposure among rural smallholders involved in the formal and informal pork sectors. This study aimed to characterize gender roles and WASH access in the Nyamagabe District (Southern Province) pork value chain (PVC) to better inform future interventions for disrupting T. solium transmission. We conducted Focus Group Discussions with 23 men and 21 women across five nodes of the PVC (farmers, animal health workers, butchers, vendors, consumers) and interviewed six key informants. Audio-recordings were transcribed verbatim, translated into English and coded as part of inductive thematic analysis. PVC participants identified numerous biosecurity gaps in the Nyamagabe PVC, such as free-range pig production, re-use of human waste, lack of prevention services (deworming, vaccination), informal slaughter, and consumption of infected and/or undercooked pork. Traditional gender roles were prevalent, with women managing domestic roles related to pig husbandry and men managing roles related to building pens, buying/selling pigs and slaughtering/butchering. Water and sanitation facilities were frequently inadequate, causing serious lapses in human and pig hygiene. Participants identified poverty as a major barrier for implementing T. solium control but demonstrated enthusiasm for receiving information and resources to support this goal. Altogether, these findings support the need for One Health programming to reduce the burden of T. solium and other zoonotic diseases in people and pigs in Rwanda. Gendered norms among rural smallholders indicated a need for gender transformative information campaigns targeting specific recipients along the PVC nodes.

title: Evaluating the cost of self-care: Impact of enhanced morbidity management protocol on people living with lymphatic filariasis in Bangladesh
abstract: by Tijana Williams, Mohammad Jahirul Karim, Samid Siddiqui, AKM Fazlur Rahman, Salim Chowdhury, Sharmin Jahan, Sultan Mahmood AMS, Shaun P. Forbes, Hannah Betts, Mark J. Taylor, Louise A. Kelly-Hope Background Lymphatic filariasis (LF) causes chronic lymphoedema requiring long-term self-care, often at personal cost. In post-elimination settings such as Bangladesh, understanding the financial burden of self-care is critical for sustaining morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP). This study evaluated self-care costs and the impact of an enhanced morbidity management protocol among people affected by filarial lymphoedema in Bangladesh. Methodology A longitudinal cohort study was conducted in Lalmonirhat and Thakurgaon districts (2020–2021). People affected by mild, moderate, and severe lymphoedema (n = 290) were assessed at baseline, trained in an enhanced self-care protocol, and assessed at a 3-month follow-up and a final follow-up conducted at 6 months in Lalmonirhat and 9 months in Thakurgaon. Data were collected on clinical characteristics (lymphoedema stage, acute attacks, pain), self-care items (soap, cream, pain relief), related costs, and adherence. Results At baseline, participants with mild (11.2–54.7%), moderate (21.9–39.5%), and severe (23.4–49.3%) lymphoedema were included, reflecting variation across districts. Acute attacks were reported by 62.8–79.6% of participants and severe pain by 40.6–54.6%. Following the intervention, acute attacks decreased to 25.2–35.2% and severe pain to 22.4–28.0% (p Conclusions Enhanced self-care training was associated with reductions in reported acute attacks and pain and changes in spending towards preventive self-care practices but did not eliminate the ongoing financial burden of lymphoedema, particularly for individuals with severe disease. Exploratory adjusted analyses supported the descriptive findings, indicating that expenditure was influenced by follow-up time, district and disease severity. Sustainable MMDP programmes should prioritise equitable access to essential self-care supplies to reduce out-of-pocket costs and support long-term adherence.

title: The growing repertoire of putative pathogen interaction genes in the Biomphalaria glabrata vs Schistosoma mansoni system
abstract: by Javier Calvelo, Stephanie R. Bollmann, Jacob A. Tennessen, Michael S. Blouin Schistosomiasis is major neglected tropical disease of humans that is caused by trematodes in the genus Schistosoma . Humans are infected during contact with water in which schistosomes are being shed from their intermediate hosts, freshwater snails. Snail control is effective at reducing transmission, but can be expensive and ecologically problematic. Therefore, there is substantial interest in understanding the genetic mechanisms behind variation in snail resistance to infection by schistosomes, with the goal of leveraging that information to reduce transmission at the snail stage. Biomphalaria glabrata is an important host snail for transmission of S. mansoni in the New World. Here we reanalyzed an older Genome-Wide Association Study (GWAS) dataset from Biomphalaria glabrata snails challenged by the trematode, Schistosoma mansoni . We identified two new regions of association with resistance to infection, named LG5R and LG11L. LG11L contains a cluster of genes for a diverse set of secreted lectins, which could be involved in some type of recognition. LG5R contains a cluster of genes for what appear to be membrane-bound receptors. These genes are very similar to those identified in an adjacent genomic region by a recent GWAS on the African snail, B. sudanica challenged by S. mansoni . Clusters of genes for single-pass transmembrane proteins also characterize two other genomic regions of association with resistance to S. mansoni that were previously described for B. glabrata (the PTC1/GRC and PTC2 regions). We hypothesize that the proteins coded for in such clusters of genes are involved in some type of matching polymorphism that may explain the ubiquitous parasite-population by snail-population interaction in compatibility that characterizes the B. glabrata-S. mansoni system. We discuss our results in light of the state of the field of genome-wide mapping studies on Biomphalaria sp. , and discuss what types of loci found to date would be the best targets for reducing transmission in natural populations.

title: Cross-sectional study on the association between seroprevalence among children and their parents’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices in a dengue-endemic city in Bangladesh
abstract: by Claudia Ximena Robayo Gonzalez, Bouchra Nasri, Marie-Catherine Gagnon-Dufresne, Avijit Saha, Laura Pierce, Mushfiqur Rahman, John Barnard Mackfield, Yang Zhang, Mrittika Barua, Md. Mizanur Rahman, Malay Kanti Mridha, Valéry Ridde, Kate Zinszer Introduction Bangladesh is experiencing a drastic increase in dengue infections since 2019, with a record number of cases exceeding 300,000 in 2023 and 102,082 cases in 2025. Control of dengue, spread by Aedes mosquitoes, requires an in-depth understanding of knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding prevention strategies and their association with the risk of infection. This association has been rarely examined in adults and even more rarely in relation to the risk of infection in children. This study aimed to investigate the association between parents’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) and children’s dengue seropositivity in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Methodology A cross-sectional study was conducted in four neighborhoods of Dhaka in November and December 2023. A total of 297 parents and 412 children aged 2–12 years participated in the study. Parents completed a questionnaire that collected data on their previous dengue experiences, sociodemographic characteristics, social capital, and knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) related to dengue. Children’s capillary blood samples were collected via finger prick and tested for IgM and IgG dengue antibodies. The relative risk (RR) of dengue seropositivity was estimated using a modified Poisson regression model with robust error variance. Results The median ages of the parents and children were 32.5 and 6.7 years, respectively. The adjusted seroprevalence of dengue for both IgM and IgG in children was 14.0% (95% CI 10% -19%). Parents’ KAP scores were classified as intermediate knowledge of the disease in 60.3% of participants; 64.3% reported positive attitudes towards dengue control and prevention actions; and 62.0% had a high score for dengue prevention practices. A higher parent attitude score was associated with lower child seropositivity (aRR 0.77, 95% CI 0.60-0.99). Conclusions These findings provide preliminary insight into the factors associated with dengue seropositivity in children in Dhaka, offering additional information about parents’ attitudes towards dengue risk and prevention and the relationship with child’s seropositivity. This information can guide public health interventions, such as dengue control campaigns. A more in-depth exploration of the context will help to understand the cultural and social factors that shape KAP in Dhaka.

title: Temporal trends in reported vector-borne diseases in China before and after the onset of COVID-19 from 2004 to 2023
abstract: by Zhiqun Lei, Qianying Liu, Zhixin Lei Background Vector-borne diseases (VBDs) continue to pose a public health burden in China. However, changes in the reported incidence and mortality of VBDs during the COVID-19 period remain insufficiently characterized. Methods We analyzed five major VBDs—typhus, dengue, leishmaniasis, malaria, and epidemic encephalitis B (EEB)—in China from 2004 to 2023. Province- and age-specific surveillance data for 2004–2020 were obtained from the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, whereas national aggregate data for 2021–2023 were obtained from the National Health Commission. Accordingly, spatial and age-specific analyses were restricted to 2004–2020, while national trend analyses were extended through 2023. Annual trends were evaluated using Joinpoint regression, monthly seasonal patterns were assessed using STL decomposition, monthly changes after January 2020 were evaluated using interrupted time-series analysis, and expected monthly trajectories for 2020–2023 were estimated using SARIMA models trained on pre-COVID data. Results From 2004 to 2020, incidence and mortality of VBDs declined significantly, especially for malaria, dengue, and EEB, and spatial hotspots were concentrated mainly in southern provinces. Compared with 2013–2019, overall incidence and mortality during 2020–2023 were 59.86% lower (95% CI: –60.36 to –59.36; P Conclusions During the COVID-19 period in China, reported VBD incidence and mortality decreased substantially. However, it would be overly simplistic to attribute these changes entirely to COVID-19-related interventions, as other factors were also likely involved. These findings highlight the need for reliable surveillance and reporting during public health emergencies, together with forecasting tools that can be adapted to changing conditions, to support future vector-borne disease control.

title: Direct and indirect entomological efficacy of Targeted Indoor Residual Spraying against Aedes aegypti in Iquitos, Peru
abstract: by Helvio Astete, Gissella M. Vasquez, Victor M. López-Sifuentes, Beyquer Zambrano, Becker Reyna, Ryan C. Moore, Amy C. Morrison, Gonzalo M. Vazquez-Prokopec, Ryan T. Larson Background Control of Aedes aegypti , the primary vector of dengue and other Aedes -borne viruses, is challenged by insecticide resistance, limited efficacy of existing tools, and that control activities often occur in the context of large dengue epidemics that overwhelm control programs. Targeted Indoor Residual Spraying (TIRS), a modification of traditional indoor residual spraying focused on Ae. aegypti resting sites, has demonstrated promising results, yet its indirect community-wide effects remain underexplored. Methodology/principal findings We conducted an entomological cluster-randomized controlled trial in Iquitos, Peru, to evaluate the direct and indirect entomological impacts of TIRS using pirimiphos-methyl. Thirty clusters were randomized to receive either TIRS (15 clusters, 898 structures) or standard Ministry of Health vector control activities (15 clusters, 1,018 structures). Aedes aegypti indoor densities were assessed in the 45 days pre-intervention and at four time points up to 255 days post-intervention using Prokopack aspiration. Generalized linear mixed models with a negative binomial link were used to estimate incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and calculate efficacy (1–IRR) for houses that received TIRS (direct effect) and untreated houses in TIRS clusters (indirect effect). Direct efficacy reached a 96% decrease in Ae. aegypti captured in sprayed houses at 15 days post-spraying and remained significant (40%) at 255 days post-spraying. Indirect efficacy reached 69% at 15 days and declined to 7% by 255 days post-spraying. Despite only 57% household-level TIRS coverage, both direct and indirect impacts on Ae. aegypti were significant during early post-intervention surveys, and after 8 months in TIRS clusters. Conclusions/significance TIRS provided substantial and sustained reductions in indoor Ae. aegypti density, including measurable indirect effects in untreated homes within intervention clusters. These findings demonstrate the entomological value of TIRS even at moderate coverage levels and highlight its potential for both preventive and reactive vector control programs and should be considered for implementation by Ministries of Health in dengue-endemic urban settings as well as by the U.S. military when deployed to tropical or subtropical locations.

title: Bacterial immune priming and Wolbachia -mediated dengue blocking in Aedes albopictus mosquitoes
abstract: by Abdullah A. Alomar, Dongmin Kim, Barry W. Alto, Eric P. Caragata Background Wolbachia is a maternally-transmitted bacterial endosymbiont that is highly prevalent amongst arthropods. Many Wolbachia strains induce pathogen blocking, thereby protecting their hosts from pathogenic microbial infections. Blocking against pathogenic bacteria occurs in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, where Wolbachia has been artificially established by microinjection. However, in Drosophila fruit flies, it occurs after oral bacterial challenge but not after systemic challenge via injection. Pathogen blocking has been linked to increased host immune activity associated with Wolbachia infection. This is similar in principle to immune priming, a memory immune response in insects, where sub-lethal exposure to a pathogen increases the ability to survive future infections. Aedes albopictus mosquitoes naturally harbor Wolbachia ; however, the extent to which native Wolbachia -mediated pathogen blocking and immune priming influence host response to infection remains unclear. Accordingly, we sought to characterize the response of Wolbachia -infected Ae. albopictus to bacterial challenge, and to determine whether the combination of these microbes could hinder a subsequent infection with dengue virus (DENV). Methodology/principal findings We challenged adult female Ae. albopictus with and without their native Wolbachia infection with a sub-lethal dose of four mosquito-associated bacteria: Micrococcus, Staphylococcus (gram positive), Brevundimonas , Enterobacter (gram negative). Assessing post-challenge mortality, we observed that Wolbachia infection reduced cumulative mortality and delayed the onset of senescence amongst mosquitoes challenged with each bacterium. However, this protective effect was stronger against gram positive bacteria. Bacteria-primed Ae. albopictus were then orally challenged with DENV. We observed that mosquitoes that experienced a pre-challenge with gram negative bacteria were associated with reduced DENV prevalence and viral load, whereas Wolbachia -infected mosquitoes exhibited further reductions in viral load. Conclusions/significance We highlight novel characteristics of native Wolbachia infection in Ae. albopictus mosquitoes, with protection against bacterial-induced mortality, and interactions between pathogen blocking and bacterial priming that may depend on bacterial gram status. These findings provide insight into the immune interactions associated with native Wolbachia and build on our understanding of adaptive immunity in mosquitoes.

title: Immune-mediated remodelling of tissue architecture in Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL)
abstract: by Deep Goswami, Shriya Saha, Madhurima Roy, Ebrahim Mohammad, Ratnaprabha Maji, Ritika Sengupta, Shilpa Sengupta, Sutopa Roy, Surya Jyati Chaudhuri, Nilay Kanti Das, Bidhan Chakraborty, Uttara Chatterjee, Mitali Chatterjee Background Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL), a dermal sequel of apparently cured visceral leishmaniasis (VL), presents with macular or polymorphic lesions. A relationship, if any, between immune cell infiltration and cytokines potentially causing tissue-remodelling remains poorly defined, and was the focus of this study. Methodology/principal findings Skin biopsies along with plasma from PKDL patients and healthy controls were analyzed. Tissue sections were assessed for immune cell subsets (CD8 ⁺ T cells, CD68 ⁺ macrophages, CD20 ⁺ B cells, CD66b⁺ neutrophils), associated cytokines/chemokines, adhesion molecules (E-cadherin, Intercellular Adhesion Molecule-1), extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins (fibronectin, collagen I/IV, laminin), matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) using immuno-histochemistry/fluorescence, while circulating cytokines/chemokines, and MMP9 were quantified using multiplex assays/ELISA. PKDL lesions exhibited increased cell infiltration, monocytes/macrophages>CD8 ⁺ T cells>> neutrophils >B cells. E-cadherin was significantly downregulated, especially in macular lesions, whereas ICAM-1 was elevated. In both PKDL forms, ECM components were significantly reduced, and correlated inversely with immune cell infiltration. The raised levels of circulating chemokines (CCL2, CCL3, CCL4, CCL5, CXCL9, CXCL10, IL-8) positively correlated with their corresponding immune populations; additionally, circulating pro- (TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-1β) inflammatory cytokines and IL-4 was elevated. Additionally, lesional TNF-α, IFN-γ and MMP9 was elevated, and correlated inversely with E-cadherin and ECM proteins. Conclusions/significance In PKDL lesions, there was an elevated presence of monocytes-macrophages/CD8 + T cells, B cells and neutrophils; the increased presence of their respective chemokines endorsed their homing to lesional sites. Furthermore, the increased presence of dermal MMP9, TNF-α and IFN-γ possibly facilitated the breakdown of E-cadherin and ECM components, which could cause a site-specific loss of melanocytes, and contribute to the hypopigmentation associated with PKDL.

title: Disclosing pathogenic processes of monkeypox (MPOX) and drug repurposing through host-transcriptomics analysis
abstract: by Sabkat Mahmud, Alvira Ajadee, Md. Ahad Ali, Md. Feroj Ahmed, Reaz Ahmmed, Md. Masud Rana, Tasfia Noor, Md. Fahim Faysal, Md. Hadiul Kabir, Md. Nurul Haque Mollah Monkeypox (MPOX) virus infection outbreak in Africa in 2022 was initially considered a neglected tropical disease (NTD). Now it is recognized as a global health problem. The recent global spread has emphasized the need for increased attention to combat MPOX. Although there are some vaccines against MPOX, most people worldwide are still not vaccinated due to their unawareness or unavailability. However, so far, there is no approved drug against MPOX yet. Therefore, effective drugs against MPOX are also essential. This study attempted to disclose pathogenic processes and therapeutic strategies of MPOX based on MPOX-associated host key-genes (hKGs). At first, three transcriptomic profile datasets were analyzed, identifying 166 common host differentially expressed genes (hDEGs) between MPOX patients and control groups, comprising 75 upregulated and 91 downregulated hDEGs. Subsequently, six top-ranked host key genes (hKGs): ALB, HSP90AA1, CDH1, PTPRC, IGF1, and ABL1, were identified as potential MPOX-causing genes through protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis. Functional enrichment analysis of these hKGs revealed critical pathogenic processes of MPOX infection, including biological processes, molecular functions, cellular components, and KEGG pathways. Regulatory network analysis involving transcription factors and miRNAs provided further insights into disease mechanisms. Based on molecular docking analysis, five top-ranked drug molecules Tecovirimat, Beclabuvir, Maraviroc, Raltegravir, and Brincidofovir were identified as potential repurposable therapeutics against MPOX. ADME/T and drug-likeness evaluations confirmed favorable pharmacokinetic properties for these candidates. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the top three complexes (ALB-Tecovirimat, CDH1-Maraviroc, and PPARG-Beclabuvir) demonstrated strong binding stability, supported by RMSD, RMSF, and MM-GBSA results. Therefore, the results provided in this study might be potential resources for diagnosis and therapies of MPOX patients. However, the findings require experimental validation in wet lab for further confirmation.

title: The RLR-MAVS-IRF3 axis activates the IFN pathway to restrict Tonate virus infection
abstract: by Thomas Labadie, Roger Eloiflin, Zoé Denis, Marie Motos, Joanna Re, Moritz Schüssler, Morgane Chemarin, Isabelle Moltini-Conclois, Valérie Courgnaud, Dorothée Missé, Nadine Laguette, Karim Majzoub Tonate virus (TONV) is a neglected mosquito-borne alphavirus of the Venezuelan equine encephalitis complex associated with febrile illness, encephalitis, and fetal central nervous system abnormalities. Yet, host pathways that sense TONV infection and restrict its replication remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated the interaction between TONV and the type I interferon (IFN-I) system in human T98G and A549 cells. We show that TONV infection led to the accumulation of cytosolic double-stranded RNA and a robust IFN response. RIG-I and MDA5 depletion as well as that of MAVS and IRF3 strongly reduced TONV-induced IFN response. Disruption of RIG-I, MDA5, MAVS, or IRF3 resulted in an increase of dsRNA-positive cells and a higher viral RNA accumulation. Finally, we found that treatment with exogenous IFN-I strongly inhibits TONV replication, reducing both viral RNA loads and infectious particle production. Thus, together, our results identify the RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS-IRF3 axis as a major pathway sensing TONV infection and establishing an IFN-I-dependent antiviral state, providing the first molecular characterization of TONV innate immune sensing in human cells.

title: Barriers to biomedical care: Qualitative insights into health-seeking behaviors and systemic challenges among people affected by leprosy in Tanzanian communities
abstract: by Sylivester Asimwe Muhigi, Kijakazi Mashoto, Mercy Chiduo Background Delayed diagnosis in leprosy reflects both how people interpret symptoms and seek care, and how effectively health systems recognize and manage the disease. Qualitative evidence from Tanzania remains limited on how the interaction between patients and health care workers affect provision of care to people affected by leprosy in a timely manner. The main aim of this study was to explore health-seeking behaviors and systemic challenges affecting access to biomedical care among people affected by leprosy in selected Tanzanian communities. Methods Ethics Statement: Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the Medical Research Coordinating Committee (MRCC) through the National Health Research Ethics Committee (NatHREC) with reference number NIMR/HQ/R.8a/Vol.IX/4587. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before data collection. Identifying information was removed from transcripts, data were anonymized before analysis, and audio files and transcripts were stored on password-protected computers accessible only to the data manager and the principal investigator. Data will be retained for up to 10 years per NIMR policy. An anonymized coding framework and de-identified extracts are available upon reasonable request. Given the sensitive nature of gender-based violence disclosures, referral procedures were established to ensure that participants requiring additional support could be linked to appropriate services This qualitative study was conducted in Tanga and Morogoro regions, Tanzania. Semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions were held with people affected by leprosy, community members, District Tuberculosis and Leprosy Coordinators, Community Health Workers, and Prevention of Disability officers. Data were audio-recorded, transcribed, translated into English, and analyzed thematically. Results Our findings revealed various factors which contributed to delays in seeking for biomedical care among people affected with leprosy. First, early symptoms were often normalized or attributed to witchcraft and curses, prompting initial care from traditional healers. Second, stigma, fear of rejection, and advice from relatives and community members delayed disclosure and transition to biomedical care. Third, health-system barriers including misdiagnosis, limited provider familiarity with leprosy, referral delays, medicine shortages, and inadequate support for disability management delayed confirmation of diagnosis and initiation of appropriate treatment. Conclusion Health-seeking behaviors among people affected by leprosy were shaped by stigma, social influence, and health-system barriers that delayed or limited access to biomedical care. Evidence-based interventions, including culturally sensitive education, stigma reduction, and strengthening of frontline biomedical services, can help overcome these barriers. Policy efforts should prioritize biomedical care alongside community-based awareness to reduce stigma and promote timely care-seeking.

title: Zika virus serologic responses during pregnancy in a dengue-endemic setting: A prospective cohort study in Thailand
abstract: by Salin Sirinam, Dennopporn Sudjai, Supawat Chatchen, Watcharee Arunsodsai, Weerawan Hattasingh, Laura Pezzi, Thomas Jaenisch, May Chu, Thitiya Yakasaem, Kriengsak Limkittikul Background Zika virus (ZIKV) infection during pregnancy has been associated with adverse birth outcomes, including severe neurological abnormalities. Confirmation of infection remains challenging due to the disease’s predominantly asymptomatic or mild nature. While real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) is the gold standard, its use in clinical settings and surveillance is limited. Serological point-of-care tests offer alternatives but pose interpretation challenges in Flavivirus-endemic regions. Methods and Findings We conducted a prospective cohort of 199 pregnant women attending the antenatal clinic at Rajavithi Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand, in 2021–2022 to describe the incidence of ZIKV serologic responses detected by a rapid test and associated pregnancy outcomes. Participants were monitored using the DPP ZCD IgM/IgG (Zika/Chikungunya/Dengue IgM/IgG) System rapid immunochromatography test (Chembio), with RT-qPCR and plaque reduction neutralization testing performed for further assessment. A ZIKV serologic response was defined as a reactive ZIKV immunoglobulin M (IgM) result at enrollment or seroconversion from non-reactive to reactive ZIKV IgM or IgG between study visits. The DPP ZCD rapid test revealed incident ZIKV-reactive serologic responses at 15.4 per 100 person-years, with all affected participants being asymptomatic. All RT-qPCR results were negative, and participants with ZIKV IgG seroconversion had neutralizing antibodies against ZIKV and all 4 Dengue virus (DENV) serotypes. A prior history of DENV infection was associated with increased odds of ZIKV-reactive serologic response (OR 3.53, P value 0.046). Conclusion This prospective study identified serologic responses detected by a ZIKV-reactive rapid test among pregnant women in Thailand. In a highly dengue-immune setting, these responses could reflect true ZIKV exposure, DENV reinfection, flavivirus immune boosting, or serologic cross-reactivity, and therefore cannot be attributed specifically to ZIKV. Rapid serologic testing may support screening and surveillance but cannot establish ZIKV infection or ZIKV-specific exposure without careful interpretation and additional testing.
