title: An improved hybrid ANFIS-BA model for accurate water quality prediction
abstract: The industrialization and modernization process has increased water pollution, significantly affecting aquatic ecosystems and increasing the demand for reliable water quality prediction tools. This study proposes a hybrid model integrating Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) and the Bees Algorithm (BA), referred to as ANFIS-BA, for accurate Water Quality Index (WQI) prediction. In the proposed framework, the Bees Algorithm is employed to optimize the premise parameters of ANFIS. To further enhance the search capability, a dual-perturbation strategy is introduced, in which uniform noise is incorporated to strengthen global exploration while Gaussian noise refines local exploitation. This strategy improves population diversity, mitigates premature convergence, and enhances optimization stability. To further assess practical applicability, the model was evaluated under two input configurations: five water quality parameters and a reduced set of three parameters. The second scenario was designed to investigate whether reliable prediction accuracy can be maintained with fewer monitoring variables, thereby reducing data acquisition costs and improving real-world feasibility. The proposed model was evaluated using a publicly available water quality dataset from India. All models were trained and validated using 5-fold cross-validation. The results demonstrate that the proposed ANFIS-BA achieves outstanding performance in both scenarios. With five input attributes, the model obtained MAE = 0.1311, RMSE = 0.1727, and R² = 99.98%. When reduced to three inputs, the performance remained highly competitive with MAE = 0.8919, RMSE = 1.2078, and R² = 99.55%, indicating strong generalization capability under reduced information conditions. Compared with other advanced machine learning models, the proposed ANFIS-BA demonstrated superiority and achieved state-of-the-art results with a higher R² than existing studies. In addition, the model provides interpretability regarding the influence of water quality factors on WQI. Overall, the proposed framework offers both methodological innovation and practical significance, providing an accurate, stable, and interpretable decision-support tool for sustainable water quality management.

title: Lightweight detection and classification of RISC-V hardware exploits using machine learning techniques
abstract: This work proposes a hardware-assisted malware detection framework leveraging the HARPY-V-GEM5 dataset for RISC-V architectures. Using the GEM5 full-system simulator, we collect microarchitectural telemetry, specifically Hardware Performance Counters (HPC) and committed instruction mnemonics–from a balanced corpus of 32 benign and malicious applications. Unlike previous approaches relying on complex deep learning models or synthetic data augmentation, we employ a rigorous undersampling strategy to create a balanced dataset of 12,890 execution samples per program, collected at a fine-grained interval of 10,000 instructions. We evaluate supervised learning algorithms, demonstrating that Random Forest (RF) and Decision Tree (DT) classifiers achieve superior efficacy compared to Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Naive Bayes. The results show detection accuracies above 99.5% when using HPC features and 99.0% when using instruction-level features. We further evaluate zero-day resilience, showing that generalization to unseen programs is strongly attack-dependent: while some families remain reliably detectable, others exhibit very low detection rates. These findings indicate that the proposed lightweight models provide partial and selective zero-day robustness, rather than uniform generalization across all attack types.

title: Evaluating Arabic embeddings in retrieval-augmented generation: a comprehensive multi-LLM study with advanced re-ranking strategies
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become an effective approach for improving factual question answering, yet its design remains insufficiently understood for Arabic, particularly in specialized domains requiring both linguistic precision and domain expertise. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of Arabic RAG architectures for Maliki Islamic jurisprudence, investigating the interaction between retrieval components and downstream language models. A total of 198 RAG configurations, combining 11 embedding models, 6 neural re-ranking strategies, and 3 large language models (Allam-7B, Fanar-9B, and Llama3-8B), were evaluated on a benchmark of 140 expert-curated multiple-choice questions. The best configuration, combining CAMeLBERT, a lightweight Arabic neural re-ranker, and Allam-7B, achieved 89.29% accuracy, substantially outperforming standalone generation. Paired statistical analyses (Cochran’s Q, McNemar’s test, and Holm–Bonferroni correction) further show that the benefit of retrieval refinement varies substantially across generators: it is largest for the multilingual model, more modest for one Arabic-specialized model, and smallest for another Arabic-specialized model with comparable standalone accuracy, indicating that intrinsic Arabic competence alone does not fully determine how much a generator benefits from retrieval. To explain these results, two domain experts independently assessed 800 retrieval instances, evaluating retrieval relevance, retrieval sufficiency, and error attribution. The qualitative analysis confirms that Arabic-specific retrieval provides more relevant supporting evidence and reveals that residual errors increasingly reflect generation-stage limitations, rather than retrieval quality, as retrieval improves. These findings motivate the concept of Capacity–Retrieval Alignment, which characterizes retrieval effectiveness as emerging from the interaction between retrieval quality, generator capacity, and the generator’s capacity to utilize retrieved evidence, providing a principled framework for designing Arabic retrieval-augmented systems.

title: FairJEn: media bias analysis using ensemble learning approach for fair journalism
abstract: Recently public opinion is mostly shaped or modified by the media and digital social platforms. The presence of increasing media bias deviates the users from the original and objective information. This fosters a skewed perception, underscoring the importance of transparency in media. Addressing this, we propose a system that detects and mitigates media bias using Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques. Our ensemble model for analysing media bias to provide fair and transparent news journalism (FairJEn), combining RoBERTa, Bi-LSTM, with XGBoost meta-classifier, achieved superior performance with 77.5% accuracy and a Macro Average F1 score of 0.705. To mitigate identified biases, we employed Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) for bias identification and BERT-based contextual replacements for content refinement. This approach maintained high semantic similarity score of 0.9997 with minimal semantic shift of 0.0047. This ensures the integrity of the original content. A news recommendation system leveraging Siamese Networks was developed to diversify the content exposure. Transitioning from cluster-based recommendations to a dataset-wide approach improved bias coverage and diversity, with the score of 0.6 and 1.52 respectively. Our proposed ensemble technique for bias detection and mitigation enhances the usage of media consumption with balanced content delivery.

title: Decentralized federated learning over noisy labels: a majority voting method
abstract: This paper introduces majority voting based decentralized federated learning (DFLMV), a general DFL framework for learning from noisy data without relying on any assumptions about local client noise models while maintaining data privacy for all clients. In contrast to conventional majority voting methods that are based on voting on data, a critical novelty of the proposed voting mechanism is to vote on models. Specifically, (1) Clients first perform traditional DFL training on their original local datasets for a predetermined number of communication rounds. (2) Clients use each of their neighbors’ models to make a prediction of every data point in their training datasets, then correct the labels based on majority voting. (3) Clients further fine-tune their models based on their updated training dataset. Theoretically we are able to prove that such a vote-on-model method has the benefit of always being able to improve model accuracy after the voting under any noisy label rate, while the conventional voting-on-data methods do not. Extensive experiments conducted on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-10N, CIFAR-100N, Clothing1M, and ANIMAL-10N validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach at various noise levels and different data settings in mitigating the adverse effects of noisy labels.

title: Attention–guided cross-representation distillation for Alzheimer’s stage identification employing MRI scans
abstract: This paper presents an attention–guided cross-representation distillation framework for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) stage identification employing MRI, targeting the discrimination of subtle and spatially distributed anatomical variations across: axial (A x ), coronal (C r ), and sagittal (S g ) views. Existing attention-based approaches often struggle to capture subtle anatomical changes occurring in critical brain regions, such as hippocampal atrophy, ventricular enlargement, and cortical thinning, which are key indicators of AD progression. In addition, many approaches rely on either global or local attention representations, limiting their ability to jointly capture long-range anatomical dependencies and subtle region-specific abnormalities that characterize AD progression. Hence, an attention–guided cross-representation distillation framework integrating Vision Transformer (ViT) and Swin Transformer (SWT) is proposed to capture global and local representations, respectively. The framework employs a novel gated dual-teacher single-student architecture in which interfusion attention fusion (IFA) forms the teacher network, while a lightweight ViT-Lite serves as the student model trained through an online response-based distillation mechanism. This process enables the student to replicate the teacher’s spatial attention patterns and learn discriminative anatomical cues essential for accurate AD stage identification. Experimental validation was conducted on two benchmark datasets, ADNI and AIBL, achieving classification accuracies of up to 98.8%. Further, Grad-CAM visualizations with an Attention Consistency Score (ACS) of up to 96% demonstrate effective spatial reasoning transfer, while Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) yield Intersection over Union (IoU) scores of up to 0.61 and Dice similarity coefficients of up to 0.72, confirming strong agreement in the anatomically relevant regions emphasized by both the teacher and student networks. In addition, Bland–Altman analysis verifies strong probabilistic agreement between teacher and student predictions. Finally, ablation and comparative studies confirm the robustness of the proposed framework, highlighting its ability to achieve both high predictive performance and clinically meaningful interpretability.

title: LLM-driven automated rule generation for heterogeneous power grid data governance
abstract: With advances in the Internet of Things, multi-source power grid data have been collected for operational optimization. The nature of power grids is changing due to renewable energy, distributed generation, and changing demand patterns. Conventional management techniques are not able to keep up, and adaptive systems are required to manage multiple data types and quickly react to changes. In this paper, we propose an LLM-based framework for automating data governance in power grids, leveraging the strengths of Large Language Models (LLMs), Knowledge Graphs (KGs), and Reinforcement Learning (RL). The LLM processes unstructured regulations and generates executable SQL constraints. The KG creates a domain ontology representing equipment, parameters, and compliance rules within a single semantic network, connecting data across modalities. The RL agent then sweeps through this rule space using a reward system that assigns a punishment to deviations observed in the records and adjusts the threshold until convergence. Results on real-world grid data demonstrate 91.2% accuracy for the generated rules and a 3.2x speedup compared to manual rule creation. The approach provides a scalable approach to automated data management in sustainable energy infrastructure.

title: Detecting noisy labels using checkpoint ensembles
abstract: We are concerned with the problem of identifying samples with noisy labels in a given dataset. Using the predictions of well-generalizing models to flag incorrectly predicted labels as noisy is a known method, but it is generally not considered competitive. At the same time, it has been observed recently that gradient descent fits clean samples first, and the noisy samples are memorized later. Inspired by related theoretical results, we revisit the idea of using the predictions of well-generalizing model checkpoints during training to classify samples as noisy or clean. We offer two key improvements that allow this strikingly simple approach to outperform some well-known methods. Our first method, ES-Prediction, classifies a sample as noisy if the model checkpoint predicts its label incorrectly. Our second method, ES-BGSS, is based on the observation that the sum of the per-sample gradients of the loss with respect to the feature layer bias parameters tends to be negative for clean samples and positive for noisy ones. Both methods are applied to an ensemble of model checkpoints collected around the early stopping point of a standard training run, which reduces the variance of the predictions and improves detection accuracy. Both methods operate in-sample, meaning they evaluate each checkpoint on its own training set and directly exploit the clean priority learning phenomenon. Our approaches only passively observe a normal training run and collect checkpoints. No extra input samples are added, and no pretrained models are used. Through empirical evaluations, we demonstrate that our methods are competitive with other approaches from related work for both detecting noisy samples and for noise-filtered training.

title: Enhancing clinical trust in brain tumor MRI: a meta-analysis of AI classification, segmentation, and explainability
abstract: Accurate detection of brain tumors using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial for improving patient outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), now enables rapid and precise analysis of MRI scans, transforming the landscape of neuro-oncology diagnosis. Despite their outstanding performance, many AI models operate as “black boxes”, providing predictions without interpretable reasoning, which limits clinical trust and regulatory approval. Recent advances in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) have aimed to bridge this gap by making algorithmic decisions more understandable to clinicians. However, there remains limited systematic evidence quantifying both the diagnostic performance and transparency of AI-based brain tumor MRI models. This study presents a systematic review and meta-analysis of artificial intelligence models for brain tumor analysis using MRI. Rather than proposing a new predictive model, the work synthesizes existing studies to evaluate diagnostic performance, explainability, and transparency practices in current AI-based approaches. It addresses the critical challenge of integrating diagnostic accuracy with interpretability, which is essential for clinical deployment. A structured literature search framework was developed using predefined databases, search terms, eligibility criteria, and research questions, providing a transparent and reproducible approach that may support future evidence synthesis studies in medical artificial intelligence. The study systematically evaluates the influence of model architecture, dataset variation, and explainability techniques on performance outcomes, while also highlighting reproducibility gaps caused by insufficient code-sharing and lack of uncertainty quantification. A meta-analysis of 39 studies revealed a pooled classification accuracy of 96.8% and a segmentation Dice coefficient of 0.877, with convolutional neural network (CNN) and hybrid models achieving approximately 98.5% accuracy. Although the adoption of explainability techniques has increased since 2022, transparency remains limited; only 32% of studies shared code and fewer than 5% incorporated uncertainty estimation. These findings demonstrate that while AI models already approach expert-level performance, their successful clinical integration depends on advancing explainable, transparent, and reproducible frameworks. By aligning diagnostic innovation with ethical and regulatory standards, explainable AI has the potential to strengthen medical trust and enable safer, more accountable clinical decision-making systems.

title: A domain-aware explainable AI framework for multi-class intrusion detection with cybersecurity-oriented semantic interpretation
abstract: This study presents a domain-aware Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework for multi-class network intrusion detection that integrates SHAP-based feature attribution with cybersecurity-oriented semantic interpretation. The framework explicitly separates predictive modeling, SHAP attribution, and semantic-layer evaluation. Its semantic layer combines dataset-specific feature-to-concept mappings with multi-condition rules derived from training data, pruned using internal validation data, and frozen before testing; rule activations lacking local SHAP evidence are explicitly quantified as unsupported. The framework was evaluated on UNSW-NB15 and CIC-IDS2017 under balanced and natural class distributions using Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Extra Trees, and Gated Recurrent Unit models. Random Forest achieved the strongest predictive performance and was selected as the reference model following complete pairwise McNemar comparisons using two-sided exact-binomial p-values and Holm correction. SHAP attribution was assessed separately through five-seed ranking stability and seed-42 feature-masking fidelity. The semantic layer was directly audited on reproducible stratified subsets of held-out natural-distribution records across five independently seeded Random Forest models. The audit retained 67 rules for UNSW-NB15 and 86 for CIC-IDS2017, of which 60 and 83 were activated, respectively. Record-level semantic coverage reached 87.39% and 85.39%; macro-class rule precision reached 0.529 and 0.885, and weighted rule lift reached 4.006 and 7.155, respectively. SHAP-supported rule–instance activations achieved mean pairwise Jaccard similarities of 0.989 ± 0.002 and 0.921 ± 0.041, while mean unsupported-statement rates were 1.06% and 6.40%. Ablation and permutation-based negative-control analyses showed that the frozen rules carried class-discriminative information beyond randomized rule labels and that stricter SHAP-evidence requirements improved rule-instance precision at the cost of reduced statement coverage. Threshold-crossing perturbations mechanically deactivated all audited rule activations but were not interpreted causally. Once local SHAP values were available, complete evidence-bounded semantic postprocessing required approximately 0.016–0.027 ms per audited record under the evaluated conditions, whereas SHAP generation dominated the measured explanation latency. These findings provide direct technical evidence concerning semantic coverage, class-discriminative value, attribution support, component contribution, and repeated-seed reproducibility across the two benchmarks. Analyst usability, trust, and operational effectiveness require future human-centered evaluation.

title: Detecting efficiency based on machine learning and neural networks approaches in DEA involving big data
abstract: Traditional data envelopment analysis (DEA) methods face computational complexity and growing calculation time when dealing with big data, particularly when the number of decision-making units (DMUs) is very large or when the input-output space is high-dimensional. To address this challenge, this study integrates machine learning techniques—specifically artificial neural networks (ANN), genetic algorithm neural networks (GANN), and particle swarm optimization neural networks (PSO-ANN)—into the DEA framework for efficient DMU classification. The proposed models are evaluated on two datasets, and their performance is assessed in terms of computational time, mean squared error (MSE), accuracy metrics, and misclassification rate. In addition, the effects of different network configurations, including the activation function and the number of hidden neurons, are investigated. The results show that the standard ANN exhibits stronger generalization and more reliable classification performance than the hybrid GANN and PSO-ANN models. In particular, ANN provides a better balance between computational efficiency and frontier preservation, making it a promising surrogate for large-scale DEA evaluation.

title: Robust zero watermarking of color medical images using enhanced VGG19, DCT, and cyclic chaos
abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) requires the safe transfer of sensitive medical images to ensure patient privacy and data integrity. In this paper, a deep learning-based zero-watermarking scheme for color medical images is proposed by integrating VGG19-based feature extraction, the discrete cosine transform (DCT), and cyclic chaos encryption. High-frequency DCT components are omitted, and a zero-watermark is generated by combining the generated binarized features with a scrambled binary watermark using an exclusive OR operation, without modifying the original image. The generated copyright verification key is further safeguarded with cyclic chaos encryption. Extensive studies show that the proposed technique is highly resistant to geometric distortions and common image-processing attacks, while remaining computationally efficient for IoMT systems. Extensive experiments have been conducted, and the results demonstrate high robustness to geometric distortions and common image-processing attacks while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for IoMT systems.

title: A lightweight multi-scale attention-driven YOLO V11 for accurate student behavior recognition in smart classroom environments
abstract: This study proposes an efficient and accurate student behavior recognition framework for smart classroom environments, addressing challenges such as small object scales, posture similarity, occlusion, dense multi-student scenarios, and the trade-off between detection accuracy and real-time performance. A lightweight multi-scale attention-driven YOLOv11 architecture is developed, integrating three key modules: Cross-Stage Partial Multi-Feature Attention (CSP-MFA) for directional multi-scale feature aggregation and enhanced sensitivity to small behaviors, a Feature Enhancement Module (FEM) for discriminative feature refinement and background suppression, and a Multi-Head Contextual Attention (MHCA) module for modeling long-range spatial dependencies among students. The proposed model is evaluated on the SCB-12 dataset using standard object detection metrics, including Precision, Recall, mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, and F1-score. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance, achieving 75.650% Precision, 79.158% Recall, 78.314% mAP@0.5, and an F1-score of 0.77, outperforming conventional two-stage detectors and lightweight YOLO variants. The model shows improved robustness in small-object detection and fine-grained behavior classification under dense and occluded classroom conditions. Although the architecture introduces moderate computational overhead compared to ultra-lightweight models, it provides a favorable balance between accuracy and efficiency. The proposed framework offers a novel integration of directional multi-scale fusion, discriminative feature enhancement, and contextual attention modeling within a unified YOLO-based architecture, demonstrating its potential for practical smart classroom deployment.

title: SteRGAN: An Improvised Framework based on Generative Adversarial Network for Image Steganography
abstract: Image steganography is the practice of concealing data within cover images, thereby enhancing confidentiality and protection of information. Nevertheless, traditional methods frequently have issues with low payload capacity, poor imperceptibility, or susceptibility to attacks. In this paper, SteRGAN, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) based framework is proposed for accurate and visually consistent image steganography. The proposed SteRGAN comprises of Embedder and Extractor modules, each of which contains a generator and discriminator. Further, a deep network named RCBNet is proposed as a discriminator in the Embedder module, which improves embedding capacity. The network employs residual connections and dilated convolutions to enhance feature extraction and preserve fine-grained visual details, thereby enabling the generation of high-quality stego-images with minimal perceptual distortion. The model is trained with composite loss function enhancing the visual imperceptibility. SteRGAN achieves superior Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) while retaining accuracy and reconstruction quality, as demonstrated by experimental evaluations conducted on the ImageNet and Microsoft COCO datasets. On the ImageNet dataset, the SteRGAN achieves a PSNR value of 42.50 dB and SSIM value of 0.992 on the cover-stego image pair and a PSNR value of 42.50 dB and SSIM value of 0.989 on the secret-recovery image pair. In contrast, the SteRGAN yields a PSNR value of 42.34 dB and SSIM value of 0.979 on the cover-stego image pair and a PSNR of 41.99 and SSIM of 0.991 on the secret-recovery image pair on MS COCO dataset. These outcomes validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework with the existing steganography methods.

title: A novel AF-CBA framework for accurate and interpretable EEG cognitive state classification
abstract: Accurate and interpretable classification of cognitive states from electroencephalography (EEG) signals represents an important area of research in cognitive neuroscience, adaptive learning systems, and intelligent human–machine interfaces. Conventional EEG-based classification methods rely on fixed-threshold and accuracy-driven optimization, resulting in unstable decision boundaries and higher misclassification costs under cognitively ambiguous conditions. Moreover, several machine learning classifiers often have similar baseline accuracy, making it difficult to determine which model is most reliable and cost-effective. To overcome these constraints, the proposed work introduces a novel Adaptive Fuzzy–Cost Benefit Analysis (AF–CBA) framework that integrates fuzzy inference and cost-sensitive adaptive threshold optimization for EEG cognitive state classification. Emotional resilience and thinking ability are modeled as cognitive indicators using fuzzy inference to provide a transparent and structured decision-making layer. The resultant cognitive load features are then applied to the machine learning algorithms such as Decision Tree (J48), Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Naive Bayes to evaluate their classification performance. The baseline experimental results show classification accuracy ranging from 80.21% to 96.85%, with a small performance gap among the SVM, RF and J48 classifiers. Thus, to increase the reliability of decision-making, the proposed AF-CBA framework uses cost-sensitive optimization, stochastic correction-based stabilization, and adaptive threshold refinement to reduce false classifications and increase decision stability. Experimental results show that the proposed AF-CBA framework significantly improves classification performance and reduces misclassification cost compared with baseline classification approaches. The optimized J48 classifier achieved the highest classification accuracy of 99.95% among the classifiers evaluated. The proposed framework is interpretable, adaptive, and cost-effective for EEG-based cognitive load classification. It has high potential for intelligent cognitive monitoring, adaptive neurocognitive systems and real-time human-centred AI applications.

title: COSMOS: continuous subspace manifold operating system learning as gauge dynamics on the Grassmannian
abstract: This work presents an operational study of COSMOS, a structured geometric learning framework that formulates neural network training as the evolution of representation subspaces rather than the optimization of Euclidean weights. In COSMOS, the learnable content is a unified global state composed of orthonormal bases and Grassmann projectors. Learning proceeds through a single global conjugation-based update that evolves these Grassmann frames, forward computation is carried out by a gradient-free arrangement of projections onto the learned subspaces, and supervised classification is read out through a geodesic-margin Class Manifold Region criterion based on principal angles to class anchor subspaces. Across controlled experiments on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10, geometric integrity holds at machine precision independent of the retraction schedule. Parameter-matched baselines locate the flat input interface below a two-layer MLP (76.30 vs 88.28 test accuracy on Fashion-MNIST), while a patchwise input interface reaches statistical parity with the MLP on both datasets (88.21 vs 88.28 on Fashion-MNIST; 51.62 vs 52.09 on CIFAR-10) and lies above per-frame Riemannian SGD (66.25). The blockwise conjugation update lets the geometric core scale: a per-block update costs 3.8 ms at $$n = 4096$$, against roughly $$4\times 10^{3}$$ s for a dense matrix exponential. The information-dilution mechanism in deep sequential arrangements is measured directly: the flow ratio and the class-manifold margin both vanish in the collapsed deep chains. These results span two small-scale, vector-input image-classification benchmarks evaluated with CPU-scale models; the design positions COSMOS as a controlled benchmark for geometric consistency in subspace-based learning, rather than as a general framework for geometric neural architectures.

title: Multi-resolution speckle priors for scale-aware and simultaneous probabilistic digital image correlation
abstract: Digital Image Correlation (DIC) models are directed by texture-awareness means and the guidance signal loses crucial, fine-grained detail in the process when naively downsampled to modulate the abrasive, semantic feature maps in the encoder’s deeper layers. While current state-of-the-art models like RAFT achieve high precision through iterative refinement, they, in addition, undergo significant computational latency, limiting their efficacy in real-time industrial monitoring. The proposed model makes use of a five-level U-Net backbone joined with a hierarchical decoder that creates four-channel displacement and uncertainty priors across three resolution scales (1/4, 1/2, and full scale), ensuring that the expansive path obtains geometrically founded signals to do away with the need for recurrent loops. Experimental validation on a structured dataset of 36,000 reference-deformed images shows that the proposed method offers a highly optimized accuracy-latency tradeoff. DNet-MRSP achieves a mean End-Point Error (EPE) of $$0.00302 \pm 0.00050\text { px}$$, exceeding baseline designs such as Deep DIC $$\text {(EPE} = 1.97721\text { px)}$$ and unconstrained optical flow models like RAFT-DIC ($$\text {EPE} = 4.42217\text { px}$$). The framework has a rapid feed-forward execution latency of $$2.23 \pm 1.70\text { ms}$$, which results in an operational processing throughput of 448.3 frames per second. This profile offers a slight latency trade-off with traditional Deep DIC ($$1.75\text { ms}$$) that is totally justified by a significant leap in sub-pixel tracking accuracy.

title: Adaptive state-space modeling of EEG dynamics for real-time sleep spindle detection
abstract: Sleep spindles are transient sigma-band (11–16 Hz) oscillations that reflect thalamocortical coordination during non-rapid eye movement sleep and are widely used as biomarkers of sleep stability and cognitive processing. Automatic spindle detection remains challenging because scalp EEG recordings exhibit low signal-to-noise ratio, marked nonstationarity, and pronounced inter-subject variability. In this study, spindle detection is formulated as a state-space inference problem rather than a purely event-centric classification task. We propose an innovation-driven adaptive Kalman filtering (AKF) detector based on a low-dimensional kinematic state model of sigma-band amplitude. The main decision variable is an exponentially weighted innovation-variance proxy, which provides an interpretable and causal measure of local model mismatch. In addition to the proposed AKF configuration, we evaluate covariance-matching, Sage–Husa, normalized innovation squared (NIS), and dual adaptive Kalman filtering variants within the same experimental framework. Experiments on six full-night C3–M2 EEG recordings demonstrate that the proposed AKF method produces stable duration-constrained catalogues of spindle-like sigma events, while covariance matching, Sage–Husa adaptation, and dual adaptive Kalman filtering provide informative responsiveness–conservativeness contrasts within the same recursive framework. A strict normalized-innovation-squared (NIS) configuration was also examined, but it suppressed all accepted events under the chosen consistency and duration constraints and is therefore discussed qualitatively rather than retained as a zero-valued comparison table. Rather than positioning the method as a replacement for modern learning-based detectors, we present it as an interpretable, uncertainty-aware, and low-latency state-space alternative. The Kalman recursion itself is causal; the present experimental results use offline zero-phase sigma filtering as a proof-of-concept preprocessing step, whereas a causal sigma-band filter would be used in deployment. These findings support adaptive state-space modeling as an interpretable alternative to purely amplitude-based detection and as a promising foundation for future hybrid deep learning + Kalman filtering systems.

title: A lightweight target detection model for long-distance accurate detection of underwater small targets
abstract: To address the issue of long-distance detection of small targets in underwater environments, we propose a lightweight target detection model integrating self-attention enhanced YOLOv5 and target 3D size information fusion for small-sized, low-power, and easily installable 2D image sonar. The model optimizes the YOLOv5 backbone with a self-attention mechanism to strengthen long-distance feature capture, and ensures lightweight performance through model compression, enabling fast detection and localization of underwater small targets. By combining sonar data and target acoustic features to complete 3D reconstruction, the model achieves fine-grained detection of small targets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model can effectively extract key features such as the target’s sonar highlight area and acoustic shadow area, and accurately realize long-distance detection of small underwater targets.

title: Principal stratification with U-statistics under principal ignorability
abstract: Abstract Principal stratification is a popular framework for causal inference in the presence of an intermediate outcome. While the principal average treatment effects are the standard target of inference, they may be insufficient when interest lies in the relative ordering of potential outcomes within a principal stratum. We introduce the principal generalized causal effect estimands to accommodate nonlinear contrast functions, providing robust, probability-scale summaries suitable for ordinal outcomes and win–loss comparisons with composite endpoints. Under principal ignorability, we expand the theoretical results in Jiang et al. ( J R Stat Soc Series B. , 2022, 84 (4), 1423–1445) to a broader class of causal estimands in the presence of a binary intermediate variable. We develop nonparametric identification results and derive efficient influence functions for the generalized causal estimands in principal stratification analyses. These efficient influence functions motivate multiply robust estimators and lay the ground for obtaining efficient debiased machine learning estimators via cross-fitting based on U-statistics. The proposed methods are illustrated through simulations and the analysis of a data example.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Combining evidence across filtrations
abstract: Abstract In sequential anytime-valid inference, any admissible procedure must be based on e-processes : generalizations of test martingales that quantify the accumulated evidence against a composite null hypothesis at any stopping time. This paper proposes a method for combining e-processes constructed in different filtrations but for the same null. Although e-processes in the same filtration can be combined effortlessly (by averaging), e-processes in different filtrations cannot because their validity in a coarser filtration does not translate to a finer filtration. This issue arises in sequential tests of randomness and independence, as well as in the evaluation of sequential forecasters. We establish that a class of functions called adjusters can lift arbitrary e-processes across filtrations. The result yields a generally applicable ‘adjust-then-combine’ procedure, which we demonstrate on the problem of testing randomness in real-world financial data. Furthermore, we prove a characterization theorem for adjusters that formalizes a sense in which using adjusters is necessary. There are two major implications. First, if we have a powerful e-process in a coarsened filtration, then we readily have a powerful e-process in the original filtration. Second, when we coarsen the filtration to construct an e-process, there is a logarithmic cost to recovering validity in the original filtration.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Beyond the mean: limit theory and tests for infinite-mean autoregressive conditional durations
abstract: Abstract Integrated autoregressive conditional duration (ACD) models serve as counterparts to integrated generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedastic models used for financial returns. However, despite their resemblance, asymptotic theory for ACD is still incomplete. Central challenges arise from the facts that (i) integrated ACD processes imply durations with infinite expectation and (ii) conventional asymptotic approaches break down due to the randomness in the number of durations within a fixed observation period. We fill this gap in the literature and provide a unified asymptotic theory for the (quasi)maximum likelihood estimator for integrated ACD models. Based on the new theoretical results, we also provide a novel framework for hypothesis testing in duration models, enabling inference on a key empirical question: whether durations possess a finite or infinite expectation. We apply our results to high-frequency cryptocurrency exchange traded fund (ETF) trading data. Motivated by parameter estimates near the integrated ACD region, we assess whether durations between trades in these markets have finite expectation, an assumption often made implicitly in the literature on point process models. Our empirical findings indicate infinite-mean durations for all five cryptocurrency ETFs examined, and we reject the integrated ACD hypothesis in favour of heavier-tailed alternatives for four out of the five ETFs.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Double cross-fit doubly robust estimators: Beyond series regression
abstract: Abstract Double cross-fit doubly robust (DCDR) estimators, which train nuisance function estimators on separate samples, are effective new estimators for causal functionals. We establish several novel theoretical results for them, building on recent work. We provide a structure-agnostic error analysis, which holds with generic nuisance functions and estimators. Then, we propose n-consistent DCDR estimators with undersmoothed local polynomial regression and k-Nearest Neighbours and a minimax rate-optimal DCDR estimator with undersmoothed kernel regression. Finally, we demonstrate inference is possible even in the non-root-n regime with a central limit theorem for an undersmoothed DCDR estimator. We reinforce our theoretical results with simulation experiments.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Proximal causal inference for conditional separable effects
abstract: Abstract Scientists regularly pose questions about treatment effects on outcomes conditional on a posttreatment event. However, causal inference in such settings requires care, even in perfectly executed randomized experiments. Recently, the conditional separable effect (CSE) was proposed as an interventionist estimand that corresponds to scientifically meaningful questions in these settings. However, existing results for the CSE require no unmeasured confounding between the outcome and posttreatment event, an assumption frequently violated in practice. In this work, we address this concern by developing new identification and estimation results for the CSE that allow for unmeasured confounding. We establish nonparametric identification of the CSE in observational and experimental settings with time-varying confounders, provided that certain proxy variables for hidden common causes of the posttreatment event and outcome are available. For inference, we characterize an influence function for the CSE under a semiparametric model where nuisance functions are a priori unrestricted. Using modern machine learning methods, we construct nonparametric nuisance function estimators and establish convergence rates that improve upon existing results. Moreover, we develop a consistent, asymptotically linear, and locally semiparametric efficient estimator of the CSE. We illustrate our framework with simulation studies and a real-world cancer therapy trial.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Statistical inference for cell type deconvolution
abstract: Abstract Integrating heterogeneous datasets across different measurement platforms poses fundamental challenges for statistical inference. An important example is cell type deconvolution, where cell type proportions in bulk RNA-seq data are estimated using reference single-cell data from different sources, leading to platform-specific scaling effects, measurement noise, and biological heterogeneity. Existing methods often treat estimated proportions as observed in downstream analyses, potentially compromising validity when comparing multiple individuals. We introduce measurement error adjusted deconvolution, a statistical framework for estimation and inference in deconvolution with externally approximated design matrices. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for identifiability under arbitrary gene-specific cross-platform scaling differences and develop valid inferential procedures for both individual-level proportions and comparisons across individuals, accounting for gene–gene correlation and shared estimation uncertainty. Simulations and real-data analyses demonstrate competitive estimation accuracy and reliable statistical inference.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: The causal effects of modified treatment policies under network interference
abstract: Abstract Modified treatment policies are a widely applicable class of interventions useful for studying the causal effects of continuous exposures. Approaches to evaluating their causal effects assume no interference, meaning that such effects cannot be learned from data in settings where the exposure of one unit affects the outcomes of others, as is common in spatial or network data. We introduce a new class of intervention—induced modified treatment policies—which we show identify such causal effects in the presence of network interference. Building on recent developments for causal inference in networks, we provide flexible, semi-parametric efficient estimators of the statistical estimand. Numerical experiments demonstrate that an induced modified treatment policy can eliminate the causal, or identification, bias that results from network interference. We use the methodology developed to evaluate the effect of zero-emission vehicle uptake on air pollution in California, strengthening prior evidence.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Anytime validity is free: inducing sequential tests
abstract: Abstract Anytime valid sequential tests permit us to stop testing based on the current data, without invalidating the inference. Given a maximum number of observations N , one may believe this must come at the cost of power when compared to a conventional test that waits until all N observations have arrived. Our first contribution is to show that this is false: for any valid test based on N observations, we show how to construct an anytime valid sequential test that matches it after N observations. Our second contribution is that we may use the outcome of a [0,1]-valued test as a conditional significance level in subsequent testing, leading to an overall procedure that is valid at the original significance level. This shows that anytime validity and optional continuation are readily available in traditional testing, without requiring explicit use of e -values. We illustrate this by deriving the anytime valid sequentialized z -test and t -test, which at time N coincide with the traditional z -test and t -test. Finally, we characterize the Sequential Probability Ratio Test by invariance under test induction, and show that it is induced by the Neyman–Pearson test for a tiny level and huge N under an i.i.d. assumption.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: The synthetic instrument: from sparse association to sparse causation
abstract: Abstract In many observational studies, researchers are often interested in the effects of multiple exposures on a single outcome. Standard approaches for high-dimensional data, such as the Lasso, assume that the associations between the exposures and the outcome are sparse. However, these methods do not estimate causal effects in the presence of unmeasured confounding. In this paper, we consider an alternative approach that assumes the causal effects under consideration are sparse. We show that under sparse causation, causal effects are identifiable even with unmeasured confounding. Our proposal is built around a novel device called the synthetic instrument, which, in contrast to standard instrumental variables, can be constructed directly from the observed exposures. We demonstrate that, under the assumption of sparse causation, the problem of causal effect estimation can be formulated as an ℓ0-penalization problem and solved efficiently using off-the-shelf software. Simulations show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both low- and high-dimensional settings. We further illustrate our method using a mouse obesity dataset.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Penalized empirical likelihood over decentralized networks
abstract: Abstract Empirical likelihood encounters serious computational challenges when applied to massive datasets or multiple data sources distributed across decentralized networks. This paper proposes a constrained empirical likelihood framework for decentralized networks, utilizing a novel penalization technique to obtain a penalized empirical log-likelihood. The resulting empirical log-likelihood ratio statistic is proved to be asymptotically standard chi-squared even for a divergent machine number. However, the optimization problem with the fused penalty is still hard to solve in the decentralized distributed network due to the coupling structure. To address the problem, two novel algorithms are developed to solve the optimization problem in a decentralized manner, with established convergence properties and linear convergence for the second algorithm in specific network structures. The methods are validated through simulations and real data analyses of census income and Ford gobike datasets.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Inference on function-valued parameters using a restricted score test
abstract: Abstract It is often of interest to make inference on an unknown function that is a local parameter of the data-generating mechanism, such as a density or regression function. Such estimands can typically only be estimated at a slower-than-parametric rate in nonparametric and semiparametric models, and performing calibrated inference can be challenging. In many cases, these estimands can be expressed as the minimizer of a population risk functional. Here, we propose a general framework that leverages such representation and provides a nonparametric extension of the score test for inference on an infinite-dimensional risk minimizer. We demonstrate that our framework is applicable in a wide variety of problems. As both analytic and computational examples, we describe how to use our general approach for inference on a mean regression function under (i) nonparametric and (ii) partially additive models, and evaluate the operating characteristics of the resulting procedures via simulations. Assessment of effect heterogeneity, inference on density functions, and conditional independence testing are discussed as additional examples.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Online kernel CUSUM for change-point detection
abstract: Abstract We present a computationally efficient online kernel Cumulative Sum method for change-point detection that utilizes the maximum over a set of kernel statistics to account for the unknown change-point location. Our approach exhibits increased sensitivity to small changes compared to existing kernel-based change-point detection methods, including the Scan-B statistic, corresponding to a non-parametric Shewhart chart-type procedure. We provide accurate analytic approximations for two key performance metrics: the average run length (ARL) and expected detection delay, which enable us to establish an optimal window length to be on the order of the logarithm of ARL to ensure minimal power loss relative to an oracle procedure with infinite memory. Moreover, we introduce a recursive calculation procedure for detection statistics to ensure constant computational and memory complexity, which is essential for online implementation. Through extensive experiments on both simulated and real data, we demonstrate the competitive performance of our method and validate our theoretical results.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: ART: distribution-free and model-agnostic changepoint detection with finite-sample guarantees
abstract: Abstract We introduce ART, a distribution-free and model-agnostic framework for changepoint analysis with finite-sample guarantees. ART transforms independent observations into real-valued scores via a symmetric function; under the null hypothesis of no changepoint these scores are exchangeable. Ranking and aggregating the scores yields test statistics whose null distribution is known exactly from the permutation law of ranks, enabling exact finite-sample Type I error control without repeated refitting under permutations. ART extends naturally to a multi-scale setting: by locally ranking scores over a family of intervals and aggregating them, it supports multiple changepoint testing, localization with inference, and post-detection inference, while retaining distribution-free calibration. The approach is model-agnostic: it imposes minimal structural or distributional assumptions and accommodates diverse score constructions, including features learned by statistical or machine-learning models. Across simulations and real-data applications, ART delivers valid error control and competitive power across a range of models and distributions. These properties make ART a reliable and versatile tool for modern changepoint analysis.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Scalability of Metropolis-within-Gibbs schemes for high-dimensional Bayesian models
abstract: Abstract We study general coordinate-wise Markov chain Monte Carlo schemes (such as Metropolis-within-Gibbs samplers), which are commonly used to fit Bayesian non-conjugate hierarchical models. We relate their convergence properties to the ones of the corresponding (potentially not implementable) random scan Gibbs sampler through the notion of conditional conductance. This allows us to study the performances of popular Metropolis-within-Gibbs schemes for non-conjugate hierarchical models, in high-dimensional regimes where both number of datapoints and parameters increase. Given random data-generating assumptions, we establish dimension-free convergence results, which are in close accordance with numerical evidences. Application to Bayesian models for binary regression with unknown hyperparameters is also discussed. Motivated by such statistical applications, auxiliary results of independent interest on approximate conductances and perturbation of Markov operators are provided.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Skew-symmetric approximations of posterior distributions
abstract: Abstract Popular deterministic approximations of posterior distributions from, e.g. the Laplace method, variational Bayes and expectation-propagation, generally rely on symmetric families, often taken to be Gaussian. This choice facilitates optimization and inference, but typically affects the quality of the approximation. In fact, even in basic parametric models, posterior distributions often display asymmetries that yield bias and reduced accuracy when considering symmetric approximations. Recent research has moved towards more flexible approximations incorporating skewness. However, current solutions are often model specific, lack general supporting theory, increase the computational complexity of the optimization problem, and do not provide broadly applicable solutions to incorporate skewness in any symmetric approximation. This article addresses such a gap by introducing a general and provably optimal strategy to perturb any symmetric approximation of a generic posterior distribution. The proposed solution is derived without additional optimization steps, and yields a similarly tractable approximation within the class of skew-symmetric densities that enhances the finite sample accuracy of the original symmetric counterpart. Furthermore, under suitable assumptions, it improves the convergence rate to the exact posterior by at least a n factor, in asymptotic regimes. These advancements are illustrated in numerical studies focusing on skewed perturbations of state-of-the-art Gaussian approximations.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: A new integrative learning framework for integrating multiple secondary outcomes into primary outcome analysis: a case study on liver health
abstract: Abstract In the era of big data, secondary outcomes have become increasingly important alongside primary outcomes. These secondary outcomes, which can be derived from traditional endpoints in clinical trials, compound measures, or risk prediction scores, hold the potential to enhance the analysis of primary outcomes. Our method is motivated by the challenge of utilizing multiple secondary outcomes, such as blood biochemistry markers and urine assays, to improve the analysis of the primary outcome related to liver health. Current integration methods often fall short, as they impose strong model assumptions or require prior knowledge to construct over-identified working functions. This article addresses these challenges and opens a new avenue in data integration by introducing a novel integrative learning framework applicable in a general setting. The proposed framework allows for the robust, data-driven integration of information from multiple secondary outcomes, promotes the development of efficient learning algorithms, and ensures optimal use of available data. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces variance in primary outcome analysis, outperforming existing integration approaches. Additionally, applying this method to UK Biobank reveals that cigarette smoking is associated with increased fatty liver measures, with these effects being particularly pronounced in the older adult cohort.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Using a two-parameter sensitivity analysis framework to efficiently combine randomized and nonrandomized studies
abstract: Abstract Causal inference is vital for informed decision-making across fields such as biomedical research and social sciences. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are considered the gold standard for internal validity of inferences, whereas observational studies (OSs) often provide the opportunity for greater external validity. However, both data sources have inherent limitations preventing their use for broadly valid statistical inferences: RCTs may lack generalizability due to their selective eligibility criterion, and OSs are vulnerable to unobserved confounding. This paper proposes an innovative approach to integrate RCT and OS that borrows the other study’s strengths to remedy each study’s limitations. The method uses a novel triplet matching algorithm to align RCT and OS samples and a new two-parameter sensitivity analysis framework to quantify internal and external validity biases. This combined approach yields causal estimates that are more robust to hidden biases than OSs alone and provides reliable inferences about the treatment effect in the general population. We apply this method to investigate the effects of lactation on maternal health using a small RCT and a long-term observational health records dataset from the California National Primate Research Center. This application demonstrates the practical utility of our approach in generating scientifically sound and actionable causal estimates.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Bayesian quantile estimation and regression with martingale posteriors
abstract: Abstract Quantile estimation and regression within the Bayesian framework is challenging as the choice of likelihood and prior is not obvious. In this paper, we introduce a novel Bayesian nonparametric method for quantile estimation and regression based on the recently introduced martingale posterior (MP) framework. The core idea of the MP is that posterior sampling is equivalent to predictive imputation, which allows us to break free of the stringent likelihood-prior specification. We demonstrate that a recursive estimate of a smooth quantile function, subject to a martingale condition, is entirely sufficient for full nonparametric Bayesian inference. We term the resulting posterior distribution as the quantile martingale posterior (QMP), which arises from an implicit generative predictive distribution. Associated with the QMP is an expedient, MCMC-free and parallelizable posterior computation scheme, which can be further accelerated with an asymptotic approximation based on a Gaussian process. Furthermore, the well-known issue of monotonicity in quantile estimation is naturally alleviated through increasing rearrangement due to the connections to the Bayesian bootstrap. Finally, the QMP has a particularly tractable form that allows for comprehensive theoretical study, which forms a main focus of the work. We demonstrate the ease of posterior computation in simulations and real data experiments.
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B: Statistical Methodology

title: Mixing time of the conditional backward sampling particle filter
abstract: Abstract The conditional backward sampling particle filter (CBPF) is a powerful Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler for general state space hidden Markov model (HMM) smoothing. It was proposed as an improvement over the conditional particle filter (CPF), which has an O(T2) complexity under a general ‘strong’ mixing assumption, where T is the time horizon. Empirical evidence of the superiority of the CBPF over the CPF has never been theoretically quantified. We show that the CBPF has O(TlogT) time complexity under strong mixing: its mixing time is upper bounded by O(logT), for any sufficiently large number of particles N independent of T . This O(logT) mixing time is optimal. To prove our main result, we introduce a novel coupling of two CBPFs, which employs a maximal coupling of two particle systems at each time instant. The coupling is implementable and we use it to construct unbiased, finite variance, estimates of functionals which have arbitrary dependence on the latent state’s path, with a total expected cost of O(TlogT). We use this to construct unbiased estimates of the HMM’s score function, and also investigate other couplings which can exhibit improved behaviour. We demonstrate our methods on financial and calcium imaging applications.

title: Localizing support-set changepoints in high-dimensional linear models
abstract: ABSTRACT Existing changepoint localization methods for high-dimensional regression models typically focus on scenarios where the regression coefficients follow a piecewise constant structure over time. However, this assumption can be overly restrictive in many practical applications due to the complex temporal dynamics of the coefficients. Additionally, in sparse regression models, the primary interest sometimes lies not in changes in the magnitudes of the coefficients, but rather in identifying the time points at which covariates transition between inactive and active states. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for detecting changepoints in the support set, allowing the coefficients to vary continuously over time. Theoretically, we establish the minimax lower bound on the localization error that nearly matches the upper bound achieved by the proposed method, and show that the required signal-to-noise condition is essentially the weakest possible based on the impossibility region in a minimax sense. Extensive numerical studies further demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method. It is also applied in the analysis of real air quality data from Northern Taiwan in 2015. An R package “SCP” is developed to implement the proposed method.

title: Bayesian multiple imputation for functional data
abstract: ABSTRACT Missing data are pervasive in modern functional datasets, where trajectories are often sparsely or irregularly observed. Although functional principal component analysis is widely used to reconstruct incomplete curves, existing approaches typically employ single imputation, leading to overly optimistic inferences in downstream analyses. To address these challenges, we develop a novel Bayesian multiple imputation framework for functional data (BAMIFun). For single-level functional data, we impose a Bayesian low-rank model that incorporates penalized spline representations to enforce smoothness of the functional domain and derive an efficient Gibbs sampler algorithm for posterior computation. In addition, we demonstrate and validate how to properly account for estimation uncertainties in downstream analysis. Furthermore, we extend the framework to multiway functional data using Functional Tensor Singular Value Decomposition model, enabling Bayesian multiple imputation in settings not supported by existing methods. Simulation studies show that BAMIFun achieves substantially improved coverage and more reliable downstream inference compared to existing methods, while maintaining similar imputation accuracy. Case studies using a physical activity dataset and an infant gut microbiome dataset further demonstrate the practical advantages of our proposed methods under severe missingness.

title: A Gaussian process model for chemoinformatics with application to the hazard classification of organic solvents
abstract: ABSTRACT With the proliferation of screening tools for chemical testing, it is now possible to create vast databases of chemicals easily. However, rigorous statistical methodologies employed to analyze these databases are in their infancy, and further development to facilitate chemical discovery is imperative. In this paper, we address the challenge of predicting an organic solvent’s water pollution class based on its chemical structure. We hypothesize that solvents with similar chemical structure are more likely to belong in the same hazard class. This chemical similarity is measured by the Tanimoto distance, a non-Euclidean metric on the chemical space. To incorporate the similarity between chemical structures in the model, we propose a Gaussian process model on the chemical space, with the kernel being a function of the Tanimoto distance. A novel feature of the proposed model is the inclusion of a scale parameter in the kernel, which controls the strength of the correlation between compounds and offers additional flexibility. We find that accounting for correlation between chemical compounds substantially improves predictive performance over the uncorrelated model, where compound similarity is unaccounted for. Our model also compares favorably against other established models in the literature. Furthermore, we present a genetic algorithm designed to identify important features to a compound’s efficacy, with the goal of facilitating chemical discovery. The algorithm operates based on two criteria derived from the proposed model. Simulation studies are conducted to demonstrate the suitability of the proposed methods.

title: Transportable inference using target population summary statistics under covariate shift
abstract: ABSTRACT Transporting findings from a study population to a target population is central to evidence-based decision-making in real-world settings. Most existing methods require individual-level data from both populations to account for covariate shift. However, privacy regulations and data-sharing constraints often preclude access to such data from the target population, leaving only covariate summaries available for analysis. In this paper, we develop transportability methods that enable valid inference using source individual-level data and target covariate summaries. First, we apply entropy balancing (EB) to transportability, enabling source individual-level data to be adjusted to match the target covariate moments. We establish asymptotic normality for the EB estimator and propose a variance estimator to account for uncertainty in covariate summaries. Second, we develop a new transportability method that allows more flexible modeling of covariate shift, thereby accounting for covariate shift and uncertainty in covariate summaries simultaneously. Asymptotic normality for the proposed estimator is established, and its asymptotic variance is consistently estimated. The proposed method offers greater flexibility in accounting for covariate shift and thus permits consistent estimation and valid inference when the validity of EB is not guaranteed. The proposed methods are evaluated by simulations and illustrated with an analysis of Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results breast cancer data.

title: Pseudo-data augmentation for exact conditional likelihood inference in meta-analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT In meta-analyses of binary outcomes, two-stage methods based on the DerSimonian–Laird-type random-effects model have been widely used, but these methods fix the within-study variances to their asymptotic estimates and rely on normality assumptions of the outcome measures. Such strict and often unrealistic assumptions can yield biased or inefficient inference. Likelihood-based approaches such as the binomial–normal generalized linear mixed model and the hypergeometric-normal (HGN) model alleviate some of these issues but are intrinsically restricted to the odds-ratio scale, limiting interpretability and precluding direct estimation of the risk-ratio—a more clinically meaningful measure. To overcome these limitations, we propose a unified likelihood-based framework that enables direct estimation of the risk-ratio under the HGN formulation. The proposed method introduces a pseudo–data augmentation approach that preserves the conditional likelihood structure of the HGN model while yielding an unbiased estimating function for the log-risk-ratio. Higher-order inference is achieved via jackknife bias and variance corrections, ensuring accurate coverage even in small or sparse datasets. Simulation studies confirm nearly unbiased estimation and well-calibrated confidence intervals across a wide range of conditions. Applications to published meta-analyses demonstrate that this approach yields interpretable, coherent, and computationally tractable inference.

title: Meta-analytical federated surveillance for incubation period with interval- and right-censored data with stochastic variational inference
abstract: ABSTRACT Accurate estimation of incubation period is fundamental to surveillance for infectious diseases. This task faces two major challenges: (1) surveillance data are often coarsely observed, comprising interval- and right-censored observations, and (2) patient-level data are frequently fragmented across multiple facilities and cannot be pooled due to privacy constraints. While traditional meta-analysis (MA) aggregates summary statistics, its one-shot nature limits the ability to fit complex hierarchical models. We propose a novel federated Bayesian framework, Federated Stochastic Variational Inference (Fed-SVI), which extends the summary-statistic philosophy of MA into an iterative, model-based federated approach. Our method fits a hierarchical lognormal model, explicitly modeling heterogeneity while estimating a global distribution. To fit this model privately, Fed-SVI iteratively exchanges summary statistics (local variational parameters). Each facility analytically computes these local parameters, rigorously incorporating the likelihood contributions of coarsely-observed data via expectations of the truncated normal distribution. A central server aggregates these parameters using stochastic natural-gradient ascent, enabling efficient information borrowing and mini-batch updates. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that Fed-SVI achieves accuracy nearly identical to a fully centralized analysis, while substantially outperforming naive federated or MA methods that discard censored information. We apply Fed-SVI to a distributed COVID-19 line list from 177 facilities, yielding results consistent with centralized estimates. Fed-SVI provides a scalable, accurate, and privacy-preserving solution for robust surveillance in modern data networks.

title: Causal decomposition framework for quantifying intervenable cancer health disparities
abstract: ABSTRACT This study proposes a nonparametric decomposition framework to quantify and prioritize the impact of multiple intervenable mediators contributing to disparities in health outcomes. Identifying modifiable components of health disparities is essential for informing policy and guiding resource allocation, but several methodological challenges remain. These include formulating hypothetical interventions for immutable characteristics such as race or ethnicity, mitigating bias from potentially incompatible statistical models used to represent causal pathways, and evaluating multiple mediators for their joint and individual effects. To address these challenges, we integrate recent advances in health disparities research with modern machine learning techniques. A key assumption, common to causal disparity frameworks, is the absence of unmeasured confounding in the mediator-outcome relationship. We extend existing methods in mediation analysis and introduce a nonparametric sensitivity analysis that provides sharp bounds on modifiable disparity estimates in the presence of unmeasured confounding. Together, these methods offer a robust and flexible approach to causal disparity analysis, enabling the identification of high-impact, actionable interventions. We demonstrate the utility of the methods in the context of colorectal cancer survival disparities, a setting where persistent differences across racial, ethnic, and underserved populations in the United States underscore the urgent need for analytic strategies that uncover effective intervention points.

title: Prediction intervals for random-effects meta-analysis based on confidence distributions and Edgington’s method
abstract: ABSTRACT Statistical inference about the average effect in random-effects meta-analysis has been considered insufficient in the presence of substantial between-study heterogeneity. Predictive distributions are well suited for quantifying heterogeneity since they are interpretable on the effect scale and provide clinically relevant information about future events. We construct predictive distributions accounting for uncertainty through confidence distributions from Edgington’s p -value combination method and the generalized heterogeneity statistic. Simulation results suggest that 95% prediction intervals typically achieve nominal coverage when more than three studies are available and effectively reflect skewness of effect estimates in scenarios with 20 or fewer studies. Formulations that ignore uncertainty in heterogeneity estimation typically fail to achieve correct coverage, underscoring the need for this adjustment in random-effects meta-analysis.

title: Generative estimation of conditional survival function
abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a deep generative approach to nonparametric estimation of conditional survival and hazard functions with censored data. The key idea of the proposed method is to first learn a conditional generator for the joint conditional distribution of the observed time and censoring indicator given covariates, and then construct the Kaplan–Meier and Nelson–Aalen estimators based on this conditional generator for conditional hazard and survival functions. Our method combines ideas from the recently developed deep generative learning and classical nonparametric estimation in survival analysis. We establish the convergence properties of the generative nonparametric estimators. Our numerical studies validate the proposed method.

title: A Bayesian deep learning framework for brain dynamic functional connectivity linked with cognition
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent neuroimaging studies have revealed that brain functional networks exhibit temporal fluctuations during cognitive tasks, sparking growing interest in dynamic functional connectivity (FC). However, few existing methods effectively incorporate temporal dynamics when examining the relationship between brain connectivity and cognition. In this work, we propose a Bayesian deep learning framework that decomposes FC into dynamic and stationary components, thereby disentangling transient fluctuations from stable network structures. By leveraging deep kernel learning, the model flexibly represents transient functions as continuous processes, allowing the data to guide the discovery of meaningful temporal patterns beyond conventional assumptions. Building on this representation, the dynamic component is modeled via a thresholded Gaussian process, which captures smooth temporal variations while inducing sparsity to highlight significant temporal signals. Simultaneously, the stationary component is modeled using a deep neural network with an integrated thresholding layer, enabling the learning of complex nonlinear relationships and enhancing interpretability by emphasizing key connections. This integrative approach balances model flexibility, temporal resolution, and interpretability, providing a powerful tool for predicting cognitive outcomes from functional neuroimaging data. We demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in both prediction accuracy and feature selection through extensive simulations. Applied to data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, our framework uncovers dynamic brain signals during cognitive tasks that significantly contribute to variations in cognitive performance.
