title: Third medium contact in the finite cell method
abstract: Modelling of contact in the finite cell method (FCM) has been challenging due to immersed boundaries. Traditional approaches known from finite element methods (FEM) are not straight forward to use in immersed finite element methods, since explicit boundary descriptions are usually needed. A simple approach to introduce contact is the third medium contact (TMC) formulation, where the void domain is filled with a soft material which acts as a barrier between possible contact pairs. In the present work, we apply the TMC to the FCM by using a local enrichment strategy. By doing so, the weak discontinuity induced by the material interface to the third medium can be resolved. Various numerical examples show, that the combination of TMC and FCM and local enrichment opens the field for further research into contact formulations using TMC and the FCM.

title: Lower-bound shakedown analysis of mixed-dimensional shell-solid structures using virtual node-based RBF coupling
abstract: Assessing the shakedown capacity of large-scale thin-walled structures under cyclic loading is essential for ensuring their long-term service safety. Existing direct shakedown methods are mostly based on a single type of finite element discretization, which leads to a persistent trade-off between computational efficiency and local accuracy for large-scale engineering structures: full solid models involve a prohibitive number of degrees of freedom, whereas pure shell models cannot adequately capture local three-dimensional stress gradients in regions such as joints and nozzle-shell intersections. To address this issue, this study proposes a lower-bound direct shakedown analysis framework for mixed-dimensional shell-solid structures according to which the linearized virtual nodes are constructed on the shell side, and an interface kinematic mapping matrix is established using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation. The corresponding static equilibrium conditions are derived from the principle of virtual work so as to accurately transfer generalized forces and moments across the interface. For the yield conditions, the von Mises criterion in the solid subdomain and the Ilyushin criterion in the shell subdomain are adopted. Both of them are formulated into standard second-order cone constraints, leading to a mixed-dimensional second-order cone programming (SOCP) model. The proposed method is systematically validated using a square plate with a hole, a three-dimensional pipe joint, and a pressure vessel with a nozzle. The results show that the shakedown limits predicted by the hybrid models agree well with those of full solid benchmarks, demonstrating the accuracy and engineering applicability of the proposed method. The framework provides an efficient and accurate analysis tool for shakedown assessment of large-scale thin-walled structures.

title: Collagen and myocyte interplay in cardiac volume overload: a multi-constituent growth and remodeling framework
abstract: Hearts subjected to volume overload (VO) are prone to detrimental anatomical and functional changes in response to elevated mechanical loading, ultimately leading to heart failure. Experimental findings now emphasize that organ-scale changes following VO cannot be explained by myocyte growth alone, as traditionally proposed in the literature. Collagen degradation, in particular, has been associated with VO and assumed to play a central role in both its acute and chronic stages. This hypothesis, however, remains to be substantiated by comprehensive mechanistic evidence, and each constituent contribution to myocardial growth and remodeling (G&R) processes is yet to be quantified. In this work, we present a multi-constituent G&R framework that integrates a mixture-based constitutive model within the kinematic growth formulation. This framework enables us to mechanistically assess the relative contributions of collagen and myocyte changes to alterations in tissue properties, ventricular dimensions, and growth phenotype. Our numerical results confirm that collagen remodeling affects the passive mechanical response of the myocardium, whereas myocytes predominantly influence the extent and phenotype of VO-induced growth. Importantly, collagen degradation exacerbates myocyte hypertrophy, revealing a synergistic interplay that accelerates the left ventricular eccentric growth and thereby promotes systolic dysfunction. This work constitutes an important step towards an integrated characterization of the early compensatory stages of VO-induced cardiac G&R.

title: Topology optimization for geometrically nonlinear structures with process-induced anisotropy
abstract: In the development of topology optimization methods for Additive Manufacturing (AM), accounting for the AM process-induced anisotropy of fabricated materials and the large deformations of slender members constitutes two significant engineering challenges. This paper proposes a novel structural topology optimization method that concurrently considers both effects. Firstly, the method introduces the print-off angle as an additional design variable, extending the orthotropic material model to characterize the anisotropic properties of AM-formed materials. Then, based on the finite deformation theory, the geometrically nonlinear mechanical behavior is simulated using the total Lagrangian formulation. The process-induced anisotropic constitutive relation is embedded into the geometrically nonlinear finite element equations, forming a coupled mechanical analysis framework that combines these two aspects. Furthermore, the Newton–Raphson method is applied to satisfy equilibrium conditions under large deformations. Additionally, numerical techniques, including density filtering, threshold projection, and adaptive control of the angular variable’s feasible domain, are integrated into the optimization process to stabilize the iterations. Finally, to enable efficient solutions via gradient-based optimization algorithms, sensitivity analyses with respect to both density and angle variables are derived in detail. Representative numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and reveal characteristic features of the optimized designs. The results show that the process-induced anisotropy can influence geometrically nonlinear design, with its effect tending to intensify as anisotropy deepens. The extent of this influence, however, appears to be problem-dependent. Optimizing the printing direction may offer performance benefits, particularly when design conditions are complex.

title: Generative design of funicular shells via physics-guided diffusion
abstract: Funicular shells carry loads predominantly through membrane action, achieving high structural efficiency with little material. Their computational design is difficult: the space of feasible forms is large, and classical optimisation explores it through local, problem-specific searches. Diffusion models offer an alternative by sampling from a learned distribution of plausible geometries, but coupling them with structural constraints is challenging, because physical guidance must act on noisy intermediate states whereas continuum-mechanical operators are defined on smooth geometries. Evaluating a non-linear shell operator on a denoised point estimate therefore yields a response that differs from the conditional mechanical response of the current diffusion state. We propose a modular two-branch Architect–Engineer pipeline. The Architect is a velocity-parameterised denoising diffusion model that learns an unconditional geometric prior over shell elevation maps. The Engineer is a time-conditioned Physics-Based Parallel UNet surrogate trained directly on noisy diffusion states, so that it predicts the mechanical response associated with the states visited during reverse sampling. The two models are trained independently and coupled only at inference, through a differentiable Membrane-Factor guidance pathway modulated by a bell-shaped schedule that concentrates the correction in the mid reverse process. On a dataset of funicular shells, the guided sampler raises the mean predicted Membrane Factor from 0.67 to 0.96, with 89% of samples above the 0.90 high-funicularity threshold, while preserving more geometric diversity than constant guidance. A guidance-strength sweep reveals a smooth transition between diversity-preserving and quality-prioritising regimes without architectural or training changes.

title: An efficient proper generalized decomposition framework with high-order absorbing boundaries for 3D viscoelastic seismic wave modeling
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) viscoelastic wave modeling is essential in seismic applications, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive as domain size and simulation duration increase. To address this challenge, this study proposes a reduced-order modeling framework based on Proper Generalized Decomposition (PGD). A partially separated 2D + 1D representation decomposes the original 3D problem into coupled lower-dimensional subproblems. A high-order absorbing boundary condition based on the multi-transmitting formula (MTF) is embedded into the PGD framework, together with a singular value decomposition (SVD)-based recompression strategy that preserves the low-rank structure. Viscoelastic attenuation and point moment-tensor seismic sources are also incorporated. Numerical experiments are conducted on elastic full-space and half-space benchmarks, viscoelastic media spanning quality factors from purely elastic to strongly attenuating, multiple moment-tensor source mechanisms, and a horizontally layered half-space. The results demonstrate that the PGD-MTF effectively suppresses spurious boundary reflections and accurately reproduces the tested 3D wavefields in homogeneous and horizontally layered media. Performance benchmarks against the conventional spectral element method show that runtime and memory consumption are consistently reduced on the same benchmark mesh, with the gain depending on the scaling pattern. For the volume-scaling scenario at the largest tested mesh, the runtime speedup reaches 17.28, while the memory consumption is reduced by a factor of 33.98. Out-of-plane scaling further amplifies the advantage because it best matches the separated representation. The gain grows monotonically with problem size, indicating that PGD-MTF is an efficient and scalable tool for large-scale 3D seismic wave simulations in settings compatible with the adopted separated representation.

title: Homogenization of one-dimensional periodic rod networks as special Cosserat rods
abstract: One-dimensional periodic rod networks are the structures that are obtained by periodically assembling its microstructural unit, a network of rods itself, in just one direction. In this work, we present a scheme for obtaining the nonlinear constitutive response of such structures when homogenized macroscopically as a continuum rod. To accurately capture arbitrary and large deformations, the geometrically exact special Cosserat rod theory is used for modeling the rod at both micro- and macroscales. By assuming the periodic structure to be strained uniformly, at macroscale, along its arc length, the full structure problem is reduced to just that of its microstructural unit but subjected to helically periodic boundary condition. The microscale problem, consisting of a network of rods and formulated in a variational setting, is solved in the presence of rod-joint constraints and helically periodic boundary conditions. The expressions for the macroscale rod’s stress resultants, i.e. internal contact force and moment, and stiffnesses are then obtained. Finally, several numerical examples having different microstructural units are presented to demonstrate our method. First, the results corresponding to simpler square and cross microstructural units are presented and validated with the existing literature. Square microstructural units having helical constituent rods are then taken up which have application as artificial muscle fiber material. Eventually, homogenization of auxetic tubular metamaterials is performed. It is shown how various design parameters of these microstructural units can be tuned to obtain the desired macroscopic response.

title: Splinenet: an isogeometric deep learning method for complex shells
abstract: We present a novel isogeometric deep learning method, termed SplineNet , for the seamless design and analysis of shell structures with complex geometries. The proposed approach is built upon watertight spline representations, analysis-suitable unstructured T-splines, and features exact geometric descriptions of computer-aided design (CAD) models in neural networks. Bézier extraction is used to build the network architecture, where Bernstein polynomials serve as the nonlinear activation functions. SplineNet can be applied in a data-free or data-driven way. In the data-free case, energy-based formulations can be naturally incorporated as loss terms, which fulfill the need of computer-aided engineering (CAE) and can be accurately calculated. In particular, the Kirchhoff–Love model is adopted to solve for the mechanical behaviors of shell structures. This way, CAD and CAE can be tightly integrated in a deep neural network without the time-consuming model/data exchange process. In the data-driven case, SplineNet can be used as the trunk net of deep operator networks to provide interpretability. Given such a trained network and unseen input data, results can be immediately obtained without retraining the network or repeatedly performing the traditional workflow for analysis. In the end, a variety of numerical examples are studied to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, especially when real-world complex geometries are involved. Comparisons with baseline models demonstrate the benefits of the spline representation in both solution learning and operator learning. The proposed method achieves lower relative $$L^2$$ and $$H^1$$ seminorm errors, together with shorter training time for operator learning. Incorporating derivative supervision further reduces the $$H^1$$ seminorm errors and improves the relative $$L^2$$ results.

title: A model order reduction method of transient topology optimization for non-viscously damped systems
abstract: In this paper, an efficient model order reduction method for transient topology optimization of non-viscously damped system is developed. The damping force of the non-viscously damped system depends on the past motion history through convolution integrals with suitable kernel functions. The topology optimization problem is formulated to minimize the mean dynamic compliance, subject to a prescribed volume fraction constraint, with elemental relative densities as design variables. The time domain equations of motion are first constructed and a low dimensional projection basis is constructed via the multi-model method to reduce the dimension of the original system. Then, the equations are transformed into a state-space formulation to eliminate the convolution term. Within this reduced state-space system, the transient responses are computed using a modified precise integration method, followed by a differentiate-then-discretize adjoint variable method for design sensitivity analysis, and the design variables are updated using the method of moving asymptotes. The optimized designs, computational efficiency, relative error and implementation effort for topology optimization are discussed. Several 2D and 3D numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of the proposed method. The results show that the proposed framework provides a practical and robust tool for large scale transient topology optimization of non-viscously damped systems, enabling significant time savings without compromising solution quality.

title: Autoencoder-based non-intrusive model order reduction for anisotropic and multi-physics problems
abstract: We propose a non-intrusive, Autoencoder-based framework for reduced-order modeling in continuum mechanics. Our method integrates three stages: (i) an unsupervised Autoencoder compresses high-dimensional finite element solutions into a compact latent space, (ii) a supervised regression network maps problem parameters to latent codes, and (iii) an end-to-end surrogate reconstructs full-field solutions directly from input parameters. To overcome limitations of existing approaches, we propose two key extensions: a force-augmented variant that jointly predicts displacement fields and reaction forces at Neumann boundaries, and a multi-field architecture that enables coupled field predictions, such as in thermo-mechanical systems. The framework is validated on nonlinear benchmark problems involving heterogeneous composites, anisotropic elasticity with geometric variation, and thermo-mechanical coupling. Across all cases, it achieves accurate reconstructions of high-fidelity solutions while remaining fully non-intrusive. These results highlight the potential of combining deep learning with dimensionality reduction to build efficient and extensible surrogate models.

title: A primal–dual active set framework for adhesive contact of structured interfaces with arbitrary tip geometry, roughness, and buckling
abstract: Structured fibrillar adhesives exhibit contact responses governed by the coupled effects of surface roughness, tip geometry, load redistribution, and structural instability. While increasing preload enhances contact, it can trigger fibril buckling, leading to a catastrophic loss of adhesive capacity—a trade-off difficult to capture with existing computational tools. This study addresses the limitations of traditional lumped models, which fail to resolve intra-fibril contact heterogeneity, by presenting a computationally efficient primal–dual active set (PDAS) framework. The formulation simulates adhesive contact for arbitrary tip geometries and stochastic rough counter-surfaces by discretizing each fibril tip into nodal degrees of freedom. This enables the resolution of partial contact, localized detachment, and heterogeneous traction within an individual fibril footprint. Local axial stiffness is assigned through nodal tip height, while a Laplacian-based coupling operator replicates the lateral load redistribution characteristic of continuum mechanics. Adhesive interaction is modeled using a bounded nodal tensile-force condition, and buckling-induced adhesion loss is incorporated through a history-dependent degradation law. The resulting constrained contact problem is solved using a PDAS strategy based on both primal nonpenetration and dual force-admissibility conditions. Verification confirms discretization convergence and consistency with Hertzian scaling, while simulations of spherical-cap, wedge-shaped, and periodic tips reproduce geometry-dependent contact nucleation and detachment mechanisms. Results identify an operating range in which contact recruitment and retained adhesive capacity are favorably balanced. The framework therefore provides an efficient tool for screening fibril geometries and operating conditions and for identifying adhesion windows governed by roughness, preload, and structural instability in reusable dry-adhesive interfaces.

title: A shell-in-shell homogenization approach for internally resolved structures
abstract: In this work we introduce a numerical framework for a multiscale shell-in-shell homogenization. It represents internally resolved shell structures, where on both scales structural shell elements are employed. In contrast to classical shell homogenization strategies, which employ shell elements with displacement degrees of freedom, the present approach considers additionally rotational degrees of freedom. A central novelty is the development of periodic boundary conditions enriched with rotational degrees of freedom so that representative volume elements (RVEs) may contain shell intersections or lack a continuous thickness. In addition, an internal constraint, the so-called moment reduction constraint, and its associated finite element formulation are introduced to ensure that the effective stiffness is independent of the size of the RVE. Furthermore, integration by parts techniques are employed to eliminate rigid body motions and rotations. The proposed approach is validated through linear-elastic benchmark tests. Several linear examples, including corrugated plates and honeycomb structures, are analyzed and compared with corresponding three-dimensional reference solutions.

title: Design for additive manufacturing: simultaneous optimization of structural integrity and minimal support structures using SIMP
abstract: In additive manufacturing of topology optimized designs, support structures represent a significant challenge, leading to substantial material waste, prolonged build times, and intensive post-processing requirements. This study introduces a sequential three-stage optimization framework aimed at achieving support-free designs by concurrently optimizing structural performance and minimizing the overhang perimeter. The proposed methodology encompasses the generation of an initial freeform design, followed by the determination of an optimal build direction, and culminating in a constrained overhang-perimeter optimization. A primary contribution of this work is the extension of the framework to incorporate stress-based topology optimization alongside compliance-based optimization, enabling support-free, additively manufacturable designs through print-orientation optimization. To ensure manufacturability, a robust formulation and relatively large filter radius are utilized to mitigate the formation of unprintable hanging features. Validated through numerical examples and physical 3D prints, the approach demonstrates that support-free designs are achievable with modest performance trade-offs.

title: A new, simple, and effective variationally consistent mixed finite element formulation for the geometrically exact planar analysis of beams and frames
abstract: A robust and efficient mixed finite element formulation, applicable to both shear-rigid (Kirchhoff-type) and shear-flexible (Reissner-type) beam theories, is proposed for the geometrically exact planar analysis of beams and frames. The formulation is derived from a Hellinger–Reissner-type variational principle, in which the spatial components of the internal forces, bending moment, and cross-sectional rotation are adopted as primary unknowns. Equilibrium of the spatial internal forces is satisfied in strong form at the member level, while the assumed bending moment field is $$C^0$$-continuous and satisfies equilibrium boundary conditions. The formulation is intrinsically free from shear- and membrane-locking phenomena, admits explicit closed-form expressions for both the residual vector and the consistent symmetric tangent matrix, and yields a highly sparse and banded global system with a reduced number of unknowns compared with conventional displacement-based formulations and previously proposed hybrid-mixed formulations. Displacement fields are recovered a posteriori by integrating the kinematic compatibility relations, producing globally $$C^0$$-continuous fields that satisfy all prescribed kinematic boundary conditions. Nonlinear equilibrium paths are traced using an arc-length strategy with a linear extrapolation predictor, and critical points are identified through the determinant of a Schur-complement-based equivalent stiffness matrix that emerges naturally from the formulation. Numerical examples demonstrate the accuracy, convergence, and robustness of the proposed approach, including verification against analytical solutions under pure bending, assessment of shear-locking performance, and the simulation of complex nonlinear responses involving snap-through, snap-back, and symmetry-breaking bifurcation phenomena.

title: A novel variationally consistent nodal integration method based on quadrature weight correction for meshfree reproducing kernel particle method
abstract: Accurate and stable nodal quadrature remains a major challenge in Galerkin meshfree methods, such as the reproducing kernel particle method (RKPM), due to the rational form of the approximation and the need to satisfy variational consistency. This study proposes a novel generalized nodal quadrature rule, termed VCI-w, which optimizes quadrature weights subject to integration constraints, geometric moment constraints, and positivity conditions. The optimized weights are shown to recover optimal convergence rates and provide robust numerical stability by effectively suppressing spurious low-energy oscillatory modes. Unlike geometric smoothing approaches that rely on conforming domains, VCI-w eliminates the dependency on background meshes and preserves the fully meshfree nature of the formulation. In contrast to gradient-modified variationally consistent integration methods that lead to a Petrov–Galerkin structure, VCI-w retains the Bubnov–Galerkin framework, preserving the symmetry of the discrete system. Numerical examples demonstrate optimal or near-optimal convergence across different basis orders, along with improved robustness in both 2D and 3D problems.

title: Optimal design of perforated plates
abstract: This study presents a structural optimization framework for silicon nanopore membranes used in bioartificial kidneys. While micromachined slit-pores are essential for blood filtration, they significantly reduce the membrane’s structural stiffness. To maximize rigidity for a fixed total pore area, we optimize the distribution of slit heights across the membrane. Due to the high number of pores ($$\approx 10^5$$ in the membrane), direct numerical simulation is computationally prohibitive. We therefore apply homogenization theory and for a given hole height derive an approximate homogeneous anisotropic plate model. For the obtained effective elasticity tensor, using linear least squares, we determine a smooth surrogate model. This approach transforms the complicated geometry optimization problem into a smooth parametric optimization problem. Then, using the finite element method in a gradient descent algorithm, we minimize two objective functions: the structural compliance and the maximum displacement. This yields, in each case, the optimal distribution of holes of different heights in the perforated membrane. The results provide an efficient computational strategy for designing mechanically robust, high-performance filtration membranes.

title: Correction: The shifted boundary collocation immersogeometric method: an application to Poisson problems
Parametric phase-field brittle fracture computations with convolutional Fourier neural operators
abstract: The variational phase-field approach to fracture has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling complex fracture phenomena, yet in the computational setting its reliance on discretizations that resolve small length scales makes it very expensive for parametric studies and real-time applications. In this paper, we propose the use of the Convolutional Fourier neural operator (C-FNO)—a data-driven operator learning architecture that enhances the global spectral capabilities of Fourier neural operators (FNOs) with local spatial convolutions—to surrogate phase-field brittle fracture simulations. We evaluate the performance of the C-FNO on two-dimensional single-edge notched specimens under varying geometric (initial notch length) and loading (magnitude and angle) parameters. Our results demonstrate that the C-FNO accurately predicts crack propagation, kinking, and branching across unseen parameter combinations, achieving very low mean absolute errors with a training time of a few hours and an inference time of the order of ten seconds. Notably, the addition of local convolution layers allows the model to capture nearly sharp cracks that are typically smoothed out by vanilla FNOs. This work highlights the potential of operator learning frameworks to provide high-fidelity, high-speed predictions for computational fracture mechanics.

title: A discontinuous SPH approach for simulating blast-induced rock fracture and multi-material interaction
abstract: Blast-induced rock fracture is a critical challenge in mining, geotechnical, and defense engineering, involving complex dynamic processes such as high-strain-rate deformation, fragmentation, and multi-material interaction. This paper presents a novel computational framework based on a discontinuous Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) approach to simulate crack propagation and damage in rock under blast loading. The framework integrates the Grady–Kipp model for tensile damage and the Drucker–Prager criterion for shear failure. Fracture is explicitly modeled using a pseudo-spring crack treatment, while a robust multi-material contact algorithm handles interfacial forces under compression. The implementation is rigorously validated through four benchmark cases: three-dimensional crack branching, a uniaxial compression test, frictional block-sliding, and unconfined compression of cylindrical specimens. The framework is further applied to simulate explosive detonation in a cylindrical rock sample, blast damage near empty holes, and rock blasting with multiple boreholes. These simulations help to understand damage mechanisms under varied initial conditions. The predicted damage patterns and fragmentation results show strong agreement with available experimental data, demonstrating the method’s capability to accurately capture dynamic fracture and complex blast-induced failure in rock.

title: Sensitivity of blast responses in a reinforced concrete slab to damage evolution parameters
abstract: Accurate prediction of blast-induced damage in reinforced concrete (RC) structures requires constitutive models that offer transparent control over softening behavior. This study develops a user-defined material (UMAT) subroutine that extends the built-in concrete damage model in commercial finite element software by exposing four key brittle damage parameters: the evolution rate ($$A_b$$), shape ($$B_b$$), saturation limit ($$d_{\max }$$), and deletion threshold ($$d_{\textrm{th}}$$), of which the latter two are internally fixed and inaccessible in the built-in implementation. Numerical simulations of an RC slab under near-field blast loading are validated against experimental midspan deflection and observed cracking patterns. A structured parametric study, varying each parameter independently, reveals that although all configurations can yield similar peak deflection magnitudes, they produce markedly different peak response times and fracture morphologies. Specifically, $$A_b$$ governs the rate of stiffness degradation; $$B_b$$ controls the curvature of the damage evolution function; $$d_{\max }$$ sets the saturation level of strength reduction; and $$d_{\textrm{th}}$$ critically advances the peak response time by triggering early element erosion. These distinctions highlight that global deflection alone is insufficient to characterize structural behavior under blast loading, and that physically meaningful control over damage evolution parameters is essential for reliable failure prediction and blast-resistance assessment.

title: Weighting disagreements with likelihood for boolean matrix factorization and correlation clustering
abstract: Boolean matrix factorization is a popular technique for summarizing a binary matrix. The goal in such summary is to find k tiles that are denser than the rest of the data: a typical objective is to minimize the number of (weighted) disagreements with the input data. Another instance of minimizing weighted disagreements is correlation clustering, where we are given a graph with signed edges and are asked to partition a graph minimizing the negative intra edges and the positive inter edges. We argue that weighting disagreements in both cases is crucial, especially for sparse datasets. This leads to a problem of selecting an appropriate weight: a non-trivial problem as we cannot use the original objective directly. To solve this issue we propose an alternative strategy: we search for results that maximize the likelihood of a simple model, based on two Bernoulli variables. We then show that we can find good solutions using a grid search. We develop 2 grid search strategies. The first approach requires $$\mathcal {O}\left( (1 + \epsilon ^{-1}) \log \ell \right)$$ queries, where $$\ell$$ is the size of the input, and yields $$(1 + \epsilon )\alpha$$ guarantee if we can $$\alpha$$-approximate the original weighted disagreement problem. The second approach is a pruning technique, based on fractional programming, that reduces the number of queries significantly in practice, especially for small $$\epsilon$$. This approach yields $$(1 + \epsilon )$$ approximation guarantees, if we can solve the original weighted disagreement problem exactly. We demonstrate empirically that weighting disagreements produces more accurate results, and study the cases where the grid search yields better likelihood scores than the selected baselines.

title: Core-driven local community detection in multiplex networks via seed optimization and multilayer modularity
abstract: Local community detection in multiplex networks faces two critical challenges. First, the result is sensitive to the query seed position. A core seed yields more accurate detection than a peripheral one. Second, nodes near community boundaries often have ambiguous memberships, making their community assignment difficult. These issues limit the accuracy and robustness of existing methods. To address these issues, this paper proposes MLCD-CND (Local Community Detection in Multiplex Networks via Core Node Detection), a two-stage method for local community detection in multiplex networks. In the first stage, MLCD-CND mitigates seed dependency by detecting high-quality core nodes through a novel Node Relation Strength metric, which integrates cross-layer structural similarity (via Jaccard Similarity Coefficient) and interaction density (via Node Influence Area Density). These core nodes replace the initial query seed to form a robust initialization. In the second stage, the algorithm expands the community by optimizing a hybrid metric that balances multiplex local modularity and community relation strength, effectively preventing over-expansion into sparse regions. The experimental results demonstrate that MLCD-CND improves the performance of the F-score by up to $$72\%$$ compared to the baseline model. The method effectively addresses seed dependency and over-expansion, offering robust performance across diverse networks.

title: Meta additive model: interpretable sparse learning with auto weighting
abstract: Sparse additive models have attracted much attention in high-dimensional data analysis due to their flexible representation and strong interpretability. However, most existing models are limited to single-level learning under the mean-squared error criterion, whose empirical performance can degrade significantly in the presence of complex noise, such as non-Gaussian perturbations, outliers, noisy labels, and imbalanced categories. The sample reweighting strategy is widely used to reduce the model’s sensitivity to atypical data. However, it typically requires prespecifying the weighting functions and manually selecting additional hyperparameters. To address this issue, we propose a new meta additive model (MAM) based on the bilevel optimization framework, which learns data-driven weights of individual losses by parameterizing the weighting function via an MLP trained on meta data. MAM is capable of a variety of learning tasks, including variable selection, robust regression estimation, and imbalanced classification. Theoretically, MAM provides guarantees for optimization convergence, algorithmic generalization, and variable selection consistency under mild conditions. Empirically, MAM outperforms several state-of-the-art additive models on both synthetic and real-world data under various types of corruption. The implementation is available at https://github.com/zxlml/MAM .

title: Self-distilled label graph learning for adaptive multi-label feature selection in biological data
abstract: Multi-label feature selection (MFS) is vital for high-dimensional biological data analysis, where samples such as genes or proteins are annotated with multiple functional labels. A major challenge in this setting is that MFS methods must identify informative features while simultaneously modeling complex, and often noisy,inter-label dependencies. Existing MFS methods, however, suffer from three critical limitations in real-world biological applications: (i) prevalent annotation noise, which compromises model reliability; (ii) limited integration of domain-specific knowledge, leading to biologically implausible or spurious label dependencies; and (iii) instability in hierarchical dependency modeling, which propagates errors across prediction stages. To address these challenges, we propose Self-Distilled Label Graph Learning for Adaptive Multi-Label Feature Selection (SDMFS), a unified optimization framework that simultaneously performs feature selection and adaptive label graph learning. First, a self-distillation mechanism generates temporally smoothed teacher targets from the model’s own historical predictions, mitigating annotation noise and stabilizing optimization. Second, an adaptive prior-guided label graph learning module integrates empirical label prior knowledge with data-driven label dependency discovery, ensuring the learned structures are both reliable and interpretable. Finally, the framework jointly leverages these modules to select discriminative features that preserve functional relationships across labels. We develop an efficient alternating minimization algorithm with guaranteed convergence and demonstrate, through extensive experiments on seven benchmark biological datasets, that SDMFS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art MFS methods in predictive performance, robustness, and biological interpretability.

title: NoDE: noise-decorrelation embedding for robust long-term multivariate time series forecasting
abstract: In long-term multivariate time–series forecasting, longer input windows are often assumed to help. However, on some standard benchmarks we observe that, for certain model–dataset combinations, performance becomes non-monotonic and unstable as the look-back length grows. Taking a data-mining perspective, we first characterize correlated input noise on the Weather benchmark, a widely used multivariate forecasting dataset. Residual-denoising analyses on this dataset show that, for some variables and time periods, input perturbations exhibit substantial short-lag autocorrelation rather than behaving as white noise. Building on this evidence, we provide a window-conditional second-order interpretation that relates whole-window embeddings to variance inflation (for linear forecasters) and curvature-dependent bias (for nonlinear forecasters) arising from residual lag covariance under temporally correlated perturbations, and discuss how this interpretation connects to both squared and absolute error criteria used in evaluation. To address this issue in real-world datasets, we introduce NoDE (Noise-Decorrelation Embedding) , a simple and model-agnostic structured linear embedding that reduces effective lag covariance via downsampling, permutation-based reshaping (shuffle/unshuffle), and shared affine mappings, while preserving a drop-in interface to common backbones. Our protocol automatically selects the downsampling window in a data-driven manner through a two-stage procedure: candidate resolutions are proposed based on ACF-energy statistics, and the final choice is made via a lightweight quick-train validation. An explicit no-op option is included to disable NoDE when downsampling is not beneficial. Comprehensive experimental evaluations validate that NoDE stabilizes performance under long look-back windows across multiple datasets and backbone families (Transformer, CNN, and MLP). In addition, the protocol’s ability to automatically activate or deactivate NoDE via a no-op option allows it to support standard, patch-wise, and multi-scale front-ends through the same selection interface, enabling robust and architecture-agnostic deployment. Code and models are open-source at https://github.com/lmh9507/NoDE .

title: Feature selection for partial multi-label learning via noise removal and dynamic label correlation
abstract: As an emerging weakly supervised learning paradigm, partial multi-label learning (PML) aims to derive robust predictors from multi-label data with noisy labels. However, apart from label noise, multi-label data usually contain thousands of feature dimensions. Existing PML methods overlook the curse of dimensionality caused by high-dimensional features, which prevents their models from achieving optimal performance. To address the above issues, this paper proposes a novel partial multi-label feature selection method named PMFS-NRDLC, which unifies label noise removal and dimensionality reduction within a single optimization framework. First, by fully utilizing the exclusive prior of PML label noise, we construct a position-constrained regression model with strict zero constraints on noise terms corresponding to non-candidate labels, which fundamentally avoids spurious confidence assignment and achieves precise label denoising. Second, we introduce feature-space manifold topology under the smoothness assumption to regularize label confidence learning, ensuring consistent local structural characteristics between original features and estimated label confidences. Meanwhile, we design an iterative dynamic label graph update strategy to capture time-varying latent label correlations, and further regularize feature weights to guarantee that correlated labels share similar feature importance. Finally, we adopt the $$l_{2,1}$$-norm to impose sparse constraints on feature weights to implement embedded feature selection. Extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that PMFS-NRDLC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art competitors.

title: Critical node identification through triplet node influence in complex networks
abstract: Identifying influential nodes is crucial to understanding and managing the structural and functional dynamics of complex networks. While traditional methods focus on either local or global influence, hybrid approaches aim to integrate both for improved accuracy. This paper presents a novel hybrid method, Triplet Node Influence (TNI), which combines degree centrality, communicability, and gravity-based H-index to evaluate node influence from local, global, and gravitational perspectives. To ensure computational efficiency without sacrificing precision, an optimal truncation radius is introduced. The effectiveness of TNI is evaluated against several state-of-the-art algorithms using three key metrics: (1) SIR-based spreading simulations with Kendall’s tau, (2) the Monotonicity Index, and (3) robustness analysis through node removal. TNI is tested on twelve unweighted and three weighted real-world networks. The results show that TNI consistently demonstrates effectiveness in identifying influential nodes, achieving superior accuracy and strong discriminatory power. It also maintains acceptable network robustness and time performance, offering a more generalized and adaptable node evaluation framework for diverse network types.

title: A novel graph-based patient embedding method for the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease from microRNA expression data
abstract: As key players of gene expression regulation, microRNAs (miRNAs) are involved in the onset and progression of many diseases. Because of their presence in organic fluid, such as blood or urine, they are optimal candidates as disease biomarkers that can be easily detected in liquid biopsy, which is less invasive and expensive than traditional techniques. In this paper, we propose a novel patient embedding method, called GraphiRNA, to support the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease from miRNA expression values. GraphiRNA is capable of capturing information about the relationships among miRNAs, estimated through the correlation of their expression values over a set of patients, and also integrate the information about their RNA sequences. Notably, GraphiRNA is able to properly model negative correlations by introducing synthetic nodes into the network, to avoid discarding the sign of correlations (and the associated information), as done by existing approaches. Our experimental evaluation, performed on real data from three studies on Alzheimer’s disease, showed superior classification performances of GraphiRNA, especially in patients affected by Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), which outlines the potential of GraphiRNA of being adopted as a diagnostic tool for the early intervention. Finally, our ablation study on the approach adopted to handle negative correlations showed an improvement reaching 30.9% in terms of F1-score over an approach that discards the sign of correlations, confirming our initial intuition about the importance of properly considering such information.

title: IGA: isomorphism-aware graph alignment for robust unsupervised anchor link prediction
abstract: The proliferation of social platforms has led users to participate in multiple networks, giving rise to anchor links that connect accounts of the same individual across platforms. Anchor Link Prediction (ALP) seeks to uncover these links and underpins various downstream applications such as user profiling and cross-platform recommendation. While early methods rely on labelled anchor links for supervised training, real-world scenarios often lack such supervision, making unsupervised ALP both more practical and significantly more challenging. Existing unsupervised methods typically focus on learning from observed network data. However, they rarely take into account the generative processes underlying different networks. In this work, we propose an unsupervised framework, Isomorphism-aware Graph Alignment (IGA), based on the practical assumption that the source and target networks may contain regions that reflect shared structural information arising from partially overlapping network formation patterns, providing stable backbone components consistently observed across networks. IGA leverages the Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) to align these backbone structures through a consistency-disparity learning principle. Additionally, we introduce a refinement strategy that adaptively augments structural and semantic information to improve alignment quality. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that IGA consistently outperforms existing unsupervised methods in both accuracy and robustness, particularly under noisy and sparse conditions.

title: Sparse oblique rule boosting for simpler additive rule ensembles
abstract: Small additive ensembles of symbolic rules offer interpretable prediction models. Traditionally, these ensembles use rule conditions based on conjunctions of simple threshold propositions $$x \ge t$$ on a single input variable x and threshold t , resulting geometrically in axis-parallel polytopes as decision regions. While this form ensures a high degree of interpretability for individual rules and can be learned efficiently using the gradient boosting approach, it relies on having access to a curated set of expressive input features so that a small ensemble of axis-parallel regions can describe the target variable well. Absent such features, reaching sufficient accuracy requires increasing the number and complexity of individual rules, which diminishes the interpretability of the model. Here, we extend classical rule ensembles by introducing logical propositions with learnable sparse linear transformations of input variables, i.e., propositions of the form $$\mathbf{x}^\textrm{T}\mathbf{w}\ge t$$, where $$\mathbf{w}$$ is a learnable sparse weight vector, enabling decision regions as general polyhedrons with oblique faces. We propose a learning method using gradient boosting based on a weighted logistic regression. Empirical results across 14 regression and classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves lower model complexity than competitive baselines while maintaining similar or better predictive accuracy. Hence, the approach provides a favorable trade-off between interpretability and accuracy and reduces the reliance on manual feature engineering.

title: Evolution of sentiment analysis toward aspect-based sentiment analysis: a scientometric analysis of research trends, knowledge structures, and emerging technologies (2015–2025)
abstract: As sentiment analysis and opinion mining evolve from simple polarity detection to complex cognitive reasoning and contextual understanding, it is important to map the growth of this field for guiding future research and technological innovation. This study presents a comprehensive scientometric analysis to examine the evolution of sentiment analysis and its progression toward Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA). Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic retrieval strategy was employed to collect 4269 unique publications from the dual database. Advanced bibliometric techniques, including co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, keyword co-occurrence analysis, and citation burst detection, were performed using CiteSpace and VOSviewer to visualize and interpret the field’s knowledge landscape. The analysis identified a sequence of technological paradigms that have shaped the field’s evolution. The study highlights a globally interconnected collaboration structure with strong regional hubs and increased international cooperation. Analysis shows a convergence between sentiment analysis, explainable AI, and multimodal machine learning. Emerging research areas include contrastive learning, multimodal fusion, prompt learning, and aspect sentiment extraction, indicating a shift toward foundation-model-driven sentiment intelligence. By explicitly linking shifts in collaboration structures to transitions in computational methodologies, the findings provide valuable guidance for developing robust, interpretable, and context-aware sentiment-understanding systems for next-generation artificial intelligence applications.

title: One-step tensor low-frequency learning for incomplete multi-view clustering
abstract: Tensor-based incomplete multi-view clustering has attracted considerable attention due to its strong capability in modeling higher-order cross-view correlations. However, many existing incomplete multi-view clustering methods still face challenges, including high computational cost, limited characterization of higher-order consistency, and potential performance degradation induced by two-step optimization frameworks. To address these challenges, we propose one-step Tensor Low-Frequency learning for Incomplete Multi-View Clustering (TLF-IMVC). Specifically, the proposed method jointly models low-frequency and low-rank structures on stacked spectral embedding tensors to enable efficient and consistent cross-view information fusion. Furthermore, a Tensor Low-Frequency nuclear norm is introduced to impose discriminative frequency-domain constraints, selectively preserving informative low-frequency components and suppressing noisy high-frequency components. In addition, an efficient alternating optimization algorithm is developed, and extensive experiments on eight datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of TLF-IMVC compared with state-of-the-art methods.

title: Multimodal knowledge graph completion method for addressing imbalance of modal information
abstract: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Completion (MMKGC) focuses on predicting missing triples in multimodal knowledge graphs by effectively leveraging both relational triples and multimodal information. However, existing MMKGC methods often overlook the imbalance of modal information among entities, resulting in an overreliance on the dominant modalities and degrading the performance of completion. To address the problem caused by the modality imbalance, a novel Multimodal Knowledge Graph Completion method (shorted by MI-MKGC) is proposed in this paper. It addresses the problem from two aspects: (1) the relation knowledge-guided dynamic modal fusion module dynamically adjusts the weights of each modality by using the relational types between entities as prior knowledge, and (2) the joint modality adversarial training module generates negative samples to enhance weak modality information. The extensive experimental results on three public datasets with 16 state-of-the-art baselines have verified the advancement of the proposed method. Specially, the metric Hit@1 of MI-MKGC increases by up to 5.2% than that of the best exiting compared method. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/yuhongcqupt/MI-MKGC.

title: DiaSeg: diagonal segment extraction from DTW paths for interpretable gait analysis
abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the dominant approach for measuring similarity between time series, yet standard practice discards the optimal warping path after computing a single distance value, losing precisely the local alignment information most relevant to clinical diagnosis. We introduce DiaSeg, a framework that recovers this discarded information by extracting diagonal segments from DTW paths with controlled breaks, characterizing each segment by five geometric features, and enabling unsupervised pattern discovery without domain-specific feature engineering. Validated on 91 subjects across six clinical conditions (healthy aging, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s, ALS, brain tumor, and stroke), three findings emerge. First, diagonal segments form consistent unsupervised patterns (silhouette 0.33) aligned with biomechanical phase annotations, with external validation confirming near-perfect separation of healthy and pathological gait (ARI up to 0.986). Second, segments discriminate pathology at 69% (supervised) and 75% (patient-level clustering), with pathology manifesting through distributional shifts in segment length rather than individual segment properties; combining segment and cycle-level features further improves classification to 91.7%. Third, while cycle-based methods achieve higher accuracy (91%), diagonal segments provide phase-specific interpretability unavailable in global representations, localizing where coordination breaks down within the gait cycle. DiaSeg thus transforms DTW from a black-box distance into a source of interpretable temporal features for neurodegenerative disease assessment.

title: Minimum length estimation in longest frequent itemsets mining
abstract: Discovering frequent itemsets is a core aspect of data mining, widely used in market basket analysis, bioinformatics, and recommendation systems. When dealing with datasets containing many items, extracting all frequent itemsets often generates a huge number of itemsets, complicating their effective use. However, in some practical applications, mining only a representative subset of frequent itemsets is sufficient. The researcher recently introduced Longest Frequent Itemsets (LFI), which are frequent itemsets that contain the maximum number of frequent items. The number of LFI is usually very small, sometimes even just one. This type of set is useful in many real-world applications including personalized tourism recommendations, insurance coverage optimization, clustering, and healthcare. The length of LFI is a crucial factor that influences the efficiency of mining algorithms. This study presents a novel method for estimating the minimum length of the LFI. Estimating this minimum length helps to significantly reduce the search space by pruning items and transactions that cannot contribute to the final solution. We propose two-level tree structures to store the information necessary for the frequent k -itemsets, where $$k\le 2$$. Building a two-level tree structure requires only a single pass over the database. We also present algorithms that use this structure to estimate the minimum length of the longest frequent itemsets and apply the proposed pruning strategies. Preliminary empirical results on both real and synthetic datasets confirm the precision of the proposed method and demonstrate a reduction in overall extraction time.

title: When, how long and how much? Interpretable neural networks for time series regression by learning to mask and aggregate
abstract: Time series extrinsic regression (TSER) aims to predict a continuous target variable from an input time series. It arises in domains such as healthcare, finance, environmental monitoring, and engineering, where both accuracy and interpretability are essential. Despite strong predictive performance, state-of-the-art TSER models typically operate as black boxes, making it difficult to understand which temporal patterns drive their predictions. Post-hoc explanation methods attempt to address this issue but often produce coarse, noisy, or unstable explanations. Inherently interpretable approaches based on additive decompositions or concepts offer an alternative, yet they often require concept supervision, struggle to capture multivariate interactions, and lack expressiveness for complex temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we propose Mask-and-Aggregate Networks for Time Series (MAGNETS), an inherently interpretable neural architecture for TSER. MAGNETS learns a compact set of human-understandable concepts directly from data, without requiring concept annotations. Each concept corresponds to a learned, mask-based aggregation over selected input features, revealing both which features influence the prediction and when they matter. Predictions are expressed as transparent combinations of these concepts, yielding faithful, input-specific explanations by design. Experiments on synthetic and real-world univariate and multivariate TSER datasets show that MAGNETS achieves accuracy comparable to black-box models while substantially outperforming existing interpretable baselines, particularly on tasks involving multivariate feature interactions.

title: Large-scale structured subspace clustering
abstract: Subspace clustering has become an essential technique in data mining and pattern discovery for revealing low-dimensional structures embedded within high-dimensional data. By modeling data as a union of multiple linear or affine subspaces, it effectively captures complex latent relationships among samples. However, existing methods still face two major challenges: (1) scalable representations may not adequately preserve intrinsic structural relationships under complex data distributions; (2) global self-representation models incur prohibitive computational costs as data scale increases. To address these limitations, we propose a Large-scale Structured Subspace Clustering (LSSC) framework that integrates anchor-based reconstruction, locality-aware coefficient initialization, distance-weighted structure regularization, and coefficient regularization to learn a compact nonnegative sample-to-anchor representation. The proposed method achieves strong clustering performance while avoiding the construction of a full sample-to-sample affinity matrix, thereby providing favorable scalability on large datasets. Extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets demonstrate that LSSC achieves the best overall average rank across ACC, NMI, Purity, and ARI among the compared methods that completed all nine datasets, while maintaining competitive clustering performance and scalability on large-scale datasets. These findings characterize both the practical scalability of LSSC and its sensitivity to highly imbalanced data distributions, thereby clarifying its empirical strengths and limitations.

title: Hierarchical graph networks for breast cancer subtype classification
abstract: Breast cancer histopathological diagnosis relies on the expert assessment of Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) stained slides. This process is both time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. Deep learning methods have shown great potential for automating cellular analysis; however, conventional patch-based approaches do not explicitly model relational spatial dependencies between biological entities, potentially limiting structural interpretability. We present a hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for ROI-level breast cancer subtype classification that represents nuclei and tissue regions as linked graph structures. The study provides a validation-driven design-space analysis of graph topology, node features, spatial pooling, and fusion of cell and tissue information within this hierarchical pipeline. The proposed approach was evaluated on the BRACS dataset, which comprises 547 whole-slide images and over 4500 annotated regions spanning seven histopathological classes. Results show that sequential hierarchical fusion is the most effective configuration in this setting, outperforming alternative strategies for integrating cell and tissue information and yielding particularly consistent improvements for Atypical Ductal Hyperplasia, Flat Epithelial Atypia, and Ductal Carcinoma in situ.

title: DNetEx: FDR-controlled differential network analysis for knowledge discovery from graphs
abstract: This paper studies change detection in graph structures through differential network analysis between two Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs), where the underlying graphs are unknown and only samples from each model are available. We consider the setting in which only a small subset of edges differs between the two GGMs, while the base graphs themselves may be dense. This framework is substantially more general than existing approaches that rely on restrictive structural assumptions such as sparsity of the base graphs. We propose DNetEx, a novel framework for identifying structural changes between GGMs with false discovery rate (FDR) control. DNetEx combines sample splitting, data screening, and statistical validation within an e-value and e-BH multiple testing framework. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that the proposed method asymptotically controls the FDR under mild conditions without imposing restrictive assumptions on the underlying graphical structures. In addition, the proposed screening mechanism improves computational efficiency and scalability by reducing the number of candidate edges considered during inference, while a tunable screening parameter provides a practical trade-off between statistical power and computational cost. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate that DNetEx achieves accurate FDR control and strong detection power, including settings where competing approaches fail to control the FDR. In a real-world fMRI connectivity study, DNetEx successfully identifies meaningful differential edges between neurotypical individuals and individuals with autism spectrum disorder, whereas competing methods detect none.

title: Time series classification with random convolution kernels: pooling operators and input representations matter
abstract: Time series classification (TSC) is a fundamental problem in supervised learning, with applications in domains ranging from healthcare and finance to industrial monitoring. Recent advances based on random convolution kernels, such as ROCKET, MiniRocket, MultiRocket, and HYDRA, have demonstrated that large sets of randomly generated convolutional features combined with simple linear classifiers can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy at very low computational cost. These methods typically rely on fixed input representations and a small number of pooling operators, most commonly the proportion of positive values (PPV), to extract features from activation maps. However, the optimal choice of pooling operator and representation can vary substantially across datasets. In this work, we first provide an empirical analysis on the UCR archive showing that using a fixed pooling operator does not generally yield optimal performance, and that the best choice depends on the data. Motivated by this observation, we propose SelF-Rocket (Selected Features Rocket), a novel extension of MiniRocket that dynamically attempts to select the most appropriate combination of input representation and pooling operator during training. SelF-Rocket incorporates a feature selection module that adapts to each dataset, allowing it to select the most appropriate pooling operator and representation. Extensive experiments on the UCR benchmark demonstrate that SelF-Rocket achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared with existing random convolution kernel methods.

title: Preserving Clinical Decision Traceability in AI Systems with Constrained Outputs
When the Patient Record Outlives the Clinical Encounter: Lessons from the Aesto Health Data Breach
A Web-Based Registry Framework Linking Transfusion Practice to Long-Term Patient Outcomes: Design and Single-Center Feasibility Study
abstract: Blood transfusions are among the most common medical interventions performed worldwide. Several comprehensive databases link transfusions to routinely collected health data but do not include the indication and the decision-making basis for a particular administration, nor patient-reported long-term outcomes. We developed a web-based registry for the standardized assessment of transfusion practice and patient outcomes, designed for an observation period of up to 30 years. The framework combines clinical data captured at the point of care with patient-reported outcome measures collected through automated digital follow-up, ensures privacy by design through physical separation of identifying and medical data, and codes diagnoses and procedures in SNOMED CT. We evaluated feasibility in a single-center pilot at Goethe University Hospital Frankfurt (11 September 2024–15 January 2026), with patient-reported follow-up collected through 13 August 2026. A total of 408 patients were enrolled, yielding 1,298 administrations across nine treatment categories in a predominantly cardiac surgical cohort. The pilot demonstrated that the registry integrates into routine clinical workflows, captures the parameters required for guideline-adherence monitoring, and supports sex-disaggregated, descriptive analyses of transfusion practice. Follow-up was completed by 12.5% of patients at 3 months and 15.2% of patients at 1 year; paired baseline–follow-up assessments of physical capacity and frailty demonstrate the data structure for capturing functional recovery. Risk-adjusted benchmarking, network-wide analyses, and donor outcomes are designed capabilities of the framework that were not evaluated in this pilot. The platform is available in 16 languages and participation is open to further institutions.

title: Development and Exploratory Evaluation of a Large Language Model-Supported Scoping Review Workflow
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated human-level performance in literature review screening phases and have been evaluated in systematic-review workflows. However, LLM performance in scoping reviews, which are broader and more heterogeneous, remains understudied. We developed a modular LLM-supported framework for scoping-review workflows and compared the performance of two general-purpose LLMs against human reviewers on a reference scoping review. The reference review’s keyword search results ( n = 1336) and prompt sets mirroring workflow stages were provided to GPT-5 and gpt-oss-20b (OpenAI, August 2025). Outputs were benchmarked against human decisions for agreement; disagreements were adjudicated. For title-abstract screening and final-inclusion concordance, unanimous and adjudicated decisions were combined into a composite reference standard. In title-abstract screening, GPT-5 and gpt-oss-20b workflows showed substantial interrater agreement with human consensus (AC1: 0.769; 0.722); reference concordance was 90.9% ( p = 0.08) and 92.4% ( p = 0.004) versus humans’ 89.0%.
