BaRatin shows the most favourable overall performance according to the evaluation criteria, including high-flow estimation, extrapolation and behaviour of prediction intervals. However, Diebold-Mariano tests indicate that the differences in predictive accuracy between BaRatin and other models are not statistically significant at the 5% level for the entire testing dataset and high-flow subset. Therefore, the study demonstrates the importance of evaluating rating curve models through a unified comparative design incorporating multiple evaluation criteria under the specific hydraulic and hydrometeorological conditions, with implications for hydrologic and hydraulic applications in this basin.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: An improved representation of spatial precipitation over Türkiye using multiscale geographically weighted regression
abstract: Accurately estimating the spatial distribution of precipitation is essential for numerous applications that depend on distributed solutions, including hydrological modeling. This is typically achieved by applying interpolation methods, such as inverse distance weighted interpolation or kriging, to gauge-based precipitation data. However, these methods often struggle to capture spatial variability in regions with complex terrain fully. In this study, we propose using Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) for spatial interpolation of precipitation. Although MGWR is an extension of Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), its application to precipitation interpolation remains limited, and few studies have comprehensively compared its performance with conventional interpolation methods. Both GWR and MGWR consider spatially varying relationships between precipitation and explanatory variables, such as elevation and distance to the coast, to estimate values for unsampled locations. However, MGWR differs from GWR in that it incorporates multiple spatial scales, providing a better representation of spatial heterogeneity. We used precipitation data collected at 237 stations across Türkiye from 1980 to 2020, along with elevation and distance to coast, as explanatory variables. The performance of the MGWR was evaluated against several commonly used methods, including inverse distance weighted interpolation, local polynomial interpolation, Kriging, empirical Bayesian Kriging, co-kriging, and GWR. The results showed that the inclusion of explanatory variables considerably improved the results. MGWR and GWR outperformed the other methods in representing local variations in precipitation, with MGWR providing additional improvements by allowing a scale-dependent analysis. The MGWR also offered the lowest level of uncertainty. This study demonstrated that MGWR can potentially improve the spatial models of hydrological and climatic variables.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Stochastic simulation of Yangtze River fluvial terraces via Bayesian generalized Coupled Markov Chains
abstract: Stratigraphic heterogeneity is a primary driver of spatial uncertainty in environmental and geotechnical risk assessments. Accurately characterizing this complex spatial variability using stochastic models is a fundamental prerequisite for evaluating the reliability of infrastructure in dynamic geological environments. Coupled Markov Chain (CMC) models have proven effective in characterizing lithological spatial distributions, but are largely confined to regular rectangular domains and assume uniform borehole depths. This paper proposes a Bayesian Generalized Coupled Markov Chains (BG-CMC) simulation method to overcome these limitations. First, an Active Domain Masking technique is introduced to map physical topographic boundaries directly onto the geostatistical grid, avoiding geometric distortions associated with traditional coordinate transformation methods. Second, a Spectral Decomposition of the transition probability matrix is utilized to enable variable-step conditional simulation; this effectively addresses data sparsity caused by unequal borehole lengths by ensuring that deep unconstrained regions asymptotically converge to the global stationary distribution. Third, a dynamic directional decoupling mechanism is established to handle irregular non-sedimentary boundaries (e.g., water bodies), preventing computational discontinuity while isolating the inference strictly within the active domain. Finally, a discrete inverse transform sampling algorithm is employed for the rigorous generation of geological states. Validated against the highly dynamic fluvial terraces of the lower Yangtze River, the results demonstrate the high capability of the proposed BG-CMC to reproduce stratigraphic patterns under undulating topography. The method provides robust, high-fidelity stochastic predictions in borehole-sparse regions, offering essential geological models for probabilistic environmental analysis and risk assessment in complex terrains.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Dynamics and probability density function of a stochastic cholera model with Black-Karasinski process and weak kernel distributed delays: application to Somalia outbreak data
abstract: Incorporating the ubiquitous nature of stochastic factors, delay effects, and the varying infectivity of Vibrio cholerae strains on cholera transmission, this paper proposes a stochastic cholera model with infinite distributed delay and Black-Karasinski process. First, the basic reproduction number is validated as the threshold governing the global dynamics of the corresponding deterministic model, and the existence and uniqueness of a global solution for the stochastic model are established, laying a foundation for subsequent analysis. Second, by constructing a stochastic Lyapunov function and employing stability theory for Markov processes, sufficient conditions for the existence of a stationary distribution of the stochastic model are derived. Furthermore, an exact expression for the probability density function near the quasi-endemic equilibrium is obtained. Additionally, sufficient conditions leading to disease extinction are provided. Finally, our numerical simulations indicate that neglecting delay effects leads to a significant overestimation of both the scale of the epidemic and the timing of its peak. Using the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, we validated the effectiveness of our model based on cholera data from Somalia, estimated the basic reproduction number of this outbreak, and provided a basis for formulating disease control strategies through sensitivity analysis.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Uncertainty-aware heavy-metal screening in urban stormwater runoff using SWMM-derived EMC records and ranking-robustness analysis
abstract: Urban stormwater drainage systems can rapidly transfer traffic-related heavy metals to receiving waters, particularly in highly impervious semi-arid catchments where long dry periods promote pollutant build-up. Resource-efficient, uncertainty-aware screening tools are therefore needed where continuous monitoring data are limited. This study examined Zn, Pb, and Cu in untreated stormwater runoff from District 10 of Tehran, Iran, using six Storm Water Management Model (SWMM)-derived event mean concentration (EMC) screening records evaluated against previously reported stormwater monitoring information. The retained records comprised six metal-specific EMC vectors and were not linked one-to-one to individually defined rainfall-runoff events or record-specific hydrometeorological descriptors. They were therefore treated as comparative screening inputs rather than as event-specific simulations. The model-derived EMCs were converted into benchmark-normalized metal quotients. Lognormal Monte Carlo simulation, empirical resampling, and upper-tail analysis were used to characterize aggregate uncertainty arising from inter-record concentration variability, while deterministic record rankings were evaluated through benchmark- and SWMM-sensitivity analyses. Record 4 produced the largest deterministic cumulative benchmark-normalized value within the reported EMC matrix, whereas Record 5 produced the smallest, but neither record was interpreted as a specific storm or hydrometeorological condition. Although Zn showed the highest model-derived EMCs, Pb was the dominant benchmark-normalized contributor because of its lower freshwater predicted no-effect concentration (PNEC). The framework separates sensitivity-based record-ranking robustness from aggregate probabilistic uncertainty and provides a transparent comparative screening method whose operational application requires validation using event-tagged monitoring and simulation outputs.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Network-aware deterioration risk and renewal prioritization for aging urban sewers: a gis-based simulation framework applied to Nam-gu, Ulsan, South Korea
abstract: Municipalities must decide which of their ageing sewers to renew first, yet many hold no inspection record at all. This paper asks how far renewal prioritization can be taken using only the attributes a utility already holds in its sewer geographic information system (GIS), and proposes a network-aware simulation framework to answer it: a material-specific Weibull model converts pipe age and its environmental stressors into a failure likelihood; a Manning-based hydraulic model on a geometrically rebuilt network graph converts pipe position into a failure consequence; their product defines pipe risk; an interpretable gradient-boosted surrogate emulates the deterioration engine; and a multi-objective genetic algorithm traces the trade-off between renewal spending and residual network risk. The framework is demonstrated on the complete public sewer network of Nam-gu, Ulsan, South Korea — 19,849 gravity pipes over 886.5 km, 68% of them older than thirty years, and without any inspection record. Its principal methodological contribution is a decision-relevant accuracy benchmark: although the surrogate reproduces only 57% of the variance of the simulated condition score, prioritizing on predicted rather than engine-computed risk retains 98.6–99.7% of the achievable risk reduction, because renewal decisions consume a rank order rather than a point estimate. Deterioration likelihood and failure consequence were approximately uncorrelated in rank across this network ( ρ = −0.03), so network position, and not age alone, sets the priority. All results are internal to the simulation: without inspection labels the surrogate emulates a mathematical process rather than measured defects, and its accuracy is not evidence of field-diagnostic skill. The framework is offered as a reproducible screening procedure for utilities holding a sewer GIS and no inspection data, designed to be recalibrated as inspection records arrive.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Fast-AHPSO for efficient source strength estimation of leakage sources with diverse spatial distribution patterns: application to industrial park (for CO$$_2$$, SO$$_2$$, NO$$_x$$) emergency response
abstract: Conventional source term estimation methods for elevated point sources are mostly limited to single-source scenarios and fail to quantify multiple simultaneous releases under dynamic meteorological conditions. Moreover, traditional Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Altruistic Heterogeneous Particle Swarm Optimization (AHPSO) suffer from premature convergence and long runtime. To address these issues, this paper proposes a fast source term estimation algorithm that integrates an improved Altruistic Heterogeneous Particle Swarm Optimization (Fast-AHPSO) with a multi-source coupled Gaussian plume correction model incorporating wind field, superposition, and temperature–humidity effects. Fast-AHPSO reduces computational time by lowering the frequency of altruistic operations and employing an early stopping mechanism. Experimental results show that Fast-AHPSO achieves high accuracy under both clustered and dispersed source layouts (average relative errors of 1.29% and 0.22%, respectively) and runs approximately ten times faster than AHPSO. The sensitivity analysis quantifies the impact of measurement noise (0–10%) and monitoring network density (6–18 sensors). Fast-AHPSO maintains a mean relative error below 5% even under 10% noise, and the 95% confidence intervals of inverted source strengths can be obtained. The spatial distribution of sources significantly affects inversion accuracy. Overall, this study offers an efficient and robust tool for multi-source term estimation in industrial parks, with explicit uncertainty quantification that supports stochastic environmental risk assessment and real-time emergency response.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Stochastic risk analysis of baltic emissions pathways under net-zero commitments
abstract: National net-zero targets are usually stated as fixed future commitments but emissions evolve under uncertainty. This paper develops a stochastic framework for assessing the likelihood that such targets will be met. The method is applied to the Baltic states and the results are compared with a wider European sample. The model combines sector-level emissions dynamics with uncertainty in land-use sinks and evaluates target attainment, breach duration, cumulative overshoot, and tail risk across five policy scenarios. The results show that the 2030 milestone is reached with high probability in all Baltic states. This mainly reflects the fact that current emissions are already relatively close to the required pathway from the 1990 baseline. Moreover, the short-run result does not extend to longer horizons: 2040 attainment differs across countries and scenarios, while probabilities of reaching the 2050 threshold remain close to zero in nearly all cases. Stronger policy assumptions reduce the size of overshoot but still do not produce a sufficient probability of meeting 2050 targets. For the Baltic states, moving from the passive to the aggressive scenario lowers tail-risk exposure by about 35%–59%, even though the chance of reaching the 2050 net-zero target remains very low.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Bayesian modelling of salinity profiles in the Volturno River mouth under depth dependence
abstract: Saltwater intrusion is a recurrent environmental hazard for Mediterranean coastal systems, and identifying which physico-chemical variables track salinity is central to monitoring design. Estimating such associations from depth-resolved profiles requires two features of the data to be addressed: the uncertainty of each depth-bin summary, arising from pooling readings taken at several stations along a steep longitudinal gradient, and the residual vertical dependence left after conditioning on the covariates. This paper proposes a Bayesian errors-in-variables-like model with a Gaussian process component for residual depth structure, applied to two synoptic campaigns in the Volturno River mouth (Italy) under contrasting winter and summer hydrological conditions. The results show that temperature is consistently associated with salinity, but the sign of the association differs between the two seasonal conditions during sampling: it is positive in winter and negative in summer within the reach occupied by the salt wedge. Dissolved oxygen is important in winter only. The residual depth amplitude is small in both campaigns, while the complementary full river reach analysis for the summer campaign yields a substantially larger residual depth component, showing that the fitted relationship is sensitive to the sampled river reach. Under near-perfect collinearity the ordering of the covariates is better identified than any individual coefficient, and is reported through posterior rank probabilities. A simulation study shows that the specification maintains nominal credible-interval coverage where a naive regression collapses to a few per cent and reverses a tracer coefficient’s sign in up to 45 per cent of replicates. Cross-validation on held-out depth bins supports predictive adequacy within each campaign, while over comparable river reaches the estimated relationships are specific to the contrasting hydrological regimes represented by the two campaigns and do not transfer between them.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Analysing uncertainty and sensitivity for riparian revegetation flood mitigation modelling in river networks
abstract: Uncertainties of hydraulic parameters in representing land-surface characteristics of revegetating riparian zones remains a critical limitation in hydrodynamic flood modelling, particularly when riparian revegetation is implemented as a nature-based solution (NbS) for downstream flood mitigation. This study presents an integrated and systematic framework for uncertainty and sensitivity analysis to evaluate the effectiveness of riparian revegetation in reducing downstream flood hazard, demonstrated in the Bundamba Creek sub-catchment, Australia. The framework combines efficient parameter space exploration using multiple sampling techniques, rain-on-grid hydrodynamic modelling, and an Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) surrogate model. Key hydraulic parameters, particularly Manning’s roughness associated with vegetation, are analysed within a realistic range of n = 0.07–0.26, representing sparse grass to dense riparian vegetation. An optimal sampling strategy is selected to ensure both global coverage and concentration within the most probable range of roughness ( n ≈ 0.10–0.20). The ANFIS model demonstrates strong predictive performance (NSE = 0.94; RMSE= 564 m 2 ), enabling rapid evaluation of a large number of scenarios. Results reveal that the most significant reduction in downstream high-hazard area occurs within critical roughness intervals ( n ≈ 0.13–0.16 and 0.22–0.24), where small increases in roughness lead to disproportionately large decreases in hazard extent. Sensitivity peaks at AEP = 1%, indicating that NbS effectiveness is maximized under moderate flood conditions, while the influence diminishes for extreme events. Uncertainty analysis demonstrates that maximum uncertainty occurs at intermediate-to-high rainfall thresholds, where flow transitions from channel-controlled to floodplain-dominated conditions, while uncertainty is significantly reduced during extreme events or very high rainfall. Ignoring uncertainty in Manning’s roughness may lead to misestimation of flood hazard, particularly near threshold rainfall conditions. The proposed framework provides a robust and computationally efficient approach for evaluating NbS performance while accounting for uncertainty at the catchment scale.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: A hybrid spectral-neurocomputing framework for stochastic risk assessment in aquatic nekton-plankton dynamics
abstract: The persistence and stability of aquatic ecosystems are strongly governed by nonlinear trophic interactions among zooplankton, phytoplankton, and piscivorous fish. While numerous computational studies exist, most rely on deterministic assumptions that overlook environmental randomness. To incorporate ecological uncertainty more realistically, we develop a stochastic extension of a tri-trophic aquatic ecosystem model by embedding random environmental perturbations into nutrient cycling, predation, and harvesting processes. The resulting system is formulated using stochastic differential equations with multiplicative noise to reflect variability arising from fluctuating toxin transfer, external disturbances, and nutrient irregularities. To efficiently solve this nonlinear stochastic model, we introduce a hybrid numerical strategy that couples spectral collocation with feedforward neural networks, enabling stable and high-fidelity approximations of the stochastic dynamics. The framework is employed to investigate stability transitions, ecological thresholds, and long-term persistence under fluctuating environments. Numerical experiments confirm the robustness of the proposed methodology, achieving absolute errors as low as $$10^{-11}$$ in the deterministic regime and $$10^{-3}$$ under stochastic forcing-outperforming spectral schemes by several orders of magnitude. Convergence is further validated through error distribution metrics and regression-based diagnostics. The stochastic framework reveals critical insights into how random perturbations influence ecological resilience and extinction risks, offering advantages over purely deterministic models. These findings demonstrate that hybrid stochastic neuro-computing provides an effective pathway for risk-aware modeling, forecasting, and sustainable management of aquatic food webs under environmental variability.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Censor-aware interrupted time-series modeling with a Bayesian hierarchical framework for multi-regime environmental time series under detection-limit censoring
abstract: Environmental monitoring programs frequently generate long-term time-series data affected by detection-limit censoring, structural disturbances, and non-stationary variability, creating challenges for reliable environmental inference. This study develops a censor-aware stochastic framework that integrates regression-on-order-statistics reconstruction, interrupted time-series analysis, Bayesian hierarchical modeling, counterfactual reconstruction, and physically constrained forecasting. The framework is applied to airborne radionuclide monitoring data collected between 2000 and 2024 at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP), a deep geological radioactive waste repository in the United States, following an underground radiological release event in 2014. The analysis identified distinct radionuclide response regimes following the disturbance. Gross alpha and gross beta activities exhibited transient increases followed by gradual recovery toward baseline conditions, consistent with short-term atmospheric perturbations. In contrast, americium-241 ( 241 Am) and plutonium-239 + 240 ( 239+240 Pu) showed sustained post-event elevation, indicating a persistent structural shift associated with long-lived particle-reactive radionuclides and ongoing resuspension processes. Plutonium-238 ( 238 Pu) displayed intermediate behavior characterized by prolonged elevation and nonlinear stabilization. Gamma-radiation-emitting radionuclides remained largely below detection limits, suggesting that apparent variability was primarily constrained by analytical sensitivity rather than environmental change. Bayesian hierarchical modeling improved uncertainty characterization under sparse detection conditions, while physically constrained forecasting produced stable projections through 2030. The proposed framework provides a transferable methodology for environmental monitoring systems characterized by detection-limit censoring, regime transitions, and long-term uncertainty, with potential applications in contamination assessment, atmospheric monitoring, and environmental risk evaluation.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Fitting the background intensity in ETAS models using regression-based poisson point process models
abstract: The Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence model (ETAS) is a widely used self-exciting spatio-temporal point process for earthquake occurrence, in which seismicity is represented as the superposition of background events and triggered events. In many ETAS implementations, the background component is estimated non-parametrically, typically through kernel smoothing. Although flexible, this approach can limit formal inference and make it difficult to incorporate structured information, such as spatial covariates and mark-related features, into the background component. This paper proposes an ETAS formulation with a regression-based background component. The standard ETAS triggering structure and declustering logic are preserved, while the background component is modelled using a regression-based approach. This provides a more interpretable representation of background seismicity and extends the range of information that can be incorporated into ETAS models. We evaluate the proposed methodology through a simulation study and illustrate its practical usefulness with an application to an Italian earthquake catalogue. The results show that the proposed approach improves the recovery of structured background intensities while maintaining competitive estimation of the triggered component.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: A novel severity categorization methodology for compound dry and hot events and its spatiotemporal analysis over the Mediterranean CORDEX domain
abstract: Compound dry and hot events (CDHEs), driven by the simultaneous occurrence of dry and hot conditions, pose increasing threats to socio-ecological systems under a changing climate. While there is extensive literature focusing on droughts and heatwaves individually, studies addressing their combined impacts remain limited. Given that the compound effects of these extremes can exceed the sum of their individual consequences, adopting a compound-event perspective is essential for effective risk assessment and management. This study investigates the spatiotemporal variability in the frequency, duration, and severity of summer CDHEs over land areas of the Mediterranean CORDEX domain during a 75-year period. In addition, a novel classification framework is proposed to assess CDHE severity by combining the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) and the Heatwave Magnitude Index daily (HWMId). Through this integrated approach, CDHEs are classified into three levels, with C3 representing the most severe category. Temporal analyses revealed breakpoints in time series of both CDHE duration and affected area extent across all categories around the 1990s, followed by a shift toward significantly increasing trends. Over the last 25 years, CDHEs have occurred across all but a very small portion of the study area, and the total number of CDHE days has exceeded 120 in some regions. During this period, summer heatwaves were more frequently accompanied by droughts than in earlier decades, especially across Western Asia, North Africa, and European Russia. The results offer valuable insights for decision-makers and stakeholders in developing effective adaptation strategies to reduce the adverse impacts of CDHEs in hotspot areas.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: An enhanced quantum reservoir computing framework for hydrological time series modeling
abstract: Accurate streamflow forecasting is essential for water resource management, yet it remains challenging due to the highly non-stationary and volatile nature of hydrological time series. This study examines an enhanced Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) framework for one-step-ahead monthly dischage forecasting of the Buzău River across three periods. The framework implements a dual-axis rotation encoding scheme to map scalar inputs onto the Bloch sphere, coupled with a fixed, multi-layered parametric reservoir featuring a cyclic Controlled-Z (CZ) entanglement topology. Operating under a continuous state-passing strategy, the network processes historical dependencies through a single forward pass over a static 4-qubit system, shifting all learning optimization to a lightweight classical ridge regression readout. QRC achieved test NSE values of 0.693–0.738. While QNN and VQR yielded lower MAE and RMSE values across all three configurations, QRC consistently outperformed BPNN. ESN achieved slightly lower errors throughout, whereas performance comparisons with ELM and LSTM varied by configuration. The primary empirical contribution of this study is a compact, fixed-reservoir architecture that successfully avoids the iterative optimization of quantum-gate parameters.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: Spatiotemporal dependence in floods with the Heffernan and Tawn conditional exceedance model: from synthesis to a new application
abstract: Flood behavior is characterized by complex spatial and temporal interdependencies that have been often overlooked in hazard and risk assessment, where traditional approaches have been either assuming independence across large regions or imposing uniform return periods within catchments. By contrast, the need for a crucial change in flood risk assessment has been recognized in recent decades. The conditional extremes model by Heffernan and Tawn, originally proposed in 2004, has emerged as an effective tool to represent extremal spatial dependence across scales, enabling the simulation of synthetic events that preserve observed multivariate dependence structures. The first part of the present manuscript presents a thematic synthesis of studies applying the Heffernan and Tawn model to floods, covering methodological developments, characterization of spatiotemporal dependence, derivation of boundary conditions for hydraulic modelling, integration with risk and impact modelling, and continental-scale applications. The synthesis organizes a fragmented body of literature, identifies common underlying patterns, and aims at facilitating the application of the model in operational flood risk assessment. The second part of the manuscript illustrates a practical implementation of the model to discharges measured at five stations along the Lambro River (Northern Italy). In the presented application, specific attention has been devoted to the scaling properties of joint return periods for synthetic events generated through Monte Carlo simulations, comparing them with the limiting cases of complete dependence and independence. The generation of 10,000 years of events demonstrated that, even within a small river system, simultaneous exceedances at all stations were substantially rarer than implied by complete dependence, supporting the explicit modelling of spatial dependence when estimating joint return periods.
journal: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

title: The political economy of flavored tobacco: comparative policy mapping of flavor restrictions for cigarettes and e-cigarettes
abstract: Background In the past five years, the market for flavored tobacco and nicotine products has become increasingly global, while policies have fragmented along national lines. Flavors attract new consumers, keep existing consumers addicted, and can worsen the negative health effects of smoking. Many of these concerns apply to newer products such as e-cigarettes, but with the added complexity for policymakers of differential risks for certain groups within the population. We conduct a comparative policy mapping of flavored cigarette and e-cigarette regulations in 200 national jurisdictions to build an original dataset of global flavor policy. We classify the policy combinations into four distinct approaches and generate several hypotheses to explain global policy variation. Results By comparing flavor restrictions across a large number of jurisdictions, we show that countries fall into four distinct groups. 41 countries restrict flavors in neither product, 16 restrict both, 40 restrict flavored e-cigarettes more than cigarettes, and 39 restrict flavored cigarettes more than e-cigarettes. In exploring several potential explanations for policy variation, we find that countries’ political systems, state capacity, and the role of states in the global tobacco economy correlate with different policies on flavor restrictions in cigarettes and e-cigarettes. Conclusions Despite global calls to ban flavored tobacco and nicotine products, policymakers, tobacco control advocates, tobacco industry representatives and other relevant actors are divided as to how to regulate them, resulting in a patchwork of national policies. Comparing how countries regulate flavored cigarettes and flavored e-cigarettes highlights the barriers to adopting a global approach to a globalizing market: government capacity, governance type, and a country’s place within the global economy all contribute to countries taking different policy approaches despite a globalized product market and shared body of current scientific evidence.

title: The gates of influence: a mixed-methods analysis of gates foundation media funding and discourse in global health
abstract: Background Over the last century, philanthropic foundations have become prominent global health actors increasingly involved in shaping the global health agenda. Concurrently, media organisations have become increasingly reliant on philanthropic funding as media consumption patterns have changed. Philanthropic foundations, such as the Gates Foundation, are positioned to offer financial support to media organisations while being provided with a strategic avenue to draw attention to particular issues and garner support. However, positive media narratives of the Gates Foundation and their focus on market-oriented vertical solutions to global health may divert attention and efforts away from other important horizontal approaches. While these critiques exist, no systematic analyses of the Foundation and their portrayal in the media has been conducted to date. This study aimed to analyse media portrayals of the Gates Foundation across the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia between 2013 and 2023, and to examine whether the Foundation’s grant funding of media organisations influences these portrayals. Results Utilising a mixed-methods approach, this empirical study uncovered that media portrayals predominantly frame the Gates Foundation positively and favour coverage of vertical, disease-specific approaches to global health, particularly infectious diseases, while giving limited coverage to broader horizontal approaches. We found the Foundation donated $291 million USD in grants to media organisations across the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia between 2013 and 2023. However, we found insufficient evidence of an association between this grant funding and positive portrayals ( p = > 0.05, OR = 0.5). Limitations associated with sourcing comprehensive funding data, and the complexities of intermediary funding raise important questions about transparency and media independence that requires further exploration. Conclusions Media coverage of global health philanthropic organisations and the influence of media funding on this coverage has had limited scholarly attention to date. The predominance of positive portrayals and coverage of vertical interventions, despite insufficient evidence of an association with grant funding, highlights the value of independent reporting that critically examines prominent philanthropic actors and adequately addresses the full spectrum of global health challenges and solutions.

title: Impact of COVID-19 outbreaks and border control measures on dengue cases in four Asia-Pacific countries
abstract: Background Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) and COVID-19-related border controls might have influenced global dengue transmission dynamics. Taking the imposition of travel restrictions during the pandemic as a natural experiment, this study aimed to explore potential associations between border restrictions and dengue prevalence in selected non-endemic and endemic Asia-Pacific countries during the pandemic using a retrospective prediction approach. Methods Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) were employed to model dengue case trends from 2009 to 2019, characterizing transmission periodicity and incidence patterns during the pandemic. Correlation analyses were conducted to examine possible associations between air passenger arrivals and reported dengue cases across four countries in 2020, using passenger volume data. SARIMA models were used to estimate counterfactual dengue incidence in the absence of COVID-19-related NPIs, and predicted cases were compared with observed cases to assess deviations potentially attributable to control measures. Results Compared with the 2009–2019 epidemic seasons, dengue activity in China and Australia remained below historical levels in 2020, while Thailand’s activity was slightly lower than its historical peak, with cases fluctuating within the moderate-to-high range. Singapore’s dengue activity remained consistently above historical maximum levels. Correlation analyses suggested a positive linear association between international air passenger arrivals and dengue cases in non-endemic countries, with Pearson correlation coefficients exceeding 0.75; however, such associations were not apparent in countries with endemic (Thailand and Singapore). Retrospective predictions indicated that COVID-19-related border restrictions might be associated with lower dengue case counts in China and Australia (96.97% and 98.16% lower than predictions, respectively), whereas observed data in Thailand and Singapore were 79.62% and 164.31% higher than historical trend-based predictions. Conclusion Prior to 2020, the four countries exhibited distinct seasonal dengue patterns. This study indicated that pandemic-related border controls might have influenced dengue trends in selected non-endemic countries but appeared to have a limited association in endemic settings, where local transmission remained predominant. These findings suggested that mitigating dengue importation required an integrated framework that synchronised risk-stratified screening for arrivals, vector surveillance, and strengthened multilateral collaboration. These insights offer a strategic roadmap for global efforts against the increasing threat of dengue.

title: Correction: Lived experiences of migrant men witnessing and surviving sexual violence in European transit spaces
Non-communicable diseases mortality attributable to lifestyle risk factors in 5 Latin American countries: a PRIME model study
abstract: Background Non-communicable diseases (NCD) are the leading causes of death in Latin American countries, yet the burden of NCD attributable to lifestyle risk factors in the region remains poorly understood. In this study, we aimed to estimate the proportion and number of NCD deaths attributable to lifestyle risk factors in five Latin American countries. We used data from national surveys conducted in five Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and El Salvador), comprising 259,327 participants. Self-reported data on fruit and vegetable consumption, physical activity, alcohol use, and tobacco smoking were stratified by sex and age group. The Preventable Risk Integrated Model (PRIME) was applied to compare baseline distributions of lifestyle risk factors with a counterfactual scenario based on World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations, estimating changes in annual NCD deaths due to cardiovascular disease (CVD), diabetes, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in 2021. Results We estimated that 184,111 NCD deaths could have been prevented or delayed across the five countries by adhering to WHO lifestyle recommendations. Brazil (46.1%) and Argentina (30.1%) accounted for the largest shares of preventable deaths. CVD represented 46.3% of the total preventable deaths. Tobacco smoking contributed to 56.8% of the preventable deaths, followed by physical inactivity (25.0%), inadequate fruit and vegetable intake (11.0%), and alcohol use (6.9%). Conclusions Our findings provide population-level estimates of NCD mortality attributable to modifiable lifestyle risk factors in Latin America. Strengthening preventive strategies that target these key behaviors could substantially reduce the NCD burden in the region.

title: Integrating the social and solidarity economy into global health: towards structural transformation for equity, resilience, and sustainability
abstract: Global health is shaped by complex and interdependent challenges across social, commercial, environmental, technological, and political domains that cannot be solved by the health sector alone. In response, alternative economic models and paradigms have gained attention. The concept of the Social and Solidarity Economy (SSE)—formally recognized in a 2023 United Nations resolution—has emerged as a promising approach. This paper examines how SSE has been addressed in global health scholarship and explores its potential contributions to equity, resilience, and sustainability, not simply as a normative framework but to provide an institutional approach to realize these norms. To illustrate this potential, we focus on migration health, a key global health agenda that highlights how multiple determinants of health interact to influence the health of populations. Migration health exemplifies how SSE’s inclusive and solidarity-based practices can engage with these determinants while promoting cross-border learning and advocacy for more equitable, resilient, and sustainable systems. We conducted a targeted literature review to examine the extent to which SSE has been addressed in global health scholarship, followed by an analytic mapping of SSE contributions to social, commercial, and environmental determinants of health, as well as to cross-cutting areas of advocacy and reform. The review shows that explicit engagement with SSE in global health literature remains scarce. Nonetheless, illustrative examples demonstrate that SSE initiatives can reduce inequalities, create inclusive employment, strengthen community networks, counter harmful commercial practices, and promote sustainable food, energy, and housing systems. These examples highlight SSE’s capacity to address determinants of health in ways that conventional approaches often overlook, and to address the lack of traction experienced by other transformative frameworks. We argue that, although SSE remains marginal in global health discourse, it holds substantial and underrecognized potential as an integrative and community-driven approach for advancing equity, resilience, and sustainability. Recognizing and embedding SSE within global health frameworks is both timely and necessary for addressing the diverse determinants that shape population health. Noting why previous equity-oriented health and economic frameworks have struggled to achieve structural change, we situate SSE within this broader question of accountability in global health governance.

title: Profiling health for equitable benefit-sharing in the global critical mineral value-chain: a lens from East and Southern Africa
abstract: Critical minerals used in low-carbon technologies are vital for the global energy transition, but with disproportionate benefit for wealthy countries and risks from their extraction in the Global South. Globally, African countries, particularly in East and Southern Africa, are reported to hold high shares of global reserves of critical minerals such as cobalt, manganese, graphite, copper, nickel and lithium. Large- and small-scale extraction of these critical minerals has thus escalated due to global demand. Despite regional policies to protect health, in practice limited attention is given to health in the sector. The paper outlines the under-reporting of health risks and impacts, particularly in artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM), in vulnerable workers, and in adjacent and displaced communities, women and children in both small and large-scale mining. This leaves a significant information gap in implementing the 2025 South Africa-led G20 Summit call for more equitable benefit-sharing with local communities in the global critical mineral value-chain. Evidence presented in this paper on efforts to assess and manage the health risks in East and Southern Africa points to the role that Health Impact Assessment (HIA) can play as an internationally recognised tool to lever recognition of the distribution of health risks, and to link this to options and duties to plan for, regulate and embed prevention and control of these risks in sector activities, including through inclusive decision-making on the findings. Evidence indicates that Environmental Impact Assessments do not meet this need. The authors thus argue for HIA to be institutionalised as a duty in sites of critical mineral extraction and processing. In East and Southern Africa this calls for strengthened capacities, legal mandates and duties for, and widened implementation and reporting of HIAs, responsive also to ASM contexts, to embed this process as a key early step for equitable benefit-sharing in the global value chain, and as one lever for a more just green transition.

title: Institutional barriers and professional integration of physicians with an Arab migration background in Germany: a qualitative study
abstract: Background Germany faces a persistent physicians shortage f, particularly in hospitals and rural regions. Migrant physicians, especially from Arab countries, represent a crucial component. However, their professional integration is shaped by complex licensure procedures, demanding working conditions, administrative burdens and sociocultural dynamics. While previous research has examined structural and regulatory barriers, limited empirical evidence exists on integration processes from the perspective of Arab physicians themselves. Purpose This study aimed to explore the challenges and experiences of professional integration among physicians with an Arab migration background in the German healthcare system. Particular attention was paid to credential recognition, workplace conditions, language-related challenges, discrimination, cultural dynamics and patient-related barriers in order to identify institutional factors shaping integration processes. Methods A qualitative research design was employed. Twenty physicians (16 men, 4 women) originating from Syria, Lebanon, Egypt and Yemen participated in semi-structured interviews conducted in Arabic or German. Participants were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling. Interviews lasted 45–60 min and were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and translated where necessary. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify patterns and overarching themes across narratives. The analysis involved iterative coding and theme development, reflexive consideration of researchers’ interpretive roles and examination of divergent and contradictory cases. Theoretical saturation was assessed after approximately 18 interviews, with two additional interviews conducted to confirm that no new core topics emerged. Results Five interconnected themes were identified. Participants described the German healthcare system as structurally reliable and well-resourced but characterized by high administrative workload, staff shortages and time pressure. Licensure procedures were experienced as lengthy, opaque and psychologically stressful. Administrative complexity and insufficient onboarding hindered early integration. Language barriers were primarily situational, relating to dialects and colloquial communication rather than medical terminology. Approximately half of participants reported experiences of discrimination, mainly from patients. Shared language and cultural background with Arab patients were perceived as professional resources that enhanced trust and communication. Participants also highlighted systemic barriers affecting patients with migration backgrounds, particularly language barriers and limited knowledge of the healthcare system. Participants additionally described an intermediary role in which their linguistic and cultural resources helped bridge communication and institutional gaps between patients with migration backgrounds and healthcare services. Across themes, professional integration emerged as a multidimensional and relational process shaped by institutional structures, workplace conditions, cultural dynamics and experiences of belonging and difference rather than solely as an individual adaptation process. Conclusion Professional integration of Arab migrant physicians in Germany is strongly influenced by institutional structures, administrative processes and workplace conditions. While Germany offers robust structural prerequisites for medical practice, deficits in recognition procedures, onboarding, intercultural institutionalization and administrative support pose significant challenges. The findings suggest that integration should be approached as a reciprocal institutional process rather than solely as an adaptation task for migrant physicians. Structural reforms including streamlined licensure processes, structured induction programs, expanded interpreting services and systematic intercultural training are essential to support migrant physicians and strengthen the resilience and equity of the German healthcare system.

title: Factors associated with suboptimal adherence to type 2 diabetes medications among internally displaced persons in camps in Al-Dana subdistrict, Northwest Syria: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Background Chronic disease management is challenging in conflict settings, with fragmented health care systems and unstable access to health care. In Northwest Syria, millions of internally displaced persons (IDPs) live in camps where insecurity, geographic barriers, and disrupted health care services complicate the management of noncommunicable diseases, such as type 2 diabetes mellitus. This study aimed to assess medication adherence among Syrian IDPs living in camps in Al-Dana subdistrict in Northwest Syria and to identify the factors associated with suboptimal medication adherence. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted between January and March 2025 among adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus attending two health centers serving IDP camps. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, clinical history, health care access, health literacy, and medication adherence, which was also determined using the Arabic version of the Adherence to Refills and Medications Scale (ARMS). Descriptive statistics and stepwise logistic regression modeling and adjusted odds ratios (AOR) were used to identify the factors associated with adherence. Results Medication adherence was low, with 99.1% of participants demonstrating some degree of nonadherence (mean ARMS score = 21.10 ± 5.59). Higher adherence was associated with attending the Albarakeh health center (AOR = 37.68; 95% CI: 13.02–132.67) and receiving encouragement through regular physician visits and access to health information (AOR = 4.732; 95% CI: 2.022–12.40). Lower adherence was associated with female sex (AOR = 0.332; 95% CI: 0.149–0.713), skipping medication due to long distances to health facilities (AOR = 0.309; 95% CI: 0.089–0.993), and discontinuing medication due to side effects (AOR = 0.280; 95% CI: 0.098–0.728). Conclusions Adherence to type 2 diabetes mellitus medications among IDPs in Northwest Syria is critically low and influenced by a combination of structural, geographic, and behavioral factors. Adherence is determined primarily by structural factors, whereas patients’ demographic characteristics play a significantly smaller role in medication adherence in the cohorts in the region studied.

title: Global systematic review of how climate change degrades the wellbeing and health of Indigenous children
abstract: Background Climate change worsens global health, with Indigenous children among the most vulnerable. Despite increasing research on climate-related health impacts, Indigenous children’s unique vulnerabilities remain underrepresented. This is the first review to synthesise systematically the global evidence on how climate change impacts the health of Indigenous children. Methods We consolidated reported health outcomes directly caused by climate change in Indigenous children. We adhered to PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines and followed a reflexive framework that considered researcher positionality, Indigenous definitions of health, and ongoing Indigenous engagement. We did a systematic search of five databases on 2 March 2025 and collaboratively screened eligible studies on climate-related health outcomes in Indigenous children and pregnant women, assessing them using the mixed-methods appraisal tool. A convergent integrated synthesis approach mapped exposure-outcome patterns and guided a theme-based narrative analysis. Meta-analysis was not feasible due to study heterogeneity. Results Fifty-three studies met inclusion criteria, comprising 16 qualitative, 23 quantitative non-randomised, 6 quantitative descriptive and 8 mixed-method designs. Five main health outcomes emerged: ( i ) psychosocial and cultural wellbeing, ( ii ) malnutrition, ( iii ) infectious diseases, ( iv ) perinatal health, and ( v ) morbidity and mortality. Reflecting the interconnected and relational nature of Indigenous health conceptualisations, most studies addressed multiple climate exposures and outcomes. Psychosocial and cultural wellbeing was the most cross-cutting theme, interconnected with all other health domains. Heat exposure and seasonal and hydroclimatic variability were the most frequently linked climate exposures. Conclusions Indigenous children across diverse contexts are experiencing adverse climate-related health outcomes. Our review consolidates the evidence base to inform culturally grounded, strengths-based responses that engage Indigenous Knowledge systems and younger generations. Advancing this field requires more geographically diverse, disaggregated, and methodologically rigorous research.

title: The securitization of global slow-onset risks/threats: long COVID, a case study
abstract: This paper investigates why Long Covid, despite affecting millions globally and posing a serious threat to public health and economic stability, remains largely absent from contemporary security agendas. It argues that the condition’s chronic, diffuse nature presents a temporal mismatch with existing security frameworks designed for acute, visible crises. Drawing on the Copenhagen School’s securitization theory and Olaf Corry’s concept of “riskification,” the paper shows how structural, normative, and political obstacles—namely the difficulty of constructing chronic disability as collective harm within dominant security imaginaries—prevent Long Covid from being framed as an existential threat. Comparing the response to Long Covid with that of climate change and acute Covid-19, it reveals how scientific uncertainty, fragmented governance, and limited public awareness undermine mobilization. U.S. reluctance to lead, domestic political fragmentation, and a cultural emphasis on individual responsibility further diminish the prospects for securitizing moves. Internationally, institutions like the UN and WHO exhibit similar inertia due to ambiguous mandates and competing priorities. The paper concludes that Long Covid exposes critical gaps in traditional security thinking, particularly in addressing slow-onset, mass-disabling threats. As similar slow-onset disabling conditions may emerge in future biological crises, prevailing security conceptions could leave societies insufficiently prepared. The paper therefore uses securitization theory diagnostically to argue that political conceptions of security should better account for chronic harm and disability.

title: Nursing as a systems profession in One Health: opportunities across the Quadripartite action tracks
abstract: The One Health agenda has progressed from a conceptual acknowledgement of human–animal–environment interdependence to a global framework for coordinated action, exemplified by the Quadripartite One Health Joint Plan of Action (2022–2026). The Joint Plan sets out high-level objectives across six action tracks, while the 2023 national implementation guide supports countries in adopting and adapting those objectives to their own contexts. This paper examines nursing as a systems profession within One Health, using the six action tracks as an analytic framework. Across the tracks, we distinguish established nursing functions from opportunities for those functions to be more explicitly recognised, formalised and evaluated during national implementation. We identify four recurring functions: continuity and coordination; early recognition, monitoring and escalation; risk communication, education and community engagement; and the implementation of preventive and protective practices. Their application varies across action-track objectives, including outbreak preparedness and response, food safety, antimicrobial stewardship and environmental health. The scope and form of these contributions also vary according to professional regulation, education, workforce capacity, service configuration and participation in governance. We derive track-informed implications for national adaptation, workforce development, service design and research, and identify the conditions under which nursing contributions can be explicitly recognised and evaluated within national One Health implementation.

title: Quantitative assessment of national essential medicines lists processes: a descriptive study of 143 countries
abstract: Background The National Essential Medicines List (NEML) selection process is a foundational component of an essential medicines based policy, and the NEML itself is a key policy tool. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidance for policy development that aligns with the Accountability for Reasonableness (AFR) framework, along with a model Essential Medicines List (EML) to support NEML selection process development. An effective selection process is one that aligns with international guidelines and leads to the selection of a NEML that addresses the priority healthcare needs of a nation. This study uses a previously developed 16-item instrument to measure NEML selection process design effectiveness for all countries with publicly available information and examines AFR condition sub scores. Methods NEML selection process design for countries with publicly available information was identified through a document review. A 16-item instrument was used to score the NEML selection process design effectiveness. AFR conditions sub scores were also determined by aggregating item scores mapped to each condition. Results Of 159 WHO member countries with a NEML, 143 (90%) with publicly available process information were identified and included by the author. NEML selection process design total effectiveness scores (TES) ranged from 2% (Mauritius) to 88% (Brazil), with a mean of 47% (SD 18.7%), a median of 49%, and mode 41%; 6 countries (4%) scored above 80%. Mean AFR sub scores were highest for relevance (61%), followed by publicity (40.4%), enforcement (35%), and revisions and appeals (29.1%). By WHO region, mean total scores were highest in South-East Asia (57.7%), followed by Europe (54%) and the Americas (53.3%), and lowest in the Eastern Mediterranean (17.8%). When aggregated by World Bank Income Classification (WBIC), mean TES was greatest for Lower-Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) (50%), followed by, Upper-Middle-Income Countries (UMICs) (49%), High-Income Countries (HICs) (47%), and finally Low-Income Countries (LICs) (38%). Conclusions National Essential Medicines List selection process design effectiveness varies widely across countries and regions, with consistently low scores for revisions and appeals. Assessing processes using standardized tools can highlight areas for improvement and support alignment with WHO guidelines and AFR conditions. Strengthening these processes may improve policy design, responsiveness to national health priorities, and equitable access to essential medicines.

title: Commercial interests in health policy dialogues: a qualitative content analysis of NEDLAC’s engagement with South Africa’s Health Promotion Levy
abstract: Background Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are rising rapidly in South Africa, prompting the introduction of the Health Promotion Levy (HPL) in 2018 to reduce the consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages. However, the levy remains below the rate recommended by the World Health Organization. One of the central institutions involved in the policy process leading up to and following the introduction of the HPL was the National Economic Development and Labour Council (NEDLAC), a statutory body designed to promote dialogue between government, business, labour, and community constituencies. This study examined NEDLAC’s mandate and its actual role in the HPL process, with particular attention to the inclusivity and transparency of its deliberations. Results Using an exploratory case study design, the research drew on qualitative content analysis of documents obtained through an access to information request made under South Africa’s Promotion of Access to Information Act 2 of 2000. The findings indicate that NEDLAC’s engagement with the HPL process fell short of its mandate to advance social equity and inclusive participation in economic decision-making. Community representatives, one of NEDLAC’s four official constituencies, were absent from all deliberations on the levy. In contrast, business representatives dominated the discussions, often advancing arguments aligned with the interests of the sugar industry and emphasising potential job losses despite limited supporting evidence. Moreover, the process lacked transparency, particularly regarding the authorship of NEDLAC’s HPL Report and the presentation of evidence used to support its conclusions. Conclusions NEDLAC’s handling of the HPL illustrates how participatory governance structures may, in practice, enable industry influence and weaken public health objectives. To enhance the integrity and effectiveness of policy dialogue on health-related fiscal measures, NEDLAC should adopt clearer procedural guidelines to ensure inclusive representation, strengthen transparency through public access to documentation, and institutionalise the role of civil society in its processes. Such reforms are essential to align participatory mechanisms with public health goals and to safeguard them from corporate capture.

title: Artificial intelligence for climate–health early warning systems in the Horn of Africa: opportunities, challenges, and a roadmap for action
abstract: Climate extremes, conflict, and population displacement converge in the Horn of Africa to accelerate outbreaks of climate-sensitive infectious diseases, whereas existing health surveillance systems remain fragmented and largely reactive. This Perspective examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to strengthen climate–health early warning by integrating satellite earth observations, routine disease surveillance, and mobility-based vulnerability indicators into anticipatory decision support systems. Drawing on global experience and region-specific constraints, we identified critical barriers to implementation, including data fragmentation, infrastructure gaps, workforce shortages, governance silos, and unresolved ethical risks. We propose a five-layer conceptual framework for an AI-enabled Climate–Health Early Warning System (CHEWS) tailored to fragile and conflict-affected settings, alongside a phased regional policy roadmap anchored within the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD). Emphasizing data sovereignty, participatory governance, and privacy-by-design, this study positions AI-CHEWS as a feasible pathway for shifting the region from reactive outbreak responses to anticipatory public health actions that enhance climate resilience and equity. Clinical Trial Number: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

title: Organising cross-border care after arrival: receiving-system challenges in a China–Vietnam border region
abstract: Background Cross-border healthcare is increasingly visible in border regions where patient mobility develops faster than the institutional arrangements needed to support care. Existing research has often examined why patients seek care abroad, while less is known about how receiving health systems organise care after cross-border patients enter local hospitals. This study examined the receiving-system challenges faced by Guangxi, China, in responding to cross-border healthcare demand from Vietnamese patients. Methods A qualitative study was conducted in Guangxi using semi-structured interviews with 35 participants, including 6 policymakers, 9 hospital administrators, 11 healthcare providers, and 9 Vietnamese patients. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling. Data were collected between March 2024 and May 2025. Interviews were conducted in Chinese, with Vietnamese-Chinese interpretation provided when needed for Vietnamese patients. Data were analysed using thematic analysis. Results Six interrelated receiving-system challenges were identified across the pre-treatment, treatment, and post-treatment stages of care: pre-arrival preparation and hospital admission coordination, patient-authorized clinical documentation transfer and verification, language mediation and culturally responsive communication, patient-and-family navigation and inpatient support, billing documentation and claim-support navigation, and structured post-discharge follow-up after return to Vietnam. These challenges show that receiving cross-border patients requires practical arrangements that connect admission preparation, usable clinical information, communication, family involvement, payment documentation, and follow-up into a coherent care process. Conclusions Cross-border healthcare in the Guangxi-Vietnam border setting should be understood as a receiving-system coordination challenge. For border-region health systems where formal cross-border arrangements remain limited, strengthening receiving-system readiness may help make care safer, more understandable, and more continuous for patients whose treatment trajectories cross national boundaries.

title: From rupture to recourse: building a new economic order for health
Institutional quality and pandemic resilience: cross-country evidence on health and economic outcomes during COVID-19
abstract: Background The COVID-19 pandemic exposed large cross-country differences in mortality, vaccination rollout, and economic recovery. We examine whether stronger pre-pandemic institutions were associated with better pandemic performance and whether vaccination rollout helps explain part of that relationship. We combine 2019 World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators with COVID-19 outcomes, policy measures, World Development Indicators, and V-Dem electoral democracy data, estimating cross-country regressions and a temporally ordered exploratory mediation model using vaccination by September 2021 and deaths accrued in the fourth quarter of 2021. Results In full multivariable specifications, a one-unit increase in the WGI composite is associated with 384 fewer reported COVID-19 deaths per million, 1,860 fewer excess deaths per million, and 15.5% points higher full vaccination coverage by end-2021. These associations remain in robustness checks using V-Dem electoral democracy controls, WGI principal-component measures, timing-specific outcomes, and influence diagnostics. Institutional quality is not robustly associated with GDP growth in 2020; its positive association with GDP growth in 2021 persists but is weaker after controlling for OxCGRT economic-support policies. The exploratory mediation decomposition is consistent with an indirect path through vaccination representing about 35% of the total association between institutional quality and late-2021 mortality. Conclusions Pre-pandemic institutional quality was consistently associated with pandemic health outcomes and vaccine deployment, while economic associations were more phase-specific. The findings are observational and should not be read as definitive causal estimates, but they underscore the relevance of governance capacity for future pandemic preparedness.

title: Political prioritization of alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverage taxation in Uganda: Agenda dynamics amidst a shifting funding landscape
abstract: Introduction Uganda faces a rising burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) at a time when pressure to mobilize domestic health financing is increasing. These challenges have become more acute since January 2025, when geopolitical shifts and donor fiscal tightening led to substantial reductions in external health funding. Consequently, policymakers have renewed interest in health taxes as a mechanism both to reduce consumption of harmful products and generate domestic revenue for health. While tobacco taxation has received sustained policy attention, largely due to the influence of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, considerably less is known about the political dynamics shaping alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) taxation. This study therefore examines the factors contributing to the relatively low prioritization of alcohol and SSB taxes within Uganda’s policy agenda. Methods Guided by the framework on political priority, we conducted 25 semi-structured interviews with stakeholders from government, parliament, civil society, academia, industry, and the media. We also reviewed 22 documents from 2015 to 2025, including policy papers, fiscal records, parliamentary debates, and industry materials. We analyzed the data thematically following an inductive thematic analysis approach. Coding was informed by the framework and strengthened through triangulation across interviews and documentary sources to enhance credibility. Results We identified three levels of barriers. First, transnational norms promoted health taxes, but regional tax harmonization commitments within the East African community constrained national policy space. Second, domestic advocacy was weakened by fragmented ministerial mandates, limited local evidence, retreating policy entrepreneurs, and industry lobbying. Third, within the national political environment, the multiparty legislative dynamics, the high cost of sponsoring private members’ bills, and revenue-centric fiscal framing limited traction. The 2025 donor financing contraction acted as a focusing event that revived debate on health taxes primarily as domestic health financing stabilization instruments rather than NCD prevention tools. Conclusion While policymakers support health taxes to curb NCDs and increase domestic revenues, taxes on alcohol and SSBs remain underprioritized in Uganda due to institutional fragmentation, political-economic incentives, and legislative resource constraints. As external financing declines, it will be essential to strengthen locally grounded evidence, cross-sector coalitions, and integration of health objectives into fiscal reforms. In this way, health taxes represent a durable policy option for quickly mobilizing financial resources for health and preventing NCDs.
